pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that the ninety and first year had passed away; and it was six hundred years from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem; and it was in the year that Lachoneus was the Chief Judge and the governor over the land.

provenance.other: “The governor over the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 42:6. The nearest others are Genesis 45:26 and Acts 7:10, both also of Joseph, and Jeremiah 40:5 of Gedaliah.
provenance.significance: If the phrase is a borrowing, it is a quiet one and it is placed at the head of the book. The only man the King James Bible calls the governor over the land is Joseph in Egypt, and the Book of Mormon's Lehites are Joseph's descendants by their own repeated claim. Lachoneus governs in the year the sign of Christ's birth is given, and the verse the title comes from is the verse where Joseph's brethren, not knowing him, bow before him. The catalogue records the possibility and does not press it.

links.note: 'Lachoneus was the Chief Judge and the governor over the land.' The five-word run is a King James singleton, which is normally decisive evidence in this catalogue; here it is not, because the phrase is also ordinary English for an ordinary office, and nothing else in the verse touches Genesis 42. Recorded at low confidence so that a reader who wants the Joseph resonance can see it and a reader who does not can decline it.
links.whyNot: Rarity is the only thing this row has. There is no shared syntax beyond the title itself, no narrative contact with Genesis 42, and no reason a writer needing an English word for a provincial ruler would have had to take one from scripture. A five-word King James singleton that is also a natural English phrase is the one shape of rarity evidence this project cannot lean on, and the row is filed to say so.
links.text: And Joseph was the governor over the land, and he it was that sold to all the people of the land: and Joseph’s brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth.

pericopes.text: And Nephi, the son of Helaman, had departed out of the land of Zarahemla, giving charge unto his son Nephi, which was his eldest son, concerning the plates of brass, and all the records which had been kept, and all those things which had been kept sacred, from the departure of Lehi out of Jerusalem:
then he departed out of the land, and whither he went, no man knoweth; and his son Nephi did keep the records in his stead, yea, the record of this people.

And it came to pass that in the commencement of the ninety and second year, behold, the prophecies of the prophets began to be fulfilled more fully; for there began to be greater signs and greater miracles wrought among the people.

provenance.other: “Wrought among the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:12, which is also the only verse holding the whole of “signs and wonders wrought among the people”. “Signs and wonders” by itself occurs in fourteen.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:12 is the summary verse of the apostolic church at its high point — the whole company with one accord in Solomon's porch while signs are worked among the people — and it is immediately followed by the arrest of the apostles. The Book of Mormon has used it once already, at Helaman 16:23, where the signs are worked and the people are not held. Here it opens the year of the nativity sign, and the same pattern follows: the signs come, and the chapter ends with lyings, dissension and robbers. The borrowed clause carries its sequel with it.

links.note: 'There began to be greater signs and greater miracles wrought among the people.' The four-word run is a King James singleton and belongs to Acts 5:12, where it is signs and wonders rather than signs and miracles. This is the second use of the verse in the Book of Mormon; it was adjudicated at Helaman 16:23, seven verses earlier in a continuous reading but in a different book and under a different heading, and the argument for the source is made there. The row is written again rather than cross-referenced because 3 Nephi is a separate reader page and the borrowing is the first thing this book does.
links.text: And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people; (and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.

pericopes.text: But there were some which began to say, That the time was past for the words to be fulfilled, which was spoken by Samuel, the Lamanite.

provenance.other: “Is past already” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 2:18. The King James Bible has no other place where a promised event is denied on the ground that its time has run out.
provenance.significance: Paul's Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection is past already and thereby overthrow the faith of some. The Nephite dissenters say the time for Samuel's sign is past and thereby try to overthrow the faith of the believers — and the next verse says exactly that, 'your joy and your faith concerning this thing, hath been vain'. The Book of Mormon's argument against a delayed sign is built out of the King James Bible's one passage about a denied resurrection, which is also the event the sign announces the possibility of. Recovering that context is what makes the mockery legible as more than local scepticism.

links.note: 'The time was past for the words to be fulfilled, which was spoken by Samuel, the Lamanite.' The structure is 2 Timothy 2:18's: a claim that the awaited thing is already past, made by named parties within the community, with the overthrow of others' faith as its stated effect. The verbal contact is 'concerning' and 'past' and the faith-overthrowing consequence rather than a reproduced run, which is why this is moderate rather than high; but 2 Timothy 2:18 is the only King James verse that makes this move, and 1 Corinthians 15 supplies the vocabulary of the answer one verse later.
links.text: Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some.

pericopes.text: And they began to rejoice over their brethren, saying, Behold, the time is past, and the words of Samuel are not fulfilled; therefore, your joy and your faith concerning this thing, hath been vain.

provenance.other: “Your faith is vain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:17, and “your faith is also vain” in exactly one, 1 Corinthians 15:14. The two are eight words apart in Paul's argument and nowhere else in the King James Bible is a reader's faith called vain.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a conditional he means to refute: if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain. The Nephite mockers use it as an assertion — your faith has been vain — about a Christ who has not yet been born. And the believers' reply, at 1:8, is Paul's own conclusion in Paul's own words: 'that they might know that their faith had not been vain.' So the chapter stages 1 Corinthians 15 as a live argument, with the mockers holding the protasis and the sign settling it. Nothing in the Book of Mormon's narrative requires this vocabulary; the King James Bible's one passage about a faith made vain supplies it.

links.note: 'Your joy and your faith concerning this thing, hath been vain' (1:6) against 'your faith is vain' (1 Corinthians 15:17) and 'your faith is also vain' (15:14), the King James Bible's only two verses in which faith is called vain, both in the same paragraph. The Book of Mormon then answers with the same phrase negated at 1:8, 'that their faith had not been vain', which is the shape of Paul's refutation. Below Skousen's threshold for a quotation and catalogued as an allusion on the §2 rule.
links.text: And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did make a great uproar throughout the land; and the people which believed, began to be very sorrowful, lest by any means those things which had been spoken, might not come to pass.
But behold, they did watch steadfastly for that day, and that night, and that day, which shall be as one day, as if there were no night, that they might know that their faith had not been vain.

provenance.other: “Shall be one day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “not day, nor night” occurs in exactly one, both Zechariah 14:7, which also carries the only King James occurrence of “at evening time”. Revelation 21:25 and 22:5 supply “there shall be no night there”, but neither has the day-that-is-one-day.
provenance.significance: Zechariah 14 is the King James Bible's day of the LORD: the mount of Olives splits, the nations are gathered against Jerusalem, and the one day known to the LORD is neither day nor night but light at evening. The Book of Mormon takes that day and makes it the night of the nativity. Recover the source's context and the sign given to the Nephites is not merely astronomical but eschatological — the day Zechariah dates to the LORD's coming in judgement is spent, in 3 Nephi, on his coming in a body. The chapter then works through the rest of Zechariah's verse in order: 'at evening time it shall be light' becomes 1:15's going down of the sun with no darkness, and 'not day, nor night' becomes 1:19's night as light as mid-day.

links.note: 'That day, and that night, and that day, which shall be as one day, as if there were no night.' Two King James singletons stand behind this, both in Zechariah 14:7: 'shall be one day' and 'not day, nor night'. The 1830 reading is what shows it — 'which SHALL be as one day' reproduces Zechariah's 'it shall be one day which shall be' word for word, and the 1920 edition's change to 'should' moves the clause away from its source (CONVENTIONS §8). Samuel's original prophecy at Helaman 14:4 has the idea — 'as if it were one day, and there were no night' — but not this wording; the King James phrasing enters the Book of Mormon here, in the narrator's summary of it, and not in the prophecy itself. That is the sort of thing a running text in first-edition wording exists to make visible.
links.text: But it shall be one day which shall be known to the LORD, not day, nor night: but it shall come to pass, that at evening time it shall be light.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that there was a day set apart by the unbelievers, that all those who believed in those traditions, should be put to death, except the sign should come to pass, which had been given by Samuel the prophet.
Now it came to pass that when Nephi, the son of Nephi, saw this wickedness of his people, his heart was exceeding sorrowful.

And it came to pass that he went out and bowed himself down upon the earth, and cried mightily to his God, in behalf of his people; yea, those which were about to be destroyed because of their faith in the tradition of their fathers.

provenance.other: “Down upon the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 18:42, and so does “himself down upon the earth”. Prostration is ordinarily 'on his face to the ground' or 'to the earth' in the King James Bible; the preposition pair here belongs to Elijah on Carmel alone.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible's one man who casts himself down upon the earth is Elijah, on the top of Carmel, praying for the sign that will settle a public contest between the prophet of the LORD and a people who have gone after other gods — a contest in which the unbelieving party has already been told to name the terms and the day. 3 Nephi 1 is that scene: a day has been set, the sign is the whole question, and the prophet goes apart and puts himself on the ground. Whether the borrowing was deliberate or not, the posture it copies is the posture of a prophet waiting on a sign he has staked lives on.

links.note: 'He went out and bowed himself down upon the earth, and cried mightily to his God.' The four-word run is a King James singleton, and its verse is 1 Kings 18:42, Elijah at the end of the Carmel contest. The machine stream found it and ranked it first for this verse, which is unusual — the n-gram stream is a recall floor and rarely puts the right verse on top (CONVENTIONS §9) — but the context test independently agrees, because the situation is Carmel's: a public trial of a prophet's word, a deadline, and a prophet on the ground waiting for the sky.
links.text: So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees,

provenance.other: “Cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8, and so does “mightily unto God”. The Book of Mormon has made the phrase its own from Mosiah 9:17 onward.
provenance.significance: Jonah 3:8 is a city under a dated sentence of destruction crying mightily unto God, and the sentence is lifted. 3 Nephi 1 is a body of believers under a dated sentence of destruction, and the prophet cries mightily on their behalf, and the sentence is lifted — by the arrival of the very sign the sentence was framed to punish them for expecting. The correspondence is closer here than at any of the Book of Mormon's earlier uses of the phrase, which is the reason for writing the row rather than only cross-referencing it.

links.note: 'Cried mightily to his God' (1:11), repeated at 1:12 as 'cried mightily unto the Lord'. The King James Bible says this once, at Jonah 3:8. By 3 Nephi the phrase is a Book of Mormon formula — Mosiah 9:17, Alma 8:16, Alma 22:17 — and a formula recurring is ordinarily registered as a recurrence and not re-argued (ADJUDICATING §4). It is written out here because the deadline structure of Jonah 3 is present in this chapter and nowhere else the phrase has been used, so the second occurrence is doing more than the formula.
links.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he cried mightily unto the Lord, all the day; and behold, the voice of the Lord came unto him, saying:

Lift up your head and be of good cheer: for behold, the time is at hand, and on this night shall the sign be given, and on the morrow come I into the world, to shew unto the world that I will fulfil all that which I have caused to be spoken by the mouth of my Holy Prophets.

provenance.route: Luke 21:28 (with Revelation 1:3) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Lift up your heads” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 24:7 and 24:9, where the heads belong to gates, and Luke 21:28. “The time is at hand” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 1:3 and 22:10, the opening and closing of that book.
provenance.significance: Luke 21:28 stands inside the Olivet discourse, where the signs precede the coming of the Son of man, and its consolation is addressed to people watching a terrifying sky. The Lord's word to Nephi reproduces both halves — the imperative and the causal clause that grounds it — but changes what is imminent: not redemption at the end but the birth at the beginning. The one text in the King James Bible that tells frightened watchers to lift their heads because deliverance is near is a text about the second coming, and the Book of Mormon has put it in the mouth of the Lord on the eve of the first.

links.note: 'Lift up your head and be of good cheer: for behold, the time is at hand.' Luke 21:28 has 'lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh' — the same imperative followed by the same causal 'for' announcing an imminent deliverance. The 1830 singular 'head' is a departure from all three King James occurrences of the phrase, which weakens the verbal case and does not touch the syntactic one. 'The time is at hand' is Revelation's frame-phrase, used twice in the chapter (1:13, 1:14) as Revelation uses it twice; it is folded in as a composite rather than given its own row.
links.text: And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.

provenance.other: “Came I into the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:37. 'Into the world' unqualified occurs in eighteen, most of them Johannine, but the first-person perfect with the inverted pronoun is Pilate's hall alone.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest metalepsis and it is easy to miss. The only place in the King James Bible where Jesus says 'came I into the world' is his answer to Pilate at the trial: 'To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth.' It is a statement about his birth made on the day of his death. The Book of Mormon takes it back to the night before the birth and has the unborn Christ say it in the future tense — 'on the morrow come I into the world' — and then completes the sentence with John's own purpose clause turned outward: 'to shew unto the world that I will fulfil all.' Recover the source and the annunciation to Nephi is worded out of the interrogation by Pilate; the beginning is announced in the words of the end.

links.note: 'On the morrow come I into the world, to shew unto the world that I will fulfil all.' The run is a King James singleton and belongs to John 18:37, where the same clause is followed by 'that I should bear witness unto the truth' — a purpose clause in the same position that the Book of Mormon fills with fulfilment rather than witness. The machine stream did propose John 18:37 here, on the shared strings 'i into the world' and 'the world that i', without any way of seeing what makes the verse the right one.
links.text: Pilate therefore said unto him, Art thou a king then? Jesus answered, Thou sayest that I am a king. To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice.

provenance.route: Acts 3:18, with Luke 1:70 and Acts 3:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “By the mouth of all his prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:18, which also carries the only occurrence of “he hath so fulfilled”. “Mouth of his holy prophets” occurs in exactly one, Luke 1:70, and “mouth of all his holy prophets” in exactly one, Acts 3:21.
provenance.significance: Three King James verses hold this formula and all three are third-person statements about God: he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, he hath so fulfilled what he shewed by the mouth of all his prophets. The Book of Mormon puts the formula in the first person and the future — 'I will fulfil all that which I have caused to be spoken by the mouth of my Holy Prophets' — so that the speaker becomes both the God who spoke through the prophets and the thing they spoke of. Luke 1:70 is the sharpest of the three to recover, because it is Zacharias's Benedictus, said over the birth of the forerunner; the formula that belongs to the New Testament's nativity is here spoken by the one about to be born.

links.note: 'I will fulfil all that which I have caused to be spoken by the mouth of my Holy Prophets.' Acts 3:18 is the closest of the three candidates because it alone joins the mouth-of-the-prophets formula to the verb 'shew' and to fulfilment — 'those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets … he hath so fulfilled' — and the Book of Mormon has 'to shew unto the world that I will fulfil'. The 1830 spelling 'shew' preserves the King James form that later editions modernized to 'show', which is part of the evidence (CONVENTIONS §8). Luke 1:70 and Acts 3:21 supply 'holy prophets', which Acts 3:18 lacks, and are folded in as composites. The formula is an established Book of Mormon borrowing from 1 Nephi 3:20 onward; what is new here is the first person.
links.text: But those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled.

pericopes.text: Behold, I come unto my own, to fulfil all things which I have made known unto the children of men, from the foundation of the world, and to do the will, both of the Father, and of the Son of the Father, because of me, and of the Son, because of my flesh. And behold, the time is at hand, and this night shall the sign be given.

provenance.other: “Unto his own” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, of which only John 1:11 has it as the object of a coming; the others are a man returning to his own house, family or place. The Book of Mormon converts the third person to the first.
provenance.significance: John 1:11 is the Prologue's verdict — 'He came unto his own, and his own received him not' — and the second half is what the Book of Mormon leaves unsaid here. At 3 Nephi 1:14 the coming is announced and nothing is said about reception; the chapter then supplies its own answer in narrative, since the people the sign is given to are the people who had set a day to kill the believers, and by 1:22 Satan is at work to keep them from believing what they have seen. The unstated clause is the point of quoting the stated one.

links.note: 'Behold, I come unto my own.' John 1:11 in the first person and the present tense. The Book of Mormon uses the sentence twice, here on the eve of the birth and again at 3 Nephi 9:16 after the destruction, where it appears in full with the rejection clause attached — so the second use closes what this one opens.
bibliography: Frederick 2016 — in his discussion of 3 Nephi 9:16 ('I came unto my own and my own received me not') as an allusion to the Johannine Prologue, he points back to 3 Nephi 1:14 as an earlier Book of Mormon passage where 'the pre-mortal Jesus proclaimed that “Behold, I come unto my own”'. He treats this verse as an earlier instance of the same Johannine wording; his argument is about Joseph Smith's use of John and about a nineteenth-century audience, not about a source apparatus.
links.text: He came unto his own, and his own received him not.

provenance.other: “The Son of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 John 1:3. Matthew 28:19's 'of the Father, and of the Son' is the far commoner formula and is a different construction: two coordinate members, not one in the genitive of the other.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 1:14 is the most tangled christological sentence in the chapter — 'to do the will, both of the Father, and of the Son of the Father, because of me, and of the Son, because of my flesh' — and the 1837 and later editions of the Book of Mormon are famously nervous about exactly this kind of Father-Son identification. The title that carries the tangle is a King James singleton from a two-hundred-word epistle. Whatever the sentence means, its distinctive term is not free-standing English; it is 2 John's.

links.note: 'The Son of the Father.' A King James singleton, at 2 John 1:3, and a title the New Testament otherwise avoids. The machine stream proposed both 2 John 1:3 and Matthew 28:19 here; Matthew's is the formulaic coordinate pair that any trinitarian sentence produces, while 2 John's is the genitive construction the Book of Mormon actually has. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is generable — a writer working out a Father-and-Son sentence could arrive at it without a source — and because there is no other contact with 2 John anywhere in the verse.
links.text: Grace be with you, mercy, and peace, from God the Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the words which came unto Nephi, was fulfilled, according as they had been spoken: for behold, at the going down of the sun, there was no darkness; and the people began to be astonished, because there was no darkness when the night came.

provenance.other: “At the going down of the sun” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 16:6. Sunset is normally 'at even', 'when the sun was down', or 'about the going down of the sun' (Joshua 10:27, 2 Chronicles 18:34); this exact form is unique.
provenance.significance: The one King James verse that fixes an hour with these words fixes the hour of the passover: 'there thou shalt sacrifice the passover at even, at the going down of the sun, at the season that thou camest forth out of Egypt.' The Book of Mormon uses it for the hour at which the night failed to fall before Christ was born. So the moment of the nativity sign is dated by the formula that dates the killing of the passover lamb, at the one place in the law where that hour is legislated — and the connection between the birth and the sacrifice is made by the clock rather than by any statement in the text. Compare the Zechariah 14:7 borrowing at 1:8: Zechariah's 'at evening time it shall be light' is the other half of this same evening, and Zechariah 14 ends in a feast too.

links.note: 'At the going down of the sun, there was no darkness.' A six-word King James singleton, and its verse is the passover legislation of Deuteronomy 16:6. The machine stream ranked it second here on the shared run and had no way to weigh what the run's only verse is about. Note that the borrowing supplies the hour and then negates what the hour ordinarily brings: in Deuteronomy the sun goes down and the lamb is killed, here the sun goes down and the darkness does not come.
links.text: But at the place which the LORD thy God shall choose to place his name in, there thou shalt sacrifice the passover at even, at the going down of the sun, at the season that thou camest forth out of Egypt.

pericopes.text: And there were many which had not believed the words of the prophets, fell to the earth, and became as if they were dead, for they knew that the great plan of destruction which they had laid for those who believed in the word of the prophets, had been frustrated; for the sign which had been given was already at hand;

provenance.other: “Became as dead men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 28:4. The King James Bible's other 'as dead' constructions are Revelation 1:17 ('I fell at his feet as dead'), Hebrews 11:12 ('as good as dead') and Isaiah 59:10 ('as dead men' in desolate places), none of which is a fall at a sign.
provenance.significance: Matthew 28:4 is the resurrection morning: the men posted to guard against the sign shake for fear of it and become as dead men, while the women who came expecting something are told not to fear. 3 Nephi 1:16 is the same tableau at the other end of the life. The men who had appointed a day to put the believers to death fall to the earth and become as if they were dead, at the sign they had staked the executions on not coming; the believers, who watched steadfastly, are the ones left standing. The Book of Mormon's nativity is described in the words of the King James Bible's resurrection, and the party that is struck down is in both cases the guard.

links.note: 'There were many which had not believed the words of the prophets, fell to the earth, and became as if they were dead.' Matthew 28:4 is the only King James verse in which people become as dead men, and it is the only one in which they do so out of fear at a sign they were posted to prevent. The Book of Mormon expands 'as dead men' into 'as if they were dead', which is why this is catalogued as an allusion and not a quotation; the situation, not the run, is what carries it. Note the 1830 reading 'the word of the prophets' in the second half of the verse, changed to 'words' in 1920 — the singular is the older text, and this catalogue prints it.
links.text: And for fear of him the keepers did shake, and became as dead men.

pericopes.text: and they began to know that the Son of God must shortly appear; yea, in fine, all the people upon the face of the whole earth, from the west to the east, both in the land north and in the land south, were so exceedingly astonished, that they fell to the earth;

for they knew that the prophets had testified of these things for many years, and that the sign which had been given, was already at hand; and they began to fear because of their iniquity and their unbelief.

And it came to pass that there was no darkness in all that night, but it was as light as though it was mid-day. And it came to pass that the sun did rise in the morning again, according to its proper order; and they knew that it was the day that the Lord should be born, because of the sign which had been given.
And it had come to pass, yea, all things, every whit, according to the words of the prophets.
And it came to pass also, that a new star did appear, according to the word.

provenance.route: Matthew 2:1-10 (with Numbers 24:17) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: No distinctive wording is shared. Matthew 2:2 has 'we have seen his star in the east'; Numbers 24:17 has 'there shall come a Star out of Jacob'. The Book of Mormon's clause is four words long and its only content word is 'star'.
provenance.significance: This is the only element of the Nephite sign that has no function in the narrative. The night without darkness is what saves the believers from execution and is argued about for three chapters; the new star does nothing, is never referred to again, and is reported in a single sentence with no witnesses named. It is there because the King James nativity has a star. The catalogue records it as a figural link for that reason: the borrowing is of a scene, not of words, and a reader who is shown nothing here has been told there is no borrowing, which is not true.

links.note: 'A new star did appear, according to the word.' There is no verbal contact worth the name, and the row is filed as figural on the §2 rule. What justifies it is that the sign is otherwise inert: Samuel promised it at Helaman 14:5 and nothing in the Book of Mormon ever uses it. In Matthew the star is the whole machinery of the second chapter, and in Numbers 24:17 — the verse the Christian tradition reads Matthew's star out of — it is the sign of a ruler out of Jacob. The Nephite star is a sign with no consequence, which is what a borrowed one looks like.
links.whyNot: One shared noun. Nothing in the wording points at Matthew rather than at Numbers, or at either rather than at nothing; a writer inventing a birth-sign for a people watching the sky might reach for a star unaided. Numbers 24:17 was already tried at Helaman 14:5 and taken there at low confidence for the same reason. The row would be withdrawn if the star were ever put to narrative use elsewhere in the Book of Mormon, since the argument here rests on its having none.
links.text: Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that from this time forth, there began to be lyings sent forth among the people, by satan, to harden their hearts, to the intent that they might not believe in those signs and wonders which they had seen; but notwithstanding these lyings and deceivings, the more part of the people did believe, and were converted unto the Lord.—

provenance.mt: Isaiah 6:10, of which John 12:40 is the New Testament's citation; the King James forms differ substantially.
provenance.route: Isaiah 6:10 → John 12:40 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Hardened their heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “blinded their eyes” occurs in exactly one, both John 12:40. “And be converted” occurs in exactly two, John 12:40 and Acts 3:19; Isaiah 6:10 reads 'and convert'.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 6:10, the verse John is quoting, which has 'make the heart of this people fat' and 'convert' where John has 'hardened their heart' and 'be converted'.
provenance.significance: John 12:40 stands three verses after 'though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him' — which is the exact complaint of 3 Nephi 1:22, where the hardening is worked so that the people 'might not believe in those signs and wonders which they had seen'. John's citation is his explanation for signs that fail to persuade, and the Book of Mormon has borrowed the explanation along with the words. The difference is the ending: John's people are not converted and are not healed; the Book of Mormon's more part are converted unto the Lord.

links.note: `mediation-check.py` returns a decisive result at one word. Isaiah 6:10 reads 'and convert, and be healed'; John 12:40 reads 'and be converted, and I should heal them'; the Book of Mormon reads 'were converted unto the Lord'. The passive is John's and it is not Isaiah's, and the two verbs framing the sentence — hardening the heart and blinding the eyes — are King James singletons in John 12:40 and are absent from the Isaiah verse he is quoting. This is the fourth Book of Mormon use of John 12:40 the catalogue has recorded and the first where the diagnostic word is 'converted' rather than the hardening pair; the earlier rows at 1 Nephi 12:17, Mosiah 11:29 and Alma 10:25 rest on the verbs alone. Together they make the same finding four times: where the King James Old Testament and its own New Testament citation diverge, the Book of Mormon has the New Testament's form.
links.text: He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

provenance.other: “Lying wonders” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Thessalonians 2:9, which is also the only King James verse joining Satan, signs and wonders, and lying in one clause. 'Signs and wonders' alone occurs in fourteen.
provenance.significance: Paul's man of sin comes 'after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders', and God sends strong delusion 'that they should believe a lie'. The Book of Mormon has every element and has inverted the mechanism: the wonders here are genuine and it is the report about them that Satan falsifies, so the lying attaches not to the signs but to the account of them. That inversion is the interesting part. A writer with 2 Thessalonians 2 in mind and a true sign to narrate has to move the lie somewhere, and the place it moves to is the press.

links.note: 'There began to be lyings sent forth among the people, by satan … that they might not believe in those signs and wonders which they had seen.' The three distinctive elements of 2 Thessalonians 2:9 — Satan working, signs and wonders, and lying — are all present, but redistributed. Moderate rather than high because no run is reproduced and because the sense is turned around; the row is written rather than excluded because the co-occurrence of these three in one King James verse is unique, and because 2 Thessalonians 2:11's 'that they should believe a lie' is the purpose clause the Book of Mormon's 'to the intent that they might not believe' answers.
links.whyNot: The parallel is a redistribution, not a reproduction: in Paul the wonders are the lie, here the wonders are true and the lies are about them. A reader could reasonably hold that a narrator describing propaganda against a miracle would arrive at 'lyings … that they might not believe' without help, and that 'signs and wonders' — fourteen King James verses — is doing no identifying work.
links.text: Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders,

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Nephi went forth among the people, and also many others, baptizing unto repentance, in the which, there were a great remission of sins. And thus the people began again to have peace in the land;

provenance.route: Mark 1:4 (with Luke 3:3 and Matthew 3:11) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Baptism of repentance” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Mark 1:4, Luke 3:3, Acts 13:24 and Acts 19:4 — and in the first two it is joined to 'for the remission of sins', which is the whole of the Book of Mormon's clause. “Unto repentance” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 3:11 and Hebrews 6:6.
provenance.significance: Mark 1:4 and Luke 3:3 describe John the Baptist, in the wilderness, baptizing unto repentance for the remission of sins immediately before the one he is preparing for arrives. 3 Nephi 1:23 puts Nephi in that position exactly: the birth has just happened, the appearance is coming, and the prophet goes out baptizing in John's formula. The Book of Mormon does not call Nephi a forerunner; the borrowed clause does it instead, and the reader who recovers the source finds that Nephi has been given the Baptist's job description at the moment when a forerunner is what the narrative needs.

links.note: 'Baptizing unto repentance, in the which, there were a great remission of sins.' The two halves are Mark 1:4's and Luke 3:3's, 'the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins', with 'unto repentance' from Matthew 3:11 supplying the preposition. Mark 1:4 is taken as the proximate form because it alone puts the baptizing and the preaching in the wilderness before the coming one, which is Nephi's position here. The 1830 reading is 'there were a great remission of sins', corrected to 'was' in 1920.
links.text: John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.

pericopes.text: and there were no contentions, save it were a few that began to preach, endeavoring to prove by the Scriptures, that it was no more expedient to observe the law of Moses. Now in this thing they did err, having not understood the Scriptures.

provenance.other: “Ye do err” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “not knowing the scriptures” occurs in exactly one, both Matthew 22:29. Mark 12:24 is the same saying in the second person interrogative, 'Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 22:29 is Jesus' answer to the Sadducees, who have used a scriptural argument — the levirate law — to disprove the resurrection. The Book of Mormon uses his rebuke against Nephites who have used a scriptural argument to abolish the law of Moses. In both cases the error is not ignorance of scripture but a wrong inference from it, and in both cases the corrective is a point about what the law is for rather than about what it says. The chapter has now run Sadducee to Sadducee: it opened with people denying a promised event because its time was past (1:5, and see 2 Timothy 2:18 there) and closes with people mis-reading the law, which are the two errors Matthew 22 and 2 Timothy 2 respectively assign to that party's argument.

links.note: 'Now in this thing they did err, having not understood the Scriptures.' Both halves are Matthew 22:29's and both are King James singletons: 'ye do err' and 'not knowing the scriptures'. The Book of Mormon changes the person and the participle — third for second, 'having not understood' for 'not knowing' — and keeps the order and the logic. Already an established borrowing at Jacob 2:23; the row is written again because 3 Nephi is a different book and because the object of the rebuke here, a scriptural argument about the law of Moses, is much closer to Matthew's situation than Jacob's was.
links.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.

pericopes.text: But it came to pass that they soon became converted, and were convinced of the error which they were in: for it was made known unto them that the law was not yet fulfilled, and that it must be fulfilled in every whit; yea, the word came unto them that it must be fulfilled; yea, that one jot nor tittle should not pass away, till it should all be fulfilled; therefore in this same year, were they brought to a knowledge of their error, and did confess their faults.

provenance.other: “One jot or one tittle” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:18. “Jot” occurs in exactly one; “tittle” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17. Both words are Tyndale's coinages for the Greek iota and keraia and have no independent English life.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:18 belongs to the Sermon on the Mount, which the resurrected Christ will deliver to this same people twenty-one chapters later, at 3 Nephi 12-14 — and when he does, he will say at 3 Nephi 12:18 that the law is fulfilled in him. The Book of Mormon has therefore given the Nephites the sentence before the sermon that contains it, and used it to settle the opposite question: Matthew's 'till all be fulfilled' is deployed here to prove the law is still binding, and will be quoted again in this same book to prove it is not. Recovering the source turns 1:25 into a set-up for 3 Nephi 12, which is the chapter that resolves it.

links.note: 'That one jot nor tittle should not pass away, till it should all be fulfilled.' Matthew 5:18 has 'one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled'. Both content words are King James rarities — 'jot' a singleton, 'tittle' in two verses — and neither exists in English outside the translation of this saying. The 1830 reading is 'one jot NOR tittle', changed to 'or' in 1920 toward the King James form; the direction of that change is worth recording (CONVENTIONS §8), since the later edition is the one that looks more like the source. Twelve continuous words is below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and this is not among his thirty-six; it is catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule, because the clause is complete and its verse is unmistakable.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 1.25 (Matthew 5:18)
links.text: For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.

provenance.other: “Confess your faults” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 5:16. 'Faults' occurs in four verses altogether — Genesis 41:9, Psalm 19:12, James 5:16 and 1 Peter 2:20 — and only James has them confessed.
provenance.significance: James 5:16 makes the confession of faults a mutual act within the congregation, 'one to another', and attaches healing to it. The Book of Mormon's dissenters confess in the same terms and are restored to the body they had divided; the whole episode of 1:24-25 is a congregational dispute settled without discipline, which is James's subject in that chapter.

links.note: 'Did confess their faults.' A King James singleton in the second person, moved to the third. The word 'faults' is rare enough in the translation to make the phrase noticeable, but it is three words and the construction is unremarkable English, so the row is an echo at moderate rather than an allusion. It is recorded because 1:25 is otherwise a Matthew 5 verse and this is the one clause in it that is not.
links.text: Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.

pericopes.text: And thus the ninety and second year did pass away, bringing glad tidings unto the people because of the signs which did come to pass, according to the words of the prophecy of all the Holy Prophets.

provenance.other: “Glad tidings” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Luke 1:19, Luke 8:1, Acts 13:32 and Romans 10:15. The angelic announcement at Luke 2:10 reads 'good tidings of great joy', not 'glad'.
provenance.significance: Luke 1:19 is Gabriel to Zacharias: 'I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.' It is the King James Bible's first nativity announcement, and it is made to a man who has just refused to believe the sign. 3 Nephi 1:26 is the year's summary — glad tidings brought to a people because of signs that came to pass — and the people it is brought to are the ones who spent the year refusing to believe those signs. The parallel is at the level of the situation, and it is the reason for preferring Luke 1:19 to the other three occurrences.

links.note: 'Bringing glad tidings unto the people because of the signs which did come to pass.' Two words, in a phrase the King James Bible uses four times, so the row rests on context rather than rarity and is filed as an echo. What tips it toward Luke 1:19 rather than Romans 10:15 is that the tidings are tied to a sign and that the chapter is a nativity chapter; the machine stream instead proposed Revelation 22:18 here on 'the words of the prophecy of', which is a King James singleton and the wrong verse — see the exclusion register.
links.text: And the angel answering said unto him, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the ninety and third year did also pass away in peace, save it were for the Gadianton robbers, which dwelt upon the mountains, which did infest the land; for so strong were their holds and their secret places, that the people could not overpower them; therefore they did commit many murders, and did do much slaughter among the people.

provenance.other: “Murder the innocent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 10:8, which is also one of only two verses with “in the secret places” (the other is Song of Solomon 2:14, of a dove in the clefts of a rock). 'Secret places' unqualified occurs in nine.
provenance.significance: Psalm 10 is the King James Bible's portrait of the organised predator: he sits in the lurking places, he murders the innocent in the secret places, he lies in wait secretly as a lion in his den, he catches the poor and draws them into his net. That is the Gadianton robbers entire, and Psalm 10's complaint — 'Why standeth thou afar off, O LORD? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble?' — is the note 3 Nephi 1 ends on, with the sign given and the land no safer.

links.note: 'Their holds and their secret places … therefore they did commit many murders.' The agreement with Psalm 10:8 is split across the sentence — secret places at one end, murder at the other — which is precisely the shape the n-gram stream cannot see, and it did not propose the verse (CONVENTIONS §9). What it did propose here, Ezra 3:13 on 'the people could not', is boilerplate. Moderate rather than high: the two elements are separated in the Book of Mormon by twenty words, and 'secret' is the Book of Mormon's own standing word for the Gadiantons, so the collocation could be its own.
links.text: He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that in the ninety and fourth year, they began to increase in a great degree, because there were many dissenters of the Nephites which did flee unto them, which did cause much sorrow unto those Nephites which did remain in the land;

and there was also a cause of much sorrow among the Lamanites: for behold, they had many children which did grow up and began to wax strong in years, that they became for themselves, and were led away by some which were Zoramites, by their lyings and their flattering words, to join those Gadianton robbers;

provenance.route: Luke 1:80 and Luke 2:40 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Waxed strong” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 1:80 and Luke 2:40, and both read 'And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit'. The bare phrase “wax strong” occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: Luke uses the sentence twice and only twice: once for John the Baptist and once for Jesus, as the hinge between each nativity account and the ministry it leads to. The Book of Mormon puts it, in a chapter about the nativity, on the Lamanite children who grow up and are led away to the Gadianton robbers — and substitutes 'in years' for Luke's 'in spirit', which is the whole of the difference. The children in the King James verses grow strong in spirit and become the forerunner and the Lord; these grow strong in years and become brigands. If the borrowing is deliberate it is bitter, and if it is not, the chapter has still ended by spending Luke's growth formula on the rising generation it is lamenting.

links.note: 'They had many children which did grow up and began to wax strong in years.' The King James Bible has 'waxed strong' in exactly two verses, Luke 1:80 and Luke 2:40, and both are the identical clause 'the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit'; the Book of Mormon has the growing and the waxing strong in Luke's order and replaces the qualifier. Moderate rather than high because the shared material is one verb phrase and because 'wax strong' is available from the Old Testament's 'waxed great' family; what holds the row up is that the exact form is Luke's alone, that both its occurrences are nativity verses, and that this is a nativity chapter.
links.text: And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel.

pericopes.text: and thus were the Lamanites afflicted also, and began to decrease as to their faith and righteousness, because of the wickedness of the rising generation.

And it came to pass that thus passed away the ninety and fifth year also, and the people began to forget those signs and wonders which they had heard, and began to be less and less astonished at a sign or a wonder from Heaven, insomuch that they began to be hard in their hearts, and blind in their minds, and began to disbelieve all which they had heard and seen,

links.text: If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder,

provenance.other: “a sign or a wonder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 13:1. The plural “signs and wonders” occurs in fourteen and is worthless as a pointer; the singular disjunctive pair is Deuteronomy's alone, and it is the pair the Book of Mormon has.
provenance.significance: Recover the statute and the verse changes character. Deuteronomy 13 is the one place in the King James Bible where a sign or a wonder is a thing to be discounted: the sign may come to pass, and the prophet is still to be refused, 'for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God.' The people of Zarahemla, nine years after a sign that did come to pass, decide it was 'wrought by men, and by the power of the Devil' — which is to say they apply Deuteronomy 13 to the nativity of Christ, and use the law's licence to discount a fulfilled sign as their reason for discounting this one. The statute's own next clause supplies the verdict they cannot see: the sign is the proving, and they are failing it.

links.note: 'Began to be less and less astonished at a sign or a wonder from Heaven.' The five-word run is the chapter's clearest verbal contact with the KJV and it lands on the Bible's only occurrence of the phrase. The wider frame is already an established borrowing in this corpus: 1 Nephi 2:11 builds Laman and Lemuel's complaint against Lehi out of the same statute's 'dreamer of dreams' and its penalty. What is new here is the first half of the statute rather than the second, and the borrowing is a good deal more literal. Note that the machine ranked Deuteronomy 13:1 first in this chapter and was, for once, right.

links.text: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.

provenance.other: “they had heard and seen” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 2:20. The order is the unusual one: “seen and heard” occurs in five KJV verses and is the ordinary English sequence, “heard and seen” in three, and only Luke 2:20 has the full four-word run the Book of Mormon reproduces.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is exact and it is an inversion. Luke 2:20 is the last verse of the shepherds' night: they have been given a sign, they have gone and found it as told, and they return glorifying God 'for all the things that they had heard and seen.' 3 Nephi 2:1 is the same sentence with the verb reversed — the people 'began to disbelieve all which they had heard and seen.' Both populations have received the same news by the same route, an angelic announcement followed by a verified sign; the shepherds' response is the KJV's, and the Nephites' response is the KJV's clause with belief taken out of it. Helaman 16:14 had already put the Zarahemla crowd in the shepherds' position by borrowing Luke 2:10; nine years later, in a different book, the narrator uses the closing verse of the same episode to say what became of them.

links.note: 'And began to disbelieve all which they had heard and seen.' The four-word run is a KJV singleton and its verse is the nativity — which is the event this chapter is counting the years from. The machine ranked Luke 2:20 here on the n-gram alone, without seeing why it mattered. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; the case rests on the singleton and on the fact that the source verse is the one Gospel verse describing how people who received this particular sign responded to it.

links.text: He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

provenance.route: Isaiah 6:10 → John 12:40 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV renders Isaiah 6:10 four times and only one of them supplies these two verbs. Isaiah 6:10 itself has 'make the heart of this people fat' and 'shut their eyes'; Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 have 'waxed gross' and 'their eyes they have closed'; Mark 4:12 drops the clause. “blinded their eyes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “hardened their heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, John 12:40. mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence, because the Book of Mormon reproduces none of the points at which Isaiah and John overlap — the case is made instead by the two words Isaiah does not contain at all.
provenance.significance: John 12:40 is not quoted here for its verbs alone. Its setting is John 12:37, 'though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him' — a population that has watched signs and declined them, which is precisely 3 Nephi 2:1's subject and 3 Nephi 2:3's ('they did not believe that there should be any more signs or wonders given'). The suppressed correspondence is the agent. In John the blinding and the hardening are God's judicial act on people who have already refused; in 3 Nephi 2:2 the same two verbs are given to Satan. The Book of Mormon takes John's diagnosis of unbelief after miracles and reassigns its subject, which is the reassignment 2 Corinthians 4:4 had already made (see the row at 2:2).

links.note: 'They began to be hard in their hearts, and blind in their minds', and at 2:2 'he did blind their eyes'. The pairing of blinded eyes with a hardened heart is confined in the KJV to John 12:40, and it is an established route in this corpus — adjudicated at 1 Nephi 12:17, again at Mosiah 11:29 and Alma 10:25, each time with the same OT-via-NT result. Written as a fresh row rather than a cross-reference because this is a new book and because the chapter does something the earlier three do not: it splits the pair across two verses and swaps 'minds' for 'heart' in the first half, which is 2 Corinthians 3:14's noun, not John's.

pericopes.text: imagining up some vain thing in their hearts, that it was wrought by men, and by the power of the Devil, to lead away and deceive the hearts of the people; and thus did satan get possession of the hearts of the people again, insomuch that he did blind their eyes, and lead them away to believe that the doctrine of Christ was a foolish and a vain thing.

links.text: Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?

provenance.route: Psalm 2:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon, not via Acts 4:25
provenance.alternative: Acts 4:25, which quotes the psalm and is the reading Helaman 16:22 leans toward.
provenance.other: “imagine a vain thing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 2:1; “imagine vain things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:25. The two verses differ at four points and the Book of Mormon reproduces one of them: mediation-check.py returns 'thing', Psalm 2:1's singular, against Acts 4:25's plural, and finds no other divergence the verse touches. The qualification is real and should be stated: the decision rests on a single word, and the Book of Mormon's own formula flexes in number — Helaman 16:22 has 'many more things did the people imagine up in their hearts, which were foolish and vain', which is the plural and was left 'uncertain' there for exactly this reason. What the pair of verses shows is that the formula has taken both KJV forms; what this verse shows is that here it has the psalm's.
provenance.significance: Psalm 2 is the conspiracy of the nations 'against the LORD, and against his anointed'. Acts 4 hears that psalm fulfilled in Herod, Pilate and the crowd who had just crucified Jesus. 3 Nephi 2:2 is the psalm's opening line applied to a population deciding, in the tenth year after his birth and twenty-four years before Acts 4, that 'the doctrine of Christ was a foolish and a vain thing'. The recovered context supplies the object the Book of Mormon's clause conspicuously lacks: what is being imagined against is not an argument but an Anointed, and the singular 'thing' that is vain in the psalm is the imagining, while the thing called vain in 3 Nephi 2:2 is the doctrine of Christ. The verse hands the psalm's own verdict back to the people who pronounce it.

links.note: 'Imagining up some vain thing in their hearts.' The collocation of a people imagining with a vain thing belongs in the KJV to Psalm 2:1 and to the one verse that quotes it. This is the second use of the formula in as many chapters of narrative across a book boundary; the argument for the source was made at Helaman 16:22 and is not restated. What is new is that this occurrence can decide its own mediation and that one could not. Filed at 'high' rather than 'moderate' because the singular strengthens the case Helaman 16:22 could only gesture at, and because the doctrinal context here — an anointed one denied — is the psalm's own, not merely compatible with it.

links.text: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them.

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 4:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon; with 2 Corinthians 3:14
provenance.other: “blinded the minds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 4:4; “minds were blinded” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:14. The participle 'blinded' occurs in only five KJV verses altogether — John 12:40, Romans 11:7, 2 Corinthians 3:14, 2 Corinthians 4:4 and 1 John 2:11 — and 3 Nephi 2:1-2 draws on three of them: the two that blind minds and the one that blinds eyes.
provenance.significance: This is the verse that reassigns the agent. John 12:40 has God blinding eyes; 2 Corinthians 4:4 has 'the god of this world' doing it, and doing it specifically to 'them which believe not', and doing it so that the gospel of Christ shall not shine on them. Every element is in 3 Nephi 2:2 in that order: an adversary takes possession, he blinds, the blinded are the unbelieving, and the effect is that the doctrine of Christ is not seen for what it is. Recovering Paul's clause supplies the motive the Book of Mormon's sentence states as a bare result — the blinding is not incidental to the disbelief, it is done for it.

links.note: 'And thus did satan get possession of the hearts of the people again, insomuch that he did blind their eyes, and lead them away to believe that the doctrine of Christ was a foolish and a vain thing.' The clause runs the two halves of 2 Corinthians 4:4 in Paul's own sequence, satanic agent then blinded unbelievers then obscured gospel of Christ. Its neighbour at 2:1, 'blind in their minds', is the KJV's noun for the object of that blinding and appears in no other collocation in the Bible outside these two Corinthian verses. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his thirty-six; the case is the double singleton plus the sequence.

links.text: For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.

provenance.other: “deceive the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 16:18. The Book of Mormon reproduces five consecutive words of it, 'deceive the hearts of the', and completes the phrase with 'people' where Paul has 'simple'.
provenance.significance: The three nouns of 3 Nephi 2:2 — deceived hearts, the doctrine of Christ, and Satan — sit within four verses of each other in Romans 16 and nowhere else in the KJV in that combination. Paul warns against those who 'cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned' (16:17), says they 'deceive the hearts of the simple' (16:18), and closes 'the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly' (16:20). Recovering the paragraph turns the Book of Mormon's sentence into a compressed reading of it — the deceivers work against a doctrine, the doctrine is Christ's, and the power behind them is the one Paul expects to be trodden down.

links.note: 'To lead away and deceive the hearts of the people.' A five-word run on a KJV singleton, and the machine's own top-ranked candidate for this verse. Moderate rather than high because 'deceive the hearts of X' is a natural English completion and because nothing else of Romans 16 is verbally present; what carries the row above an accident is that the rest of the verse assembles the other two terms of Paul's paragraph.
links.whyNot: The shared string is one clause and its final noun is changed. 'Deceive' and 'hearts' are both ordinary Book of Mormon vocabulary — 'deceive the hearts' is not a phrase this text needed Paul to supply — and the doctrine-and-Satan context could be coincidence of subject matter rather than of source, since a chapter about a population being turned against Christ has nowhere else to go.

links.text: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils.

provenance.route: Matthew 12:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon; adjudicated at Helaman 16:6
provenance.significance: The Beelzebub charge is the Gospels' one settled answer to an undeniable sign, and it is the answer 3 Nephi 2:2 gives: the works are conceded and their power is reassigned. What has changed since Helaman 16:6 is who is making the charge. There it was a crowd shouting at a preacher; here it is the population's considered account of the heavens, arrived at over nine years and recorded by the narrator as the settled state of the country.

links.note: 'That it was wrought by men, and by the power of the Devil.' The reasoning is Matthew 12:24's — the sign happened, therefore the devil did it — and this corpus adjudicated it at Helaman 16:6, where the same crowd's cry assembled Matthew 12:24 with John 10:20 and John 19:15. The row is given again rather than cross-referenced because 3 Nephi is a new book and a reader shown nothing here would be told there is no borrowing. Recorded as an echo, not an allusion: “power of the devil” occurs in no KJV verse, and the contact is with the argument rather than with any wording.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact whatever. The link rests on the shape of the accusation and on its having been established in the immediately preceding chapter of narrative; a reader who declines the Helaman 16:6 row should decline this one with it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the people began to wax strong in wickedness and abominations; and they did not believe that there should be any more signs or wonders given; and satan did go about, leading away the hearts of the people, tempting them and causing them that they should do great wickedness in the land.
And thus did pass away the ninety and sixth year; and also the ninety and seventh year; and also the ninety and eighth year; and also the ninety and ninth year;
and also an hundred years had passed away, since the days of Mosiah, which was king over the people of the Nephites.
And six hundred and nine years had passed away, since Lehi left Jerusalem;
and nine years had passed away, from the time which the sign was given, which was spoken of by the prophets, that Christ should come into the world.

links.text: But those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled.

provenance.route: Acts 3:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon; predicate from John 11:27
provenance.other: The four-word run 'prophets that Christ should' is shared with Acts 3:18 and with no other KJV verse. “should come into the world” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 6:14 and John 11:27, both of them confessions that Jesus is the one the prophets meant.
provenance.significance: Acts 3 is a page this corpus already works from: 1 Nephi 22:20 takes Deuteronomy 18 in Acts 3:22's wording rather than Moses's. Here the frame is Acts 3:18's — what the prophets said Christ should do — and the predicate is swapped from Peter's 'suffer' to John's 'come into the world'. That swap is the chapter's argument in miniature. Peter is looking back at a passion; 3 Nephi 2:7 is nine years past a nativity and has not reached the passion yet, so it takes the apostolic sentence about prophecy fulfilled and fills it with the only event that has happened.

links.note: 'From the time which the sign was given, which was spoken of by the prophets, that Christ should come into the world.' Two KJV frames fused: Acts 3:18's clause about the prophets and what Christ should do, and John's 'should come into the world'. Moderate because both halves are short and the second is doctrinally ordinary; what recommends the row is the syntactic frame, which is Acts 3:18's and not Matthew 3:3's, and the fact that the Book of Mormon has already drawn on Acts 3 in a chapter the catalogue treats as one of its principal results.
links.whyNot: Four words and five words, neither a singleton, in a verse whose purpose is chronological bookkeeping rather than argument. A writer stating that prophets foretold Christ's coming would produce something close to this without a source.

pericopes.text: Now the Nephites began to reckon their time from this period which the sign was given, or from the coming of Christ; therefore, nine years had passed away,
and Nephi, which was the father of Nephi, which had the charge of the records, did not return to the land of Zarahemla, and could no where be found in all the land.

links.text: And when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, Send. They sent therefore fifty men; and they sought three days, but found him not.

provenance.route: 2 Kings 2:16-17 → KJV → Book of Mormon, through the Book of Mormon's own disappearance type-scene
provenance.other: There is no shared distinctive wording, and the row should be read as making no claim to any. “and was not found” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:5, and the Book of Mormon's clause is 'could no where be found', which is not it; see the exclusion register at this verse for the 1 Samuel 10 phrases that are verbally closer and thematically wrong.
provenance.significance: The Bible has one scene for the disappearance of a prophet who has not been reported dead, and it is Elijah's: the sons of the prophets suspect the Spirit of the LORD has taken him up, they send fifty men, they search, and they do not find him. Deuteronomy 34:6 supplies the other half of the pattern, a grave no man knows. The Book of Mormon has already run both of them together and said so out loud at Alma 45:19, where Alma is 'taken up by the spirit, or buried by the hand of the Lord, even as Moses'. 3 Nephi 2:9 gives the same scene without the gloss and with the search made explicit — 'could no where be found in all the land' — and puts it at the point where the record changes hands. The unstated correspondence is what the type is for: a reader who has met Alma 45 knows what a Nephite record-keeper who cannot be found has become, and the narrator does not have to say it.

links.note: 'And Nephi, which was the father of Nephi, which had the charge of the records, did not return to the land of Zarahemla, and could no where be found in all the land.' Nine words of narrative, and they reproduce the elements of 2 Kings 2:16-17 in order: a prophet who does not come back, a search, a search that covers the country, a failure to find. The Book of Mormon's own precedent at Alma 45:18-19 is what licenses reading it that way, since that passage names Moses and offers translation and burial as the two options for exactly this kind of exit. Filed as figural because there is no wording to test, and the row would be dishonest at any confidence that implied there were.
links.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared with 2 Kings 2, and a narrator who wanted to record only that a man went missing would write this sentence. The whole weight is on the type-scene and on Alma 45:19 having used it; if that Alma row is withdrawn, this one goes with it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the people did still remain in wickedness, notwithstanding the much preaching and prophesying which was sent among them; and thus passed away the tenth year also; and the eleventh year also passed away in iniquity.

And it came to pass in the thirteenth year, there began to be wars and contentions throughout all the land: for the Gadianton robbers had become so numerous, and did slay so many of the people, and did lay waste so many cities, and did spread so much death and carnage throughout the land, that it became expedient that all the people, both the Nephites and the Lamanites, should take up arms against them;

therefore all the Lamanites which had become converted unto the Lord, did unite with their brethren, the Nephites, and were compelled, for the safety of their lives, and their women and their children, to take up arms against those Gadianton robbers; yea, and also to maintain their rights, and their privileges of their church, and of their worship, and their freedom, and their liberty.
And it came to pass that before this thirteenth year had passed away, the Nephites were threatened with utter destruction, because of this war, which had become exceeding sore.
And it came to pass that those Lamanites which had united with the Nephites, were numbered among the Nephites;
and their curse was taken from them, and their skin became white like unto the Nephites;
and their young men and their daughters became exceeding fair, and they were numbered among the Nephites, and were called Nephites. And thus ended the thirteenth year.

And it came to pass in the commencement of the fourteenth year, the war between the robbers and the people of Nephi did continue, and did become exceeding sore; nevertheless, the people of Nephi did gain some advantage of the robbers, insomuch that they did drive them back out of their lands into the mountains, and into their secret places.

And thus ended the fourteenth year. And in the fifteenth year they did come forth again against the people of Nephi; and because of the wickedness of the people of Nephi, and their many contentions and dissensions, the Gadianton robbers did gain many advantages over them.

And thus ended the fifteenth year; and thus were the people in a state of many afflictions; and the sword of destruction did hang over them, insomuch that they were about to be smitten down by it, and this because of their iniquity.

And now it came to pass that in the sixteenth year from the coming of Christ, Lachoneus, the Governor of the land, received an epistle from the leaders and the Governor of this band of robbers; and these were the words which were written, saying:

Lachoneus, most noble and Chief Governor of the land: behold I write this epistle unto you, and do give unto you exceeding great praise because of your firmness, and also the firmness of your people, in maintaining that which ye suppose to be your right and liberty; yea, ye do stand well, as if ye were supported by the hand of a God, in the defence of your liberty, and your property, and your country, or that which ye do call so.

provenance.route: Acts 23:26 + 24:2-3 (the letter and the exordium to a governor) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “most noble” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Esther 6:9 (“the king’s most noble princes”, plural and adjectival), Acts 24:3 and Acts 26:25. Both New Testament instances are vocatives addressed to a Roman provincial governor — Felix and Festus. The epistolary form of the same address is Acts 23:26, “Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting”, which is the KJV’s one letter from a military commander to a governor.
provenance.alternative: Esther 6:9 is the only Old Testament carrier of the phrase, and Esther is a book of royal letters carried through a province (8:10, 8:13) that this chapter has otherwise touched only at the level of noise. It will not account for the vocative, which is what is being reproduced.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis of genre rather than of sentence. Recover the context of “most noble” and the letter’s addressee is standing where Felix and Festus stand: a provincial governor being worked on, in his own title, by a professional advocate. Acts 24:2-3 is the KJV’s set-piece of official flattery — Tertullus opening the prosecution with “Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness, and that very worthy deeds are done unto this nation by thy providence, we accept it always, and in all places, most noble Felix, with all thankfulness” — and Giddianhi’s exordium does the identical work in the identical order: praise of the governor’s administration (“your firmness, and also the firmness of your people”), a concession that the praise is sincere (“ye do stand well, as if ye were supported by the hand of a God”), and only then the demand. The unstated correspondence is that Tertullus is lying and everyone in Acts 24 knows it. The Book of Mormon narrator supplies at 3:11-12 the reply Felix never gave: Lachoneus “was exceedingly astonished, because of the boldness of Giddianhi” and “could not be frightened by the demands and the threatenings of a robber”.

links.note: “Lachoneus, most noble and Chief Governor of the land”, and again a sentence later at 3:3, “most noble Lachoneus”. Two words, and on their own they would be nothing; what makes the link is that the King James Bible uses this vocative twice and both times to a governor, that the Book of Mormon supplies the office in the same breath, and that the sentence it opens is a captatio benevolentiae of exactly the Acts 24 shape. Well below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and not a quotation on any definition — the case is rarity plus office plus epistolary genre, argued together, and it should be read as such rather than as a reproduced clause.
links.whyNot: Two words. “Noble” is ordinary English and “most noble” is the natural superlative a nineteenth-century writer would reach for in a mock-formal salutation without any biblical prompting at all; the Acts parallel may be a fact about English epistolary convention rather than about this text’s sources.
links.text: We accept it always, and in all places, most noble Felix, with all thankfulness.

pericopes.text: And it seemeth a pity unto me, most noble Lachoneus, that ye should be so foolish and vain as to suppose that ye can stand against so many brave men, which are at my command, which do now at this time stand in their arms, and do await, with great anxiety, for the word, Go down upon the Nephites and destroy them.

And I knowing of their unconquerable spirit, having proved them in the field of battle, and knowing of their everlasting hatred towards you, because of the many wrongs which ye have done unto them, therefore if they should come down against you, they would visit you with utter destruction;

therefore I have wrote this epistle, sealing it with mine own hand, feeling for your welfare, because of your firmness in that which ye believe to be right, and your noble spirit in the field of battle;

provenance.other: “with mine own hand” occurs in exactly five KJV verses: 1 Samuel 25:33, 1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11, 2 Thessalonians 3:17 and Philemon 1:19. Four of the five are Pauline letter-closings and the fifth (Abigail on David’s avenging himself) is not epistolary at all. Philemon 1:19 is the one that pairs the formula with a verb of writing in the perfect — “I Paul have written it with mine own hand” — which is the construction 3:5 has.
provenance.significance: In the KJV the autograph formula is a mark of authentication a dictating writer adds so the recipient can trust the letter; 2 Thessalonians 3:17 says so outright, “the token in every epistle: so I write.” Giddianhi is authenticating a threat. He also signs twice — “I am Giddianhi” at the end of 3:9 and again at the end of 3:10 — which is the signature repeated where Paul repeats it, after the argument rather than before it. The datum that matters most here is the 1830 reading. The first edition has “therefore I have wrote this epistle, sealing it with mine own hand”; the 1920 correction to “have written” is a grammatical tidy-up that happens to move the text onto Philemon 1:19’s exact participle. That is CONVENTIONS §8’s second case running the usual direction in reverse — a later edition correcting the text back toward its source — and it means the modern text shows this borrowing more plainly than the running text does, not less.

links.note: “Therefore I have wrote this epistle, sealing it with mine own hand.” Four words from a five-verse KJV phrase, four of whose five carriers are the closing autograph of a Pauline letter, dropped into the closing movement of a letter. The link matters chiefly because of what stands two verses later: 3:7 reproduces the slave/brother/partner triad of Philemon 1:16-17, so a single twenty-five-verse epistle is being touched twice, once in the signature position and once in the argument. Either contact alone would be thin; the pair is not.
links.text: I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.

pericopes.text: therefore I write unto you desiring that ye would yield up unto this my people, your cities, your lands, and your possessions, rather than that they should visit you with the sword, and that destruction should come upon you;

or in other words, yield yourselves up unto us, and unite with us, and become acquainted with our secret works, and become our brethren, that ye may be like unto us; not our slaves, but our brethren, and partners of all our substance.

provenance.other: Three absolute rarities from one short letter. “not now as a servant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “a brother beloved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Philemon 1:16; “receive him as myself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philemon 1:17, whose governing noun is the one Giddianhi uses — “if thou count me therefore a partner”. “partner” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Proverbs 29:24, 2 Corinthians 8:23, Philemon 1:17) and “partners” in exactly two, both in Luke 5’s fishing boats.
provenance.alternative: The Book of Mormon writes “slaves” where the KJV writes “servant”. “slaves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 18:13, in a cargo list — so the word is not from this source and is the writer’s own English. What is reproduced is the antithesis and its terms, not the noun.
provenance.significance: Philemon is the only letter in the Bible whose whole business is converting a slave into a brother, and Giddianhi’s offer states its three terms in Philemon’s own order: not a slave, a brother, a partner.
