Recover the context and every term inverts. Paul asks a master to surrender a legal claim over one man and undertakes the cost himself — “I will repay it”, 1:19, the very verse whose autograph formula stands at 3:5; Giddianhi asks a nation to surrender its cities, lands and possessions and calls the surrender fraternity. Paul’s “partner” is a bond of the gospel; Giddianhi’s partnership is “of all our substance”, i.e. of plunder, and its condition is that Lachoneus’ people “become acquainted with our secret works”. The one New Testament letter about manumission has been made the script for an offer of confederacy in a robber band, and the fact that the same twenty-five verses supply the signature line two verses earlier is what turns a coincidence of vocabulary into a reading of the epistle as a whole.

links.note: “Yield yourselves up unto us, and unite with us … and become our brethren, that ye may be like unto us; not our slaves, but our brethren, and partners of all our substance.” No clause is reproduced, but the argumentative skeleton of Philemon 1:16-17 is — the not-a-slave-but-a-brother antithesis, which the KJV states once, followed immediately by the reception of that brother as a “partner”, which the KJV also states once. Taken with 3:5 this is two contacts with one very short epistle in three verses of a single letter, in the two positions (argument and signature) a reader of Philemon would notice first.
links.text: Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?

provenance.route: Genesis 34:15-23 → KJV → Book of Mormon (narrative form, not wording)
provenance.other: The Genesis phrases are all singletons and none of them is reproduced. “be as we be” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (34:15), “become one people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (34:16), “consent unto us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (34:22). The Book of Mormon’s corresponding phrases — “unite with us”, “that ye may be like unto us” — share no distinctive word with any of them; “unite” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 86:11, and not in this sense at all.
provenance.significance: Genesis 34 is the King James Bible’s one negotiated merger between an armed party and a people it could destroy, and its terms are Giddianhi’s terms in Giddianhi’s order: dwell with us, be as we be, become one people, and then — said aside, to his own city — “Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of theirs be ours?” That last is the sentence 3:7 says out loud: “partners of all our substance”. The type-scene is a confederacy offered in bad faith by the party that means to end up with the other’s goods, and it closes in Genesis with a general slaughter and the taking of the flocks and herds — which is what 3:13 and 3:22 are moving out of reach when Lachoneus gathers the flocks and herds into one place. The inversion worth naming is that in Genesis the deceit is on the side that accepts and in 3 Nephi it is on the side that offers.

links.note: Under CONVENTIONS §0a this is put on the table rather than left out. The sentence is a bad-faith offer of merger from an armed party to a people it has just threatened, stating its terms as kinship and shared substance while intending the substance; that is the Shechem negotiation of Genesis 34 in outline, and Genesis 34 is the only such negotiation in the KJV. The wording is entirely the Book of Mormon’s own, so this is figural in the strict sense and is catalogued as such.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact at all — not one distinctive shared word — and the resemblance is at the level of a situation that any writer inventing an extortionate ultimatum could arrive at independently. Circumcision, intermarriage and the rape of Dinah, which are what Genesis 34 is actually about, have no counterpart here. If the Philemon link above accounts for the verse’s wording, this row is a reading of the scene and not a claim of dependence, and it should be withdrawn the moment a source with actual wording is found for it.
links.text: But in this will we consent unto you: If ye will be as we be, that every male of you be circumcised;

pericopes.text: And behold, I swear unto you, if ye will do this, with an oath, ye shall not be destroyed; but if ye will not do this, I swear unto you, with an oath, that on the morrow month, I will command that my armies shall come down against you, and they shall not stay their hand, and shall spare not, but shall slay you, and shall let fall the sword upon you, even until ye shall become extinct.

And behold, I am Giddianhi, and I am the Governor of this the secret society of Gadianton; which society, and the works thereof, I know to be good; and they are of ancient date, and they have been handed down unto us.

And I write this epistle unto you, Lachoneus, and I hope that ye will deliver up your lands, and your possessions, without the shedding of blood, that this my people may recover their rights and government which have dissented away from you, because of your wickedness in retaining from them their rights of government; and except ye do this, I will avenge their wrongs. I am Giddianhi.

provenance.other: “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22. tools/mediation-check.py was run against Leviticus 17:11, the law the Hebrews verse summarizes, and returned one decisive point: the Book of Mormon has Hebrews 9:22’s “without shedding of blood” and nothing of Leviticus’ atonement clause. So the phrase is the New Testament’s formulation of the law, not the law’s own.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 9:22 is the KJV’s statement that remission cannot be had without blood. Giddianhi’s letter offers precisely a remission without blood — hand over the lands and possessions and nobody dies — and prices a nation’s surrender in the sentence the epistle uses to say that nothing is remitted cheaply. The within-book arc is the part worth recording: the same three words return in 3 Nephi at 9:19, in the voice of Christ, abolishing the thing Hebrews says is indispensable — “ye shall offer up unto me no more the shedding of blood”. Six chapters separate a robber’s bloodless bargain from a bloodless sacrifice, and the phrase they share is a KJV singleton.

links.note: “I hope that ye will deliver up your lands, and your possessions, without the shedding of blood.” Three words, absolutely rare, and the argument for the row is the rarity plus the placement rather than any further contact with Hebrews 9. The phrase was adjudicated for this catalogue at Alma 34:13, where Alma’s last-sacrifice argument genuinely runs alongside Hebrews 9; the row is written again here because 3 Nephi is a new book and a new hand, and because 3 Nephi 9:19 will take the same words up in the opposite direction. The argument for the source is made at Alma 34:13 and is not restated.
links.whyNot: “Without the shedding of blood” is the Book of Mormon’s standing idiom for a bloodless military outcome — Alma 58:28 takes a city “without the shedding of blood” in exactly this neutral sense — so its appearance in an ultimatum proves only that the writer had the phrase, not that he was thinking of Hebrews when he used it. The sense in the source (no remission of sin) and the sense here (no casualties) are not the same sense.
links.text: And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass when Lachoneus received this epistle, he was exceedingly astonished, because of the boldness of Giddianhi, demanding the possession of the land of the Nephites, and also of threatening the people, and avenging the wrongs of those that had received no wrong, save it were they had wronged themselves, by dissenting away unto those wicked and abominable robbers.

Now behold, this Lachoneus, the Governor, was a just man, and could not be frightened by the demands and the threatenings of a robber; therefore he did not hearken to the epistle of Giddianhi, the Governor of the robbers, but he did cause that his people should cry unto the Lord for strength against the time that the robbers should come down against them;

yea, he sent a proclamation among all the people, that they should gather together their women, and their children, their flocks and their herds, and all their substance, save it were their land, unto one place.

provenance.route: Genesis 12:5 + Genesis 46:32-47:1 (two patriarchal migrations) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “and all their substance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 12:5, Abram's own departure from Haran carrying "all their substance that they had gathered." “flocks and their herds and all” occurs in exactly two, Genesis 46:32 and 47:1, Jacob's household bringing their flocks and herds down into Egypt. Lachoneus's proclamation fuses both: “their flocks and their herds, and all their substance”.
provenance.significance: Two migrations answer to two motives. Abram's move is a call away from a besieging famine toward a promise; Jacob's is flight from a famine into a foreign king's protection. Lachoneus's gathering is neither a call nor a flight to safety abroad but a mustering against robbers, ordered by a native governor rather than God or Pharaoh — the vocabulary of patriarchal migration applied to a wartime evacuation. The verse is quoted again in summary at 3 Nephi 4:3 (an exclusion, see that row), so the phrase is used twice for the one event: commanded here, executed there.

links.note: “Their flocks and their herds, and all their substance” welds Genesis 12:5's KJV singleton to the two-verse phrase of Genesis 46:32/47:1 in one clause. Both are Genesis migrations carrying a household's substance to a place of safety; Lachoneus's proclamation borrows the vocabulary of patriarchal relocation for a defensive gathering of the whole Nephite nation into one place.
links.text: And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came.

pericopes.text: And he caused that fortifications should be built round about them, and the strength thereof should be exceeding great. And he caused that there should be armies, both of the Nephites and of the Lamanites, or of all them which were numbered among the Nephites, should be placed as guards round about, to watch them, and to guard them from the robbers, day and night;

provenance.other: “a watch against” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 4:9, and “set a watch” occurs in exactly two (Nehemiah 4:9 and Psalm 141:3, which is about the mouth). Neither string is reproduced here; what the Book of Mormon has is the collocation of praying, watching and “day and night” against a named enemy, and “day and night” by itself occurs in exactly 28 KJV verses and settles nothing.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 4 is the King James Bible’s one sustained account of a people fortifying a place against a threatened raid, and 3 Nephi 3:12-26 reproduces its whole programme in Nehemiah’s order: prayer to God for strength (3:12; Nehemiah 4:9a), fortifications built (3:14; Nehemiah 4:6), a watch set round about against the enemy day and night (3:14; Nehemiah 4:9b, 4:22), armament with shields and bucklers under one commander’s direction (3:26; Nehemiah 4:13, 4:16), and the enemy’s design frustrated without a battle. Nehemiah’s enemies are also, like the Gadianton band, an adversary drawn partly from within the province.

links.note: “Guards round about, to watch them, and to guard them from the robbers, day and night”, preceded two verses earlier by a governor causing his people to “cry unto the Lord for strength”. Recorded as an echo, at the level of the paragraph rather than the phrase: no clause of Nehemiah 4 is reproduced, but the chapter is the KJV’s only template for what Lachoneus does, and the Book of Mormon runs the template’s items in the template’s order across 3:12-26.
links.whyNot: Every individual element is common. Fortifying, watching and praying under threat are what any besieged people do, and the only rare string in the source (“a watch against”) is not in the Book of Mormon at all. If this row is right it is right about the shape of a chapter, which is the weakest kind of evidence in the apparatus and the easiest to construct after the fact.
links.text: Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night, because of them.

pericopes.text: yea, he said unto them, As the Lord liveth, except ye repent of all your iniquities, and cry unto the Lord, that they would in no wise be delivered out of the hands of those Gadianton robbers.

And so great and marvellous were the words and prophecies of Lachoneus, that they did cause fear to come upon all the people, and they did exert themselves in their might, to do according to the words of Lachoneus.
And it came to pass that Lachoneus did appoint Chief Captains over all the armies of the Nephites, to command them at the time that the robbers should come down out of the wilderness against them.
Now the chiefest among all the Captains, and the great Commander of all the armies of the Nephites, was appointed, and his name was Gidgiddoni.

Now it was the custom among all the Nephites, to appoint for their Chief Captains, save it were in their times of wickedness, some one that had the spirit of revelation, and also of prophecy; therefore this Gidgiddoni was a great prophet among them, and also was the Chief Judge.

provenance.route: Ephesians 1:17 + Revelation 19:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The Book of Mormon’s pairing has no single KJV carrier and has to be assembled from two. “the spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10; “the spirit of wisdom and revelation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 1:17. “spirit of revelation” on its own occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses, which is the fact that keeps kjvSpecific at ‘uncertain’: half the formula is not King James English.
provenance.significance: The chapter is defining a Nephite constitutional rule — that the commander of the armies must be a man with the spirit of revelation and of prophecy, except in times of wickedness — and it defines it with the two KJV phrases that treat prophecy and revelation as a possessed faculty rather than an event. Revelation 19:10 is where the New Testament identifies that faculty with “the testimony of Jesus”, which is a striking thing to have standing behind a rule about who may command an army. The catalogue records the composite rather than choosing between the halves, because the Book of Mormon’s sentence is a fusion and not a citation of either.

links.note: “Some one that had the spirit of revelation, and also of prophecy.” Proposed under CONVENTIONS §0a as a composite: neither half of the formula is the Book of Mormon’s invention, both halves are KJV singletons, and no KJV verse joins them. What makes it worth a row rather than silence is that the phrase is doing institutional work here — it is the stated qualification for high command — and that its two sources are the KJV’s two verses about a permanent spiritual endowment.
links.whyNot: “Spirit of revelation” is not a KJV phrase, and the pairing of revelation with prophecy is common enough in nineteenth-century religious English (and in the Book of Mormon’s own usage) to need no biblical model. A reader who declines this row loses nothing but the observation that the two halves are separately rare.
links.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

pericopes.text: Now the people said unto Gidgiddoni, Pray unto the Lord, and let us go up upon the mountains, and into the wilderness, that we may fall upon the robbers and destroy them, in their own lands.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 1:41-44, with its Numbers 14:40-45 parallel → KJV → Book of Mormon (narrative form)
provenance.other: Verbal contact is slight and is honestly reported as such. “let us go up” occurs in exactly six KJV verses and none of them is this story; the shared elements are ‘go up’, the mountain and the proposal to fight, all common. “weapons of war”, which is Deuteronomy 1:41’s distinctive noun phrase and reappears at 3 Nephi 3:26, occurs in exactly 9 KJV verses and cannot carry weight on its own.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible has one scene in which a people proposes, on its own initiative, to go up into the mountain and fall upon its enemies, and is told not to. Numbers 14:40-42 and its retelling at Deuteronomy 1:41-43 give the oracle in the form Gidgiddoni gives it: ‘Go not up … that ye be not smitten before your enemies’, because the LORD is not among you. In Deuteronomy they gird on their weapons of war, go up presumptuously anyway, and are chased ‘as bees do’ and destroyed. 3 Nephi 3:20-26 runs the same scene and inverts its outcome at every joint: the people propose the ascent, the prophet-commander forbids it in the same terms (‘if we should go up against them, the Lord would deliver us into their hands’), the people obey, and the arming with weapons of war that in Deuteronomy 1:41 precedes disobedience here follows obedience, at 3:26, as preparation for waiting. The unstated correspondence is that the Nephites at Zarahemla are the Exodus generation given a second run at Hormah, and they pass.

links.note: “Pray unto the Lord, and let us go up upon the mountains, and into the wilderness, that we may fall upon the robbers and destroy them, in their own lands.” No wording is borrowed; the scene is. What makes it more than a coincidence of military common sense is the completeness of the sequence — popular initiative, ascent into the hill country, a prophet’s refusal on the ground that the Lord would not be with them, and the arming that follows — and the fact that Gidgiddoni’s reply at 3:21 is built out of King James idiom from a different but adjacent refusal (1 Samuel 26:10-11, catalogued at that verse). The catalogue records this one as figural and expects a reader to be able to decline it.
links.whyNot: There is no distinctive shared wording, and a besieged people wanting to take the offensive while its commander refuses is the commonest situation in the literature of war. The Deuteronomy scene turns on the presence or absence of the LORD among a rebellious people; nothing in 3 Nephi 3 says the Nephites who propose the sortie are rebelling, and they obey at once.
links.text: Then ye answered and said unto me, We have sinned against the LORD, we will go up and fight, according to all that the LORD our God commanded us. And when ye had girded on every man his weapons of war, ye were ready to go up into the hill.

pericopes.text: But Gidgiddoni saith unto them, the Lord forbid; for if we should go up against them, the Lord would deliver us into their hands; therefore we will prepare ourselves in the centre of our lands, and we will gather all our armies together, and we will not go against them, but we will wait till they shall come against us; therefore, as the Lord liveth, if we do this, he will deliver them into our hands.

provenance.other: “the Lord forbid” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 1 Samuel 24:6, 1 Samuel 26:11 and 1 Kings 21:3 — and “as the Lord liveth” occurs in exactly 27, which alone would prove nothing. What locates the source is that 3 Nephi 3:21 uses both idioms inside one speech, and the only place in the King James Bible where they stand in adjacent verses is 1 Samuel 26:10-11: ‘As the LORD liveth, the LORD shall smite him … The LORD forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the LORD’s anointed.’ tools/mediation-check.py was run on 1 Samuel 26:10 against 1 Samuel 24:6 and found no decisive divergence — the two Davidic refusals are worded too alike at the points 3:21 reproduces — so the case for chapter 26 rests on the adjacency of the two idioms rather than on a word.
provenance.significance: The two idioms come with an argument attached, and it is Gidgiddoni’s argument. David refuses to strike an enemy who is delivered into his hand, and gives as his reason that the LORD will do it in his own time and by his own means — ‘the LORD shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish’ — so that the right course is to decline the initiative and wait. Gidgiddoni refuses to go up against the robbers, on the ground that going up would deliver his people into their hands and waiting will deliver them into his: ‘we will not go against them, but we will wait till they shall come against us; therefore, as the Lord liveth, if we do this, he will deliver them into our hands.’ Recover the source and the strategic doctrine the chapter is famous for is the Davidic refusal to take a providential shortcut, argued in the KJV’s own two oath-formulas for that refusal. It also puts a hard edge on the scene: what David declines to strike is the LORD’s anointed, and what Gidgiddoni declines to strike is a band drawn from his own countrymen (3:11).

links.note: “The Lord forbid; for if we should go up against them, the Lord would deliver us into their hands … therefore, as the Lord liveth, if we do this, he will deliver them into our hands.” Neither formula is rare enough to identify a source by itself, but their co-occurrence is: 1 Samuel 26:10-11 is the one place in the KJV where they stand together, and it is a refusal to take the offensive argued exactly as Gidgiddoni argues it. This is what CONVENTIONS §3 means by confidence decoupled from volume — the shared text is two stock phrases, and the dependence is nevertheless the best explanation, because the phrases arrive together and bring their argument with them.
links.text: The LORD forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the LORD’s anointed: but, I pray thee, take thou now the spear that is at his bolster, and the cruse of water, and let us go.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass in the seventeenth year, in the latter end of the year, the proclamation of Lachoneus had gone forth throughout all the face of the land, and they had taken their horses, and their chariots, and their cattle, and all their flocks, and their herds, and their grain, and all their substance, and did march forth by thousands, and by tens of thousands, until they had all gone forth to the place which had been appointed, that they should gather themselves together, to defend themselves against their enemies.

provenance.other: “made proclamation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 32:5 and Ezra 10:7; “gather themselves together” occurs in exactly 8. Ezra 10:7 is the only KJV verse that has both, and it is the only one in which a proclamation is issued throughout a territory ordering a whole people to gather themselves together to one city. The Book of Mormon reproduces the five-word run ‘that they should gather themselves together’ at 3:22 and again at 3:24, in each case governed by Lachoneus’ proclamation ‘gone forth throughout all the face of the land’.
provenance.significance: Ezra 10 is not just the right vocabulary but the right event. A proclamation goes out through Judah and Jerusalem; everyone assembles at one place within three days on pain of forfeiting his substance (10:8); they sit trembling in the open, confess, and repent. 3 Nephi 3:13-25 does all of it — proclamation through the whole land, gathering to one appointed place with the flocks and herds and all their substance, and then, at 3:25, ‘they did fear the words which had been spoken by Lachoneus, insomuch that they did repent of all their sins’. The KJV’s one mass gathering-by-proclamation is also its one mass gathering that ends in national repentance, which is what the Book of Mormon needs this gathering to do.

links.note: “The proclamation of Lachoneus had gone forth throughout all the face of the land … to the place which had been appointed, that they should gather themselves together.” A five-word run plus ‘proclamation … throughout’, from the one KJV verse that joins the two. The link is placed here rather than at 3:13, where the proclamation is first issued, because 3:13 has only ‘gather together’ and the reflexive that matches Ezra is at 3:22; the register carries a cross-reference at 3:13 pointing here (CONVENTIONS §6a).
links.whyNot: Both halves of the phrase are ordinary King James administrative English, and a writer describing a general muster would arrive at ‘proclamation’ and ‘gather themselves together’ without a model. The row rests on the two appearing together and on the repentance at 3:25, not on anything unrepeatable.
links.text: And they made proclamation throughout Judah and Jerusalem unto all the children of the captivity, that they should gather themselves together unto Jerusalem;

pericopes.text: And the land which was appointed was the land of Zarahemla, and the land which was between the land of Zarahemla and the land Bountiful; yea, to the line which was between the land Bountiful and the land Desolation;

and there were a great many thousand people, which were called Nephites, which did gather themselves together in this land. Now Lachoneus did cause that they should gather themselves together in the land southward, because of the great curse which was upon the land northward;

and they did fortify themselves against their enemies, and they did dwell in one land, and in one body, and they did fear the words which had been spoken by Lachoneus, insomuch that they did repent of all their sins; and they did put up their prayers unto the Lord their God, that he would deliver them in the time that their enemies should come down against them to battle.

And they were exceeding sorrowful because of their enemy. And Gidgiddoni did cause that they should make weapons of war, of every kind, that they should be strong with armor, and with shields, and with bucklers, after the manner of his instruction.

provenance.other: “were exceeding sorrowful” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:22, and the 1830 reproduces its opening five words exactly: ‘And they were exceeding sorrowful’. tools/mediation-check.py was run against the Markan parallel, Mark 14:19, and returned one decisive point: the Book of Mormon has Matthew’s ‘were exceeding’ and not Mark’s ‘began to be’. The wider phrase ‘exceeding sorrowful’ occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 26:22, Matthew 26:38 and Mark 14:34, the last two both Gethsemane — so every carrier of the phrase belongs to one night.
provenance.significance: This is a CONVENTIONS §8 case of the strongest kind: the borrowing is visible in the running text and invisible in the modern one. 1830 reads ‘And they were exceeding sorrowful’; the 1920 edition regularized ‘exceeding’ to ‘exceedingly’, and “exceedingly sorrowful” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses, so a reader of the current text has no way to see that the sentence begins with five words of Matthew. Recover the source and the transfer is pointed. Matthew 26:22 is the Twelve’s reaction to ‘one of you shall betray me’ — the KJV’s one company grieving over treachery from inside its own number. 3 Nephi 3:26 applies it to a people whose besiegers are, by the narrator’s own account at 3:11, dissenters from among themselves, men ‘that had received no wrong, save it were they had wronged themselves, by dissenting away’. The sorrow is not fear of an army; it is grief at defection, which is what the source verse is about.

links.note: “And they were exceeding sorrowful because of their enemy.” Five words of a KJV singleton, in the same grammatical position, opening the sentence as it opens Matthew’s. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation, but the rarity is absolute, the mediation test decides against Mark, and the 1830 preserves the form the 1920 destroyed. The context score is held at 3 because a besieged people grieving is not, on its face, the Last Supper; the reading offered in `significance` — that the grief in both places is grief at betrayal from within — is an argument a reader may decline without touching the verbal case.
links.text: And they were exceeding sorrowful, and began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that in the latter end of the eighteenth year, those armies of robbers had prepared for battle, and began to come down, and to sally forth from the hills, and out of the mountains, and the wilderness, and their strong holds, and their secret places, and began to take possession of the lands, both which was in the land south, and which was in the land north, and began to take possession of all the lands which had been deserted by the Nephites, and the cities which had been left desolate.
But behold there was no wild beasts nor game in those lands which had been deserted by the Nephites, and there was no game for the robbers save it were in the wilderness.

And the robbers could not exist save it were in the wilderness, for the want of food; for the Nephites had left their lands desolate, and had gathered their flocks, and their herds, and all their substance, and they were in one body;

therefore there were no chance for the robbers to plunder and to obtain food, save it were to come up in open battle against the Nephites; and the Nephites being in one body, and having so great a number, and having reserved for themselves provisions, and horses, and cattle, and flocks of every kind, that they might subsist for the space of seven years, in the which time they did hope to destroy the robbers from off the face of the land. And thus the eighteenth year did pass away.

And it came to pass that in the nineteenth year, Giddianhi found that it was expedient that he should go up to battle against the Nephites, for there was no way that they could subsist, save it were to plunder, and rob, and murder.

And they durst not spread themselves upon the face of the land, insomuch that they could raise grain, lest the Nephites should come upon them and slay them; therefore Giddianhi gave commandment unto his armies, that in this year they should go up to battle against the Nephites.

And it came to pass that they did come up to battle; and it was in the sixth month; and behold, great and terrible was the day that they did come up to battle; and they were girded about after the manner of robbers; and they had a lamb-skin about their loins, and they were dyed in blood; and their heads were shorn; and they had head-plates upon them; and great and terrible was the appearance of the armies of Giddianhi, because of their armour, and because of their being dyed in blood.

provenance.other: “great and terrible” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses. Six attach it to something other than a day — a wilderness (Deuteronomy 1:19, 8:15), things done (10:21), God himself (Nehemiah 1:5, 4:14), a name (Psalm 99:3). Joel 2:31 is the only one that attaches it to a day, and Malachi 4:5, which the reader might expect, reads “the great and dreadful day of the LORD”.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 1:19 / Nehemiah 1:5, if the phrase is taken as a free-standing KJV intensifier rather than a citation.
provenance.significance: Recover Joel 2:31 and the borrowing acquires a date. “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD come.” The narrator of 3 Nephi 4 uses that adjective pair four times in five verses of a battle in the nineteenth year, and four chapters later the sun really is darkened over the land for three days (3 Nephi 8). The book also closes its Malachi transcription at chapter 25 with the great and dreadful day itself. So the phrase is not merely lurid: it is the book quietly rehearsing, on a battlefield, the vocabulary of the day it is about to narrate.

links.note: “Great and terrible was the day that they did come up to battle… and great and terrible was the appearance of the armies of Giddianhi” — then again at 4:11 for the battle and the slaughter. The phrase is a KJV one and its distribution is the argument: of the seven verses that have it, only Joel 2:31 puts it on a day, and “great and terrible was the day” is what 3 Nephi 4:7 says. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion on the discrimination rather than on the run length. The 1830 text is unchanged here, and the fourfold repetition inside five verses is the narrator adopting the phrase rather than citing it once.
links.text: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD come.

provenance.other: “dyed” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses; “skins dyed” occurs in exactly five, all of them the tabernacle’s covering of rams’ skins dyed red. The other two are Isaiah 63:1’s dyed garments from Bozrah and Ezekiel 23:15’s dyed attire.
provenance.significance: If the echo is real the effect is a vestment parody: the one thing the King James Bible dyes an animal skin for is the roof of the tabernacle, and the robbers come up to battle wearing lamb-skins dyed in blood. Isaiah 63:1-3, the other dyeing verse, would sharpen it further — the figure whose garments are red because he has trodden the winepress alone is the divine warrior, and here the red garments are on the army God is about to destroy.

links.note: “They had a lamb-skin about their loins, and they were dyed in blood.” Recorded as a gesture, not a case. The Book of Mormon’s only description of a dyed skin garment sits against a King James Bible whose only dyed skins are the rams’ skins dyed red of the tabernacle, and whose only other dyed cloth is Isaiah 63:1’s. No phrase is shared, so this is an echo at the level of a single collocation.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact beyond the word “dyed” and the presence of a skin, and “dyed in blood” is a natural description that needs no source. Exodus dyes rams’ skins red with a dye; the robbers are dyed in blood, which is not dyeing in the Exodus sense at all. A reader who declines this row is being reasonable, and the catalogue records it only so that the collocation is not silently passed over.
links.text: And rams’ skins dyed red, and badgers’ skins, and shittim wood,

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the armies of the Nephites, when they saw the appearance of the army of Giddianhi, had all fallen to the earth, and did lift their cries to the Lord their God, that he would spare them, and deliver them out of the hands of their enemies.

provenance.other: “fallen to the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 20:24 and Acts 26:14. Acts has the closer four-word run (“all fallen to the earth”, against the Book of Mormon’s “had all fallen to the earth”), and is registered as an exclusion at this verse; the Chronicles verse has the whole chapter behind it.
provenance.alternative: Acts 26:14, on the four-word run alone.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 20 is the King James Bible’s one full-dress narrative of a nation that wins a battle by not fighting it, and 3 Nephi 4 runs its whole sequence. Jehoshaphat’s people are outnumbered and besieged; they fast, gather to one place, and pray (20:4-13); the king and all Judah fall before the LORD (20:18); the LORD sets ambushments against the invaders (20:22); Judah comes to the watch tower and sees dead bodies fallen to the earth (20:24); they return to Jerusalem with singing and instruments (20:27-28); and God gives them rest round about (20:30). 3 Nephi 4 has every one of those beats in order — the gathering to one body (4:3), the prostration and cry (4:8), the ambush laid in the night that cuts off the retreat (4:24-25), the slaughter (4:11), the return to the place of security (4:15), and the breaking forth in singing and praising (4:31). The metaleptic gain is at the falling: 2 Chronicles 20 has two fallings, Judah falling before the LORD and the enemy fallen dead to the earth, and 3 Nephi 4 has exactly those two, in that order.

links.note: “The armies of the Nephites, when they saw the appearance of the army of Giddianhi, had all fallen to the earth, and did lift their cries to the Lord their God, that he would spare them, and deliver them out of the hands of their enemies.” The verbal foothold is thin — a four-word phrase the KJV uses twice — and it is offered as a foothold and nothing more. What carries the row is the shape. This is the Jehoshaphat type-scene, and the reason to catalogue it here rather than treat it as a commonplace is that the Book of Mormon reproduces the sequence and not merely the theme: prostration before the enemy, the Lord’s ambush, the dead on the field, the return, the song. Filed as figural precisely because the wording will not bear more than that; the confidence is on the sequence, not the words.
links.text: And when Judah came toward the watch tower in the wilderness, they looked unto the multitude, and, behold, they were dead bodies fallen to the earth, and none escaped.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when the armies of Gaddianhi saw this, they began to shout with a loud voice, because of their joy; for they had supposed that the Nephites had fallen with fear, because of the terror of their armies;

but in this thing they were disappointed, for the Nephites did not fear them, but they did fear their God, and did supplicate him for protection; therefore when the armies of Giddianhi did rush upon them, they were prepared to meet them; yea, in the strength of the Lord they did receive them;

provenance.route: Psalm 71:16 → KJV → Mosiah 9:17 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “in the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 (“I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD”) and Micah 5:4 (“he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD”).
provenance.significance: The phrase entered the corpus at Mosiah 9:17 with the Psalm’s verb of motion attached — Zeniff goes forth to battle — and by 3 Nephi it has become a Nephite battle formula detached from either KJV verb. Its reappearance here, in the one chapter of 3 Nephi where an army stands still and receives a charge rather than making one, is the formula at its furthest remove from the Psalm that supplied it.

links.note: “In the strength of the Lord they did receive them.” Catalogued because a reader of 3 Nephi meets the phrase here for the first time in this book and should be told where it comes from, not because a fresh borrowing is being claimed: the discrimination that made Mosiah 9:17 a link — the Psalm’s “go” against Micah’s “stand and feed” — has nothing to bite on here, since the Nephite verb is “receive”. Recorded across the book boundary under ADJUDICATING §4, with the argument made at Mosiah 9:17 and not restated.
links.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

pericopes.text: and the battle commenced in this the sixth month; and great and terrible was the battle thereof; yea, great and terrible was the slaughter thereof, insomuch that there never was known so great a slaughter among all the people of Lehi since he left Jerusalem.
And notwithstanding the threatenings and the oaths which Giddianhi had made, behold, the Nephites did beat them, insomuch that they did fall back from before them.

And it came to pass that Gidgiddoni commanded that his armies should pursue them as far as to the borders of the wilderness, and that they should not spare any that should fall into their hands by the way; and thus they did pursue them, and did slay them, to the borders of the wilderness, even until they had fulfilled the commandment of Gidgiddoni.

And it came to pass that Giddianhi, who had stood and fought with boldness, was pursued as he fled; and being weary because of his much fighting, he was overtaken and slain. And thus was the end of Giddianhi, the robber.

And it came to pass that the armies of the Nephites did return again to their place of security. And it came to pass that this nineteenth year did pass away, and the robbers did not come again to battle; neither did they come again in the twentieth year;

and in the twenty and first year they did not come up to battle, but they came up on all sides to lay siege round about the people of Nephi; for they did suppose that if they should cut off the people of Nephi from their lands, and should hem them in on every side, and if they should cut them off from all their outward privileges, that they could cause them to yield themselves up according to their wishes.

provenance.route: Luke 19:43 → KJV → Book of Mormon; Isaiah 29:3 fused in the same sentence
provenance.other: “in on every side” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 19:43, and the full clause “keep thee in on every side” occurs in exactly one KJV verse as well. “on every side” by itself occurs in thirty-two and is worthless; the discriminating word is the preposition that precedes it. The siege half of the sentence is Isaiah’s: “lay siege” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Isaiah 29:3, Ezekiel 4:2, 4:3), and “camp against thee round about” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:3, which is the only one that also has the Book of Mormon’s “round about”.
provenance.significance: Both halves of this sentence are the King James Bible’s language for the siege of Jerusalem, and they come from its two ends. Isaiah 29:3 is the Lord besieging Ariel, the city where David dwelt; Luke 19:43-44 is Jesus weeping over the same city and telling it that its enemies will compass it round and keep it in on every side, “because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.” 3 Nephi is the book of the visitation. Four chapters after this siege the Lord descends to the survivors at Bountiful, and the cities that are destroyed in 3 Nephi 8-9 are destroyed for exactly the reason Luke 19:44 gives. So the words in which Jesus dooms the city that missed its visitation are here used of the people who are about to receive theirs — and the outcome is inverted: Lachoneus’s people are hemmed in on every side and delivered.

links.note: “They came up on all sides to lay siege round about the people of Nephi… and should hem them in on every side.” Two KJV singletons inside one sentence, from the Bible’s two great siege oracles against Jerusalem. The Lukan phrase is the stronger of the two: four words, and “in on every side” is a preposition stack that occurs nowhere else in the King James Bible, so the agreement is not the common “on every side” but the awkward construction wrapped around it. Isaiah 29:3 supplies “lay siege” with “round about”, which no other KJV siege verse has together. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; the case here is rarity, not length.
links.text: For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,

pericopes.text: Now they had appointed unto themselves another leader, whose name was Zemnarihah; therefore it was Zemnarihah that did cause that this siege should take place.

But behold this was an advantage unto the Nephites; for it was impossible for the robbers to lay siege sufficiently long to have any effect upon the Nephites, because of their much provision which they had laid up in store
because of the scantiness of provisions among the robbers; for behold they had nothing save it were meat for their subsistence, which meat they did obtain in the wilderness.
And it came to pass that the wild game became scarce in the wilderness, insomuch that the robbers were about to perish with hunger.

provenance.other: “perish with hunger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:17, the prodigal son at the moment he comes to himself in a far country during a famine. The phrase is adjudicated at its first appearance in the volume, Mosiah 21:17.
provenance.significance: The parable’s hunger is what turns the prodigal round: he starves, comes to himself, and goes home to a father who receives him. 3 Nephi 4:20 puts that sentence on the robbers, and the chapters on either side follow the parable rather than the war. The hunger makes Zemnarihah’s people desire “to withdraw from their design” (4:22); many thousands then yield themselves up prisoners rather than die (4:27); and in the next chapter those of them who will covenant to keep the peace are not executed but “set at liberty” (3 Nephi 5:4-6). The one KJV verse in which starvation produces repentance is the verse the Book of Mormon reaches for at the point where starvation produces repentance.

links.note: “The wild game became scarce in the wilderness, insomuch that the robbers were about to perish with hunger.” A KJV singleton, and its second use in the corpus after Mosiah 21:17 — recorded here as a fresh link because the book is new and the reader page is per-book (ADJUDICATING §4), and because the use is different: Mosiah has a relief measure to keep widows from perishing, 3 Nephi has an enemy army starving toward surrender. Below Skousen’s threshold and not among his quotations.
links.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!

pericopes.text: And the Nephites were continually marching out by day and by night, and falling upon their armies, and cutting them off by thousands and by tens of thousands.

provenance.other: “by day and by night” — with the preposition repeated — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 28:19. The King James Bible has “day and night” everywhere and the doubled preposition only here. The Book of Mormon has the construction twice, at 3 Nephi 4:21 and, reversed, at 4:22.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 28:15-19 is the covenant with death and the overflowing scourge: “when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it… morning by morning shall it pass over, by day and by night.” What Isaiah describes is not a battle but an unresting, repeated passing-over that wears a people out, and that is exactly the Nephite tactic 4:21 describes — continual sorties, not a set engagement, until 4:22 reports the effect in Isaiah’s own terms, “the great destruction which come upon them by night and by day.” The Book of Mormon has taken the scourge oracle’s picture of relentlessness and given it to the side it approves of.

links.note: “The Nephites were continually marching out by day and by night, and falling upon their armies, and cutting them off by thousands and by tens of thousands.” The doubled preposition is the whole of the verbal evidence and it is enough to name a source, because the KJV writes it that way once. Held at moderate rather than high: four words is little, the sense of Isaiah’s clause is temporal where the Book of Mormon’s is adverbial, and a writer with the KJV in his ear could produce the doubling unprompted. The reversal at 4:22 is what tips it — the phrase is being handled, not merely used.
links.text: From the time that it goeth forth it shall take you: for morning by morning shall it pass over, by day and by night: and it shall be a vexation only to understand the report.

pericopes.text: And thus it became the desire of the people of Zemnarihah, to withdraw from their design, because of the great destruction which come upon them by night and by day.
And it came to pass that Zemnarihah did give command unto his people, that they should withdraw themselves from the siege, and march into the farthermost parts of the land, northward.

And now Gidgiddoni, being aware of their design, and knowing of their weakness because of the want of food, and the great slaughter which had been made among them, therefore he did send out his armies in the night-time, and did cut off the way of their retreat, and did place his armies in the way of their retreat;

and this did they do in the night-time, and got on their march beyond the robbers, so that on the morrow, when the robbers began their march, they were met by the armies of the Nephites, both in their front and in their rear.
And the robbers which were on the south, were also cut off in their places of retreat. And all these things were done by command of Gidgiddoni.
And there were many thousands which did yield themselves up prisoners unto the Nephites; and the remainder of them were slain;

and their leader, Zemnarihah, was taken, and hanged upon a tree, yea, even upon the top thereof, until he was dead. And when they had hanged him until he was dead, they did fall the tree to the earth, and did cry with a loud voice, saying,

provenance.other: “hanged on a tree” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Joshua 8:29, Esther 2:23, Acts 5:30, Acts 10:39 — and Deuteronomy 21:22 and Galatians 3:13 give the same idiom in other grammatical forms. The Book of Mormon reads “hanged upon a tree”, with a preposition no King James verse uses of this act. Of the four, only Joshua 8:29 hangs the defeated commander of an army after a battle won by an ambush, and only Joshua 8:29 and 10:26-27 have the body brought down and a monument made of the site.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 21:22-23 as the law behind the act, mediated by Galatians 3:13 (“Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”). tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence between the Deuteronomy and Galatians forms, because the Book of Mormon reproduces no clause that the two of them word differently; the mediation cannot be settled from this verse.
provenance.significance: The end of the robbers is the fall of Ai. Joshua 8 is a battle won by a force that marches out in the night and places itself beyond the city so that the enemy is caught between two armies — “so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side” (8:22) — and it ends with the king of Ai hanged on a tree and the site marked. 3 Nephi 4:24-25 has Gidgiddoni send his armies out in the night-time to get beyond the robbers and cut off the way of their retreat, so that on the morrow they are met “both in their front and in their rear”; 4:26 accounts for the ones on the south; and 4:28 hangs the leader on a tree. Read against Joshua 8, the felling of the tree at 4:28-29 is the Book of Mormon supplying the monument the Hebrew narrative supplies with a heap of stones, and Deuteronomy 21:23’s requirement that the body not remain on the tree is satisfied by bringing the tree down rather than the man.

links.note: “Their leader, Zemnarihah, was taken, and hanged upon a tree, yea, even upon the top thereof, until he was dead.” The idiom is the King James Bible’s and the narrative is Joshua’s. What makes this more than a commonplace is that the two preceding verses have already run Joshua 8’s tactics: a night march to a position beyond the enemy, the enemy met front and rear on the morrow, the survivors cut off in their places of retreat. The execution then lands where Joshua 8 lands. Note the departure that is not KJV: the Book of Mormon writes “upon a tree”, which no King James verse does of a hanging, and adds “even upon the top thereof”, a detail no biblical hanging has — “top thereof” occurs in exactly two KJV verses and neither is a gallows. The borrowing is of an act and its idiom, not of a clause, which is why this is filed as an allusion and not a quotation.
links.text: And the king of Ai he hanged on a tree until eventide: and as soon as the sun was down, Joshua commanded that they should take his carcase down from the tree, and cast it at the entering of the gate of the city, and raise thereon a great heap of stones, that remaineth unto this day.

pericopes.text: May the Lord preserve his people in righteousness and in holiness of heart, that they may cause to be fell to the earth all who shall seek to slay them because of power and secret combinations, even as this man hath been fell to the earth.

provenance.other: “hew down” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 12:3 (graven images) and Daniel 4:14 (the tree). Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 have “hewn down” of the fruitless tree at the root of which the axe is laid.
provenance.significance: Daniel 4 is the King James Bible’s one narrative in which a felled tree IS a deposed ruler: “Hew down the tree… It is thou, O king” (4:14, 4:22). 3 Nephi 4:28-29 makes the same identification explicitly and in the opposite direction — the ruler is put on the tree, the tree is brought down with him on it, and the crowd then reads the act as a sign, praying that all who seek to slay them may be “fell to the earth, even as this man hath been fell to the earth.” The tree and the man are made one thing by the ritual rather than by a dream.

links.note: “That they may cause to be fell to the earth all who shall seek to slay them because of power and secret combinations, even as this man hath been fell to the earth.” Recorded as a gesture toward Daniel 4, not as a demonstrated borrowing: the Book of Mormon’s felling is a real tree brought down over a real corpse, and Daniel’s is a vision, but Daniel 4 is the only place in the King James Bible where cutting down a tree is the deposing of a man, and 3 Nephi 4:29 is a chant that says exactly that. The 1830 text is evidence here — it reads the causative “fell the tree to the earth” and “cause to be fell”, twice, which 1920 regularised to “felled”; the first edition’s odd verb is what makes the felling read as a performed sentence rather than a tidying of the battlefield.
links.whyNot: There is no shared wording at all. “Hew down the tree” and “fall the tree to the earth” have the tree in common and nothing else, and a people who have just hanged a man on a tree have an obvious reason to cut the tree down that requires no source. A reader who takes this as ordinary reprisal and not as an allusion has the better of the evidence; it is here because the identification of tree with ruler is unusual enough to be worth pointing at.
links.text: He cried aloud, and said thus, Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches:

pericopes.text: And they did rejoice and cry again with one voice, saying, May the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, protect this people in righteousness, so long as they shall call on the name of their God for protection.

provenance.route: Exodus 3:6/3:15 → New Testament → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37, Acts 7:32 — and all four are New Testament. Exodus never writes it that way: 3:6, 3:15 and 4:5 all read “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, without the conjunction before Isaac, and 3:16 compresses further to “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob”.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 3:15, which is the formula’s home and which the Book of Mormon does not follow.
provenance.significance: The decisive metalepsis is Matthew’s next clause. In the Gospels this formula is not a doxology but a proof text: Jesus quotes it to the Sadducees and immediately draws the inference, “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” The Nephites cry it standing on a field where the slaughter has been the greatest ever known among the people of Lehi (4:11), over an enemy leader they have just hanged. The one thing the New Testament does with these words is argue from them that the dead are not dead, and the Book of Mormon puts them in the mouths of survivors counting corpses, four chapters before the resurrected Christ appears to them.

links.note: “May the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, protect this people in righteousness.” Fourteen words reproduced exactly, and the mediation turns on a single conjunction, as it did at 1 Nephi 6:4 and Alma 36:2. tools/mediation-check.py cannot settle it — run against Exodus 3:15 and Matthew 22:32 it reports no decisive divergence, because it ignores single common words and “and” is the only word at which the two forms differ (ADJUDICATING §4 leaves that class to the eye). By eye the answer is unambiguous: every Old Testament occurrence omits the conjunction before Isaac and every New Testament occurrence has it, and the Book of Mormon has it. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six; on run length this is nonetheless the longest continuous KJV agreement in the chapter.
links.text: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did break forth, all as one, in singing and praising their God, for the great thing which he had done for them, in preserving them from falling into the hands of their enemies;

provenance.other: “were as one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 5:13, where the trumpeters and singers were as one in praising and thanking the LORD. “break forth into singing” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all Isaiah — 14:7, 44:23, 49:13, 54:1.
provenance.significance: Both halves of the sentence look forward inside this book. 2 Chronicles 5:13 is the dedication of Solomon’s temple, and what happens the moment the congregation is as one in praising is that the house is filled with a cloud and the glory of the Lord; 3 Nephi 11 is a congregation gathered at a temple to whom the Lord in fact descends. Isaiah 54:1, the fourth of the “break forth into singing” verses, is transcribed entire seventeen chapters later as 3 Nephi 22:1, out of the mouth of the risen Christ. So a victory chant on a battlefield is made of the KJV’s language for the moment a temple is filled and for the song the book’s Christ will hand back to this people as a prophecy.

links.note: “They did break forth, all as one, in singing and praising their God, for the great thing which he had done for them.” Two KJV phrases fused, neither reproduced whole: the Book of Mormon has “all as one” against the King James “were as one”, and it splits “break forth into singing” by putting “all as one” inside it. The 2 Chronicles verse carries more weight than the count alone suggests, because it supplies not only the singleton but the two verbs the Book of Mormon pairs — “praising and thanking” against “singing and praising”. Held at moderate: neither phrase is reproduced exactly, and a congregation praising in unison is not a rare thing to describe.
links.text: It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD; and when they lifted up their voice with the trumpets and cymbals and instruments of musick, and praised the LORD, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: that then the house was filled with a cloud, even the house of the LORD;

pericopes.text: yea, they did cry, Hosanna to the Most High God; and they did cry, Blessed be the name of the Lord God Almighty, the Most High God.

provenance.other: “Hosanna” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Matthew 21:9, 21:15, Mark 11:9, 11:10, John 12:13 — and all five belong to the triumphal entry. The word is absent from the Old Testament entirely. “Hosanna to the” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both in Matthew 21, and both read “Hosanna to the son of David”.
provenance.significance: Matthew’s acclamation is a tricolon: Hosanna to the son of David — Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord — Hosanna in the highest. 3 Nephi 4:32 is the same three beats with the middle term altered: Hosanna to the Most High God — Blessed be the name of the Lord God Almighty — the Most High God. Even Matthew’s closing “in the highest” is answered, by the repetition of “the Most High”. What the crowd shouts at the gate of Jerusalem to a king riding in, the Nephites shout on a battlefield in the twenty-first year; and 3 Nephi 11:17 will have a multitude cry Hosanna again, this time with the person Matthew’s crowd was greeting standing in front of them.

links.note: “Yea, they did cry, Hosanna to the Most High God; and they did cry, Blessed be the name of the Lord God Almighty, the Most High God.” Hosanna is a New Testament word in the King James Bible and only ever a triumphal-entry word, so its appearance in a Nephite war-cry dated to the first century BC is an anachronism of the plainest kind — the second in the volume after 1 Nephi 11:6, and the first put in a crowd’s mouth. The structure is the argument as much as the word: “Hosanna to the …” is Matthew’s construction, and the acclamation that follows keeps Matthew’s order of blessing and superlative.
links.text: And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.

provenance.other: “Lord God Almighty” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Revelation 4:8, 11:17, 15:3, 16:7, 21:22 — and every one of them is in the Revelation of John. The Old Testament has “God Almighty” (Genesis 28:3 and four others) but never with “Lord” before it.
provenance.significance: The title is the one 1 Nephi 1:14 borrowed at the head of the volume, from the verse that identifies the words Lehi sings as “the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb”. Its return here puts the same Apocalypse vocabulary on the other end of the book, and in the same breath as Hosanna: a Nephite army praises God in a doxology whose two halves come from the Gospels’ account of Palm Sunday and from John’s vision of the saints singing beside the sea of glass. Both are victory songs sung to a deliverer who has not yet appeared, which is what 3 Nephi 4 is.

links.note: “Blessed be the name of the Lord God Almighty, the Most High God.” Recorded across the book boundary; the argument for the title’s KJV specificity was made at 1 Nephi 1:14 and is not restated. What is new here is the pairing. The verse sets a title the King James Bible uses only in Revelation beside a word the King James Bible uses only at the triumphal entry, and gives both to a crowd on a battlefield — so the doxology has no Old Testament vocabulary in it at all, in a chapter narrated as first-century-BC history. Filed as an echo rather than an allusion because only the title is shared and none of Revelation 15:3’s surrounding clauses.
links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

pericopes.text: And their hearts were swollen with joy, unto the gushing out of many tears, because of the great goodness of God in delivering them out of the hands of their enemies; and they knew it was because of their repentance and their humility that they had been delivered from an everlasting destruction.

provenance.other: “delivered them out of the hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 8:34, which continues “of all their enemies on every side”. The King James Bible’s ordinary idiom is the singular, “out of the hand of”; the plural “hands” with “their enemies” is Judges 8:34’s alone. The machine proposed Judges 2:14 for the same words and it is registered as an exclusion — 2:14 delivers Israel INTO the hands of enemies, which is the opposite transaction.
provenance.significance: Judges 8:34 is not a deliverance verse. It is the verse that records the forgetting of one: “And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side.” 3 Nephi 4:33 is the exact photographic negative — the people know why they were delivered, name it as their repentance and their humility, and weep. The negative does not hold for long. Within two chapters the same people are dividing into classes, “lifted up unto pride and boastings because of their exceeding great riches” (3 Nephi 6:10-15), which is what Judges 8:34 describes happening to Israel after Gideon. The catalogue’s reading is that the borrowed clause is doing the work of a warning the narrator has not yet made explicit.

links.note: “Because of the great goodness of God in delivering them out of the hands of their enemies; and they knew it was because of their repentance and their humility that they had been delivered from an everlasting destruction.” The five-word run is a KJV singleton, and the same clause is used at 4:8 as a petition before the battle — “deliver them out of the hands of their enemies” — so the chapter opens and closes on it. Held at moderate rather than high because the phrase is close to the KJV’s common deliverance idiom and the plural could be inadvertent; what recommends the identification is that the plural is Judges’, and Judges is the book whose whole shape is deliverance followed by forgetting.
links.text: And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:

provenance.other: “everlasting destruction” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Thessalonians 1:9. The phrase is adjudicated in the corpus at Helaman 8:26 and recurs across nine Book of Mormon verses.
provenance.significance: 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9 is a coming: “the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God… who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.” That paragraph is the programme of the next five chapters of 3 Nephi. Four chapters after this verse the cities burn, the earth is broken up, and a voice from heaven tells the survivors which cities were destroyed and why (3 Nephi 8-9); then the Lord is revealed from heaven and the survivors who were spared are the ones who fall at his feet. The chapter’s last word is the New Testament’s one word for the fate everyone else meets, and the Book of Mormon puts it on the people who escape it.

links.note: “They knew it was because of their repentance and their humility that they had been delivered from an everlasting destruction.” A two-word borrowing from a KJV singleton, filed as an echo for the same reason it was at Helaman 8:26: the phrase is short enough that a preacher’s ear could produce it and nothing else of 2 Thessalonians 1 is present in the sentence. It is recorded again here, across the book boundary, because the Pauline context bears on 3 Nephi in a way it did not bear on Helaman — the paragraph the phrase comes from describes a revelation from heaven in flaming fire, and 3 Nephi is the book that narrates one.
links.text: Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

pericopes.text: And now behold there was not a living soul among all the people of the Nephites, which did doubt in the least thing in the words of all the holy prophets which had spoken; for they knew that it must needs be that they must be fulfilled;

provenance.other: “holy prophets” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Luke 1:70, Acts 3:21, 2 Peter 3:2 and Revelation 22:6 — and every one of them is in the New Testament. The Old Testament never calls a prophet holy. Acts 3:21 is the one that adds the totalising 'all': 'all his holy prophets'.
provenance.alternative: 2 Peter 3:2, 'the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets', supplies the noun 'words' that 3 Nephi 5:1 has and Acts 3:21 lacks; the two verses between them account for the whole phrase.
provenance.significance: Acts 3:21 is Peter at Solomon's porch defining what all the holy prophets spoke about: 'the times of restitution of all things'. 3 Nephi 5 borrows the epithet at its first verse and then, twenty-two verses later, writes a restitution — 'the restoring all the house of Jacob unto the knowledge of the covenant' (5:25), gathered 'from the four quarters of the earth' (5:24). The chapter opens with the KJV's vocabulary for prophecy-fulfilled and closes with the specific prophecy Acts 3:21 says all of them were about. Neither text says this; the shape of the chapter does.

links.note: 'Not a living soul … which did doubt in the least thing in the words of all the holy prophets which had spoken.' The epithet is a New Testament one: “holy prophets” occurs in exactly four KJV verses and all four are in the New Testament, which is a small anachronism sitting inside a large one, since the verse is dated to the twenty-sixth year after the sign of Christ's birth. The catalogue adjudicated the fuller form of the phrase at 1 Nephi 3:20, where 'the mouth of all the holy prophets' comes with 'since the world began' attached; this row is written rather than registered as a repeat because 3 Nephi is a different book and Mormon is a different hand (ADJUDICATING §4). What is new here is the use: at 1 Nephi 3:20 the prophets are cited as a source of words, here as a body whose words are all now demonstrably true.
links.text: Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.

provenance.other: “must needs have been fulfilled” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:16, and “must needs” occurs in exactly 12. Of those twelve, Acts 1:16 is the only one whose subject is scripture and whose predicate is fulfilment.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 18:7 is the closer string — “must needs be that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that is it — but its subject is the coming of offences, not the fulfilling of prophecy. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's syntax and Acts' sense.
provenance.significance: Acts 1:16 is Peter explaining Judas: the scripture must needs have been fulfilled, and the fulfilment in question is a betrayal. The construction exists in the KJV to say that a bad outcome was nevertheless written. 3 Nephi 5:1-2 turns it to the opposite service — a people who have watched the signs arrive and now reason backward from the arrival to the necessity.

links.note: 'For they knew that it must needs be that they must be fulfilled', repeated at 5:2 as 'they knew it must needs be that all things should come to pass'. The idiom is not English of any period at large; it is the KJV's, twelve times, and only Acts 1:16 joins it to scripture being fulfilled. Held at moderate and not higher because the two candidate verses split: the exact string belongs to Matthew 18:7 and the sense belongs to Acts 1:16, and a writer with the whole KJV in his ear could reach the sentence from either. The 1830 reading is quoted; 1920 deletes 'thing' and 'in' from 5:1 without touching this clause.
links.whyNot: No word of Acts 1:16 beyond the two-word idiom is present — no Holy Ghost, no mouth of David, no Judas — and the doubled use at 5:1 and 5:2 looks more like a writer's tic than a citation. A reader who declined this row and filed both verses as formulaic would not be unreasonable.
links.text: Men and brethren, this scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Ghost by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Jesus.

pericopes.text: and they knew that it must be expedient that Christ had come, because of the many signs which had been given, according to the words of the prophets; and because of the things which had come to pass already, they knew it must needs be that all things should come to pass according to that which had been spoken;
therefore they did forsake all their sins, and their abominations, and their whoredoms, and did serve God with all diligence, day and night.

provenance.route: Acts 26:7, with Luke 2:37 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “serving God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:7, and “served God with” occurs in exactly one, Luke 2:37. Those are the only two verses in the King James Bible that predicate serving God of a continuous day-and-night practice: “serve God” occurs in exactly five verses and none of the other three (Exodus 3:12, Malachi 3:14, Hebrews 12:28) has anything to do with time of day. 3 Nephi 5:3 takes Luke's syntax — served God with [a manner] — and Acts' word order, 'day and night', where Luke 2:37 reads 'night and day'.
provenance.significance: Acts 26:7 is Paul on trial before Agrippa, and the people he describes as 'instantly serving God day and night' are 'our twelve tribes', waiting on a promise. This chapter ends by gathering those tribes: 'all the remnant of the seed of Jacob, which are scattered abroad' (5:24), 'restoring all the house of Jacob unto the knowledge of the covenant' (5:25). The one KJV verse that says what 5:3 says about worship is the one that attaches it to the twelve tribes and the promise they hope to come to — which is precisely what 5:24-25 promises them. Recover the context and 5:3's converted Nephites are put in the posture the New Testament assigns to scattered Israel, twenty verses before the chapter says they are scattered Israel.

links.note: 'They did forsake all their sins, and their abominations, and their whoredoms, and did serve God with all diligence, day and night.' Two KJV singletons in one clause, from the only two verses in the Bible that describe anyone serving God around the clock. The join is visible: the frame 'served God with —' is Luke's, the ordering 'day and night' is Acts'. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages, but the collocation is absolutely rare and the thematic payoff is in the same chapter. Note that the third element, 'with all diligence', is not from either: “with all diligence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 4:23, where it governs keeping the heart, and the Book of Mormon uses the phrase as a formula of its own throughout Mosiah and Alma. See the exclusion register at this verse.
links.text: Unto which promise our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come. For which hope’s sake, king Agrippa, I am accused of the Jews.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when they had taken all the robbers prisoners, insomuch that none did escape which were not slain, they did cast their prisoners into prison, and did cause the word of God to be preached unto them; and as many as would repent of their sins and enter into a covenant that they would murder no more, were set at liberty;

provenance.route: Isaiah 61:1 → Luke 4:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “set at liberty” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Jeremiah 34:16, Luke 4:18, Acts 26:32 and Hebrews 13:23. Isaiah 61:1, which Luke 4:18 quotes, does not have it — Isaiah reads 'proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound'. 'Set at liberty' is the form the KJV New Testament gives the verse, following the Septuagint's phrasing where the Hebrew has the release of prisoners.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py returns Isaiah 61:1 as the decisive form, on the ground that the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's 'prison' where Luke has 'blind'. That result is an artifact and is overridden here: the robbers of 3 Nephi 5:4 are literally cast into prison, so the word is supplied by the narrative and carries no evidence either way. The word that is not supplied by the narrative is 'liberty', and it is Luke's.
provenance.significance: Luke 4:18 is the Nazareth sermon — the text Jesus reads and then closes the book on, saying it is fulfilled in their ears. Its programme is preaching to the poor and liberty for prisoners. 3 Nephi 5:4 executes that programme with a jailer's literalism: the prisoners are actual prisoners, the preaching is done at them in their cells, and the liberty is conditional on a covenant to commit no more murders. The chapter is set in the years immediately after Christ's birth-sign and immediately before his appearance in 3 Nephi 11, and the Nephite state is here running the Nazareth manifesto as criminal policy.

links.note: 'They did cast their prisoners into prison, and did cause the word of God to be preached unto them; and as many as would repent of their sins and enter into a covenant that they would murder no more, were set at liberty.' Three of Luke 4:18's four clauses are here in Luke's order — preaching, captives, liberty — and the fourth, recovering of sight, is the one Luke added to Isaiah and the one the Book of Mormon has no use for. The mediation is the point: the verse behind Luke 4:18 is Isaiah 61:1, and Isaiah's English is 'proclaim liberty', not 'set at liberty'. The Book of Mormon has the New Testament's wording of an Old Testament promise, in a book whose narrator has not yet met the New Testament.
links.whyNot: 'Set at liberty' was ordinary legal English in 1829 and would need no source at all; the phrase appears in Acts 26:32 and Hebrews 13:23 of prisoners with no Isaianic freight whatever. Held at moderate because the case rests on the company the phrase keeps in this verse rather than on the phrase itself.
links.text: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,

pericopes.text: but as many as there were who did not enter into a covenant, and who did still continue to have those secret murders in their hearts; yea, as many as were found breathing out threatenings against their brethren, were condemned and punished according to the law.

provenance.other: “breathing out threatenings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:1, and the noun 'threatenings' occurs in exactly two, Acts 9:1 and Acts 4:29. The whole idiom is confined to Acts. The catalogue adjudicated the borrowing at 1 Nephi 18:17 and wrote it again at Alma 54:19 across the book boundary; this row is the third such crossing and the argument is not restated.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has recorded this phrase three times now, and 3 Nephi 5:5 is where its context finally arrives whole. Acts 9:1's breather-out of threatenings is Saul on the Damascus road, and the next thing that happens to him is conversion — he is struck down, blinded, taught, baptised, and set to preaching. 3 Nephi 5:4-5 splits the robbers into exactly those two outcomes and puts the Acts 9 phrase on the wrong half. Those who repent and covenant are 'set at liberty' in Luke 4:18's words; those 'found breathing out threatenings against their brethren' are 'condemned and punished according to the law'. The verse borrows the description of a man the New Testament goes on to convert and applies it to the men this chapter refuses to convert.

links.note: 'Yea, as many as were found breathing out threatenings against their brethren, were condemned and punished according to the law.' A four-word run from a KJV singleton, in the correct grammatical setting — breathing out threatenings *against* somebody, as Saul does against the disciples of the Lord. Written rather than registered as a repeat because 3 Nephi is a new book and a new voice (ADJUDICATING §4); the argument for KJV specificity was made at 1 Nephi 18:17 and is not made again. What this occurrence adds is that it sits one verse after a Lukan borrowing about setting prisoners at liberty, so the chapter has both halves of the Saul narrative — the threatenings and the release — within two sentences, assigned to opposite parties.
links.text: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,
