pericopes.text: And thus they did put an end to all those wicked, and secret, and abominable combinations, in the which there were so much wickedness, and so many murders committed.
And thus had the twenty and second year passed away, and the twenty and third year also, and the twenty and fourth, and the twenty and fifth; and thus had twenty and five years passed away,

and there had many things transpired which, in the eyes of some, would be great and marvellous; nevertheless, they cannot all be written in this book; yea, this book cannot contain even a hundredth part of what was done among so many people, in the space of twenty and five years;

provenance.other: “could not contain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 21:25. The Book of Mormon writes 'cannot contain', which occurs in exactly four verses, three of them the temple prayer's 'the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee' and the fourth 1 Corinthians 7:9 on continence — none of them about books. The container-too-small idiom applied to a written record is John 21:25's alone.
provenance.significance: John 21:25 is the last sentence of the Fourth Gospel and the King James Bible's only editorial apology for omission. Mormon has used it before — 1 Nephi 6:3, Words of Mormon 1:5, Helaman 3:14 — and here he uses it in the same breath as the other verse this chapter runs on: 'many things transpired which, in the eyes of some, would be great and marvellous; nevertheless, they cannot all be written in this book'. See the Revelation 15:3 row at this verse. The abridger's excuse and the hymn's adjective arrive in one sentence, and between them they say that what is being withheld is God's works.

links.note: 'This book cannot contain even a hundredth part of what was done among so many people.' The idiom is John's — a record too large for the thing meant to hold it — and it is the fourth time the catalogue has recorded it in the Book of Mormon. Written rather than excluded as a repeat because 3 Nephi is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4); the fullest argument is at Helaman 3:14, where the same abridger writes 'a hundredth part of the proceedings of this people … cannot be contained in this work' seven chapters earlier. The fraction is not John's and is not the Bible's: “hundredth part” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 5:11, where it is a rate of interest, and the Book of Mormon uses it as its own measure of what will not fit.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is a substitution, not a reproduction — 'cannot contain' for 'could not contain', 'this book' for 'the world itself'. Held at moderate on that ground, as the earlier rows in this family were.
links.text: And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.

provenance.other: “great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses and both are Revelation 15 — 15:1 of the sign in heaven and 15:3 of God's works. The 1830 prints 'marvellous' with the KJV's double l; 1920 modernized it to 'marvelous', so the first edition shows the borrowing in its spelling and the current text does not (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: This is the first half of a pair. Revelation 15:3 reads 'Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints', and Mormon takes one half of it here and the other half ten verses later: 'I know the record which I make to be a just and a true record' (5:18). In Revelation the two predicates belong to God — his works and his ways. Mormon distributes them across his own editorial problem: the deeds he cannot write down are the great and marvellous ones, and the writing he can vouch for is the just and true one. He does not claim the first for himself and he does claim the second. Note also that the same verse stands behind the catalogue's flagship link at 1 Nephi 1:14, at the head of the whole book, and behind 3 Nephi 4:32 twelve verses earlier: the Book of Mormon's opening narrator and its closing editor reach for the same hymn.

links.note: 'There had many things transpired which, in the eyes of some, would be great and marvellous.' Two words, but they are confined in the King James Bible to a single chapter, and 3 Nephi 5:18 takes the rest of the same sentence. Held at moderate rather than higher because the adjectival pair has become one of the Book of Mormon's own formulas by this point in the corpus — 1 Nephi 14:7, Jacob 4:8, Helaman 16:16 — so a writer could produce it without reaching for Revelation at all. What lifts it above a formula here is the company: the same verse's other half arrives at 5:18, in the same editorial passage, in Mormon's own voice.
links.whyNot: Two words is very little, and the qualification 'in the eyes of some' distances the narrator from the adjective in a way Revelation's doxology does not. Taken alone this row would be a formulaic exclusion; it is written because of 5:18.
links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

pericopes.text: but behold there are records which do contain all the proceedings of this people; and a more short but a true account was given by Nephi;
therefore I have made my record of these things according to the record of Nephi, which were engraven on the plates which were called the plates of Nephi.
And behold I do make the record on plates which I have made with mine own hands.

And behold, I am called Mormon, being called after the land of Mormon, the land in the which Alma did establish the church among the people; yea, the first church which was established among them after their transgression.
Behold I am a disciple of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I have been called of him to declare his word among his people, that they might have everlasting life.

provenance.route: Mark 1:1, with John 19:38 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Jesus Christ the Son of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 1:1 — the two names and the title in that order and adjacent. The near neighbours are not the same string: Acts 8:37 reads 'Jesus Christ is the Son of God' and 2 Corinthians 1:19 'the Son of God, Jesus Christ'. Separately, “a disciple of Jesus” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:38. 3 Nephi 5:13's twelve words run the two singletons together: 'I am a disciple of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.'
provenance.significance: John 19:38's one disciple of Jesus is Joseph of Arimathaea, 'but secretly for fear of the Jews' — a disciple defined by concealment, who declares himself only to ask for a body. Mark 1:1's phrase is the opposite: the title of a book, published at its head. 3 Nephi 5:13 is Mormon breaking into his own abridgement to say who he is, and the sentence he uses is the concealed disciple's designation joined to the evangelist's title page. The whole force of the verse is that the self-identification is no longer secret — it is what he has been 'called of him to declare'.

links.note: 'Behold I am a disciple of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I have been called of him to declare his word among his people, that they might have everlasting life.' Two KJV singletons spliced at the word 'Jesus'. The second half runs on into Johannine vocabulary — “have everlasting life” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 3:16 and John 6:40, and John 6:40 also supplies 'the will of him that sent me', which 3 Nephi 5:14 answers with 'according to the will of God'. This is the Book of Mormon's editor giving himself a Christian credential in the New Testament's exact words, four hundred years after the events of 3 Nephi and six hundred after Lehi; the anachronism is the finding, not an objection to it (CONVENTIONS §3a).
bibliography: Frederick 2016 (co-occurrence only: our index records that 3 Nephi 5:13 is discussed within 1,500 characters of citations of Mark 1:1 and Acts 8:37; he proposes no source here, and the argument above is the catalogue's own)
links.text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God;

pericopes.text: And it hath become expedient that I, according to the will of God, that the prayers of those which have gone hence, which were the holy ones, should be fulfilled according to their faith, should make a record of these things which have been done;
yea, a small record of that which hath taken place from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem, even down until the present time;
therefore I do make my record from the accounts which hath been given by those which were before me, until the commencement of my day;
and then I do make a record of the things which I have seen with mine own eyes.
And I know the record which I make to be a just and a true record; neverthelers there are many things which, according to our language, we are not able to write.

provenance.other: “just and true” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 15:3. The near misses are not it: Revelation 16:7 and 19:2 read 'true and righteous', Deuteronomy 32:4 'just and right', Revelation 15:3 alone has the pair in this order.
provenance.significance: The second half of the pair begun at 5:8. Revelation 15:3 is the song of Moses and of the Lamb, sung by those who have gotten the victory: 'Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.' Mormon has taken 'great and marvellous' for the deeds he cannot record and 'just and true' for the record he can. The metalepsis is a modest one and worth naming precisely: the hymn predicates both of God, and Mormon, who is scrupulous about not claiming the first — the marvellous things are only 'in the eyes of some', and he confesses at 5:18 that 'we are not able to write' much of what he has — claims the second outright for a document he made with his own hands (5:11). The one thing an abridger can offer, in the Book of Mormon's own borrowed language, is the ways rather than the works.

links.note: 'And I know the record which I make to be a just and a true record.' Three words from a KJV singleton, and the fourth borrowing this catalogue has recorded from Revelation 15:3 after 1 Nephi 1:14, 1 Nephi 14:23 and Alma 29:8. The construction with the article repeated — 'a just and a true record' — is the Book of Mormon's habit, not the KJV's, and it does not weaken the identification: the pair itself has exactly one home in the King James Bible. The row is written rather than excluded as a repeat because Revelation 15:3's earlier appearance in this book, at 3 Nephi 4:32, borrows a different phrase from it ('Lord God Almighty'), so this is not the same borrowing recurring but a different clause of the same verse arriving in the same chapter as 5:8.
links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

pericopes.text: And now I make an end of my saying which is of myself, and proceed to give my account of the things which hath been before me.

I am Mormon, and a pure descendant of Lehi. I have reason to bless my God and my Saviour Jesus Christ, that he brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem, (and no one knew it save it were himself and those which he brought out of that land,) and that he hath given me and my people so much knowledge unto the salvation of our souls.

provenance.other: “our fathers out of the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 24:17. The exodus formula at large is everywhere — 'out of the land of Egypt' fills the Pentateuch — but the first-person-plural possessive is Joshua's alone, and the catalogue adjudicated it at Mosiah 7:20 on that ground. The 1830 spells the divine title 'Saviour' with the KJV's u; 1920 Americanized it to 'Savior' (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Joshua 24 is the covenant renewal at Shechem, and 24:17 is the people's answer to 'choose you this day whom ye will serve'. Every previous Book of Mormon use of the formula keeps that setting — Limhi at a temple with a gathered people (Mosiah 7:20), Aaron before Lamoni's father (Alma 22:9). Mormon's use is private. He is alone with his plates, naming himself, and the creed that in Joshua is recited by a nation in assembly is here recited by one man as a reason to bless God for his own literacy: 'he hath given me and my people so much knowledge unto the salvation of our souls'. The parenthesis is the tell — '(and no one knew it save it were himself and those which he brought out of that land)' — an exodus with no witnesses, in the words of the exodus with the most.

links.note: 'That he brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem.' Jerusalem stands where Joshua 24:17 has Egypt, which is the Book of Mormon's standing substitution in exodus recitals and has been since 1 Nephi. This row is written rather than registered as a repeat of Mosiah 7:20 because 3 Nephi is a different book and this is Mormon speaking in his own person rather than a character in the narrative (ADJUDICATING §4). What is new is the pairing with 'my Saviour Jesus Christ' in the same sentence: Joshua's creed is being said to a Christ, six hundred years before the KJV New Testament that names him.
links.text: For the LORD our God, he it is that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way wherein we went, and among all the people through whom we passed:

pericopes.text: Surely he hath blessed the house of Jacob, and hath been merciful unto the seed of Joseph.
And insomuch as the children of Lehi hath kept his commandments, he hath blessed them and prospered them according to his word;
yea, and surely shall he again bring a remnant of the seed of Joseph to the knowledge of the Lord their God;
and as surely as the Lord liveth will he gather in from the four quarters of the earth, all the remnant of the seed of Jacob, which are scattered abroad upon all the face of the earth;

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:12 → Revelation 20:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “four quarters of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:8. “four quarters” occurs in exactly four — Deuteronomy 22:12 of a garment's corners, 1 Chronicles 9:24 of the porters' stations, Jeremiah 49:36 'the four quarters of heaven', and Revelation 20:8. The gathering prophecy the sentence is otherwise reciting, Isaiah 11:12, reads 'the four corners of the earth'; “four corners of the earth” occurs in exactly two verses, Isaiah 11:12 and Revelation 7:1.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 11:12 is the source of the thought and of everything else in 5:24-26 — the assembling, the dispersed, the remnant. It is not the source of these five words.
provenance.significance: tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point and it is this one: the Book of Mormon has 'quarters' (Revelation 20:8) where Isaiah 11:12 has 'corners'. The finding matters because of what the two verses do. Isaiah 11:12 gathers Israel home; Revelation 20:8 is Satan released from his prison after the thousand years, going out to the four quarters of the earth to deceive the nations and 'gather them together to battle'. The Book of Mormon's promise of the gathering of Jacob is worded with the King James Bible's one phrase for the mustering of Gog and Magog. The catalogue recorded the same substitution at 1 Nephi 19:16 and held it at moderate on the ground that 'quarters' and 'corners' are near-synonyms; the repetition here, in a different book and a different hand, and repeated again two verses later at 5:26, makes the reading harder to put down to chance.

links.note: 'And as surely as the Lord liveth will he gather in from the four quarters of the earth, all the remnant of the seed of Jacob.' Five words from a KJV singleton, doing the opposite of what the singleton does. The mediation is the argument: the underlying prophecy is Isaiah 11:12, which the passage follows in substance through 5:26 — assemble, gather, the dispersed — but at every point where Isaiah's English and Revelation's differ, the Book of Mormon has Revelation's. 'As the Lord liveth' is a separate matter and is not evidence: it occurs in thirty-seven KJV verses and is the standard oath formula.
links.text: And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog, and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea.

provenance.other: “which are scattered abroad” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 1:1. The bare verb is common — “scattered abroad” occurs in exactly 11 verses, five of them in Acts of the persecuted church — but the relative clause in this exact form has one home, and its antecedent there is 'the twelve tribes'.
provenance.significance: A seam is visible in this clause and it is worth marking. '…which are scattered abroad upon all the face of the earth' is two KJV singletons welded end to end: the first four words are James 1:1's address to the twelve tribes of the dispersion, and the last seven are Ezekiel 34:6's 'my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth', which the Book of Mormon adopted as its own dispersion formula back in 1 Nephi 10:12 and has used ever since. The verse reaches for the corpus's habitual phrase and prefixes it with the New Testament's address to the scattered tribes, which is exactly what the sentence is about.

links.note: 'All the remnant of the seed of Jacob, which are scattered abroad upon all the face of the earth.' The referent is identical to James's — the dispersed tribes of Jacob — and the wording of the relative clause has one KJV home. Held at moderate because 'which are scattered abroad' is a natural relative clause on an ordinary verb and a writer could compose it without James; what makes it worth recording is that the antecedent matches. See the exclusion register at this verse for the Ezekiel 34:6 half of the clause, which is standing formula and not a fresh borrowing.
links.whyNot: Four words, none of them rare individually, and the surrounding clause is demonstrably the Book of Mormon's own formula. A reader who filed the whole clause under the standing dispersion exclusion would be taking a defensible line.
links.text: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting.

pericopes.text: and as he hath covenanted with all the house of Jacob, even so shall the covenant wherewith he hath covenanted with the house of Jacob, be fulfilled in his own due time, unto the restoring all the house of Jacob unto the knowledge of the covenant that he hath covenanted with them;

and then shall they know their Redeemer, which is Jesus Christ, the Son of God; and then shall they be gathered in from the four quarters of the earth, unto their own lands, from whence they have been dispersed; yea, as the Lord liveth, so shall it be. Amen.

provenance.other: “gather together the dispersed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:12, and the substantive “the dispersed” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 11:12 and John 7:35. 3 Nephi 5:26's 'from whence they have been dispersed' is the only place in this chapter where Isaiah's own vocabulary surfaces rather than Revelation's.
provenance.significance: Two verses of one sentence divide the evidence cleanly, and the link is placed where the wording is rather than where the theme is (CONVENTIONS §6a). 5:24 gathers 'from the four quarters of the earth', which is Revelation 20:8's phrase and not Isaiah's; 5:26 gathers 'from the four quarters of the earth, unto their own lands, from whence they have been dispersed', and 'dispersed' is Isaiah's word and not Revelation's. So the passage is not following one verse or the other but holding both, and the seam runs through a single sentence. Isaiah 11:12 also accounts for what the chapter has been saying since 5:23 — an ensign, an assembling of outcasts, a remnant — and the whole peroration reads as Isaiah 11:11-12 re-narrated with one phrase swapped out.

links.note: 'And then shall they be gathered in from the four quarters of the earth, unto their own lands, from whence they have been dispersed.' The verb, the object and the destination are Isaiah 11:12's — gather together the dispersed, assemble the outcasts, from the four corners of the earth — and only the single word 'quarters' is not. The catalogue records the Revelation phrase at 5:24 and Isaiah's own word here, because that is where each sits. Note that 'unto their own lands' is not from Isaiah: “own lands” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses, and the plural is the Book of Mormon's, which has many lands where Isaiah has one.
links.text: And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

provenance.other: “thy Redeemer” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses and all seven are in Isaiah 41-60. Isaiah 49:26 is the one that joins the title to knowing and to Jacob: 'all flesh shall know that I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the mighty One of Jacob.' Isaiah 60:16 has the same three-part formula and is the only real competitor.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 60:16, 'thou shalt know that I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer', is nearly identical and is a gathering chapter too. Isaiah 49:26 is preferred only because it names Jacob, which this passage names four times, and because the Book of Mormon has it transcribed at 1 Nephi 21:26 and quoted twice more.
provenance.significance: This is why the mediation is 'OT-via-earlier-BoM' rather than 'direct-OT'. Isaiah 49 is not an outside text for a Book of Mormon writer: it stands transcribed in full at 1 Nephi 21 and is expounded at 1 Nephi 22:13 and 2 Nephi 6:18, so a later narrator reaching for 'know … Saviour … Redeemer … Jacob' is reaching for something already inside his own record. The chapter's closing sentence answers, in the corpus's own voice, the verse the corpus copied out six hundred years earlier.

links.note: Four elements of Isaiah 49:26 are present across 3 Nephi 5:20-26 and not one of them contiguously: 'my Saviour Jesus Christ' at 5:20 (1830 spelling, KJV's u), 'the house of Jacob' at 5:21 and again at 5:25, 'then shall they know their Redeemer' at 5:26. Isaiah 49:26 has all four in nine words. This is the split-agreement case CONVENTIONS §9 says the n-gram stream cannot see by construction, and it did not see it: no candidate in the dossier proposes Isaiah 49. Recorded because the peroration is otherwise built out of Isaiah 11 and it would be odd for the one Isaian gathering-verse the Book of Mormon has already copied out to be absent from it.
links.whyNot: No run longer than two words, and 'Redeemer' and 'Saviour' are among the commonest titles in the corpus. The row rests entirely on the co-occurrence of four elements spread over seven verses, which is a weaker kind of evidence than this catalogue usually accepts, and a reader could reasonably hold that the passage simply has Isaiah 11 and nothing else.
links.text: And I will feed them that oppress thee with their own flesh; and they shall be drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine: and all flesh shall know that I the LORD am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the mighty One of Jacob.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that the people of the Nephites did all return to their own lands, in the twenty and sixth year, every man, with his family, his flocks and his herds, his horses and his cattle, and all things whatsoever did belong unto them.

And it came to pass that they had not eaten up all their provisions; therefore they did take with them all that they had not devoured, of all their grain of every kind, and their gold, and their silver, and all their precious things, and they did return to their own lands and their possessions, both on the north and on the south, both on the land northward and on the land southward.

And they granted unto those robbers which had entered into a covenant to keep the peace, of the band which were desirous to remain Lamanites, lands, according to their numbers, that they might have, with their labors, wherewith to subsist upon; and thus they did establish peace in all the land.

And they began again to prosper and to wax great; and the twenty and sixth and seventh years passed away, and there was great order in the land; and they had formed their laws according to equity and justice.
And now there was nothing in all the land, to hinder the people from prospering continually, except they should fall into transgression.
And now it was Gidgiddoni, and the Judge Lachoneus, and those which had been appointed leaders, which had established this great peace in the land.
And it came to pass that there were many cities built anew, and there were many old cities repaired;
and there were many highways cast up, and many roads made, which led from city to city, and from land to land, and from place to place.

links.text: Go through, go through the gates; prepare ye the way of the people; cast up, cast up the highway; gather out the stones; lift up a standard for the people.

provenance.other: “cast up the highway” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “cast up” occurs in seven, of which only Isaiah 62:10 and Jeremiah 18:15 (“a way not cast up”) use it of making a road; the rest raise siege banks or throw dust on heads. The collocation of the verb with the noun is therefore effectively Isaiah's.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 57:14, 'Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way', has the verb in the same sense without the noun.
provenance.significance: The KJV builds a highway exactly twice, and both times it is the road by which a scattered people comes home to its God — Isaiah 40:3's highway in the desert and Isaiah 62:10's highway with the stones gathered out of it and a standard lifted over it. 3 Nephi 6:7-8 is a public-works notice: cities built anew, old cities repaired, highways cast up, roads from land to land. Read against Isaiah the notice is not neutral infrastructure. It is the language of preparing the way, placed in the last years of peace before the Lord actually comes to this people in chapter 11, and the chapter then spends twenty verses showing the people making themselves unfit to receive him. The road is built and the standard is not lifted.

links.note: 'And there were many highways cast up, and many roads made, which led from city to city.' The verb is the tell: English has many ways to say that a road was built, and 'cast up' is the KJV's, used of a highway in one verse only. Everything else here is the Book of Mormon's own — the plural 'highways', the pairing with 'roads made', the city-to-city itinerary — so this is registered as an echo and not more. What is borrowed is a single Isaianic construction, not a clause.
links.whyNot: Two words, and 'cast up' had a plain technical sense in nineteenth-century English road-building independent of any Bible. A reader who wants to call this common idiom rather than borrowing is not being unreasonable; the case rests on the KJV's own restriction of the phrase to Isaiah's homecoming road.

pericopes.text: And thus passed away the twenty and eighth year, and the people had continual peace.

But it came to pass in the twenty and ninth year, there began to be some disputings among the people; and some were lifted up unto pride and boastings, because of their exceeding great riches, yea, even unto great persecutions:

links.text: But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil.

provenance.other: “boastings” in the plural occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:16. “buy and sell, and get gain” occurs in exactly one, James 4:13. “Ye have condemned and killed the just” occurs in exactly one, James 5:6. All three are inside a single continuous denunciation.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's structure, borrowed whole. James runs: the merchant who will go into such a city and buy and sell and get gain (4:13) → 'ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil' (4:16) → 'Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you' (5:1) → 'ye have condemned and killed the just; and he doth not resist you' (5:6). 3 Nephi 6 runs: lifted up unto pride and boastings because of their exceeding great riches (6:10) → 'for there were many merchants in the land' (6:11) → the rich and the learned distinguished by ranks (6:12) → the judges condemn the prophets and put them to death secretly, and the prophets do not resist (6:23-25) → and in chapter 8 the miseries come, on the rich cities by name. Not one of James's clauses is quoted at length; his sequence is followed from end to end, and the Book of Mormon supplies the destruction that James only threatens. The metalepsis is the last verse of the sequence: 'he doth not resist you' is the whole content of 3 Nephi 6:13's other party, who receive railing and would not turn and revile again.

links.note: 'Some were lifted up unto pride and boastings, because of their exceeding great riches.' The single distinctive word is 'boastings', a KJV singleton in the plural, and by itself it would be worth no more than the moderate echo the catalogue gave it at Helaman 4:13. What lifts it here is what stands in the next verse: 'for there were many merchants in the land'. James 4:13-16 is the KJV's one passage that puts a merchant, his gain, and his boastings in that order, and 3 Nephi 6:10-11 puts riches, boastings and merchants in the same order across a verse break. The rest of James's paragraph then supplies the rest of the chapter — see the provenance note.
links.whyNot: The verbal base is one rare word plus a common noun; a reader who declines the sequence argument is left with 'boastings' alone, which is a moderate echo at best. The case is a claim about order, not about wording, and it is held at high because the order holds for four consecutive elements and not because any clause is reproduced.

pericopes.text: for there were many merchants in the land, and also many lawyers, and many officers.

And the people began to be distinguished by ranks, according to their riches, and their chances for learning; yea, some were ignorant because of their poverty, and others did receive great learning because of their riches;

some were lifted up in pride, and others were exceeding humble; some did return railing for railing, while others would receive railing, and persecution, and all manner of afflictions, and would not turn and revile again, but were humble and penitent before God;

links.text: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.

provenance.other: “railing for railing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The noun 'railing' in this reciprocal construction exists nowhere else in the Authorized Version, and no modern translation preserves it — RSV and NRSV read 'reviling for reviling', NIV 'insult with insult' — so the phrase is the KJV's English and not merely the New Testament's sense.
provenance.significance: Peter's clause is a prohibition with a promise attached: do not render railing for railing, 'knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing'. 3 Nephi 6:13 divides one people along exactly that line — 'some did return railing for railing, while others would receive railing … and would not turn and revile again' — and the next verse tells you which half inherited: the church was broken up in all the land save among the few who 'were firm, and steadfast, and immoveable'. The suppressed half of Peter's verse, the inheritance, is what 6:14 hands out.

links.note: 'Some did return railing for railing.' Three words, reproduced exactly from the only KJV verse that contains them, and the verse's own construction is preserved: Peter's 'rendering … railing for railing' becomes 'return railing for railing', a synonym in the participle and nothing else changed. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his long quotations; the strength here is absolute rarity, not length. The verse then goes on to describe the other party in the words of 1 Peter 2:23, catalogued separately below, so both of the Petrine singletons in this argument are present in one Book of Mormon sentence.

links.text: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:

provenance.other: “reviled not again” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the bare collocation 'revile again' occurs in none. The Book of Mormon's 'would not turn and revile again' inserts one verb into the KJV's phrase and keeps the adverb that makes it reciprocal.
provenance.significance: The subject of 1 Peter 2:23 is Christ under trial — reviled, suffering, and committing himself 'to him that judgeth righteously'. 3 Nephi 6:13 gives that posture to the people who will shortly be arraigned before judges who do not judge righteously, and 6:23 has those judges put them to death secretly. Peter's Christ is the model of the Nephite martyrs of 6:23 before Christ has arrived in the book at all, and the trial the chapter builds toward in 6:25-30 is a trial of the judges rather than of the just — which is Peter's clause completed rather than quoted.

links.note: 'While others would receive railing, and persecution, and all manner of afflictions, and would not turn and revile again, but were humble and penitent before God.' The second Petrine singleton in the same sentence. Peter's 'when he was reviled, reviled not again' is a description of Christ's silence under trial; the Book of Mormon converts it from a participial description to a refusal ('would not turn and revile again') and supplies the direction of the alternative — 'humble and penitent before God' where Peter has 'committed himself to him that judgeth righteously'.
links.whyNot: 'Revile' is an ordinary English verb, and the reciprocal 'again' could be reached without Peter. It is held at high rather than certain on its own; the reason it is not registered lower is that the immediately preceding clause of the same Book of Mormon verse quotes 1 Peter 3:9's singleton, which makes an independent arrival at 2:23's very unlikely.

pericopes.text: and thus there became a great inequality in all the land, insomuch that the church began to be broken up; yea, insomuch that in the thirtieth year the church was broken up in all the land, save it were among a few of the Lamanites, which were converted unto the true faith; and they would not depart from it, for they were firm, and steadfast, and immoveable, willing with all diligence to keep the commandments of the Lord.

links.text: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

provenance.other: “stedfast, unmoveable” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “unmoveable” in exactly two, the other being the grounded ship of Acts 27:41. The 1830 spells the second adjective 'immoveable', keeping the -eable of the KJV's own orthography, where 1920 modernises to 'immovable'.
provenance.significance: Paul's pair closes his resurrection chapter: because the dead rise, be stedfast and unmoveable, 'forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord'. 3 Nephi 6 has just described men 'testifying unto them concerning the redemption which the Lord would make for his people; or in other words, the resurrection of Christ' (6:20), and the only people in the land who hold when the church breaks up are described in the adjectives Paul attaches to that doctrine. The chapter puts the resurrection preaching and the resurrection-grounded steadfastness in the same twenty verses, which is the order of 1 Corinthians 15 itself.

links.note: 'They were firm, and steadfast, and immoveable, willing with all diligence to keep the commandments of the Lord.' Paul's adjective pair, in Paul's order, with a third adjective prefixed. The catalogue adjudicated this at 1 Nephi 2:10 and it has since become one of the Book of Mormon's own formulae (Mosiah 5:15, Alma 1:25); the row is written again here because a new book is a new hand and because 3 Nephi's use is not simply the formula recurring — the converted Lamanites are the exception that survives the breaking up of the church, and the argument for the phrase's source was made at 1 Nephi 2:10 rather than restated here.

pericopes.text: Now the cause of this iniquity of the people, was this: Satan had great power, unto the stirring up of the people to do all manner of iniquity, and to the puffing them up with pride, tempting them to seek for power, and authority, and riches, and the vain things of the world.
And thus satan did lead away the hearts of the people, to do all manner of iniquity; therefore they had not enjoyed peace but a few years.

And thus in the commencement of the thirtieth year, the people having been delivered up for the space of a long time, to be carried about by the temptations of the Devil whithersoever he desired to carry them, and to do whatsoever iniquity he desired they should; and thus in the commencement of this, the thirtieth year, they were in a state of awful wickedness.

links.text: And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.

provenance.other: “taken captive by him at his will” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “carried about” occurs in four, of which Ephesians 4:14 ('carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive') is the only one about deception.
provenance.alternative: Ephesians 4:14 supplies the verb the Book of Mormon actually uses; 2 Timothy 2:26 supplies the doctrine. The verse may be reaching for both.
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy 2:26's peculiarity is the possessive: the captives act at the devil's will, not their own, which is as close as the KJV comes to saying that the damned are moved by another's volition. 3 Nephi 6:17 states that doctrine twice over in one sentence — 'whithersoever he desired to carry them, and to do whatsoever iniquity he desired they should' — and then, in the very next verse, revokes it: 'they did not sin ignorantly … therefore they did wilfully rebel.' Paul's clause exists to explain why such people can be recovered; the Book of Mormon quotes the captivity and then withdraws the excuse.

links.note: 'The people having been delivered up … to be carried about by the temptations of the Devil whithersoever he desired to carry them, and to do whatsoever iniquity he desired they should.' The verbal contact is thin and the conceptual contact is exact: the devil's desire, not the sinner's, is the grammatical subject of what the sinner does, which in the KJV is 2 Timothy 2:26's construction alone. Registered as an allusion at moderate because the wording is the Book of Mormon's throughout — 'delivered up', 'carried about', 'whithersoever' are all reachable without Paul.
links.whyNot: No phrase of more than two words is shared with either candidate. If the doctrine of the devil's directing will was already the Book of Mormon's own — and 2 Nephi 1:18 and Alma 12:6 suggest it was by this point — then 3 Nephi 6:17 needs no source at all, and the row should be read as a note on where that doctrine's English came from rather than as a borrowing at this verse.

pericopes.text: Now they did not sin ignorantly, for they knew the will of God concerning them, for it had been taught unto them; therefore they did wilfully rebel against God.

links.text: For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins,

provenance.route: Numbers 15:27-31 → Hebrews 10:26 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: The distinction the verse turns on is Numbers 15:27-31, where the soul that sins bishgagah (in error) is atoned for and the soul that acts beyad ramah (with a high hand) is cut off. The KJV renders the pair 'through ignorance' / 'presumptuously'.
provenance.other: “sin wilfully” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “ignorantly” occurs in exactly four, of which Numbers 15:28 is the only one in the sacrificial law that the Hebrews argument is reworking. The Book of Mormon's sentence contains both adverbs and neither source contains the other.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 10:26 is the New Testament's restatement of the Numbers law with the terms changed — 'wilfully' where Numbers has 'presumptuously', received knowledge where Numbers has the high hand — and its consequence in 10:27 is not a penalty but the removal of the remedy, followed by 'a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries'. 3 Nephi 6:18 states the condition; two chapters later 3 Nephi 8-9 supplies the fiery indignation, by name and by city. Read the two together and the catalogue's cleanest instance of metalepsis in this book: the verse that establishes that these people cannot plead ignorance is the verse whose unquoted next clause is the fire that takes them.

links.note: 'Now they did not sin ignorantly, for they knew the will of God concerning them, for it had been taught unto them; therefore they did wilfully rebel against God.' Both halves of the KJV's ignorance/wilfulness distinction are here in one sentence, and they come from two different books. 'Wilfully', paired with prior knowledge and with rebellion rather than error, is Hebrews 10:26's singleton and Hebrews 10:26's argument. 'Ignorantly' is the Levitical adverb of Numbers 15:28, which Hebrews does not use. `mediation-check.py` on 3 Nephi 6:18 against Numbers 15:28 and Hebrews 10:26 returns decisive points in both directions and flags the verse as a composite, which is the right answer: the wilfulness is mediated through Hebrews, the ignorance is not. The catalogue already reads Hebrews 10:26-29 behind Alma 39:6, where the wilfulness is present but the ignorance clause is not; 3 Nephi 6:18 is the fuller form.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 6.18 (Hebrews 10:26)

pericopes.text: And now it was in the days of Lachoneus, the son of Lachoneus: for Lachoneus did fill the seat of his father, and did govern the people that year.

And there began to be men inspired from heaven, and sent forth, standing among the people in all the land, preaching and testifying boldly of the sins and iniquities of the people, and testifying unto them concerning the redemption which the Lord would make for his people; or in other words, the resurrection of Christ; and they did testify boldly of his death and sufferings.

links.text: He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.

provenance.route: Psalm 16:10 → Acts 2:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the resurrection of Christ” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The New Testament otherwise says 'the resurrection of the dead', 'the resurrection of Jesus Christ' (1 Peter 1:3, 3:21) or 'his resurrection'; the bare genitive with the title alone is Peter's at Pentecost and nowhere else.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:31 is Peter arguing that a prophet who lived long before the event 'seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ' — that is, it is the New Testament's own warrant for pre-Christian prophecy of a resurrection not yet accomplished. 3 Nephi 6:20 needs precisely that warrant and takes precisely that phrase: men inspired from heaven, testifying 'concerning the redemption which the Lord would make for his people; or in other words, the resurrection of Christ'. The gloss 'or in other words' is doing the work Peter's exegesis of Psalm 16 does, and it lands on Peter's four words. There is no better instance in the chapter of a borrowing whose source supplies the argument for the borrowing's own possibility.

links.note: 'Or in other words, the resurrection of Christ; and they did testify boldly of his death and sufferings.' Four words from the only KJV verse that contains them, in a sentence whose whole purpose is to say that pre-Christian prophets preached a post-Christian doctrine. The wider verse keeps Peter's company: 'testify boldly' answers to the boldness of Acts 4:13 and 4:31, and 'his death and sufferings' to Acts 3:18's 'that Christ should suffer'. Registered against Acts 2:31 alone because that is where the singleton is.

pericopes.text: Now there were many of the people which were exceeding angry, because of those which testified of these things; and those which were angry, were chiefly the Chief Judges, and they which had been High Priests, and lawyers; yea, all they which were lawyers, were angry with those which testified of these things.

links.text: Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.

provenance.other: “lawyers” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and every one of them is in Luke; four (11:45, 11:46, 11:52, and by continuation 11:53-54's reaction) belong to one scene. The singular 'lawyer' occurs in three, two of them also Luke. There is no other book of the Bible in which a lawyer exists as a party.
provenance.significance: Luke 11 is the only passage in scripture where lawyers as a class are (a) reproved, (b) made furious by the reproof, and (c) charged in the same breath with the blood of the prophets: 'I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute … it shall be required of this generation' (11:49-51), and then 11:53-54, 'the scribes and the Pharisees began to urge him vehemently … laying wait for him, to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him.' 3 Nephi 6:21-23 reproduces all three movements in order and then does what Luke only predicts: the lawyers are angry at those who testify, and the prophets are taken and put to death. The suppressed clause is 11:51's 'it shall be required of this generation' — and it is required of this generation, in chapter 8.

links.note: 'Those which were angry, were chiefly the Chief Judges, and they which had been High Priests, and lawyers; yea, all they which were lawyers, were angry with those which testified of these things.' The word is the point. The Book of Mormon's opposition party in this chapter is chief judges, former high priests and lawyers, and 'lawyers' is a King James word that exists only in Luke, only as a bloc, and only under a woe. The verse repeats the noun twice in one sentence and singles the lawyers out as the party that is angry to a man, which is Luke's own emphasis at 11:45 — the lawyer who objects that he too has been reproached.
links.whyNot: The verbal base is a single noun; no phrase is shared. The case rests on the noun's distribution and on the three-part correspondence set out in the provenance note, and a reader who takes 'lawyers' as simply the ordinary English word for the profession — which the Book of Mormon has used since Alma 10 — will decline it.

pericopes.text: Now there was no lawyer, nor Judge, nor High Priest, that could have power to condemn any one to death, save their condemnation was signed by the governor of the land.

links.text: Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death:

provenance.other: “put any man to death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “the governor of the land” occurs in none; the KJV's eight 'governor of the —' phrases are of a city, a house, the Jews, or a feast. What is borrowed is the jurisdictional rule, not the title.
provenance.significance: John 18:31 is the only verse in the Bible that states the arrangement 3 Nephi 6:22 states as Nephite law: a religious-legal establishment with full power to condemn and no power to execute, the execution reserved to a civil governor. Everything that follows in both narratives follows from that one disability. In John it produces the transfer to Pilate and the crucifixion under Roman authority; in 3 Nephi it produces the secret executions of 6:23, carried out precisely so that 'the knowledge of their death came not unto the governor of the land, until after their death'. The Book of Mormon's judges do what the Sanhedrin of John 18 is prevented from doing, by concealment rather than by referral — and the chapter that establishes this is four chapters from the crucifixion itself, which the book will narrate from the other side of the world in 3 Nephi 8.

links.note: 'Now there was no lawyer, nor Judge, nor High Priest, that could have power to condemn any one to death, save their condemnation was signed by the governor of the land.' The singleton wording sits two verses later — 6:24's 'that any man should be put to death, except they had power from the governor of the land' inverts John's 'not lawful for us to put any man to death' — but the link is catalogued here, where the rule and the personnel are given together, and 6:24 is cross-referenced in the exclusion register. The personnel are John's: a high priest, a court, and lawyers, unable to kill. The catalogue has already read the other half of John 18:31 at Mosiah 26:11, where Alma remands the accused 'that thou may judge them according to their crimes' — so the two halves of one KJV verse are used in two different books for the two different sides of the same jurisdictional problem.
links.whyNot: The shared words are reordered rather than reproduced, and a legal system in which a local court needs a governor's warrant to execute is not so peculiar that it could only be got from John. The strength of the row is that this is the one place the KJV describes such a system, and that the Book of Mormon's next verse turns on evading it.

pericopes.text: Now there were many of those which testified of the things pertaining to Christ; which testified boldly, which were taken and put to death secretly, by the Judges, that the knowledge of their death came not unto the governor of the land, until after their death.
Now behold, this was contrary to the laws of the land, that any man should be put to death, except they had power from the governor of the land;
therefore a complaint came up unto the land of Zarahemla, to the governor of the land, against these Judges which had condemned the prophets of the land unto death, not according to the law.
Now it came to pass that they were taken and brought up before the Judge, to be judged of the crime which they had done, according to the law which had been given by the people.

Now it came to pass that those Judges had many friends and kindreds; and the remainder, yea, even almost all the lawyers and the High Priests, did gather themselves together, and unite with the kindreds of those Judges which were to be tried according to the law;

and they did enter into a covenant one with another, yea, even into that covenant which was given by them of old, which covenant was given and administered by the Devil, to combine against all righteousness;

therefore they did combine against the people of the Lord, and enter into a covenant to destroy them, and to deliver those which were guilty of murder from the grasp of justice, which was about to be administered according to the law.

And they did set at defiance the law and the rights of their country; and they did covenant, one with another, to destroy the governor, and to establish a king over the land, that the land should no more be at liberty, but should be subject unto kings.

links.text: When thou art come unto the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee, and shalt possess it, and shalt dwell therein, and shalt say, I will set a king over me, like as all the nations that are about me;

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 17:14 / 1 Samuel 8:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “set a king over” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Deuteronomy 17:14, 1 Samuel 10:19 and 1 Samuel 12:13 — and all three belong to the single biblical topos of a people asking for a king. The Book of Mormon reads 'establish a king over the land', which is none of them; only the preposition and the noun are shared.
provenance.significance: The Deuteronomic and Samuel passages are the Bible's account of a people freely choosing a king and being warned what it will cost them — 'ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen'. 3 Nephi 6:30 is the same transaction with the consent removed: not a people asking, but a conspiracy covenanting in secret 'to destroy the governor, and to establish a king over the land, that the land should no more be at liberty, but should be subject unto kings'. Israel demands a king to judge it; the Nephite judges demand a king to protect them from judgment. The Book of Mormon's own version of 1 Samuel 8 is Mosiah 29, where the kingship is abolished by the voice of the people, and 3 Nephi 6:30 is the undoing of that chapter by a covenant taken in the dark.

links.note: The chapter's last verse, and it is the biblical demand for a king inverted at every point that carries weight. What survives verbally is only 'a king over', and the Book of Mormon's verb is 'establish' where all three KJV verses have 'set'; the link is registered as figural for that reason, not as an allusion. What makes it worth registering at all is that this is the closing act of the sequence the chapter has been building — merchants, ranks, angry lawyers, murdered prophets — and it lands on the one political act the Deuteronomic law legislates for in advance.
links.whyNot: Two words, one of them a preposition. If the Book of Mormon's kingship discourse is taken as self-sufficient by this point in the corpus — and after Mosiah 29 it plainly is — then 3 Nephi 6:30 needs no biblical source, and this row records a resonance rather than a dependence. It is kept because a reader who knows Deuteronomy 17 will hear it, and the catalogue should say whether it heard it too.

pericopes.text: Now behold, I will shew unto you that they did not establish a king over the land; but in this same year, yea, the thirtieth year, they did destroy upon the judgement seat, yea, did murder the Chief Judge of the land.

And the people were divided one against another; and they did separate one from another, into tribes, every man according to his family, and his kindred and friends; and thus they did destroy the government of the land.

links.text: And if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.

provenance.other: “house be divided” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:25, and “cannot stand” in exactly four, of which three are Mark 3:24, 3:25 and 3:26. The Book of Mormon's own phrase, “divided one against another”, reproduces neither, and “one against another” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, none of them the Synoptic saying. The link therefore rests on the idiom and its consequence, not on a run of words — which is why it is filed as an echo.
provenance.significance: The saying withholds the outcome — a divided kingdom 'cannot stand' — and 3 Nephi 7:2 supplies it in the same sentence: 'thus they did destroy the government of the land.' What is worth recording is not this verse alone but where it sits. Mark 3 is the chapter behind 7:16's eight-word run, and the material 3 Nephi 7 takes from it arrives in Mark's own order of concerns: the division that cannot stand (3:24-26) at 7:2, Satan as the agent of it (3:23, 3:26) at 7:5, the prophet grieved at the hardness of their hearts (3:5) at 7:16, and unclean spirits cast out by a delegated power (3:11, 3:15) at 7:19. Read alone this row is thin; read as the first stop on that route it is part of the chapter's principal finding.

links.note: 'And the people were divided one against another; and they did separate one from another, into tribes … and thus they did destroy the government of the land.' The Synoptic division saying is the King James Bible's one formulation of the idea that internal division destroys a polity, and this is the sentence in which the Nephite polity is destroyed by internal division. The Book of Mormon has already used the idiom at Helaman 10:18 in a reflexive plural that matches no single verse; 3 Nephi is a new book and a new narrator, so the row is written again here rather than cross-referenced (ADJUDICATING §4). Note that the division here runs along exactly the lines Luke 12:52-53 makes the mark of the kingdom's arrival — family, kindred, friends — but inverted: there the household divides, here the household is the unit that survives and the nation dissolves around it.
links.whyNot: No distinctive wording is reproduced. A reader who wants the connection has to accept that 'divided one against another' is reaching for 'divided against itself', and it may simply be the ordinary English way of saying what happened.

pericopes.text: And every tribe did appoint a Chief, or a leader over them; and thus they became tribes, and leaders of tribes.
Now behold, there was no man among them, save he had much family and many kindreds and friends; therefore their tribes became exceeding great.
Now all this was done, and there was no wars as yet among them; and all this iniquity had come upon the people, because they did yield themselves unto the power of satan;
and the regulations of the government was destroyed, because of the secret combination of the friends and kindreds of them which murdered the prophets.
And they did cause a great contention in the land, insomuch that the more righteous part of the people, although they were nearly all become wicked; yea, there were but few righteous men among them.
And thus six years had not passed away, since the more part of the people had turned from their righteousness, like the dog to his vomit, or like the sow to her wallowing in the mire.—

links.text: But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.

provenance.route: Proverbs 26:11 → 2 Peter 2:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “wallowing in the mire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:22, and so does “the sow that was washed”. The other half of the couplet is the Proverbs form: “to his vomit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 26:11, and 2 Peter reads 'to his own vomit again'. So the Book of Mormon's dog is Solomon's and its sow is Peter's.
provenance.alternative: Proverbs 26:11 alone. It is ruled out by the sow, which is in no Old Testament verse; the swine half of the proverb enters the Bible only at 2 Peter 2:22, where it is paired with a non-canonical saying.
provenance.significance: Recover 2 Peter 2:20-22 and the borrowing acquires its clock. Peter's proverb is applied to people who 'have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ' and 'are again entangled therein', for whom 'the latter end is worse with them than the beginning' — apostasy after knowledge, not sin in ignorance. That is precisely the arithmetic 3 Nephi 7:8 is making: 'thus six years had not passed away, since the more part of the people had turned from their righteousness', six years measured from the signs of Christ's birth in 3 Nephi 1. And 2 Peter 2:21's definition of the offence — 'after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them' — is restated seven verses later at 7:15 as their 'quick return from righteousness unto their wickedness and abominations'. The epistle is not being quoted for a picturesque image; it is supplying the category the chapter needs.

links.note: 'The more part of the people had turned from their righteousness, like the dog to his vomit, or like the sow to her wallowing in the mire.' Both animals, in Peter's order, with the mire clause reproduced word for word. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but the mediation is not in doubt: 2 Peter 2:22 is the only verse in the Bible that has the sow, and the run “to her wallowing in the mire” is its alone. What the Book of Mormon does not take is Peter's 'own' and his 'again' — 'like the dog to his vomit' is the Proverbs wording, so the verse is a composite rather than a straight lift, and the mediation-check divides three decisive points to one on that account.

pericopes.text: Now this secret combination which had brought so great iniquity upon the people, did gather themselves together, and did place at their head a man whom they did call Jacob;
and they did call him their king; therefore he became a king over this wicked band; and he was one of the chiefest which had given his voice against the prophets which testified of Jesus.—

links.text: Which thing I also did in Jerusalem: and many of the saints did I shut up in prison, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death, I gave my voice against them.

provenance.other: “gave my voice against” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:10; “voice against” occurs in exactly two, the other being Jeremiah 4:16, where it is a herald's shout at Jerusalem and not a vote. The idiom is also distinctively King James: the Greek is a ballot cast, and modern versions read 'cast my vote against them', which removes the voice entirely. A reader of any twentieth-century Bible cannot find this phrase.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a confession of judicial murder made to Agrippa — he is describing, as the chief of persecutors, his own consent to the killing of the saints, and Acts 7:58 has already shown him holding the clothes at the stoning of a witness. 3 Nephi 7:10 gives that sentence to the man the secret combination has just crowned: 'he was one of the chiefest which had given his voice against the prophets which testified of Jesus.' The metalepsis works in both directions. It makes Jacob the Nephite Saul of Tarsus, formally casting his vote for the deaths of those who testify of Jesus; and it silently withholds what makes Paul's sentence bearable in Acts, which is that the speaker has since been converted and is telling the story against himself. Jacob is made king instead. Note also that the stoning of prophets Acts 7:58 attaches to Saul turns up four verses later at 7:14.

links.note: 'And he was one of the chiefest which had given his voice against the prophets which testified of Jesus.' The KJV has exactly one verse in which a man gives his voice against people who are put to death, and it is Paul's account of his own part in the executions at Jerusalem. The Book of Mormon takes the idiom whole and keeps its legal sense — a formal assent to a death sentence, not mere speech against — which is why the verse can call Jacob 'one of the chiefest' of a body rather than a lone accuser. Whether 'chiefest' is also reaching for Paul's 'very chiefest apostles' is not decidable: “chiefest” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses across both testaments, and the word is not rare enough to carry the weight.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were not so strong in number as the tribes of the people which were united together, save it were their leaders did establish their laws, every one according to his tribe; nevertheless they were enemies, notwithstanding they were not a righteous people; yet they were united in the hatred of those who had entered into a covenant to destroy the government;

therefore Jacob seeing that their enemies were more numerous than they, he being the king of the band, therefore he commanded his people that they should take their flight into the northernmost part of the land, and there build up unto themselves a kingdom, until they were joined by dissenters, (for he flattered them that there would be many dissenters,) and they become sufficiently strong to contend with the tribes of the people. And they did so;

and so speedy was their march, that it could not be impeded, until they had gone forth out of the reach of the people. And thus ended the thirtieth year; and thus were the affairs of the people of Nephi.

And it came to pass in the thirty and first year, that they were divided into tribes, every man according to his family, kindred and friends; nevertheless, they had come to an agreement that they would not go to war one with another; but they were not united as to their laws, and their manner of government, for they were established according to the minds of them which was their chiefs and their leaders. But they did establish very strict laws that one tribe should not trespass against another, insomuch that in some degree they had peace in the land; nevertheless, their hearts were turned from the Lord their God, and they did stone the prophets, and did cast them out from among them.

And it came to pass that Nephi, having been visited by angels, and also by the voice of the Lord, therefore having seen angels, and being eyewitness, and having had power given unto him that he might know concerning the ministry of Christ, and also being eyewitness to their quick return from righteousness unto their wickedness and abominations;

links.text: For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.

provenance.other: “eyewitnesses” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 1:2 and 2 Peter 1:16, and the word occurs nowhere else in the Bible in any form. The 1830 reading is the singular 'eyewitness', twice, which 1920 hyphenated to 'eye-witness'; neither spelling is in the KJV, but the noun itself is confined to those two verses.
provenance.alternative: Luke 1:2, 'which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word' — attractive because 3 Nephi 7:15-17 pairs eyewitness with ministry twice ('the ministry of Christ', 'he did minister many things'). It is not preferred because Luke's eyewitnesses are other people, cited by a writer who was not one, whereas 2 Peter's are the writer himself, which is Nephi's position here.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 1:16-18 is the KJV's one first-person claim to have both seen and heard: 'we were eyewitnesses of his majesty … And this voice which came from heaven we heard, when we were with him in the holy mount.' 3 Nephi 7:15 builds its credential the same way and in the same order — visited by angels, and also by the voice of the Lord, therefore having seen angels, and being eyewitness. What makes the route worth naming is that the chapter has already been to this epistle: 7:8 takes the dog and the sow from 2 Peter 2:22, and 2 Peter 2:21's 'after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment' is what 7:15 calls their 'quick return from righteousness unto their wickedness'. Two contacts with a three-chapter epistle in eight verses, and both fall in the part of it that is about apostasy after knowledge.

links.note: 'Nephi, having been visited by angels, and also by the voice of the Lord, therefore having seen angels, and being eyewitness.' The word 'eyewitness' is not ordinary English scripture vocabulary — it is in two verses of the Bible and no more — and the sentence that carries it here reproduces 2 Peter's structure of a voice heard and a glory seen. The link is conceptual rather than verbal because no clause is shared; what is shared is a rare noun and the shape of the claim it underwrites.
links.whyNot: A single rare word plus a structural resemblance. Luke 1:2 has the same word and the ministry vocabulary that surrounds it here, and a reader could reasonably prefer that verse or decline both.

pericopes.text: therefore, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, and the blindness of their minds, went forth among them in that same year, and began to testify boldly, repentance and remission of sins through faith on the Lord Jesus Christ.

links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “being grieved for the hardness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does “hardness of their hearts”; both are Mark 3:5. Check the pronoun before assuming it: “hardness of your hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Matthew 19:8, on divorce, which is not this verse. The Book of Mormon has the third person, and therefore Mark.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has recorded this clause nine times before, so what earns a fresh argument here is not the phrase but what the chapter does with the rest of Mark 3. Mark 3:5 is not a lament, it is a hinge: Jesus, grieved at the hardness of their hearts, works a healing, and the healing is what makes his opponents 'take counsel … how they might destroy him' (3:6). 3 Nephi 7:16-20 runs that hinge exactly — grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he goes forth and ministers, he casts out devils and raises the dead, 'and the people saw it … and were angry with him, because of his power.' Miracle producing murderous anger is the Markan sequence and it is not the obvious one; grief usually precedes rebuke, not wonders. And the surrounding chapter keeps returning to the same page of Mark: the divided house that cannot stand (3:24-26) at 7:2, Satan as its agent (3:23) at 7:5, unclean spirits and a delegated power to cast them out (3:11, 3:15) at 7:19. 3 Nephi 7 is the Book of Mormon's most sustained single-chapter engagement with Mark 3, and this verse is the anchor that keeps the rest from being coincidence.

links.note: 'Therefore, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, and the blindness of their minds, went forth among them in that same year, and began to testify boldly.' Eight words of Mark 3:5 in order and unaltered, from a verse that is the sole KJV home of both of its distinctive phrases. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six, but dependence here is not seriously deniable. The clause is by now a Book of Mormon formula — it has appeared in five previous books — and per ADJUDICATING §4 the row is written again because 3 Nephi is a new book and a new hand; the argument for the borrowing itself was made at 1 Nephi 2:18 and is not restated. What is new is the context: this is the first time a Book of Mormon narrator uses it of himself in the situation Mark 3 gives it, a prophet grieved and then attacked for the miracle that follows.

links.text: And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “repentance and remission of sins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:47. The looser “remission of sins” occurs in exactly seven, and the near neighbours — Mark 1:4 and Luke 3:3, 'the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins' — put the two nouns in a different relation. Only Luke 24:47 conjoins them.
provenance.significance: Luke 24:47 is the risen Christ's last commission, three verses before the ascension: repentance and remission of sins 'preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem'. 3 Nephi 7 puts that commission into effect in the thirty-first year, and the rest of it turns up in the neighbouring verses — 'in his name' at 7:19-20, 'in the name of Jesus', and 'among all nations' as the whole premise of a book claiming the commission reached a people outside Jerusalem. The chronology is the finding. In Luke the words are spoken by the risen Lord and then obeyed; here they are obeyed at 7:16 and 7:23 and the risen Lord does not arrive to speak them until 3 Nephi 11. The preaching precedes the commission that authorises it, which is the Book of Mormon's characteristic anachronism stated as compactly as anywhere in the book.

links.note: 'Began to testify boldly, repentance and remission of sins through faith on the Lord Jesus Christ.' Five words of a KJV singleton, and the whole content of Nephi's preaching for the next eight verses: 7:23 repeats the phrase exactly ('he did preach unto them repentance and remission of sins') and 7:25 completes it with 'received a remission of their sins'. Because both occurrences fall in one chapter the borrowing is adjudicated here at first use and 7:23 is recorded in recurrenceRefs. Note that the KJV's own commonest form of the phrase is Mark 1:4's, which subordinates remission to baptism; the Book of Mormon has Luke's coordinate pair, and then supplies the baptism separately at 7:24-25.

links.text: Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:

provenance.route: Ephesians 4:18 + 2 Corinthians 4:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “blindness of their minds” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses. Both of its halves are KJV singletons of different verses: “blindness of their heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:18, and the blinding of minds is 2 Corinthians 4:4, 'the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not'.
provenance.significance: The phrase is a fusion, and the two verses fused are the New Testament's two accounts of why unbelievers cannot see — Ephesians 4:18's self-inflicted hardening and 2 Corinthians 4:4's blinding by the god of this world. 3 Nephi 7 has already said which of the two it means: at 7:5 'they did yield themselves unto the power of satan', which is 2 Corinthians 4:4's mechanism and not Ephesians'. So the composite is not careless; the minds come from the verse where an external power blinds them and the blindness comes from the verse where the fault is their own, and the chapter has narrated both.

links.note: 'Being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, and the blindness of their minds.' The pair of clauses is what makes this worth a row: the first is Mark 3:5 unaltered, and the second is a phrase that exists in no King James verse but is assembled out of two that do. Ephesians 4:18 supplies 'blindness of their —' and 2 Corinthians 4:4 supplies the organ, its 'blinded the minds of them which believe not' standing four words from the dossier's independently-ranked match at 7:14. Recorded as an echo because neither source is reproduced intact; recorded at all because a hybrid of two singletons is better evidence of reading than either singleton alone would be.
links.whyNot: Hearts and minds are an easy English doublet, and a writer who had just written 'hardness of their hearts' might reach for 'blindness of their minds' without any verse behind it. The case rests on the arithmetic of the two singletons, not on any run of words.

pericopes.text: And he did minister many things unto them; and all of them cannot be written, and a part of them would not suffice; therefore they are not written in this book. And Nephi did minister with power and with great authority.

links.text: And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book:

provenance.route: John 20:30-31 and 21:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “not written in this book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:30. The bare “written in this book” occurs in exactly twelve, mostly Deuteronomic curse formulae, so the negative is what identifies the source. The second half of the Book of Mormon's sentence answers to John 21:25, whose hyperbole is that 'even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written'.
provenance.significance: John's two colophons do different work — 20:30-31 says the record is a selection made so that the reader may believe, 21:25 says the whole could not be written at all — and 3 Nephi 7:17 uses both in one sentence: 'all of them cannot be written, and a part of them would not suffice; therefore they are not written in this book.' What the borrowing does is transfer the evangelist's sign-off to a prophet. In John the unwritten signs are Jesus's; here they are Nephi's, and the next verse explains why the substitution is not presumptuous — 'so great was his faith on the Lord Jesus Christ, that angels did minister unto him daily'. Recover John 20:31 and the borrowed clause carries its purpose clause with it: 'but these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ.' 3 Nephi 7:21 states the same result four verses on, of those 'which was in Jesus Christ, in whom they believed'.

links.note: 'And all of them cannot be written, and a part of them would not suffice; therefore they are not written in this book.' Six words of a KJV singleton, in order and unchanged. The catalogue has adjudicated the same formula at Mosiah 1:8 and Alma 13:31 and it is written again here because 3 Nephi is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4); what is new in this occurrence is that it is applied to signs and miracles rather than to words, which is John 20:30's own referent and not Mosiah's or Alma's. “many other signs” also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one, which is worth noticing given that 7:22 goes on to say the converts 'did shew forth signs also'.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were angry with him, even because he had greater power than they, for it were not possible that they could disbelieve his words: for so great was his faith on the Lord Jesus Christ, that angels did minister unto him daily;

links.text: And he was there in the wilderness forty days, tempted of Satan; and was with the wild beasts; and the angels ministered unto him.

provenance.other: “angels ministered unto him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 1:13. The only other angelic ministration in the KJV is Matthew 4:11, “angels came and ministered”, which also occurs in exactly one verse; both are the close of the temptation.
provenance.significance: In the King James Bible there is exactly one man to whom angels minister, and the ministration is what follows his refusal of Satan. 3 Nephi 7 has set that refusal up as the chapter's governing contrast: at 7:5 the people 'did yield themselves unto the power of satan', and at 7:18 the one man who did not is served by angels daily. The Book of Mormon has taken a phrase the gospels use once, at the end of forty days in the wilderness, and made it a standing condition — 'daily' is its own word and it is the word that converts an episode into a station. Note also what the borrowing costs the sentence: the phrase's home context makes the angelic ministry a consolation after temptation, and here it is the explanation of why a prophet's enemies cannot answer him.

links.note: 'For so great was his faith on the Lord Jesus Christ, that angels did minister unto him daily.' Four words of a KJV singleton with the auxiliary changed and 'daily' added. The rarity is absolute — the KJV gives an angelic ministration to nobody but Jesus, and gives it twice in one episode — so the claim being made about Nephi is precise and is made by the choice of phrase rather than by any assertion.
links.whyNot: Short, and the words are ordinary; a writer describing angels serving a man has few other ways to say it. The row rests on the fact that the KJV, having many angels, uses this construction for one man only.

pericopes.text: and in the name of Jesus did he cast out devils and unclean spirits; and even his brother did he raise from the dead, after he had been stoned and suffered death by the people;

links.text: And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues;
