provenance.other: “in the name of Jesus” occurs in exactly six KJV verses and “cast out devils” in exactly twelve, so neither identifies a source alone; what narrows it is the pairing of the name with the casting out, which is Mark 16:17's 'In my name shall they cast out devils'. Two further phrases are singletons: “signs following” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:20, against 7:22's 'they did shew forth signs also', and “power to heal sicknesses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:15, against 7:18-19's 'he had greater power … did he cast out devils'. “devils and unclean spirits” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses; Mark 3 has the two terms in one chapter, at 3:11 and 3:15.
provenance.significance: Mark 16:17-20 is the KJV's list of what believers will do after the ascension, and the point of the list is that the works are delegated: they are done 'in my name', by people who are not Jesus, with the Lord 'working with them, and confirming the word with signs following'. 3 Nephi 7:19-22 is that list executed — devils cast out in the name of Jesus, the dead raised, miracles done in the sight of the people, and the healed themselves showing forth signs. The chronological point is the same one Luke 24:47 makes at 7:16, and sharper: the longer ending of Mark describes the church's life after the resurrection, and here it is being lived four chapters before the resurrected Christ arrives. Mark 3:15 supplies the same commission in its pre-resurrection form — power to heal sicknesses and to cast out devils, given to men who are ordained — and 7:25 will ordain them.

links.note: 'And in the name of Jesus did he cast out devils and unclean spirits; and even his brother did he raise from the dead.' No clause is reproduced, which is why the row is conceptual, but the inventory is Mark's and so is its governing formula: works done by a man in the name of Jesus. The verses that follow keep to the list — miracles in the sight of the people (7:20), devils cast out and infirmities healed (7:22), signs shewn forth (7:22, where the 1830's 'shew' preserves the KJV spelling that 1920 modernised). Both later verses are recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than given rows of their own, since they are the same borrowing continuing.
links.whyNot: The vocabulary of casting out devils is common enough in the gospels that no single verse is demonstrable, and a case could be made for Matthew 10:1 or Mark 3:15 instead of the longer ending. The row claims the passage is working from Mark's signs-list, not that it is quoting one verse of it.

pericopes.text: and the people saw it, and did witness of it, and were angry with him, because of his power; and he did also do many more miracles, in the sight of the people, in the name of Jesus.

And it came to pass that the thirty and first year did pass away, and there were but few which were converted unto the Lord; but as many as were converted, did truly signify unto the people that they had been visited by the power and spirit of God, which was in Jesus Christ, in whom they believed.—

And as many as had devils cast out from them, and were healed of their sicknesses and their infirmities, did truly manifest unto the people that they had been wrought upon by the spirit of God, and had been healed; and they did shew forth signs also, and did do some miracles among the people.

And it came to pass that thus passed away the thirty and second year also. And Nephi did cry unto the people in the commencement of the thirty and third year; and he did preach unto them repentance and remission of sins.
Now I would have you to remember also, that there were none which were brought unto repentance, who were not baptized with water;

links.text: For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.

provenance.other: “baptized with water” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 1:5 and Acts 11:16, and the second is Peter quoting the first. John 1:26 and 1:31 have 'baptize with water' and 'baptizing with water', not the past participle. So the Book of Mormon's phrase is, in the KJV, one saying of the risen Lord and its later citation.
provenance.significance: The phrase is never neutral in the KJV. Both times it appears it is the first half of a contrast whose second half is the whole point — 'but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence' — and at Acts 1:5 the not-many-days is ten, until Pentecost. 3 Nephi 7:24-26 is emphatic that the baptism it is describing is with water and says nothing about the Holy Ghost; the reader is at the close of the thirty-third year, and 3 Nephi 9:20 will promise 'baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost', 3 Nephi 11 will bring the risen Christ, and 3 Nephi 19:13 will deliver the fire. The suppressed half of Acts 1:5 is the Book of Mormon's next four chapters. Mormon's editorial aside — 'Now I would have you to remember also' — is asking the reader to hold exactly the thing Acts 1:5 makes provisional.

links.note: 'Now I would have you to remember also, that there were none which were brought unto repentance, who were not baptized with water.' The insistence on water, twice in two verses, is the point of the passage, and 'baptized with water' in that participial form is a two-verse phrase in the KJV, both of them Acts 1:5's saying. What is being remembered is a limit: this was water only. 7:25 repeats the phrase and is recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than given its own row for it.

pericopes.text: therefore there were ordained of Nephi, men unto this ministry, that all such as should come unto them, should be baptized with water, and this as a witness and a testimony before God, and unto the people, that they had repented and received a remission of their sins.

links.text: Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.

provenance.other: “ordained to be a witness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:22. “were ordained” occurs in exactly two, Acts 13:48 and 16:4, neither of which is an ordination to office. The Book of Mormon's own phrase, 'ordained of Nephi, men unto this ministry … as a witness and a testimony', separates the two words that Acts 1:22 joins but keeps both.
provenance.significance: Acts 1:21-22 is the KJV's one description of what a man is ordained for, and the answer is: to be a witness of the resurrection. The requirement is retrospective — the candidate must have companied with the apostles from the baptism of John — and the office is filled before Pentecost, in the ten-day gap. 3 Nephi 7:25 ordains men in the same gap and to the same office, and the resurrection they are ordained to witness has not happened yet. Read with 7:24's Acts 1:5, the whole passage sits inside Acts 1: baptism with water at 7:24, ordination to be a witness at 7:25, and the Holy Ghost withheld until the Lord comes. These are the men Christ will call at 3 Nephi 11-12, and the Book of Mormon has already given them Matthias's job description.

links.note: 'Therefore there were ordained of Nephi, men unto this ministry … and this as a witness and a testimony before God, and unto the people.' Ordination plus witness is a rare conjunction in the KJV — one verse — and it belongs to the appointment of Matthias, the one apostolic ordination the New Testament narrates. Mark 3:14's 'he ordained twelve' is the alternative and is not preferred, because the Book of Mormon supplies the witness language that Mark's verse lacks and Acts 1:22 has.
links.whyNot: The shared words are 'ordained' and 'witness', both ordinary, and the Book of Mormon's sentence is about baptism rather than about apostleship. The case is that the KJV joins these two words once, and that 7:24 has already put the passage in Acts 1.

pericopes.text: And there were many in the commencement of this year, that were baptized unto repentance; and thus the more part of the year did pass away.

And now it came to pass that according to our record, and we know our record to be true: for behold, it was a just man which did keep the record; for he truly did many miracles in the name of Jesus; and there was not any man which could do a miracle in the name of Jesus, save he were cleansed every whit from his iniquity.

links.text: Jesus saith to him, He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean every whit: and ye are clean, but not all.

provenance.other: “every whit” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Deuteronomy 13:16, 1 Samuel 3:18, John 7:23 and John 13:10 — and only two of them attach it to cleanness. “clean every whit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Of the pair, John 7:23's is a healing ('I have made a man every whit whole') and John 13:10's is a washing, which is the sense 3 Nephi 8:1 needs.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowed idiom turns out to have an exception built into it. John 13:10 is spoken at the supper, over the feet of the disciples, and its second half is 'and ye are clean, but not all' — the evangelist's note that Jesus 'knew who should betray him'. Mormon uses the phrase to certify a record-keeper: no man could do a miracle in the name of Jesus 'save he were cleansed every whit from his iniquity'. The KJV's one occurrence of the phrase is the one place where being clean every whit is asserted of a company and immediately withdrawn from one of them. A chapter that is about to narrate the crucifixion opens by vouching for its witness in the words Jesus used on the night he was betrayed.

links.note: 'There was not any man which could do a miracle in the name of Jesus, save he were cleansed every whit from his iniquity.' The colophon that opens the destruction narrative is doing what a colophon does — certifying the record — and it certifies it with a Johannine idiom. 'Every whit' is not ordinary nineteenth-century English for 'entirely'; it is King James English, and its cleanness sense is confined to two verses of John. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages: the case rests on the rarity of the collocation, not on length.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass, if there was no mistake made by this man in the reckoning of our time, the thirty and third year had passed away,

and the people began to look with great earnestness for the sign which had been given by the prophet Samuel, the Lamanite; yea, for the time that there should be darkness for the space of three days, over the face of the land.
And there began to be great doubtings and disputations among the people, notwithstanding so many signs had been given.
And it came to pass in the thirty and fourth year, in the first month, in the fourth day of the month, there arose a great storm, such an one as never had been known in all the land;

links.text: And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full.

provenance.other: “there arose a great storm” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 8:24 has 'there arose a great tempest in the sea' and Luke 8:23 'there came down a storm of wind'; the exact run 'there arose a great storm' is Mark's alone.
provenance.alternative: Jonah 1:4, 'the LORD sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest', is the other candidate storm and shares no run with the verse.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible has one 'great storm' and it is the squall on Galilee that Jesus stills with 'Peace, be still', after which the disciples ask 'What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?' 3 Nephi 8 answers that question by removing the man from the boat. The storm that in Mark demonstrates his authority over wind and sea is here raised at his death and not stilled for three hours; the calm comes only in 3 Nephi 9, and it comes as his voice. Recovering Mark makes the tempest an argument rather than a catastrophe.

links.note: 'There arose a great storm, such an one as never had been known in all the land.' Helaman 14:23 had prophesied 'great tempests', not a storm; the narration reaches instead for the four-word run that in the KJV belongs to one episode. What follows in 3 Nephi 8:6-7 — tempest, thunder, lightnings — is the Book of Mormon's own vocabulary, so the borrowing is the opening clause only.

pericopes.text: and there was also a great and terrible tempest; and there was terrible thunder, insomuch that it did shake the whole earth as if it was about to divide asunder;
and there was exceeding sharp lightnings, such as never had been known in all the land.

links.text: So there was hail, and fire mingled with the hail, very grievous, such as there was none like it in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.

provenance.other: “such as there was none like” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 9:24 and Exodus 11:6, and both are plague formulae — the seventh plague and the tenth. Revelation 16:18's 'such as was not since men were upon the earth' is the only other superlative of the kind and is worded quite differently.
provenance.significance: This is the frame the whole chapter is built in, and 8:20 confirms it. The KJV's formula for an unprecedented disaster in a named land belongs to the plagues of Egypt; 3 Nephi says it twice in three verses, of a fire that takes a city (8:8, against Exodus 9:24's 'fire mingled with the hail') and of lightnings. Then 8:20 supplies the ninth plague's felt darkness and 8:21 removes the exemption Exodus 10:23 grants Israel. The destruction is narrated as an Egyptian plague sequence visited on a covenant people, which reverses the source's whole point: in Exodus the formula marks what God does to the oppressor while his people sit in the light.

links.note: 'Such an one as never had been known in all the land' (8:5), 'such as never had been known in all the land' (8:7). The doubled superlative bounded by 'in all the land' is the shape of Exodus 9:24 and 11:6, where the bound is 'in all the land of Egypt'. Not a verbal quotation — the Book of Mormon has 'never had been known' where Exodus has 'there was none like it' — and filed as an echo for that reason; what carries it is that the formula is repeated exactly as Exodus repeats it, and that the chapter goes on to take two further plagues from the same run of chapters.
links.whyNot: The shared material is a construction rather than a phrase, and any narrator describing an unprecedented storm may reach for 'such as never had been known'. Taken alone this row would not be worth writing; it is filed because 8:20's Exodus 10:21 borrowing is a KJV singleton and makes the plague frame something the chapter demonstrably has rather than something a reader supplies.

pericopes.text: And the city of Zarahemla did take fire;
and the city of Moroni did sink into the depths of the sea, and the inhabitants thereof were drowned;
and the earth was carried up upon the city of Moronihah, that in the place of the city thereof, there became a great mountain;
and there was a great and terrible destruction in the land southward.

But behold, there was a more great and terrible destruction in the land northward: for behold, the whole face of the land was changed, because of the tempest, and the whirlwinds, and the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the exceeding great quaking of the whole earth;

links.text: And all the people saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking: and when the people saw it, they removed, and stood afar off.

provenance.route: Exodus 20:18 → KJV → Helaman 14:21 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “thunderings and the lightnings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Without the articles the pair is commoner: Revelation has 'thunderings, and lightnings' four times and 'voices, and thunders, and lightnings' once. What is peculiar to Exodus 20:18 is the definite-article series, which is what 3 Nephi 8:12 and 8:17 have and what Helaman 14:21 and 14:26 do not.
provenance.significance: Exodus 20:18 is the theophany at Sinai: the people see the thunderings and the lightnings and stand afar off, and out of that noise comes the law. 3 Nephi 8 runs the same list three times over a landscape being destroyed, and out of the noise, in 3 Nephi 9, comes a voice giving a law — 'the law in me is fulfilled'. The chapter is worth reading as a Sinai in which the mountain is not one mountain but a mountain thrown up over a city (8:10).

links.note: 'The tempest, and the whirlwinds, and the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the exceeding great quaking of the whole earth.' The machine ranked Exodus 20:18 first in this chapter and it is right to; the articled series is a KJV singleton and 3 Nephi has it twice (8:12, 8:17) and again without 'the whirlwinds' at 8:19. Samuel had prophesied 'thunderings and lightnings' bare (Helaman 14:21, 14:26), so the definite articles enter with the narration, not with the prophecy. Moderate because the articles may simply be English: a narrator listing four known phenomena will article them whether or not he has Sinai in view.

pericopes.text: and the highways were broken up, and the level roads were spoiled, and many smooth places became rough,

links.text: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:

provenance.route: Isaiah 40:4 + Luke 3:5 → KJV → 1 Nephi 17:46 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “rough places” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 40:4, where the predicate is 'plain'. “made smooth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 3:5, where the noun is 'ways'. 'Smooth places' — Isaiah's noun with Luke's adjective — appears in no KJV verse at all. It appears in 1 Nephi 17:46.
provenance.alternative: Read as a fresh borrowing from the KJV, mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence at 8:13: Isaiah 40:4 and Luke 3:5 differ at 'exalted/filled' and 'made/brought', which 3 Nephi does not reproduce, and the two forms it does reproduce are one word from each. The verse cannot settle its own mediation against the Bible. It settles decisively against the Book of Mormon.
provenance.significance: 1 Nephi 17:46 argues from God's power over the landscape: 'by his word, he can cause that rough places be made smooth, and smooth places shall be broken up'. The second clause is Nephi's own invention — it reverses Isaiah's promise and has no biblical source — and 3 Nephi 8:13 is where it happens. 'The highways were broken up, and the level roads were spoiled, and many smooth places became rough.' The catalogue's normal finding is that a Book of Mormon verse is worded out of the KJV; this one is worded out of a Book of Mormon verse that was itself worded out of two KJV verses, and the intervening step is visible because the phrase it contributes exists in no Bible. Isaiah's highway prepared for the Lord is unbuilt at his death by the same vocabulary that promised it.

links.note: Helaman 14:24 had prophesied that 'many highways shall be broken up' and Helaman 14:23 that mountains and valleys would change places, which is Isaiah 40:4 read as seismology. 3 Nephi 8:13 fulfils both and adds a third clause Samuel never spoke: 'many smooth places became rough'. That clause is 1 Nephi 17:46's, inverted — Nephi had God making rough places smooth and breaking smooth places up, and here the smoothing runs backwards. The KJV supplies 'rough places' (Isaiah) and 'smooth' (Luke) but never their combination; the combination is the Book of Mormon's own, made in 1 Nephi and cashed here, four hundred years and one authorial voice later.

pericopes.text: and many great and notable cities were sunk, and many were burned, and many were shook till the buildings thereof had fallen to the earth, and the inhabitants thereof were slain, and the places were left desolate;

links.text: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and notable day of the Lord come:

provenance.other: “great and notable” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “notable” occurs in exactly five, of which this is the only one that pairs it with 'great'. Acts 2:20 is Peter's Pentecost citation of Joel 2:31, and 'notable' is where the KJV's Acts departs from the KJV's Joel.
provenance.significance: Ten verses apart, this chapter uses both halves of a King James discrepancy. Joel 2:31 reads 'the great and terrible day of the LORD'; Acts 2:20, quoting it, reads 'the great and notable day of the Lord'. 3 Nephi 8:14 has 'great and notable' and 3 Nephi 8:24-25 has 'great and terrible', and no other English pair of adjectives in the chapter behaves this way. Whatever produced this text had both readings of one verse available and distributed them — the Old Testament form to the mourners' cry, where the day of the LORD is being invoked, and the New Testament form to the cities. That is not a fact a reader can get from either testament alone.

links.note: 'Many great and notable cities were sunk.' Taken by itself the phrase is unremarkable English and would not be worth a row. It is filed because of what stands ten verses later: 'O that we had repented before this great and terrible day' (8:24, 8:25), which mediation-check.py shows decisively to be Joel 2:31's form and not Acts 2:20's. The chapter thereby contains both of the KJV's renderings of one Hebrew phrase, and the machine cannot see the pair because they are eleven verses apart.
links.whyNot: 'Notable' is ordinary English and could reach a description of cities without Acts. The row is a pairing argument, not a verbal one: it depends entirely on 8:24, and a reader who declines the pairing should decline this link and keep the other.

pericopes.text: and there were some cities which remained; but the damage thereof was exceeding great, and there were many in them which were slain;
and there were some which were carried away in the whirlwind; and whither they went, no man knoweth, save they know that they were carried away;

links.text: And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

provenance.other: 'Carried away in the whirlwind' appears in no KJV verse; “in the whirlwind” occurs in exactly one, Nahum 1:3, where it is the LORD's way and not a man's removal. “no man knoweth of his” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 34:6, of Moses' unfound grave.
provenance.significance: There are two men in the King James Bible whose end is a disappearance nobody can locate, and both are the men this book's founding chapters run on. Elijah goes up by a whirlwind and fifty men search three days and do not find him (2 Kings 2:16-17); Moses is buried and 'no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day'. 3 Nephi 8:16 gives an unnumbered crowd of ordinary people both endings at once — the whirlwind and the unknown grave — during three days in which nobody can see. The sign of a prophet's translation has become a way of dying.

links.note: 'There were some which were carried away in the whirlwind; and whither they went, no man knoweth, save they know that they were carried away.' No KJV run is reproduced, which is why this is an echo and not an allusion; the case is the coincidence of two rare narrative facts, removal by whirlwind and an unlocatable end, in a passage whose surrounding chapters have used 2 Kings 2 before (1 Nephi 4:2 draws on 2 Kings 2:8). The three days of 2 Kings 2:17 and the three days of 3 Nephi 8:23 are the same number and, as far as the wording goes, a coincidence.
links.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared. A whirlwind is the obvious agent for people vanishing in a storm, and 'no man knoweth' occurs in exactly six KJV verses, none of them Deuteronomy 34:6's construction. A reader who wants verbal contact before recording a link should decline this one; it is here because the catalogue prefers to say it looked.

pericopes.text: and thus the face of the whole earth became deformed, because of the tempests, and the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the quaking of the earth.

And behold, the rocks were rent in twain; yea, they were broken up upon the face of the whole earth, insomuch that they were found in broken fragments, and in seams, and in cracks, upon all the face of the land.

links.text: And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;

provenance.route: Matthew 27:51 → KJV → Helaman 14:21-22 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “rent in twain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, and in both it is the veil of the temple. “the rocks rent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:51, which is therefore the only verse in the Bible holding both phrases.
provenance.significance: The 1830 reading is the evidence. 3 Nephi 8:18 begins 'And behold, the rocks were rent in twain; yea, they were broken up' — and Helaman 14:22, Samuel's prophecy, reads 'yea, they shall be rent in twain, and shall ever after be found in seams, and in cracks, and in broken fragments'. The narration answers the prophecy clause for clause, 'yea' included, and reverses its order of seams, cracks and fragments to fragments, seams and cracks. The 1920 edition deleted the 'yea', and with it the plainest sign that this sentence is quoting Helaman 14 rather than Matthew 27. What Matthew supplies, at one remove, is the transferred verb: in the KJV the thing rent in twain is a temple curtain, and in the Book of Mormon it is the bedrock of a continent with no temple to tear.

links.note: The verbal case for Matthew 27:51 was made at Helaman 14:21, where three phrases from two consecutive KJV verses arrive together; it is not restated here. What 3 Nephi 8:18 adds is that the fulfilment is worded from the prophecy and not freshly from the gospel — 'in seams, and in cracks' and 'broken fragments' are Helaman 14:22's words, not Matthew's, and Matthew's 'the earth did quake' has already been used at 8:12 and 8:17 in the Book of Mormon's own 'quaking'. This is an across-the-book repeat and gets a full row on that ground (ADJUDICATING §4): a reader of 3 Nephi is meeting the rent rocks for the first time in this hand.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the storm, and the tempest, and the quakings of the earth did cease—for behold, they did last for about the space of three hours; and it was said by some that the time was greater; nevertheless, all these great and terrible things were done in about the space of three hours; and then behold, there was darkness upon the face of the land.

links.text: And it was about the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what was done, came in.

provenance.other: “about the space of three hours” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does the shorter “space of three hours”. Matthew 27:45, which is where the three hours of the crucifixion darkness actually come from, does not contain the phrase: it counts 'from the sixth hour … unto the ninth hour' and never names the interval.
provenance.significance: The chapter needs a three-hour span because the gospels have one, and the gospels do not have the words for it. So the duration comes from Matthew 27:45 by arithmetic and the phrase comes from Acts 5:7 by quotation — and Acts 5:7 is the interval between Ananias's death and Sapphira's, the three hours in which a woman walks in not knowing what has happened. 3 Nephi 8:19 is a verse about people who do not yet know what has happened either. Whether that resonance was intended or not, the borrowing is the kind this catalogue exists to record: a New Testament phrase pulled from a wholly unrelated episode to measure a New Testament event that had no phrase of its own.

links.note: 'They did last for about the space of three hours; and it was said by some that the time was greater; nevertheless, all these great and terrible things were done in about the space of three hours.' The six-word run occurs twice in one verse and in exactly one verse of the Bible. Note what the number has done: Samuel prophesied thunderings and lightnings 'for the space of many hours' (Helaman 14:21, 14:26), and the narration converts 'many' into the synoptic three — assigning to the tempest the span Matthew gives the darkness, while the darkness itself keeps Samuel's three days. The chapter has both of the crucifixion's canonical intervals and has put them on different phenomena.

links.text: He is thy praise, and he is thy God, that hath done for thee these great and terrible things, which thine eyes have seen.

provenance.other: “great and terrible things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “great and terrible” occurs in exactly seven, but the others attach it to a wilderness (Deuteronomy 1:19, 8:15), to God (Nehemiah 1:5, 4:14), to his name (Psalm 99:3) and to the day of the LORD (Joel 2:31). Only Deuteronomy 10:21 has the neuter plural, and only Deuteronomy 10:21 pairs it with 'done'.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 10:21 is a summary of the Exodus: the great and terrible things God did for Israel are the plagues and the sea, and Moses' point is that Israel's eyes saw them done to somebody else. 3 Nephi 8:19 uses the phrase, with its verb, of what has just been done to the Nephites — and the chapter has been narrating an Egyptian plague sequence since 8:5 (Exodus 9:24) and will complete it at 8:20 with the felt darkness of Exodus 10:21. So the summary formula for the plagues arrives attached to the plagues, on the wrong side of them. This is the sharpest instance in the chapter of a borrowing that inverts its source's beneficiary.

links.note: 'All these great and terrible things were done in about the space of three hours.' Five words in sequence from a KJV singleton, with the source's own verb. 'Great and terrible' is a formula this chapter likes — 8:6, 8:11, 8:12, 8:24, 8:25 — but only at 8:19 does it take Deuteronomy 10:21's exact noun and predicate, and the chapter's other uses of the formula are adjectival, of a tempest, a destruction and a day.

links.text: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.

provenance.other: “darkness over all the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 23:44, narrating the same three hours, reads 'there was a darkness over all the earth'; Mark 15:33 reads 'over the whole land'.
provenance.alternative: Luke 23:44. mediation-check.py returns 'And it was about' as a decisive point for Luke, and that result should not be used: the 'about' in 3 Nephi 8:19 belongs to 'about the space of three hours', which is Acts 5:7's idiom, and the tool has matched a generic opening. The real test is land against earth, and the tool cannot see it because it aligns 'land unto' against 'earth until' as one unit and reports neither.
provenance.significance: Every statement about the darkness in this chapter says 'land' — 8:3 'over the face of the land', 8:19 'darkness upon the face of the land', 8:20 'thick darkness upon the face of all the land', 8:22 'upon the face of the land' — while the seismic damage in the same chapter takes 'earth' (8:17, 8:18 'the face of the whole earth'). That distribution follows the King James Bible's own split: Matthew's darkness is over the land, Luke's is over the earth, and 3 Nephi assigns Matthew's noun to the darkness in all four places it mentions it. Samuel's prophecy had not: Helaman 14:27 says darkness 'should cover the face of the whole earth'. The narration corrects the prophecy toward Matthew.

links.note: 'And then behold, there was darkness upon the face of the land.' The verbal contact is short, but the phrase it belongs to is a KJV singleton and the alternative — Luke's 'over all the earth' — is available in the same chapter of the same story, which makes the choice testable. It is tested by distribution rather than by a single verse, and the distribution is four for four. What the chapter does not take from Matthew is the duration: Matthew's darkness lasts three hours and 3 Nephi's lasts three days, the three hours having gone to the tempest (8:19).
links.whyNot: A verse-by-verse mediation test fails here — mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence at 8:20, and its report at 8:19 is a false positive. The argument is cumulative across four verses and one chapter of Helaman, which is weaker than a single decisive word and is stated as such.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there was thick darkness upon the face of all the land, insomuch that the inhabitants thereof which had not fallen, could feel the vapour of darkness;

links.text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.

provenance.other: “darkness which may be felt” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “thick darkness” occurs in exactly nine, of which Exodus 10:22 is the only one that is three days long — 'a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days'. 3 Nephi 8:20 has both the thickness and the feeling in a single sentence, and 8:23 supplies the three days.
provenance.significance: Samuel the Lamanite prophesied three days of darkness and the Helaman adjudication filed Exodus 10:22 for it, noting that the ninth plague is a plague from which Israel is exempt — 'all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings' (Exodus 10:23) — and that Helaman 14:27 states no exemption. 3 Nephi 8 closes that question in the strongest terms available: 8:21 says there could be no light 'at all', not by candle, torch or kindled fire, and 8:22 that neither sun nor moon nor stars were seen. There is no Goshen. And the detail 3 Nephi adds to the prophecy is precisely the one Exodus 10:21 supplies and Exodus 10:22 does not — that the darkness can be felt. The plague has been run without the covenant exemption that was its whole point.

links.note: 'The inhabitants thereof which had not fallen, could feel the vapour of darkness.' Palpable darkness is one of the strangest images in the King James Bible and it exists in exactly one verse. Helaman 14:20, 14:27 promised three days of no light and said nothing about touching it; the narration adds the touch, and adds it from the verse immediately before the one Samuel's prophecy was built on. The 1830 spelling 'vapour' is the KJV's and was Americanised to 'vapor' in 1920, which is the usual pattern (CONVENTIONS §8) and here it removes nothing but orthography — 'vapour of darkness' is not a KJV phrase in any spelling.

pericopes.text: and there could be no light, because of the darkness, neither candles, neither torches; neither could there be fire kindled with their fine and exceeding dry wood, so that there could not be any light at all;

links.text: And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.

provenance.other: “candles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the singular 'candle' is commoner, in about a dozen. Zephaniah 1:15, three verses on, is one of the nine 'thick darkness' verses and belongs to the same oracle: 'a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness and desolation, a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness'.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one plural 'candles' are God's, and he is carrying them through a darkened Jerusalem to find the men who said he would do neither good nor harm. 3 Nephi 8:21 takes the candles away from the people who need them, in a city being punished for the same complacency, three verses before the same prophet's catalogue of a day of darkness and thick darkness. Read that way the verse is Zephaniah's oracle from the inside: the light that cannot be kindled is the light by which the search is made.

links.note: 'There could be no light, because of the darkness, neither candles, neither torches.' The word is a KJV singleton and the setting of the singleton is a punitive darkness over a doomed city, which is exactly 3 Nephi 8's setting. That is the whole case, and it is thin: candles are what a nineteenth-century writer would name first when saying that nothing would light.
links.whyNot: One common noun, in the plural, and no other contact with Zephaniah 1 anywhere in the chapter. 'Neither candles, neither torches' is a natural pair in English and needs no source; the Book of Mormon's sentence is about the physical impossibility of fire, Zephaniah's about a search. Recorded at 'low' because a reader who checks the rarity of 'candles' will find the singleton and should be told the catalogue found it too and did not think it carried weight.

pericopes.text: and there was not any light seen, neither fire, nor glimmer, neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the stars, for so great were the mists of darkness which were upon the face of the land.

links.text: These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.

provenance.other: “mist of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's plural, 'mists of darkness', appears in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The phrase entered this book at 1 Nephi 8:23, in Lehi's dream, where the mist of darkness blinds those on the path to the tree, and 1 Nephi 12:17 glosses it as 'the temptations of the devil, which blindeth the eyes and hardeneth the hearts of the children of men'. 3 Nephi 8:22 makes it weather. What was a figure for temptation in the founding vision is here a meteorological fact over a destroyed country, and the same clause that contains it also contains the sun, the moon and the stars — so the dream's image is being used to explain a physical darkness that no astronomy accounts for. 2 Peter's own context is a judgement oracle against false teachers, 'clouds that are carried with a tempest', which the chapter has had since 8:6.

links.note: Across a book boundary from its earlier adjudications, so the row is written rather than excluded (ADJUDICATING §4): a reader of 3 Nephi meets the phrase here in Mormon's hand and should be shown its source. The argument for 2 Peter 2:17 was made at 1 Nephi 8:23 and is not restated. What is new in 3 Nephi is the pluralisation and the literalisation — 'so great were the mists of darkness which were upon the face of the land' — and the fact that the phrase now sits inside the KJV's other darkness vocabulary rather than inside a vision.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that it did last for the space of three days, that there was no light seen; and there was great mourning, and howling, and weeping among all the people continually; yea, great were the groanings of the people, because of the darkness and the great destruction which had come upon them.

links.text: And the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day, saith the Lord GOD: there shall be many dead bodies in every place; they shall cast them forth with silence.

provenance.other: “howlings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The singular 'howling' is commoner — Isaiah 15:8, Jeremiah 25:36, Zechariah 11:3 and two others — but 3 Nephi 8:25 has the plural, 'thus were the howlings of the people great and terrible', which is Amos's form.
provenance.significance: Amos 8 is the oracle a reader of a crucifixion-darkness narrative most needs, and it stands behind more of this chapter than one word. Amos 8:3 turns the songs of the temple into howlings and fills every place with dead bodies; Amos 8:9-10 is the KJV's clearest promise of a darkness at midday — 'I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day' — and immediately adds 'I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation … and I will make it as the mourning of an only son'. 3 Nephi 8:23-25 has the darkness, the mourning, the howlings, and mourners crying 'in one place' and 'in another place' as Amos has dead bodies 'in every place'. The mourning of an only son is what the chapter is nominally about.

links.note: 'There was great mourning, and howling, and weeping among all the people continually.' The verse's own contact with Amos 8:3 is one word, but it is a KJV singleton and the chapter uses it twice, taking the plural at 8:25. What raises this above a lexical coincidence is Amos 8:9-10, whose sequence — sun darkened out of season, then mourning and lamentation over a land — is 3 Nephi 8:22-25's sequence. Moderate rather than high because no run of two words is shared with any verse of Amos 8; the case is one rare word plus a matched order of events.

pericopes.text: And in one place they were heard to cry, saying: O that we had repented before this great and terrible day, and then would our brethren have been spared, and they would not have been burned in that great city Zarahemla.

links.text: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD come.

provenance.other: “great and terrible day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts 2:20 quotes Joel 2:31 at Pentecost and renders the same phrase 'the great and notable day of the Lord'; Malachi 4:5 has the third English form, 'the great and dreadful day of the LORD'.
provenance.alternative: Acts 2:20, excluded by the mediation test. mediation-check.py finds one decisive divergence between the two candidates and the Book of Mormon has Joel's side of it: 'terrible', not 'notable', on a backbone of five further shared words (sun, turned, darkness, moon, blood).
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's clearest mediation result and it runs against the direction of the chapter. Everything else here has been mediated — the rocks through Helaman 14, the smooth places through 1 Nephi 17, the darkness through Matthew rather than Luke — and the mourners' cry goes straight to the Old Testament, past the New Testament sermon that quotes it. The recovery is worth having: Joel 2:31 is the verse whose first half reads 'the sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood', and two verses earlier 3 Nephi 8:22 has said that neither the sun nor the moon nor the stars could be seen. The mourners cry about the great and terrible day out of the one KJV verse that had already told them what the sky would look like on it. Peter, preaching the same verse fifty days after the events this chapter narrates, said 'notable'; the Nephites say 'terrible', and the chapter had already spent Acts's word on its cities at 8:14.

links.note: 'O that we had repented before this great and terrible day.' Four words from a KJV singleton, spoken twice (8:24, 8:25), in a passage that has just described the sun and moon going dark. The chapter's other five uses of 'great and terrible' are adjectival — a tempest, two destructions, a set of things done, the howlings — and only here does it modify 'day', which is what makes Joel and not the general formula the source.

pericopes.text: And in another place they were heard to cry and mourn, saying: O that we had repented before this great and terrible day, and had not killed and stoned the prophets, and cast them out; then would our mothers, and our fair daughters, and our children have been spared, and not have been buried up in that great city Moronihah; and thus were the howlings of the people great and terrible.

links.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

provenance.route: Matthew 23:37 → KJV → Helaman 13:33 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “killest the prophets” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34, and both continue 'and stonest them'. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between them at this verse: the two differ at 'thou that/which', 'gathereth/doth gather' and 'chickens/brood', none of which 3 Nephi reproduces.
provenance.alternative: Luke 13:34 cannot be excluded on wording. Helaman 13:25, the Book of Mormon verse that first works this material, was adjudicated to Matthew 23:30 — Matthew's form of the fathers-and-prophets saying, which Luke has at 11:47-48 in different words — so the earlier link in the same chain favours Matthew, and the mediation is recorded as such with that qualification stated.
provenance.significance: The cry is not a fresh borrowing at all: it is the fulfilment of a scripted lament. Samuel the Lamanite told the Nephites what they would say — 'O that I had repented, and had not killed the prophets, and stoned them, and cast them out' (Helaman 13:33) — and 3 Nephi 8:25 reports them saying it, in the plural and with 'before this great and terrible day' spliced in from Joel. So the chain runs Matthew 23:37 → Helaman 13:25 and 13:33 → 3 Nephi 8:25, and each step is visible. What Matthew supplies at the far end is the triad of killing, stoning and the mothers and children: 'how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens'. 3 Nephi's mourners name 'our mothers, and our fair daughters, and our children', which is the gathering that did not happen.

links.note: 'O that we had repented … and had not killed and stoned the prophets, and cast them out; then would our mothers, and our fair daughters, and our children have been spared.' The proximate model is Helaman 13:33 almost word for word, with 'I' made 'we' and Joel's day inserted; Helaman 13 in turn is built on Matthew 23, where 'cast them out' comes from Samuel's own 'ye do cast out the prophets' (Helaman 13:24) rather than from the gospel. The row sits here rather than at Helaman because a reader of 3 Nephi meets the cry as speech, in a new book and a new hand, and because the chapter's other lament (8:24) is Joel's and this one is not.
links.whyNot: The Matthew/Luke choice cannot be settled from this verse and is argued from the earlier link in the same chain, which is an inference and not a test. And because the wording is so close to Helaman 13:33, a reader may reasonably say the only real link here is to Helaman and that the biblical row belongs there.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there was a voice heard among all the inhabitants of the earth upon all the face of this land, crying,

Wo, wo, wo unto this people; wo unto the inhabitants of the whole earth, except they shall repent, for the Devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice, because of the slain of the fair sons and daughters of my people; and it is because of their iniquity and abominations that they are fallen.

links.text: And I beheld, and heard an angel flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice, Woe, woe, woe, to the inhabiters of the earth by reason of the other voices of the trumpet of the three angels, which are yet to sound!

provenance.other: “Woe, woe, woe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The King James Bible doubles a woe twice more (Revelation 18:10, 18:16, both “Alas, alas”) but trebles it only here. “Woe to the inhabiters” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 8:13 and 12:12, and the Book of Mormon's “inhabitants” for “inhabiters” is the one word it does not take over.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 24:6 or Revelation 17:2, if the phrase is read as the generic “inhabitants of the earth”, which occurs in exactly seven KJV verses.
provenance.significance: The two Revelation woes are the only two, and this verse has both of them at once. From 8:13 comes the treble woe cried by a flying angel with a loud voice — which is what 9:1 has just described, a voice heard among all the inhabitants of the earth. From 12:12 comes the rest of the sentence: “Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you.” Revelation gives the rejoicing to heaven and the woe to the earth because the devil has been cast down; 3 Nephi 9:2 keeps the woe and the devil and hands the rejoicing to the devil instead — “the Devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice.” The inversion is the argument. In Revelation the devil's descent is heaven's victory; here it is simply his triumph, and there is nobody left in the heavens to rejoice.

links.note: 'Wo, wo, wo unto this people; wo unto the inhabitants of the whole earth, except they shall repent, for the Devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice.' A threefold woe addressed to the earth's inhabitants, spoken by a voice out of heaven, with the devil named in the following clause: every element is Revelation's, and Revelation uses them in exactly two verses, both of which are here. “rejoice, ye heavens” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the devil is come down” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Revelation 12:12; the Book of Mormon keeps the verbs and reassigns them. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not a quotation — the longest continuous run is three words — but the coincidence of a treble woe, the addressees, and the devil in one sentence is not producible from anywhere else in the King James Bible.

pericopes.text: Behold, that great city Zarahemla have I burned with fire, and the inhabitants thereof.

links.text: Standing afar off for the fear of her torment, saying, Alas, alas that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come.

provenance.other: “that great city” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses. Three are Nineveh (Jonah 1:2, 3:2, 4:11), one is the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:10), and the remaining six are Babylon in Revelation 14:8, 17:18, 18:10, 18:16, 18:19 and 18:21. “utterly burned with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and Revelation 18:8 is the one that burns a city.
provenance.alternative: Jonah 1:2, on the strength of the same demonstrative and a wickedness that comes up before God; see the separate row at 9:7.
provenance.significance: The demonstrative is doing more work than a reader notices. “That great city” is not how the Book of Mormon otherwise names Nephite cities, and in the King James Bible it is overwhelmingly the epithet of one city under one sentence — the Babylon of Revelation 18, burned with fire in verse 8, cast into the sea like a millstone in verse 21, and found with the blood of prophets and of saints in her at verse 24. 3 Nephi 9 destroys its cities in precisely those three ways and gives that reason: Zarahemla burned with fire (9:3), Moroni sunk in the sea (9:4), and every one of them destroyed so that the blood of the prophets and the saints should not come up any more (9:5, 9:7, 9:8, 9:9, 9:11). Recover the context and the chapter is reading the whole Nephite civilization as Babylon — which is what makes the survivors' invitation at 9:13 an offer of exile's end rather than merely of forgiveness.

links.note: 'Behold, that great city Zarahemla have I burned with fire, and the inhabitants thereof.' The formula recurs at 9:4, 9:9 and, without the adjective, throughout 9:6-10; it is adjudicated here at first use. No single Revelation verse is being quoted, and the epithet on its own would not carry a link — ten KJV verses have it. What carries it is that the chapter takes three separate fates from Revelation 18 and distributes them across its cities in Revelation's own order, and closes each with Revelation 18:24's charge. Moderate rather than high because the individual contact is short and the argument is cumulative.
links.whyNot: “That great city” is a natural English intensifier and needs no source; Jonah's Nineveh, a great city spared for its repentance, is arguably the more apt model for a chapter that ends by inviting the survivors to repent. The Revelation reading rests on the cluster, not on this phrase.

pericopes.text: And behold, that great city Moroni have I caused to be sunk in the depths of the sea, and the inhabitants thereof to be drowned.

links.text: But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.

provenance.other: “drowned in the depth of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “depth of the sea” in the singular occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Matthew 18:6. The plural “depths of the sea” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10, Micah 7:19) and the Book of Mormon has the plural, so the number is against the link even though the collocation of drowning with the sea's depth is Matthew's alone.
provenance.alternative: Micah 7:19, 'thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea', which supplies the plural but reverses the sense: Micah drowns sins, 3 Nephi 9:4 drowns a city.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:6 is the only verse in the Bible where drowning in the sea's depth is a sentence rather than an accident, and the crime it punishes is offending one of the little ones who believe. Read the chapter to its end and the same figure returns: 'whoso repenteth and cometh unto me as a little child, him will I receive' (9:22). The chapter opens by drowning a city and closes by receiving a child, which is Matthew 18's own sequence — verse 6 sinks the offender, verse 3 sets a child in the midst. Whether the writer saw that or not, the two ends of 3 Nephi 9 sit at the two ends of one Gospel pericope.

links.note: 'That great city Moroni have I caused to be sunk in the depths of the sea, and the inhabitants thereof to be drowned.' The verb and the location together are a Matthean singleton. The case is limited by one letter: the Book of Mormon has 'depths', which is the Old Testament's plural, and Matthew has 'depth'. Recorded at moderate because the drowning is what is distinctive — the three plural verses do not drown anybody, they bring people up (Psalm 68:22), dry a way through (Isaiah 51:10), and sink sins (Micah 7:19).
links.whyNot: The singular/plural divergence is exactly the kind of one-word test that decides mediation elsewhere in this catalogue, and here it points away from Matthew. A reader who declines the link on that ground is being consistent with the catalogue's own method.

pericopes.text: And behold, that great city Moronihah have I covered with earth, and the inhabitants thereof, to hide their iniquities and their abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.

links.text: And in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints, and of all that were slain upon the earth.

provenance.other: “blood of prophets, and of saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The reverse order, “of saints and prophets”, also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:6. Those two are the whole of the King James Bible's usage: nowhere else are prophets and saints named together as the murdered. The Book of Mormon has Revelation 18:24's order, prophets before saints, at all five occurrences of its formula.
provenance.significance: Revelation 18:24 is the verdict clause of Babylon's fall — the sentence that says what the burning was for. 3 Nephi 9 attaches that clause to every city it destroys and turns it into a purpose: not 'in her was found the blood' but 'that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.' The blood is still crying; the destruction is what stops the crying. That is a harder theology than Revelation's, because Revelation's Babylon is punished for the blood while 3 Nephi's cities are buried to silence it, and the difference is visible only once the source is recovered.

links.note: 'That the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.' The pairing is not a natural English collocation; it is Revelation's, and Revelation's twice only, once in each order. The Book of Mormon takes the order of 18:24 — the Babylon verse, not the third-vial verse — and repeats it verbatim at 9:7, 9:8, 9:9 and 9:11, which is why it is adjudicated here at first use. The 1830 reading at this verse is 'shall not come **up** any more', with 'up' deleted in 1920; the first edition therefore has the blood ascending, which is what Genesis 4:10 and Jonah 1:2 both require and what the modern text obscures.

pericopes.text: And behold, the city of Gilgal have I caused to be sunk, and the inhabitants thereof to be buried up in the depths of the earth;

yea, and the city Onihah, and the inhabitants thereof, and the city of Mocum, and the inhabitants thereof, and the city of Jerusalem, and the inhabitants thereof, and waters have I caused to come up in the stead thereof, to hide their wickedness and abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.

links.text: Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.

provenance.other: “wickedness is come up before me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the shorter “come up before me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Jonah 1:2. The Book of Mormon does not have the preposition: it has wickedness hidden 'from before my face' and blood that comes 'up any more unto me'. The two halves of Jonah's clause are present, split across the sentence.
provenance.significance: Jonah 1:2 is the King James Bible's one verse in which a city's wickedness comes up before God, and it is also one of the ten verses reading 'that great city' — the epithet 3 Nephi 9 uses of Zarahemla, Moroni, Moronihah and Jacobugath. What makes the recovery worth the effort is Jonah's outcome. Nineveh's wickedness comes up before God and Nineveh is not destroyed; it repents at a prophet's preaching and is spared, and Jonah is angry about it. 3 Nephi 9 runs the same premise to the opposite conclusion, destroys the great cities whose wickedness came up, and then — at 9:13 — offers the survivors exactly what Nineveh got. The chapter is Jonah with the sequence reversed: destruction first, the invitation to repent afterward.

links.note: 'And waters have I caused to come up in the stead thereof, to hide their wickedness and abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints shall not come up any more unto me against them.' Two Jonah singletons are in play and neither is reproduced continuously: 'wickedness' + 'come up' + a first-person divine 'me' are all here, distributed across two clauses rather than the one clause Jonah has them in. Recorded as an echo, not an allusion, for that reason.
links.whyNot: Split agreement across a clause boundary is exactly what the machine streams cannot see and also what a reader can manufacture at will; 'wickedness' and 'come up' are both common words and the sentence has other business. If the Revelation 18 reading at 9:3 is right, this verse needs no second source.

pericopes.text: And behold, the city of Gadiandi, and the city of Gadiomnah, and the city of Jacob, and the city of Gimgimno, all these have I caused to be sunk, and made hills and valleys in the places thereof, and the inhabitants thereof have I buried up in the depths of the earth, to hide their wickedness and abominations from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints should not come up any more unto me against them.—

And behold, that great city Jacobugath, which was inhabited by the people of the king of Jacob, have I caused to be burned with fire, because of their sins and their wickedness, which was above all the wickedness of the whole earth, because of their secret murders and combinations: for it was they that did destroy the peace of my people and the government of the land; therefore I did cause them to be burned, to destroy them from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints should not come up unto me any more against them.

And behold, the city of Laman, and the city of Josh, and the city of Gad, and the city of Kishkumen, have I caused to be burned with fire, and the inhabitants thereof, because of their wickedness in casting out the prophets, and stoning them which I did send to declare unto them concerning their wickedness and their abominations;

and because they did cast them all out, that there were none righteous among them, I did send down fire and destroy them, that their wickedness and abominations might be hid from before my face, that the blood of the prophets and the saints which I sent among them, might not cry unto me from the ground against them;

links.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.other: “crieth unto me from the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the shorter “unto me from the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Both are Genesis 4:10; blood cries from the ground nowhere else in the King James Bible.
provenance.significance: The chapter has spent nine verses saying that the blood of the prophets must not 'come up any more unto me', and only at 9:11 does it name the mechanism, in Cain's words. That matters for what the destruction is. Genesis 4:10 is God's interrogation of a murderer — 'What hast thou done?' — and the answer to the crying blood there is not the burial of Abel but the marking and exile of Cain. Here the crying blood is answered by burying the murderers with the evidence, which is the one thing Genesis 4 refuses to do. The borrowing carries its own indictment: a reader who recovers the context finds that the God who would not let Cain's ground stay silent is here silencing it himself.

links.note: 'That the blood of the prophets and the saints which I sent among them, might not cry unto me from the ground against them.' Four continuous words of a King James singleton, with the fifth — 'cry' for 'crieth' — required by the Book of Mormon's subjunctive. Below any quotation threshold and unmistakable all the same: no other verse in the Bible has blood crying to God out of the earth. The 1830 reads 'which I sent', changed to 'whom' in 1920; the first edition's relative pronoun is the King James Bible's own usage for persons and the modern text has corrected it away from the source.

pericopes.text: and many great destructions have I caused to come upon this land, and upon this people, because of their wickedness and their abominations.
O all ye that are spared, because ye were more righteous than they! will ye not now return unto me, and repent of your sins, and be converted, that I may heal you?

links.text: He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 6:10 — 'and convert, and be healed', with no agent named for the healing.
provenance.route: Isaiah 6:10 → John 12:40 + Acts 3:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The Isaiah verse and its New Testament forms diverge at exactly two points that this verse reproduces, and the Book of Mormon has the New Testament's reading at both: 'be converted' against Isaiah's active 'convert', and a first-person divine healer against Isaiah's agentless 'be healed'. Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 read 'should be converted'; John 12:40 reads 'and be converted', without the auxiliary, which is what 3 Nephi 9:13 has. The surrounding syntax comes from a second New Testament verse: “and be converted, that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:19, and the Book of Mormon reproduces that four-word sequence with Acts's 'repent' in front of it.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 13:15 or Acts 28:27 for the healing clause, if the missing 'should' is thought too slight to separate the three; all three carry the same two decisive divergences from Isaiah.
provenance.significance: This is the same verse of John that 1 Nephi 12:17 used, and it is used here to undo what it did there. In 1 Nephi the borrowing was from the front half — the blinded eyes and the hardened heart, John's own words and not Isaiah's — as an explanation of why a people would not see. Here the chapter takes the back half, the clause John's Isaiah leaves as a road not taken, and turns it into an offer: be converted, that I may heal you. John 12:40 is a statement about why healing did not happen; 3 Nephi 9:13 addresses the survivors of a destruction with the same clause in the imperative, and the blindness Isaiah's God imposed is the blindness this voice invites them out of. Acts 3:19 supplies the frame, and its own context is worth recovering too: Peter is preaching to the people who have just killed Jesus, promising them 'times of refreshing' if they will repent and be converted. 3 Nephi 9:13 speaks the same offer to another people who have just rejected the same prophets, three days after the same death.

links.note: 'Will ye not now return unto me, and repent of your sins, and be converted, that I may heal you?' `mediation-check.py` returns two decisive points against Isaiah 6:10 and for the New Testament form. Isaiah's idiom is intransitive — the people 'convert' and 'are healed', with the healer unnamed — while every New Testament rendering makes the conversion passive and puts the healing in God's own mouth. The Book of Mormon has the passive and the first person, in a first-person divine speech where Isaiah's construction would have served just as well. Two New Testament verses are fused: Acts 3:19 gives the imperative and the syntax — “and be converted, that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon has all four words in order, with 'repent' ahead of them as Acts has it — while John 12:40 gives the completion, since Acts 3:19's own 'that' clause is about sins being blotted out and not about healing. Among the three witnesses to the Isaiah clause, John 12:40 alone drops the auxiliary 'should', which the Book of Mormon also drops.

pericopes.text: Yea, verily I say unto you, if ye will come unto me, ye shall have eternal life. Behold, mine arm of mercy is extended towards you, and whosoever will come, him will I receive; and blessed are they which cometh unto me.

Behold I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God. I created the Heavens and the earth, and all things that in them is. I was with the Father from the beginning. I am in the Father, and the Father in me; and in me hath the Father glorified his name.

links.text: Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.

provenance.other: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 14:10 and 14:11, and the two are identical across the whole of the shared span, so the pair cannot be separated on wording. John 10:38 has the same doctrine in the reverse order — 'the Father is in me, and I in him' — and is not the source.
provenance.significance: Ten continuous words of the farewell discourse, and the clause that follows them is where the metalepsis is. 'In me hath the Father glorified his name' has no King James phrase behind it, but it has a King James scene: John 12:28, where Jesus prays 'Father, glorify thy name' and 'there came a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again' — a voice the bystanders took for thunder. 3 Nephi 9 is a voice out of darkness heard by a people who have just survived thunder, and the sentence it speaks about the Father's glorified name is the sentence that voice from heaven spoke. The chapter is not only quoting John; it is occupying the one position in John's Gospel from which the Father is heard to speak.

links.note: 'I am in the Father, and the Father in me; and in me hath the Father glorified his name.' A ten-word continuous run from a two-verse King James pair, and one of the longest verbatim New Testament runs in the Book of Mormon outside its transcribed blocks. Still short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his long quotations. The speaker's situation is what makes the borrowing pointed: in John these words are spoken to Philip in a room, and here they are spoken out of darkness to a continent.

links.text: And when they heard that, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, Lord, thou art God, which hast made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all that in them is:

provenance.route: Exodus 20:11 / Acts 4:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “all that in them is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24, and Acts 4:24 is itself an echo of Exodus 20:11. `mediation-check.py` reports no decisive divergence: the two verses do not differ at any point 3 Nephi 9:15 reproduces, so the mediation cannot be settled from this verse and is recorded as uncertain.
provenance.alternative: Nehemiah 9:6, 'the earth, and all things that are therein', which supplies the Book of Mormon's 'things' but not its grammar; see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: This is a case where the 1830 first edition preserves the borrowing and every later edition erases it. 'All that in them is' is a King James construction that reads as a solecism in modern English — a singular verb governing a plural antecedent, an artefact of the 1611 translators' Hebrew. The 1830 has 'all things that in them **is**'; 1920 changed 'is' to 'are' and produced a sentence that is grammatical, idiomatic, and no longer in the King James Bible at all. CONVENTIONS §8 was written for exactly this: the first edition shows the dependence and the current text hides it.

links.note: 'I created the Heavens and the earth, and all things that in them is.' The King James Bible has this odd concord twice and nowhere else. The Book of Mormon inserts 'things' — probably under the pull of Nehemiah 9:6's 'all things that are therein' — but keeps the singular verb, which only the Exodus/Acts idiom explains. Moderate rather than high because the interpolated word breaks the run, and because the underlying creation formula is common property.

links.text: The same was in the beginning with God.

provenance.other: “in the beginning with God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the Word was with God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are the prologue of John. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'the Father' for 'God' throughout, which is the adjustment a first-person speaker requires.
provenance.significance: Verses 15 to 17 of this chapter run down John's prologue in John's order and nothing else's: creation of all things (John 1:3), pre-existence with God (1:2), coming to his own and being rejected (1:11), and the giving of sonship to those who received him (1:12). That the sequence holds across three consecutive Book of Mormon verses is stronger evidence than any one of the four contacts, and it is the reason this row sits at high on a phrase that is only four words long.

links.note: 'I was with the Father from the beginning.' The prologue's second verse in the first person, with 'the Father' for 'God'. Taken alone it would be an echo at best; taken as the second step of a four-step walk through John 1:1-12 that continues into 9:16 and 9:17, it is part of an extended borrowing and is graded accordingly.

pericopes.text: I came unto my own, and my own received me not. And the scriptures, concerning my coming, are fulfilled.

links.text: He came unto his own, and his own received him not.

provenance.other: “his own received him not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The whole of John 1:11 is nine words long and 3 Nephi 9:16 reproduces all nine, changed only from the third person to the first.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon splits this verse across thirty-four years and two speakers. At 3 Nephi 1:14, on the eve of the birth, the voice says only the first half — 'Behold, I come unto my own' — and stops before the rejection. Here, after the crucifixion and the destruction, the same voice finishes the sentence: 'and my own received me not.' The half-quotation at 1:14 is not an abbreviation; it is a sentence held open for three decades, and the reader who knows John's verse knows from 1:14 how it must end.

links.note: 'I came unto my own, and my own received me not.' John 1:11 entire, in the first person. The argument for the first-person adaptation was made at 3 Nephi 1:14, where the opening clause appears alone; what is new here is the second clause, which the earlier verse deliberately withheld. This is the completion of a quotation rather than the recurrence of a formula, so it is written as a full link under ADJUDICATING §4.

pericopes.text: And as many as have received me, to them have I given to become the Sons of God; and even so will I to as many as shall believe on my name: for behold, by me redemption cometh, and in me is the law of Moses fulfilled.

links.text: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:

provenance.other: “become the sons of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “believe on his name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are John 1:12, which is the only verse in the King James Bible joining reception of Christ, sonship, and belief in the name.
provenance.significance: The one substantive change is a deletion, and it changes the doctrine. John gives the received 'power to become the sons of God' — ἐξουσία, a warrant or entitlement, something short of the thing itself. 3 Nephi 9:17 removes the word: 'to them have I given to become the Sons of God.' What John holds at one remove the Book of Mormon grants outright, and the removal is precise enough to be a reading of John rather than a slip. The 1830's capitalized 'Sons of God' makes the same point typographically.

links.note: 'And as many as have received me, to them have I given to become the Sons of God; and even so will I to as many as shall believe on my name.' John 1:12 in the first person, following John 1:11 in 9:16 as John's own order requires, with the two King James singletons intact and 'power' dropped. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold — the longest continuous run is six words — and a quotation on any other reckoning.

pericopes.text: I am the light and the life of the world. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.

links.text: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.

provenance.other: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 21:6 and 22:13, and “the beginning and the end” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, the same two. Revelation 1:8 is excluded by a single syllable: it reads 'the beginning and the ending'. “Alpha and Omega” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all in Revelation.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 1:8, which is the best-known of the four and the one a reader is likeliest to name — but its wording is not the Book of Mormon's.
provenance.significance: Ten continuous words, and the choice among Revelation's four self-identifications is settled by one word the Book of Mormon does not have. That matters beyond bookkeeping: Revelation 1:8 is spoken 'saith the Lord' by a voice describing itself in the third person to a seer, while 21:6 and 22:13 are spoken by Christ in his own person at the end of the book, one of them ('It is done') immediately after the new heaven and the new earth. 3 Nephi 9 speaks after a destruction that has remade the face of a land, and it takes the formula from the two places in Revelation where a world has just ended.

links.note: 'I am the light and the life of the world. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.' Ten words of Revelation continuously and exactly, in a first-person divine speech, as in the source. This is the strongest single verbal contact in the chapter and one of the cleanest anywhere in 3 Nephi; the only thing standing between it and Skousen's threshold is that his count needs sixteen.

links.text: Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.

provenance.other: “the light of the world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 5:14, John 8:12 and John 9:5 — of which Matthew's is addressed to the disciples and only John's two are self-predications. “the life of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:51. The Book of Mormon's 'the light and the life of the world' fuses two Johannine titles that the Gospel never joins.
provenance.significance: The compound is not in the Bible, and recovering its halves shows why it belongs here rather than anywhere else. John 8:12 promises that whoever follows the light of the world 'shall not walk in darkness' — and this speech is delivered into three days of a darkness so thick it could not be lighted (3 Nephi 8:20-23). John 6:51 makes Christ the life of the world by the giving of his flesh, which is the death this chapter has just described the sun going out over. The chapter fuses the two titles at precisely the moment when both are literally at issue: the light speaks in the dark, and the life speaks from the far side of its own death.

links.note: 'I am the light and the life of the world.' Neither half is a quotation and the compound is the Book of Mormon's own, but both halves are Johannine self-predications and one of them is a King James singleton. Graded high on the strength of the setting rather than the run length: a formula joining light and life to the world, spoken out of a three-day darkness by one who has just died, is not reaching past John for its vocabulary.

pericopes.text: And ye shall offer up unto me no more the shedding of blood; yea, your sacrifices and your burnt offerings shall be done away, for I will accept none of your sacrifices and your burnt offerings;

links.text: And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.

provenance.other: “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The King James Bible has 'shed blood' and 'bloodshed' constantly; the nominalized 'shedding of blood' it uses once, in the verse that makes it the condition of remission.
provenance.significance: This is the sharpest metalepsis in the chapter. The single King James verse containing the phrase 3 Nephi 9:19 abolishes is the verse that says the thing being abolished is indispensable: 'without shedding of blood is no remission.' The abolition is therefore not a repudiation of Hebrews but its conclusion — the sacrifices end because the one shedding of blood that Hebrews 9 is arguing toward has now happened, three days earlier, and the chapter has just described the sky going dark over it. Hebrews 10:9 supplies the mechanism in the same first person the Book of Mormon uses: 'He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second.' 3 Nephi 9:19-20 takes away the first in verse 19 and establishes the second in verse 20.

links.note: 'And ye shall offer up unto me no more the shedding of blood; yea, your sacrifices and your burnt offerings shall be done away.' Three words, and they are a King James singleton belonging to the one New Testament argument this sentence is executing. The Old Testament has plenty of verses rejecting sacrifice — Psalm 51:16, Isaiah 1:11, Jeremiah 6:20, Amos 5:22 — but every one of them rejects sacrifice as insincere, and none of them abolishes it; Hebrews 9-10 is the only place in the Bible where the whole system is ended by a single blood-shedding, which is what 3 Nephi 9:19 announces.

pericopes.text: and ye shall offer for a sacrifice unto me a broken heart and a contrite spirit.
