And whoso cometh unto me with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, him will I baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost, even as the Lamanites, because of their faith in me, at the time of their conversion, were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and they knew it not.

links.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

provenance.other: “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “contrite spirit” occurs in exactly two, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2. Psalm 34:18 is therefore the only verse in the King James Bible containing both, and it contains them in the Book of Mormon's order. Psalm 51:17, which readers reflexively name here, has the nouns crossed: 'a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart'.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 51:17, on the strength of its subject — it is the Bible's classic statement that God prefers a contrite heart to sacrifice, which is the argument 9:19-20 is making. But its wording is not this wording; see the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: Getting the psalm right changes what the verse promises. Psalm 51 offers the broken heart as what God will not despise — a negative, a plea from a penitent that his offering not be rejected. Psalm 34:18 offers it as the condition on which 'the LORD is nigh' and 'saveth', which is exactly what 3 Nephi 9:20 goes on to give: whoever brings it is baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost. The Book of Mormon's sacrifice is not accepted grudgingly in place of a bullock; it is the thing that brings God near, and that is Psalm 34's claim and not Psalm 51's.

links.note: 'Ye shall offer for a sacrifice unto me a broken heart and a contrite spirit.' Two rare King James collocations that meet in one verse and in this order, and a distribution that decides between the two psalms a reader would propose. The catalogue has taken the same pair to Psalm 34:18 at 2 Nephi 2:7, 2 Nephi 4:32 and Jacob 2:10; this is its first appearance in 3 Nephi and its first appearance in a divine first-person speech, where the sacrificial framing of 9:19 makes the Psalm 51 alternative genuinely tempting and the wording still refuses it.

links.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.route: Matthew 3:11 / Luke 3:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “with the Holy Ghost, and with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16 — the Baptist's saying in its two fuller forms; Mark 1:8 and John 1:33 omit the fire. Both KJV verses put the Holy Ghost first and the fire second, and 3 Nephi 9:20 reverses them, twice in one verse: 'baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost'.
provenance.significance: The inversion is consistent and it is doing work. In the Gospels the fire is the second, ominous term — the next verse in both Matthew and Luke burns the chaff 'with unquenchable fire', so the Baptist's fire is judgement appended to blessing. 3 Nephi 9:20 puts the fire first, in a chapter that has just burned four cities with fire and buried the rest, and thereby claims the same element for mercy. The Lamanites who 'were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and they knew it not' are the proof offered: fire that arrives unnoticed and saves, in a chapter where fire has been arriving very noticeably and destroying.

links.note: 'Him will I baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost, even as the Lamanites … were baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and they knew it not.' The Baptist's promise, with the two elements transposed. The transposition is not an error to be explained away — it is repeated within the verse, and it is the Book of Mormon's standing order for the phrase — but it does mean the run is not continuous with either Gospel, which is why this is an allusion rather than a quotation despite the vocabulary being complete.

pericopes.text: Behold, I have come unto the world to bring redemption unto the world, to save the world from sin;

links.text: And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.

provenance.other: “to save the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:47. The nearest competitor is 1 Timothy 1:15, where “the world to save” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners' — which supplies the Book of Mormon's 'come unto the world' but not its object.
provenance.significance: John 12:47 disclaims judgement, and this chapter has just executed one. The voice that has spent eighteen verses itemizing the cities it burned, sank and buried says, in the nineteenth, that it came not to judge but to save the world — using the one King James phrase for it, and using it eight verses after quoting John 12:40 at 9:13. The chapter is working in a single stretch of John's twelfth chapter, and the part of it it takes is the part that denies doing what the chapter has done.

links.note: 'Behold, I have come unto the world to bring redemption unto the world, to save the world from sin.' A King James singleton, tripled: 'the world' three times in one sentence where John has it twice. The link is moderate because the sentence is a summary formula the Book of Mormon could reach from several New Testament places at once, and because 'come unto the world' is 1 Timothy's construction rather than John's.
links.whyNot: 'To save the world' is short and the doctrine is the New Testament's common property; a reader who takes 1 Timothy 1:15 as the source, or no single source at all, is not being unreasonable.

pericopes.text: therefore whoso repenteth and cometh unto me as a little child, him will I receive; for of such is the kingdom of God. Behold, for such I have laid down my life, and have taken it up again; therefore repent, and come unto me ye ends of the earth, and be saved.

links.text: But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.

provenance.other: “of such is the kingdom of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 10:14 and Luke 18:16; “as a little child” occurs in exactly two, Mark 10:15 and Luke 18:17. Matthew 19:14 is excluded by one word — it reads 'kingdom of heaven'. Mark and Luke cannot be separated on wording here, and the Book of Mormon has both halves of the pericope, the saying at verse 14 and the condition at verse 15.
provenance.significance: The chapter began by drowning a city in the depths of the sea and ends by receiving whoever comes as a little child. Those are the two ends of Mark's own material: the millstone and the deep for whoever offends a little one, and the kingdom for whoever becomes one. Recovering the source puts the destruction and the invitation in one frame rather than two, and answers the question the chapter otherwise leaves open — on what terms the survivors of a divine destruction are supposed to approach the God who caused it. On a child's terms, which is Mark's answer and not the chapter's own invention.

links.note: 'Whoso repenteth and cometh unto me as a little child, him will I receive; for of such is the kingdom of God.' Eight continuous words of Mark 10:14 with the following verse's 'as a little child' folded in ahead of them. 'Kingdom of God' rather than Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven' rules out Matthew; nothing rules out Luke 18:16-17, which is identical in the shared span, and Mark is named as the source only because the Book of Mormon has the whole two-verse unit that Mark and Luke both carry. Below Skousen's threshold and a quotation on the evidence.

links.text: Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.

provenance.other: “lay down my life” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, John 10:15, 10:17 and 13:37, of which Peter speaks the third. “take it again” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:17 and 10:18. Only John 10:17 has both, and it is the only verse in the Bible where laying down a life and taking it again stand in one clause.
provenance.significance: John 10:17-18 is the good-shepherd claim that no man takes the life from him — that the laying down is voluntary and the taking again is a power he holds. 3 Nephi 9:22 puts that claim in the perfect tense: 'I have laid down my life, and have taken it up again.' John's Jesus says it prospectively to opponents who are about to stone him; here it is said retrospectively, three days after the fact, to survivors who felt the earth shake when it happened. The tense is the whole distance the Book of Mormon has travelled from its source, and it is the only word it changes.

links.note: 'For such I have laid down my life, and have taken it up again.' John 10:17's two clauses in John's order, moved from the future to the perfect and given 'up' — which John does not have, and which the resurrection makes natural. The verbs are rare enough to be decisive: nowhere else in the King James Bible does anyone speak of taking a laid-down life again.

links.text: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.

provenance.other: “and be ye saved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “the ends of the earth” occurs in exactly twenty-eight, but Isaiah 45:22 is the only one in which God addresses them directly in the imperative and offers them salvation. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'come' for Isaiah's 'look', which is Matthew 11:28's verb — 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 45:22's second half is the reason the summons is worth recovering: 'for I am God, and there is none else.' It is the Old Testament's most compressed monotheistic self-declaration, and the invitation is grounded in it — look to me because there is nobody else to look to. 3 Nephi 9 opens with a voice identifying itself ('Behold I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God', 9:15) and closes by issuing Isaiah's summons to the ends of the earth in the first person. The unstated half of the source supplies the warrant the chapter never states: the speaker can call the ends of the earth to himself because he is the one Isaiah 45 says there is none else beside.

links.note: 'Therefore repent, and come unto me ye ends of the earth, and be saved.' A King James singleton and the addressees, in Isaiah's order, with one verb changed. The change is not arbitrary: 'look' becomes 'come', which is the verb of Matthew 11:28 and of this chapter's own repeated 'whosoever will come, him will I receive' (9:14) and 'cometh unto me' (9:20, 9:22). Isaiah supplies the sentence; the Gospels supply the verb that makes the sentence about approach rather than sight.

pericopes.text: And now behold it came to pass that all the people of the land did hear these sayings, and did witness of it. And after these sayings there was silence in the land for the space of many hours;

links.text: And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour.

provenance.other: “there was silence in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “space of half an hour” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same one. “the space of” by itself occurs in sixteen, so the measured interval is ordinary KJV idiom; what is not ordinary is silence being the thing measured. Revelation 8:1 is the only verse in the Bible where a silence is given a duration.
provenance.alternative: ‘Silence in the land’ could be plain English narration, and the Book of Mormon's own destruction sequence (3 Nephi 8) supplies every other element of the scene without help from Revelation.
provenance.significance: Recover Revelation 8:1's context and the borrowing acquires a position in a sequence. The silence at the opening of the seventh seal is an interval between judgments: the seals are finished, the seven trumpets have not yet sounded, and heaven waits. 3 Nephi 10:1-2 puts its silence at the same joint. The three days of destruction are over, the voice has not yet spoken again, and the people stop howling for the space of many hours. In Revelation the silence precedes the trumpet-angels; here it precedes the voice of Christ at 10:3, and then a second, longer silence of the whole book — the ministry itself — begins at chapter 11. The catalogue notes the parallel without claiming the writer worked it out: what is demonstrable is that the one KJV sentence about a timed silence stands behind this one.

links.note: ‘And after these sayings there was silence in the land for the space of many hours … therefore there was silence in all the land for the space of many hours.’ The clause is repeated at 10:2, which is itself a signal that it is being handled as a formula rather than composed twice. Four of its words are Revelation 8:1's in order, and the frame around them — a silence quantified in hours — is Revelation 8:1's and nobody else's in the King James Bible. The differences are the differences of scale a translator of an apocalypse into a chronicle would make: heaven becomes the land, half an hour becomes many hours. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his passages; it is catalogued as an allusion on rarity, not on length.

pericopes.text: for so great was the astonishment of the people that they did cease lamenting and howling for the loss of their kindred which had been slain; therefore there was silence in all the land for the space of many hours.
And it came to pass that there came a voice again unto the people, and all the people did hear, and did witness of it, saying:

O ye people of these great cities which have fallen, which are a descendant of Jacob; yea, which are of the house of Israel; O ye people of the house of Israel, how oft have I gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and have nourished you.

links.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

provenance.other: “hen gathereth her chickens” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “under her wings” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 23:37 and its Lukan parallel at Luke 13:34. Luke's form of the clause is ‘as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings’. The Book of Mormon has ‘gathereth’ and ‘chickens’, which are Matthew's two words and not Luke's two words.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon does not quote the lament once; it conjugates it. Matthew has one verb in one tense — a completed refusal, ‘how often WOULD I have gathered you … and ye would not’. 3 Nephi 10 says it three times in three tenses: ‘how oft HAVE I gathered you … and have nourished you’ (10:4), ‘how oft WOULD I have gathered you … and ye would not’ (10:5, Matthew's own form), ‘how oft WILL I gather you … if ye will repent’ (10:6). The New Testament's closed lament over a city already judged is opened at both ends: backwards into a history of care, forwards into an offer. That is the argument of the chapter, and it is made by inflecting a borrowed sentence.

links.note: ‘How oft have I gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and have nourished you.’ Ten consecutive words of Matthew 23:37, from the only verse in the KJV containing ‘hen gathereth her chickens’. The mediation test is between the two Synoptic forms, not between an Old Testament source and its New Testament citation, and it is decisive on two independent points: the Book of Mormon has Matthew's finite ‘gathereth’ against Luke's periphrastic ‘doth gather’, and Matthew's ‘chickens’ against Luke's ‘brood’. Both are Matthew's. Note what is added and what is dropped: the addressees are no longer ‘O Jerusalem, Jerusalem’ but ‘O ye people of these great cities which have fallen’, and the speaker's opening clause about killing and stoning prophets is withheld — it returns, transposed, at 10:12.

links.text: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me.

provenance.other: “nourished and brought up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. ‘Nourished’ in any form occurs in ten, and Isaiah 1:2 is the only one of the ten in which God is the subject and his own people are the object.
provenance.significance: The added clause supplies what Matthew's lament assumes but never states — the history of care that makes the refusal culpable. In the King James Bible that history has one classic expression, and it is the opening of Isaiah's prophetic lawsuit, addressed to heaven and earth as witnesses against a nation. Bringing Isaiah 1:2 into the hen sentence lets the Book of Mormon say in one breath what Isaiah and Matthew say separately: I fed you, and you would not.

links.note: ‘… and have nourished you.’ Matthew 23:37 has no such clause; the Book of Mormon adds four words to a sentence it is otherwise reproducing exactly, and the addition is the point of interest. The KJV's one verse in which God nourishes his people is Isaiah 1:2, where the nourishing is immediately answered by rebellion — which is the answer 10:5 goes on to give in Matthew's own words, ‘and ye would not’. The verbal contact is a single participle, so this is recorded as an allusion and no higher.
links.whyNot: Only one content word is shared. ‘Nourish’ is a natural verb to reach for once the image is a hen and her chickens, and a writer could arrive at it from the metaphor alone without Isaiah 1:2 in view.

pericopes.text: And again, how oft would I have gathered you, as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings; yea, O ye people of the house of Israel, which have fallen; yea, O ye people of the house of Israel; ye that dwell at Jerusalem, as ye that have fallen; yea, how oft would I have gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens, and ye would not.

links.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

provenance.other: “and ye would not” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Genesis 42:22, Deuteronomy 1:43, Isaiah 30:15, Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34 — and in all five it closes a divine or paternal reproach. On its own it would identify nothing; sitting nine words after ‘hen gathereth her chickens’ it is the last clause of the verse being quoted.
provenance.significance: Verse 5 is the member of the triad in which the borrowing is exact, and it is also the member in which Jerusalem re-enters. Matthew's lament is addressed to a city; the Book of Mormon has readdressed it to the fallen cities of the New World; and here, mid-sentence, the original addressee is folded back in — ‘ye that dwell at Jerusalem, as ye that have fallen’. The two audiences are made one audience by a comparison, and the sentence that judged Jerusalem is thereby made to judge Zarahemla on the same terms.

links.note: ‘How oft would I have gathered you, as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings … and ye would not.’ Adjudicated as a distinct row from 10:4 rather than as a repetition, because this is the verse that carries Matthew's own tense and Matthew's own closing clause, both of which 10:4 replaced. The Book of Mormon says the sentence three times and only once says it as Matthew says it; that once is here. See 10:4 for the mediation test against Luke 13:34, which the Matthaean ‘gathereth’ and ‘chickens’ decide on two independent points.

links.text: But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice, and said unto them, Ye men of Judaea, and all ye that dwell at Jerusalem, be this known unto you, and hearken to my words:

provenance.other: “ye that dwell at Jerusalem” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's usual formulae are ‘the inhabitants of Jerusalem’ (some two dozen verses) and ‘them that dwell in Jerusalem’ (Acts 1:19, Acts 13:27); ‘dwell AT Jerusalem’ with this preposition is Peter's alone.
provenance.significance: This chapter reaches into Acts 2 twice. Peter's Pentecost address opens with ‘all ye that dwell at Jerusalem’ and reaches its prophetic climax at Acts 2:19, ‘blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke’ — which is the verse standing behind 3 Nephi 10:13's catalogue of deaths. A voice from heaven addressing survivors of a darkness and an earthquake, and doing so in the vocabulary of the sermon that interprets exactly such signs as the last days, is a coherent use of one chapter and not two coincidences.

links.note: ‘Ye that dwell at Jerusalem, as ye that have fallen.’ Five words from a KJV singleton, dropped into the middle of the Matthew 23:37 quotation. The interesting thing is the syntax it lands in: Matthew's lament was addressed TO Jerusalem, and here Jerusalem is a third party compared to the addressees rather than the addressee itself. Acts 2:14 is the KJV verse that supplies a way of naming the residents of Jerusalem in the vocative-adjacent ‘ye that’ construction the sentence needs.
links.whyNot: Five words, one of which is a place-name the context requires in any case, and no other contact with Acts 2:14's sentence. A writer needing to say ‘you who live in Jerusalem’ has few English options and this is one of them.

pericopes.text: O ye house of Israel, whom I have spared, how oft will I gather you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, if ye will repent and return unto me with full purpose of heart.

links.text: And I will give them an heart to know me, that I am the LORD: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God: for they shall return unto me with their whole heart.

provenance.other: “return unto me with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it continues ‘their whole heart’. The Book of Mormon reads ‘return unto me with full purpose of heart’. “purpose of heart” also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:23; ‘full purpose of heart’ occurs in none. The Book of Mormon phrase is a splice of the two, keeping Jeremiah's clause and substituting Acts's noun for Jeremiah's ‘whole’.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 24 is the vision of the two baskets of figs, and 24:7 is the promise attached to the good figs — the exiles carried away to Babylon, whom God will bring back and give a heart to know him. 3 Nephi 10:6 is spoken to the survivors of a national catastrophe on precisely that model: a spared remnant, sorted from a destroyed majority, offered a return conditional on their heart. The verse the Book of Mormon reaches for is the KJV's own promise to the sorted-and-spared, and 10:12's account of who was spared is a sorting of good figs from bad in all but the image.

links.note: ‘How oft will I gather you as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, if ye will repent and return unto me with full purpose of heart.’ The hen clause is Matthew 23:37, adjudicated at 10:4-5, and is not re-argued here; what is new in verse 6 is the condition attached to it, and the condition is Jeremiah's. The substitution of ‘full purpose’ for ‘whole heart’ is a genuine improvement on the source's rhythm and is the phrase the Book of Mormon then uses as a formula elsewhere, which is what one would expect of a borrowing that has been absorbed rather than transcribed.
links.whyNot: Four words, and ‘return unto me’ is the standard KJV language of repentance (Joel 2:12, Zechariah 1:3, Malachi 3:7 all have a form of it). The singleton status of “return unto me with” is partly an artifact of the preposition.

pericopes.text: But if not, O house of Israel, the places of your dwellings shall become desolate, until the time of the fulfilling of the covenant to your fathers.

links.text: Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.

provenance.other: “left unto you desolate” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:38 and Luke 13:35, so the Synoptic test that decided 10:4 cannot be run here — the Book of Mormon shares none of the four distinctive words. The wording it does share is Ezekiel's: “your dwellingplaces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 6:6, where the cities in them are laid waste and the high places made desolate. ‘The places of your dwellings’ is that compound noun unpacked.
provenance.significance: The case rests on sequence, and the sequence is the finding. 3 Nephi 10:5 quotes Matthew 23:37; 3 Nephi 10:7 says what Matthew 23:38 says, in the same position and as the same consequence of the same refusal; and 3 Nephi 10:14 quotes Matthew 24:15 verbatim. Three consecutive stations of the Olivet material appear in the Book of Mormon in the source's own order, spread across ten verses. The one substantive departure is doctrinal rather than verbal: Matthew's desolation is announced flatly, and the Book of Mormon's is conditional — ‘But if not’ — and bounded, ‘until the time of the fulfilling of the covenant to your fathers’. The verse takes Matthew's sentence of abandonment and gives it a term.

links.note: ‘But if not, O house of Israel, the places of your dwellings shall become desolate, until the time of the fulfilling of the covenant to your fathers.’ What follows the hen lament in Matthew is the desolation of the house, and what follows it here is the desolation of the dwellings; the position in the argument is identical and the wording is not. The verbal supply comes instead from Ezekiel 6:6, whose ‘dwellingplaces’ is the KJV's one word for the thing being made desolate. This row is filed on the strength of its place in a sequence rather than on shared vocabulary, and it should be read as the middle term between 10:5 and 10:14 rather than as a link that would stand alone.
links.whyNot: Outside the word ‘desolate’ there is no verbal contact with Matthew 23:38 at all, and ‘desolate’ occurs in well over a hundred KJV verses. Withdraw this row if the Matthew 24:15 quotation at 10:14 is ever shown to have reached the chapter independently of Matthew 23, since the sequence argument is the whole of the case.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that after the people had heard these words, behold they began to weep and howl again, be cause of the loss of their kindred and friends.

And it came to pass that thus did the three days pass away. And it was in the morning, and the darkness dispersed from off the face of the land, and the earth did cease to tremble, and the rocks did cease to rend, and the dreadful groanings did cease, and all the tumultuous noises did pass away,

and the earth did cleave together again, that it stood, and the mourning, and the weeping, and the wailing of the people which were spared alive, did cease; and their mourning was turned into joy, and their lamentations into the praise and thanksgiving unto the Lord Jesus Christ, their Redeemer:

links.text: Then shall the virgin rejoice in the dance, both young men and old together: for I will turn their mourning into joy, and will comfort them, and make them rejoice from their sorrow.

provenance.other: “mourning into joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The passive construction the Book of Mormon uses — ‘was turned into joy’ — is John 16:20's, where the subject is ‘your sorrow’; “turned into joy” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 16:20 and Job 41:22. So the nouns are Jeremiah's and the voice of the verb is John's.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 31 is the chapter of the new covenant with the house of Israel — ‘I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel’ (31:31) — and of Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted. Three verses earlier this chapter said ‘until the time of the fulfilling of the covenant to your fathers’ (10:7) and addressed ‘O house of Israel’ (10:6). The mourners whose mourning is turned to joy at 10:10 are therefore being described in the words of the KJV's one promise to turn Israel's mourning to joy, taken from the KJV's principal chapter about the covenant that 10:7 has just named as the term of their desolation. The two verses are three apart in the Book of Mormon and twenty apart in Jeremiah, and they are doing one thing.

links.note: ‘And their mourning was turned into joy, and their lamentations into the praise and thanksgiving unto the Lord Jesus Christ, their Redeemer.’ The reversal formula is Jeremiah 31:13's, with Jeremiah's active promise (‘I will turn’) reported as an accomplished passive, which is how a chronicle records a fulfilled oracle. That the passive is also John 16:20's form is worth recording but is not needed for the case: John has ‘sorrow’ where both Jeremiah and the Book of Mormon have ‘mourning’, which is the word that carries the rarity.

pericopes.text: And thus far were the scriptures fulfilled, which had been spoken by the prophets.—

And it was the more righteous part of the people which were saved, and it was they which received the prophets, and stoned them not; and it was they which had not shed the blood of the saints, which were spared;

links.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

provenance.other: “killest the prophets” occurs in exactly two KJV verses and “stonest them” occurs in exactly two — Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34 in both cases, which is to say the clause exists in the KJV only as the opening of this lament. “them which are sent unto thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is Matthew's form of the relative; Luke has ‘them that are sent unto thee’. Compare also Matthew 10:41, where “receiveth a prophet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, for the positive form of the test.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's best row and it is a case of metalepsis in the strict sense. At 10:4-5 the Book of Mormon quotes the second half of Matthew 23:37 and conspicuously withholds the first half — ‘thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee’ — which in Matthew is the accusation that explains why the gathering failed. Seven verses later the suppressed clause returns, inverted, as the criterion of survival: the spared are ‘they which received the prophets, and stoned them not’. The unstated point of correspondence, in Hays's phrase, is that the whole population has been sorted by the standard Matthew applies to Jerusalem, and that the Book of Mormon has answered Matthew's question — why would ye not? — by exhibiting the minority who would. Nothing in either text says this; the pair of quotations says it.

links.note: ‘And it was they which received the prophets, and stoned them not.’ The clause is built out of Matthew 23:37's opening accusation by negation: Jerusalem stones the prophets sent to her, and these did not. The verbal contact is one verb, but that verb's KJV distribution is confined to this lament and its Lukan double, and this chapter has already quoted the lament twice. Read as an isolated verse the row would be thin; read as the completion of a quotation deliberately truncated at 10:4, it is the strongest thing in the chapter. Note that the criterion also runs backwards through 3 Nephi 9:11, where the destroyed are those who cast out and killed the prophets — the sorting is the same sorting, stated once positively and once negatively.

links.text: For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and thou hast given them blood to drink; for they are worthy.

provenance.other: “blood of saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “blood of the saints” occurs in exactly one; they are Revelation 16:6 and Revelation 17:6 respectively, and the Book of Mormon's ‘shed the blood of the saints’ takes the verb from the first and the article from the second. “shed the blood” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which Revelation 16:6 is the only one where the blood is a martyr's.
provenance.significance: Revelation 16:6 is not a description but a verdict: it is the angel of the waters justifying a bowl of wrath — they shed the blood of saints and prophets, therefore they are given blood to drink, therefore they are worthy. 3 Nephi 10:12 states the same principle from the other side, as the ground on which a minority was NOT destroyed. Putting the two clauses of verse 12 together, the spared are defined by not having done the two things the KJV names as grounds for judgment: not stoning the sent prophets (Matthew 23:37) and not shedding the blood of the saints (Revelation 16:6). The verse is a two-clause citation of the New Testament's criteria for deserving a catastrophe.

links.note: ‘And it was they which had not shed the blood of the saints, which were spared.’ Six words in order from a phrase that exists in the KJV only in Revelation, and only in the two verses that pronounce Babylon guilty. The word ‘saints’ doing this work in a pre-Christian narrative voice is itself worth flagging: the Book of Mormon uses the KJV's specifically apocalyptic vocabulary of martyrdom to grade the dead of a New World earthquake.
links.whyNot: ‘Shed blood’ is ordinary KJV idiom for murder, and a writer describing the killing of holy men might reach ‘shed the blood of the saints’ without Revelation in view. The rarity counts above are what carry the row.

pericopes.text: and they were spared, and were not sunk and buried up in the earth; and they were not drowned in the depths of the sea; and they were not burned by fire, neither were they fallen upon and crushed to death; and they were not carried away in the whirl-wind; neither were they overpowered by the vapor of smoke and of darkness.

links.text: And I will shew wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke:

provenance.mt: Joel 2:30 — ‘blood, and fire, and PILLARS of smoke’.
provenance.other: “vapour of smoke” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:19. “pillars of smoke” occurs in exactly two, Song of Solomon 3:6 and Joel 2:30 — and Joel 2:30 is the verse Acts 2:19 is quoting. The Book of Mormon has Peter's noun, not Joel's, here as at 1 Nephi 22:18. The 1830 spells ‘vapor’ in both places against the KJV's ‘vapour’.
provenance.significance: The mediation is doubly indirect and that is the finding. The wording is Joel's by way of Acts, which the catalogue established at 1 Nephi 22:18; but the proximate model at 3 Nephi 10:13 is not the New Testament, it is Nephi. 1 Nephi 19:11 forecast destruction ‘by tempest, by fire, and by smoke, and vapour of darkness, and by the opening of the earth’, and 3 Nephi 10:13-14 reports it as ‘the vapor of smoke and of darkness … by fire, and by smoke, and by tempests, and by whirlwinds, and by the opening of the earth’ — the same list, in nearly the same order, with the two ‘vapour’ phrases of 1 Nephi 19:11 and 22:18 fused into one. So the route runs Joel → Peter → the KJV → Nephi → Mormon, and 10:14's demand that the reader search the scriptures to see the prophecies fulfilled is, on the text's own terms, a demand to check this list against that one.

links.note: ‘Neither were they overpowered by the vapor of smoke and of darkness.’ Two KJV-derived phrases are fused: Acts 2:19's ‘vapour of smoke’, quoted at 1 Nephi 22:18, and ‘vapour of darkness’, which is 1 Nephi 19:11's own coinage and which 3 Nephi 8:20 has already used at the moment of the darkness itself. The mediation is filed as OT-via-earlier-BoM rather than OT-via-NT because Acts supplies only one of the two halves and because the whole clause sits inside a list that reproduces Nephi's prophecy item by item; the underlying divergence from Joel, however, is the same divergence adjudicated at 1 Nephi 22:18, and the Book of Mormon is on Peter's side of it in both places.

pericopes.text: And now whoso readeth, let him understand; he that hath the scriptures, let him search them, and see and behold if all these deaths and destructions by fire, and by smoke, and by tempests, and by whirlwinds, and by the opening of the earth to receive them, and all these things, is not unto the fulfilling of the prophecies of many of the holy prophets.

links.text: When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place, (whoso readeth, let him understand:)

provenance.other: “whoso readeth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “let him understand” occurs in exactly one — both Matthew 24:15. Mark's parallel is worded differently: “let him that readeth understand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 13:14. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's word order, not Mark's, and the whole of the shared material is Matthew's five words in Matthew's sequence. (The mediation tool also reports two further ‘decisive’ points against Mark; those are artifacts of the verse boundary, since Matthew 24:15 simply ends where Mark 13:14 continues. The parenthesis itself is the real test and it is unambiguous.)
provenance.significance: Matthew's parenthesis is an aside to the reader of the Gospel, and its content is that a prophecy of Daniel about desolation is about to be recognised in an event. The Book of Mormon puts the same aside in the same office at the end of its own account of a desolation, and then makes the reference explicit in the next breath: ‘he that hath the scriptures, let him search them, and see and behold if all these deaths and destructions … is not unto the fulfilling of the prophecies of many of the holy prophets.’ Where Matthew asks the reader to identify one prophecy of Daniel with one abomination, the Book of Mormon asks the reader to identify a whole class of prophecies with a whole catalogue of catastrophes. And it does so with the clause that, in the source, belongs to the Olivet discourse begun by the lament this chapter has quoted three times. 3 Nephi 10 runs Matthew 23:37 (at 10:4-5), Matthew 23:38 (at 10:7) and Matthew 24:15 (at 10:14) in the source's order.

links.note: ‘And now whoso readeth, let him understand.’ Five words verbatim from a KJV singleton, and the Synoptic test is decisive: Matthew has ‘whoso readeth, let him understand’ and Mark has ‘let him that readeth understand’, and the Book of Mormon has Matthew's. This falls below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his passages; it is catalogued as a quotation because a complete clause is reproduced exactly from a verse that is identifiably its source, which is the test CONVENTIONS §2 sets. The borrowing carries a structural claim with it — an aside from narrator to reader, in the second person, breaking a description of ruin — and the Book of Mormon reproduces the function as well as the words.

links.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

provenance.other: “search the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The nearest relative is Acts 17:11's ‘searched the scriptures daily’, of the Bereans; John 5:39 is the only imperative.
provenance.significance: Recover John 5:39 and the next three verses of 3 Nephi 10 turn out to be its second clause. John's imperative is followed immediately by its ground — ‘and they are they which testify of ME’ — and the Book of Mormon's imperative is followed by 10:16, ‘because they testified particular concerning US’, and by 10:17, ‘those things which testifies of US’. The 1830's ‘testifies’ with a plural subject preserves the singular concord of John's ‘testify of me’ more visibly than the 1920 edition's corrected ‘testify’ does. So the chapter takes over both halves of John 5:39 and changes exactly one word in the second half: the scriptures testify not of Christ but of the remnant of the seed of Joseph. That substitution is a considerable claim, and it is made entirely by a pronoun.

links.note: ‘He that hath the scriptures, let him search them.’ The KJV's one ‘search the scriptures’ is John 5:39, and the Book of Mormon has broken it into a relative clause and an object pronoun while keeping both content words. What makes the row more than a two-word match is what follows: verses 15-17 supply John 5:39's own continuation — the scriptures as a body of witness — with the object of the witness changed from the speaker to the audience. Note also the 1830 reading at 10:17, ‘those things which testifies of us’, where the later editions read ‘these things which testify of us’: the first edition keeps the singular verb that John's clause has, and the modern text does not.

pericopes.text: Behold I say unto you yea, many have testified of these things at the coming of Christ, and were slain because they testified of these things;
yea, the prophet Zenos did testify of these things, and also Zenock spake concerning these things, because they testified particular concerning us, which is the remnant of their seed.

Behold our father Jacob also testified concerning a remnant of the seed of Joseph. And behold, are not we a remnant of the seed of Joseph? And those things which testifies of us, are they not written upon the plates of brass which our father Lehi brought out of Jerusalem?

And it came to pass that in the ending of the thirty and fourth year, behold I will shew unto you that the people of Nephi which were spared, and also they which had been called Lamanites, which had been spared, did have great favors shewn unto them, and great blessings poured out upon their heads, insomuch that soon after the ascension of Christ into Heaven, he did truly manifest himself unto them,
shewing his body unto them, and ministering unto them; and an account of his ministry shall be given hereafter. Therefore for this time I make an end of my sayings.

And now it came to pass that there were a great multitude gathered together, of the people of Nephi, round about the temple which was in the land Bountiful; and they were marvelling and wondering one with another, and were shewing one to another the great and marvellous change which had taken place;
and they were also conversing about this Jesus Christ, of which the sign had been given, concerning his death.

And it came to pass that while they were thus conversing one with another, they heard a voice, as if it came out of Heaven; and they cast their eyes round about, for they understood not the voice which they heard; and it was not a harsh voice, neither was it a loud voice; nevertheless, and notwithstanding it being a small voice, it did pierce them that did hear, to the centre, insomuch that there were no part of their frame that it did not cause to quake; yea, it did pierce them to the very soul, and did cause their hearts to burn.—

links.text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.

provenance.other: “still small voice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 19:12, and the Book of Mormon has already used it at 1 Nephi 17:45, where it is adjudicated. 3 Nephi 11:3 does not repeat the phrase; it reproduces the sentence-shape around it.
provenance.alternative: The negations could be read as the narrator's own attempt to describe an unfamiliar sound, owing nothing to Elijah.
provenance.significance: Recover Horeb and the borrowing argues something the verse does not say. At 1 Kings 19:11-12 the LORD is *not* in the wind, *not* in the earthquake, *not* in the fire, and the small voice is what remains when the theophanic machinery has been cleared away — a rebuke to a prophet who wanted fire. 3 Nephi 11 comes immediately after three chapters of exactly that machinery: the tempest, the earthquakes, the fire that burned Zarahemla, the three days of darkness of 3 Nephi 8-10. The chapter that follows the destruction opens by telling the reader that the voice is not loud, and it does so in Elijah's syntax. The catastrophe was not where God was.

links.note: “It was not a harsh voice, neither was it a loud voice; nevertheless, and notwithstanding it being a small voice, it did pierce them.” The words “still small voice” are not here, and that is why the machine streams did not see this. What is here is 1 Kings 19:11-12's construction: a run of negations of loud phenomena, then an adversative, then a small voice — and “small voice” as a description of divine speech has no other model in the KJV. The Book of Mormon had already quoted 1 Kings 19:12 outright at 1 Nephi 17:45 (“he hath spoken unto you in a still small voice”), so the source is demonstrably in the corpus's repertoire; what 3 Nephi 11:3 does is take the frame rather than the phrase.

links.text: And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?

provenance.other: “our heart burn within us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:32. The n-gram stream did propose Luke 24:15 here, but only on the connective “it came to pass that while they”; the real contact is seventeen verses further down the road.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis of a precise kind. In Luke the burning heart is *retrospective*: the two disciples name it only after the breaking of bread, when “their eyes were opened, and they knew him”, and what made it burn was that “he opened to us the scriptures.” 3 Nephi 11 moves the burn to the front. The hearts burn at verse 3, and the crowd still cannot make out a word of what is being said; recognition does not arrive until verse 8, and then only wrongly (“they thought it was an angel”). Luke's readers are told what the sensation meant before they are told what caused it; the Nephites are given the sensation and made to wait five verses for the cause.

links.note: The Emmaus frame is set up before the phrase lands. Two verses earlier the people are “conversing one with another” about “this Jesus Christ, of which the sign had been given, concerning his death” — which is Luke 24:14-15's disciples “talking together of all these things which had happened” as “Jesus himself drew near”, unrecognised. Then the voice comes and “did cause their hearts to burn”, and the only KJV verse in which a heart burns at the presence of the risen Christ is Luke 24:32. Note that the 1830 punctuation closes the verse with a dash, holding the burn open into verse 4.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that again they heard the voice, and they understood it not;

and again the third time they did hear the voice, and did open their ears to hear it; and their eyes were towards the sound thereof; and they did look steadfastly towards Heaven, from whence the sound came;

links.text: And while they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel;

provenance.other: “stedfastly toward heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:10. The 1830 spells it “steadfastly” and modernises “toward” to “towards”, which is why a literal string search misses it; the collocation is Luke's and nobody else's.
provenance.significance: Acts 1:11 is the promise the whole chapter is about to cash: “this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.” 3 Nephi 11:5 puts a crowd in the posture of Acts 1:10 — eyes fixed on the sky — and three verses later a man descends out of heaven; and at 11:12 the narrator explains the crowd's collapse by saying they remembered “that Christ should shew himself unto them after his ascension into Heaven.” The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's one verse of upward staring and supplied the sequel Acts withholds. The men in white apparel tell the apostles to stop looking up. Here the looking up is rewarded.

links.note: “They did look steadfastly towards Heaven, from whence the sound came.” Two rare elements in one clause: the adverb-plus-direction collocation that the KJV uses exactly once, and the direction of gaze that in Acts belongs to the ascension. Both this verse and 11:12 keep the ascension explicitly in view, so the context is not incidental — the chapter is narrating a return, and it borrows the vocabulary of the departure to do it.

pericopes.text: and behold, the third time they did understand the voice which they heard; and it saith unto them,
Behold, my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, in whom I have glorified my name, hear ye him.

links.text: While he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.

provenance.other: “my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Matthew 3:17, Matthew 17:5, Mark 1:11, 2 Peter 1:17). “hear ye him” occurs in exactly two (Matthew 17:5 and John 10:20, where it means the opposite — “he hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?”). Only Matthew 17:5 holds both, and Mark 9:7 and Luke 9:35 read “hear him” without the “ye”.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 3:17, the baptismal voice, supplies the same eleven words and is the more famous verse; it cannot supply the imperative.
provenance.significance: The transfiguration voice, not the baptismal one. In Matthew 17:5 “hear ye him” is spoken over Moses and Elias on the mountain, and its force is that the Law and the Prophets have just been superseded as the party one listens to. 3 Nephi 11 is about to do the same thing to the Nephite record: within a chapter Christ will replace the law of Moses (3 Nephi 12:46-47, 15:4-5) as the standing authority. The Father's introduction is chosen from the one KJV scene in which the sentence already means that.

links.note: Eleven words of Matthew 17:5 in order, then its imperative, with one interpolation. What the Book of Mormon changes is instructive: “This is” becomes “Behold”, appropriate to a voice addressing a crowd rather than three men under a cloud; and “in whom I have glorified my name” is inserted, which is the third heavenly-voice scene of the Gospels, John 12:28 (“Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it”). So the verse compounds two of the KJV's three voices from heaven and drops the baptismal one — which the chapter will pick up separately at 11:35. Running mediation-check.py between Matthew 3:17 and Matthew 17:5 returns no decisive divergence, because the two agree at every point the Book of Mormon reproduces of the shared clause; the evidence here is an inclusion rather than a variant, and “hear ye him” settles it.
bibliography: Frederick 2016 (index: 3 Nephi 11:7 is discussed in proximity to John 1:2-4, 1:11-12, 1:17, 14:10 and 17:1 — co-occurrence in his argument about the Gospel of John, not a proposed source for this verse)

pericopes.text: And it came to pass as they understood, they cast their eyes up again towards Heaven, and behold, they saw a man descending out of Heaven; and he was clothed in a white robe, and he came down and stood in the midst of them, and the eyes of the whole multitude was turned upon him, and they durst not open their mouths, even one to another, and wist not what it meant: for they thought it was an angel that had appeared unto them.

links.text: And as they thus spake, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.

provenance.other: “stood in the midst of them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:36 — the risen Christ's first appearance to the assembled disciples. John 20:19 has the shorter “stood in the midst” in the same scene.
provenance.significance: Luke's next sentence is the point. “But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit” (24:37) — the appearance is met with a category error, and the rest of Luke 24 is spent correcting it by touch (“handle me, and see”). 3 Nephi 11:8 makes the same error with a different term: “they wist not what it meant: for they thought it was an angel that had appeared unto them”, and the correction that follows at 11:14-15 is likewise by touch. The Book of Mormon is not merely borrowing Luke's stage direction; it is borrowing his plot — apparition, misidentification, tactile proof — and running it at the scale of a multitude.

links.note: “He came down and stood in the midst of them.” The clause is the KJV's one description of the risen Christ arriving among his gathered disciples, and it arrives here at exactly the corresponding narrative moment. The 1830 keeps the singular verb of the following clause (“the eyes of the whole multitude was turned upon him”, corrected to “were” in 1920), which is worth noting only because it shows the sentence is the Book of Mormon's own construction around a borrowed clause rather than a transcription.

links.text: And he went out, and followed him; and wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision.

provenance.other: “wist not” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses, too many to identify a source alone; “know of a surety” occurs in exactly two (Genesis 15:13 and Acts 12:11). Acts 12:9 is the only KJV verse joining “wist not” to the misperception of an angel, and Acts 12:11 is the only one joining “know of a surety” to an angel correctly identified.
provenance.alternative: Both phrases are ordinary Jacobean English and the Book of Mormon uses “wist not” elsewhere; the sequence may be coincidence.
provenance.significance: If the borrowing is real it is inverted, which is the interesting part. Peter “wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision”, and comes to himself with “Now I know of a surety, that the Lord hath sent his angel” — a man who mistakes a real deliverance for an apparition. The Nephites make the opposite mistake in the same two phrases: they take a real man for an angel, and are brought to “know of a surety” by handling him. Acts moves from vision to fact; 3 Nephi moves from messenger to person.

links.note: Two rare phrases in Acts 12's own order, seven verses apart in Acts and seven verses apart here. 11:8 has “wist not what it meant: for they thought it was an angel that had appeared unto them”, which is Acts 12:9's “wist not … but thought he saw a vision” with the angel moved from cause to misidentification; 11:15 closes with “did know of a surety, and did bear record”, which is Acts 12:11's phrase. Filed under CONVENTIONS §0a as a link worth putting on the table rather than one I would defend hard, with the whyNot attached.
links.whyNot: Neither phrase is a singleton, the sense is inverted at both points, and nothing else of Acts 12 — Herod, the prison, the iron gate, Rhoda — appears anywhere in the chapter. A reader who declines this is being reasonable; the case rests entirely on the two phrases occurring in the same order in both texts.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he stretched forth his hand, and spake unto the people, saying:
Behold I am Jesus Christ, of which the prophets testified that should come into the world;

links.text: She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.

provenance.other: “should come into the world” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 6:14 (“that prophet that should come into the world”) and John 11:27 (“thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world”). The formula is Johannine and appears nowhere else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: John 11:27 is Martha's confession at the grave of Lazarus, spoken to a man who is about to prove it by raising the dead. 3 Nephi 11:10 turns the confession into a self-identification: the sentence the KJV gives to a mourner meeting the resurrection is here spoken by the risen man to a mourning nation. And the chapter returns the formula to the crowd at 11:15 — “of whom it was written by the prophets that should come” — so the confession is made twice, once by Christ about himself and once by the multitude about him.

links.note: “Behold I am Jesus Christ, of which the prophets testified that should come into the world.” The relative construction is John's and only John's. The 1830 reads “of which” where 1920 reads “of whom”, and 1830's “that should come” where 1920 reads “that shall come” — both changes move the sentence away from the KJV's own relative-pronoun idiom, so the first edition shows the borrowing more plainly than the current text does (CONVENTIONS §8).

pericopes.text: and behold I am the light and the life of the world, and I have drank out of that bitter cup which the Father hath given me, and have glorified the Father in taking upon me the sins of the world, in the which I have suffered the will of the Father in all things, from the beginning.

links.text: Then said Jesus unto Peter, Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?

provenance.other: “the cup which my Father hath given me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:11. “I have glorified thee” occurs in exactly one, John 17:4. The Book of Mormon reads “the Father” where John 18:11 reads “my Father”, which is John 5:36's article (“the works which the Father hath given me”); mediation-check.py run against John 5:36 and John 18:11 returns one decisive point for John 18:11, on “cup”.
provenance.significance: The two verses this sentence is built from stand on either side of the crossing of the brook Cedron. John 17:4 (“I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do”) closes the high-priestly prayer; John 18:11 (“the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?”) is spoken in the garden minutes later, at the arrest. Between them lies John 18:1, the passion's first step. So the risen Christ's summary of his own suffering is assembled out of the last two sentences he speaks in John before it begins — the prayer that says the work is done and the rebuke that says the cup will be drunk — with the drinking, which John never narrates, supplied in the past tense.

links.note: “I have drank out of that bitter cup which the Father hath given me, and have glorified the Father.” Six words of John 18:11 and the substance of John 17:4 in one sentence. Note what is not KJV: “bitter cup” occurs in no KJV verse at all — the Gospels never call the cup bitter — and “the sins of the world” in the plural occurs in none either, against John 1:29's singular singleton “taketh away the sin of the world”. The chapter is working from John's vocabulary and inflecting it, not transcribing it. The 1830 “drank” was corrected to “drunk” in 1920.

links.text: Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.

provenance.route: John 8:12 + John 1:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the light of the world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Matthew 5:14, John 8:12, John 9:5); the two Johannine ones are Jesus's self-predication. The compound “the light and the life” occurs in no KJV verse — it is a fusion, and its warrant is John 1:4, “In him was life; and the life was the light of men.”
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon does here what a reader of John's prologue does: it collapses the two predicates John holds apart. John 8:12 gives “I am the light of the world”; John 11:25 gives “I am the resurrection, and the life”; John 1:4 is the one verse that puts life and light in a single clause and makes one the source of the other. “I am the light and the life of the world” is the prologue's sentence rewritten as an ego eimi saying, which is exactly the move John himself never quite makes.

links.note: Not a quotation — the phrase is a compound the KJV does not contain — but every element is Johannine and the compound has a Johannine warrant. Recorded at moderate because the fusion is the Book of Mormon's own and the individual halves are among the most widely repeated sentences in Christian speech; the argument is the *combination*, not the vocabulary.
links.whyNot: “Light of the world” and “life of the world” are common enough in devotional English by 1830 that neither needs a KJV verse behind it, and the fusion could be independent of John 1:4 entirely.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had spake these words, the whole multitude fell to the earth, for they remembered that it had been prophesied among them that Christ should shew himself unto them after his ascension into Heaven.
And it came to pass that the Lord spake unto them saying:

Arise and come forth unto me, that ye may thrust your hands into my side, and also that ye may feel the prints of the nails in my hands, and in my feet, that ye may know that I am the God of Israel, and the God of the whole earth, and have been slain for the sins of the world.

links.text: Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.

provenance.other: “thrust it into my side” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:27; “the print of the nails” occurs in exactly one, John 20:25. The two are eight words apart in the Book of Mormon's sentence and two verses apart in John. The feet come from neither: John mentions only hands and side, and it is Luke 24:39 that reads “Behold my hands and my feet”.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon fuses the demand with the permission. In John, “the print of the nails” is Thomas's *condition* for believing — a sentence of unbelief, spoken to the other disciples in Jesus's absence — and “thrust it into my side” is Jesus's answer to it a week later, given to one man and immediately rebuked (“be not faithless, but believing”). 3 Nephi 11:14 puts both in Christ's own mouth, unprompted, as an invitation issued to a whole nation before anyone has doubted, and the reason given is not the curing of unbelief but the establishing of identity: “that ye may know that I am the God of Israel.” What John treats as a concession to one disciple's weakness, 3 Nephi treats as the evidentiary basis of a covenant, and 11:15 has the multitude take it up “one by one” — Thomas's private test administered as a public ordinance. Note also that Luke's feet are added, so the wounds catalogued are the full five of Western devotion rather than John's three.

links.note: The chapter's flagship, and the machine streams found none of it — “thrust your hands into my side” and “thrust it into my side” share no contiguous window long enough to score. Two KJV singletons from adjacent verses of one pericope, in the source's own order, with a third Gospel supplying the feet. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation, and catalogued as an allusion for that reason, though the dependence is not seriously deniable: there is no other verse in the Bible from which “the prints of the nails” could come. Note the Book of Mormon's plural “prints”, against John's singular, and the plural “your hands” for John's singular “thy hand” — the invitation has been rescaled from one man to two thousand five hundred.

links.text: For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called.

provenance.other: “God of the whole earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 54:5, where it stands beside “the Holy One of Israel”: “thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called.” The Book of Mormon's pair — “the God of Israel, and the God of the whole earth” — reproduces both halves of that apposition with the second title verbatim.
provenance.significance: Eleven chapters later, in this same sermon and to this same congregation, Christ reads Isaiah 54 aloud in full; 3 Nephi 22:5 comes back as “thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called.” So the title by which he identifies himself at the moment the wounds are shown is drawn from the one chapter of Isaiah he will later quote entire — and Isaiah 54 is the chapter of the forsaken wife regathered, “For a small moment have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I gather thee” (54:7). A people who have just spent three chapters buried in darkness are told, in Isaiah 54's own words, who is standing in front of them, and are then given Isaiah 54 to keep.

links.note: The self-identification at the centre of the chapter is a KJV singleton, and it is not a decorative one: “God of the whole earth” is the universalising title, and it is joined here to the particular one, “God of Israel”, in the order Isaiah 54:5 joins them. The link is filed here, at the wording, rather than at 3 Nephi 22 where the whole chapter is transcribed; 22:5 is recorded in recurrenceRefs so the two can be read together.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the multitude went forth, and thrust their hands into his side, and did feel the prints of the nails in his hands and in his feet; and this they did do, going forth one by one, until they had all gone forth, and did see with their eyes, and did feel with their hands, and did know of a surety, and did bear record, that it was he, of whom it was written by the prophets that should come.
And it came to pass that when they had all gone forth, and had witnessed for themselves, they did cry out with one accord, saying:
Hosanna! Blessed be the name of the Most High God! And they did fall down at the feet of Jesus, and did worship him.

links.text: And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.

provenance.other: “Hosanna” occurs in exactly five KJV verses (Matthew 21:9, 21:15, Mark 11:9, 11:10, John 12:13) and every one of them is the triumphal entry — the word enters English only through that pericope. “Blessed be the name” occurs in exactly three (Job 1:21, Psalm 113:2, Daniel 2:20), none of them with Hosanna; Matthew 21:9 has the variant “Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord”. “At the feet of Jesus” occurs in exactly one, Luke 8:35.
provenance.significance: The acclamation is imported whole from the entry into Jerusalem — the one occasion in the Gospels when a crowd greets Jesus as king — and it is here answered rather than ignored. In Matthew the Hosanna is followed within two verses by the cleansing of the temple and within a week by the crucifixion; the chief priests hear the children shouting it and are “sore displeased” (21:15). 3 Nephi 11:17 has the crowd shout it at the temple in Bountiful with nobody to object, and the worship the Jerusalem crowd could not complete — “they did fall down at the feet of Jesus, and did worship him” — is completed here.
provenance.alternative: 'Blessed be the name of the Most High God' is a standard doxological formula and its nearest KJV wording is Psalm 113:2, not Matthew.

links.note: The evidence is the word Hosanna itself, which has no existence in English scripture outside the triumphal entry, joined to a doxology whose wording is not Matthew's. Recorded as an echo at moderate confidence: the shout is unmistakably the Gospels' and the sentence after it is not. “Most High God” is common in the KJV (eleven verses, from Melchizedek to the Gerasene demoniac) and does nothing to narrow the source.
links.whyNot: Only one word is actually shared with Matthew 21:9. The rest of the verse is built from formulae the KJV distributes widely, and a Hosanna requires no particular verse behind it once the word is in the language.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he spake unto Nephi, (for Nephi was among the multitude,) and he commanded him that he should come forth.
And Nephi arose and went forth, and bowed himself before the Lord, and he did kiss his feet.—

links.text: And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment.

provenance.other: “kissed his feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 7:38 — the woman in the Pharisee's house. The gesture is named again at 7:45 (“hath not ceased to kiss my feet”) and nowhere else in scripture.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is in Luke 7:45, where the kissing of the feet is used against Simon: “Thou gavest me no kiss: but this woman … hath not ceased to kiss my feet.” In Luke the gesture belongs to a sinner, is proportioned to how much she has been forgiven (7:47), and shames the host who omitted it. Here it is Nephi — the chief disciple, the man just called out of the crowd and given authority to baptize — who performs the omitted host's courtesy in the sinner's manner. The one KJV act of kissing Christ's feet is an act of penitence, and the Book of Mormon assigns it to the man about to be ordained.

links.note: Four words, one of them a KJV singleton in this collocation, and the surrounding clause (“bowed himself before the Lord”) is generic. Moderate rather than high because the gesture is natural enough to be invented independently; but the KJV supplies exactly one precedent for it and the chapter is otherwise saturated with Gospel wording, so an independent invention here would be the exception in its own context.

pericopes.text: And the Lord commanded him that he should arise. And he arose and stood before him.
And the Lord said unto him, I give unto you power that ye shall baptize this people, when I am again ascended into heaven.

links.text: And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.

provenance.other: “All power is given unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 28:18, and “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” in exactly one, Matthew 28:19. Matthew 28:18-19 is the KJV's only conferral of baptismal authority by the risen Christ, and 3 Nephi 11:21-25 follows it in order: the power given (28:18 / 11:21), the delegation to others (28:19 / 11:22), the formula (28:19 / 11:25).
provenance.significance: Matthew's commission is given before the ascension, to eleven men, on a mountain in Galilee, and its horizon is “all nations”. 3 Nephi 11:21 reverses the chronology in the same breath as it borrows the words: “I give unto you power that ye shall baptize this people, when I am again ascended into heaven.” The authority is granted after an ascension that has already happened, for use after a second one, and it is bounded to “this people” rather than all nations. The Book of Mormon is not copying the Great Commission so much as arguing that there was a second issue of it, out of Matthew's sequence and outside Matthew's geography.

links.note: “I give unto you power that ye shall baptize this people” is Matthew 28:18's “All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth” turned outward into 28:19's “Go ye therefore … baptizing them”, with the two verses' logic (power, therefore baptize) preserved and their grammar recast as a direct grant. The verbatim material is held back for 11:25, adjudicated separately; what is borrowed here is the sequence.

pericopes.text: And again the Lord called others, and said unto them likewise; and he gave unto them power to baptize. And he saith unto them, On this wise shall ye baptize; and there shall be no disputations among you.

Verily I say unto you, that whoso repenteth of his sins through your words, and desireth to be baptized in my name, on this wise shall ye baptize them: Behold, ye shall go down and stand in the water, and in my name shall ye baptize them.

links.text: And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.

provenance.other: “went down both into the water” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:38, and “come up out of the water” in exactly one, Acts 8:39 (Mark 1:10 has the participial “coming up out of the water”). Acts 8:36-39 is the KJV's only baptism narrated as a descent into water and a return out of it, and it is the only one preceded by a stated condition of belief.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon turns a narrative into a rubric. Acts 8 tells what Philip and the eunuch did once, in a desert, on the eunuch's own initiative (“See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?”); 3 Nephi 11:23-26 converts the same two movements — “ye shall go down and stand in the water”, “come forth again out of the water” — into the standing instruction, with the condition of belief moved from the candidate's request to the officiant's warrant (“whoso repenteth of his sins through your words, and desireth to be baptized in my name”). The one immersion the KJV narrates end to end becomes the shape of every immersion.

links.note: The verbal contact is genuine but distributed: neither singleton is reproduced intact, and the Book of Mormon writes “go down and stand in the water” and “come forth again out of the water” where Acts writes “went down both into” and “come up out of”. What makes the link worth recording is that this is the only KJV passage supplying both halves of the motion in that order, and that the passage's conditional structure (repentance, desire, then the act) is reproduced with it. Acts 2:38 supplies the standing formula 'repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ'.
links.whyNot: No phrase is reproduced exactly, and the down-and-up description of immersion is entailed by the practice rather than by any text.
bibliography: Frederick 2016 (index: 3 Nephi 11:23 is discussed in proximity to Acts 2:38, Acts 8:16 and John 3:18 — co-occurrence in his argument, not a proposed source)

pericopes.text: And now behold, these are the words which ye shall say, calling them by name, saying:
Having authority given me of Jesus Christ, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen.

links.text: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:

provenance.other: “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 28:19. The n-gram stream scores this the highest candidate in the chapter — a fifteen-word run at rarity 6.66 — and it is the one place in the chapter where the machine and the reader agree without argument.
provenance.significance: Matthew's participle becomes a first-person performative. In Matthew the words describe what the eleven are to do (“baptizing them in the name of…”); in 3 Nephi 11:25 they are the words to be said aloud, prefaced by the officiant's warrant (“Having authority given me of Jesus Christ”) and closed with “Amen.” The KJV's only trinitarian baptismal phrase is thereby converted from narrative description into liturgical text — the shortest possible route from a Gospel sentence to a rubric, and one the chapter has spent four verses preparing (11:24, “these are the words which ye shall say, calling them by name”).

links.note: The clause is reproduced entire, including the KJV's doubled “and of”, which no modern version keeps in that form. This is the chapter's one unambiguous quotation on any definition, Skousen's threshold included: fifteen consecutive words from a verse that is the sole KJV occurrence of them.

pericopes.text: And then shall ye immerse them in the water, and come forth again out of the water.

And after this manner shall ye baptize in my name, for behold, verily I say unto you, that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one; and I am in the Father, and the Father in me, and the Father and I are one.

links.text: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.

provenance.route: 1 John 5:7 (Comma Johanneum) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “these three are one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 5:7, and so does “three that bear record”. This is the strongest kjvSpecific claim available anywhere in the corpus: 1 John 5:7's heavenly witnesses are absent from every Greek manuscript before the fourteenth century, absent from the critical editions, and absent from modern English versions, which read simply 'For there are three that bear witness'. A text dependent on this sentence is dependent not merely on the KJV's English but on the KJV's canon.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the chapter's structure follows from it. 1 John 5:7-8 gives two triads: three that bear record in heaven, “the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one”, and immediately three that bear witness in earth, “the Spirit, and the water, and the blood.” 3 Nephi 11 is a chapter about water. The trinitarian formula is stated at 11:27 as the *reason* for the baptismal wording just given (“for behold … the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one”), the threefold bearing of record is spelled out at 11:32, and the “are one” returns at 11:36 — so the Comma's heavenly triad is deployed exactly where its own verse deploys it, adjacent to the water. Whatever one thinks of the Comma's authenticity, the Book of Mormon has read it in its place.

links.note: “The Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one” — the KJV's one sentence asserting that the three are one, with 'the Word' replaced by 'the Son', which is the substitution the Comma's own trinitarian reading requires. The link is filed here at first use; 11:32's threefold bearing of record and 11:36's second “are one” are recorded in recurrenceRefs, and 11:32 carries its own row because it takes a different clause of the same verse.

links.text: Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me: or else believe me for the very works’ sake.

provenance.route: John 14:10-11 + John 10:30 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “I am in the Father, and the Father in me” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 14:10 and 14:11, and nowhere else in scripture. “I and my Father are one” occurs in exactly one, John 10:30. The n-gram stream caught the first (a ten-word run at rarity 2.71) and missed the second, because the Book of Mormon inverts it.
provenance.significance: The inversion is the finding. John 10:30 reads “I and my Father are one”; 3 Nephi 11:27 reads “the Father and I are one”, putting the Father first and dropping the possessive — and it does so immediately after a sentence in which the Father has already been named twice ahead of the Son. In John the sentence is a claim made under hostile questioning, and the Jews take up stones at the next verse. Here it is offered as the doctrinal ground of a baptismal formula, and the reordering quietly removes the offence: the Son is no longer the subject asserting parity but the second term in the Father's sentence.

links.note: Nine consecutive words of John 14:10-11 followed by John 10:30 reordered. Both are among the most-quoted sentences in the New Testament, which is why attestation is scored low rather than high — a link this famous is not evidence of a *reading* of John, only of access to it. What makes it worth a row is what sits around it: the KJV's two Johannine mutual-indwelling verses and its one 'are one' verse are all pulled into a single sentence, and that sentence is doing the work 1 John 5:7 does two clauses earlier.

pericopes.text: And according as I have commanded you, thus shall ye baptize. And there shall be no disputations among you, as there hath hitherto been; neither shall there be disputations among you concerning the points of my doctrine, as there hath hitherto been;

for verily, verily I say unto you, he that hath the spirit of contention, is not of me, but is of the Devil, which is the father of contention, and he stirreth up the hearts of men to contend with anger, one with another.
