links.text: Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.

provenance.route: John 8:44 + 1 John 3:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the father of it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:44 — the devil as father of lies. “Is of the devil” occurs in exactly one, 1 John 3:8. “Stirreth up” occurs in exactly eight, of which four are Proverbs on strife (10:12, 15:18, 28:25, 29:22) and one, Proverbs 15:18, contains both the stirring and the anger: “A wrathful man stirreth up strife.”
provenance.significance: The substitution is the argument. John 8:44 makes the devil the father of *lying* — “when he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it” — and it is said in the middle of the most contentious dispute in the Fourth Gospel, a chapter that ends with stones being taken up. 3 Nephi 11:29 keeps John's genitive construction exactly and changes the noun: the devil is now “the father of contention”, and what he authors is not falsehood but disputation. Read back into John 8, the substitution proposes that the dispute in which Jesus called his opponents the devil's children was itself the devil's work — which is a reading of John 8 the Book of Mormon has made by changing one word.

links.note: Two singletons and a proverb in one sentence: “is not of me, but is of the Devil” (1 John 3:8), “which is the father of contention” (John 8:44's construction with the noun replaced), and “stirreth up the hearts of men to contend with anger” (the Proverbs formula, where anger and stirring up strife are paired four times). The verse is the hinge of the chapter's argument against disputation, and it is assembled entirely from KJV parts. The 1830 “which is the father” was modernised to “who is the father” in 1920, moving away from the KJV's relative.

pericopes.text: Behold, this is not my doctrine, to stir up the hearts of men with anger, one against another; but this is my doctrine, that such things should be done away.
Behold, verily, verily I say unto you, I will declare unto you my doctrine.

And this is my doctrine, and it is the doctrine which the Father hath given unto me; and I bear record of the Father, and the Father beareth record of me, and the Holy Ghost beareth record of the Father and me, and I bear record that the father commandeth all men, every where, to repent and believe in me;

links.text: And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:

provenance.other: “all men every where to repent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 17:30, and the seven-word run is the second-highest-scoring candidate in the chapter. Critically, the 1830 prints it as two words — “all men, every where, to repent” — matching the KJV's own “every where”; the 1920 edition closed it up to “everywhere”, which appears in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Acts 17:30 does not end where the Book of Mormon stops quoting. Paul's sentence continues: “because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead.” The command to universal repentance is grounded, in its own verse, on the resurrection of a particular man — and here it is spoken by that man, standing in front of a crowd that has just handled his wounds. The Areopagus speech's warrant is the assembly's own experience an hour earlier.

links.note: Seven consecutive words of a KJV singleton, and the clearest case in the chapter for CONVENTIONS §8: the 1830's two-word “every where” is the KJV's spelling and 1920's “everywhere” is not, so the first edition preserves a borrowing the current text has quietly effaced. The surrounding clause “and believe in me” is the Book of Mormon's addition; Acts 17:30 stops at repentance.

links.text: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.

provenance.route: 1 John 5:7 (Comma Johanneum) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “three that bear record” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 5:7. The verb form the Book of Mormon uses twice here, “beareth record”, occurs in no KJV verse at all — the KJV inflects it as “bear record” (four verses) or “beareth witness”. So the phrase is borrowed and then conjugated into a form the source never uses.
provenance.significance: 1 John 5:7 asserts that there are three witnesses and that they are one; it does not say what each of them witnesses to. 3 Nephi 11:32 supplies the missing predicates and makes them reciprocal: the Son bears record of the Father, the Father of the Son, the Holy Ghost of both. The Comma's bare arithmetic is turned into a circuit, and the circuit is then used, four verses later at 11:36, to close on the Comma's own conclusion — “for the Father, and I, and the Holy Ghost, are one.” The chapter has read 1 John 5:7 as a sentence with a gap in it and filled the gap.

links.note: A separate row from 11:27 because it takes a different clause of the same verse: 11:27 has the Comma's “these three are one”, 11:32 has its “three that bear record”, and only together do they reproduce 1 John 5:7 whole. CONVENTIONS §4's trap about repeats within a book does not apply, since this is not the same phrase recurring but the second half of one verse arriving five verses after the first.

pericopes.text: and whoso believeth in me, and is baptized, the same shall be saved; and they are they which shall inherit the kingdom of God.

links.text: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.

provenance.other: “believeth and is baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:16, and “shall be damned” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. 3 Nephi 11:33-34 reproduces both halves of Mark's antithesis in Mark's order and adds nothing to its logic. “They are they which” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:39, and “inherit the kingdom of God” in exactly four, all Pauline.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's second dependence on a passage the KJV contains and the modern critical editions do not. Mark 16:16 belongs to the longer ending of Mark, absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and bracketed or footnoted in every modern version; 1 John 5:7, six verses earlier at 3 Nephi 11:27, is the Comma Johanneum. The two doctrinally load-bearing propositions of Christ's own statement of his doctrine — that the Godhead is one, and that belief plus baptism is the condition of salvation — rest on the two most famous textually disputed passages in the King James New Testament. That is a finding about availability in Hays's sense inverted (CONVENTIONS §3a): these sentences were not merely unavailable in 600 BC, they were unavailable to any Greek reader of the first four centuries.

links.note: Mark's sentence, split across two verses and recast in the Book of Mormon's “whoso” idiom: “he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned” becomes “whoso believeth in me, and is baptized, the same shall be saved” (11:33) and “whoso believeth not in me, and is not baptized, shall be damned” (11:34). The addition is “and is not baptized” in the negative limb, which Mark conspicuously omits — Mark damns unbelief alone, 3 Nephi damns unbelief and unbaptism together. Catalogued as a quotation on subtype paraphrase rather than allusion because both of the verse's distinguishing phrases are singletons and the whole propositional structure is carried over. The trailing clause “they are they which shall inherit the kingdom of God” fuses John 5:39's relative construction with Paul's formula; the 1830 “which” was modernised to “who” in 1920, moving away from the KJV.

pericopes.text: And whoso believeth not in me, and is not baptized, shall be damned.—

Verily, verily I say unto you, that this is my doctrine; and I bear record of it from the Father; and whoso believeth in me, believeth in the Father also; and unto him will the Father bear record of me; for he will visit him with fire, and with the Holy Ghost;

links.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.route: Matthew 3:11 or Luke 3:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “with the Holy Ghost, and with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, which are John the Baptist's forecast of the coming one in the two Gospels that record it. mediation-check.py cannot separate them here: its one 'decisive' point is a false positive on the word 'bear', which in 3 Nephi 11:35 belongs to 'bear record' and in Matthew 3:11 to bearing shoes. The Book of Mormon reproduces only the material the two verses share, so the Matthew/Luke question is undecidable at this verse.
provenance.significance: The chapter has now taken both halves of Matthew 3. The Father's voice at 11:7 is the beloved-Son formula that Matthew 3:17 gives at the Jordan (routed through Matthew 17:5, which alone adds 'hear ye him'); the Father's witness at 11:35 is Matthew 3:11's baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost, which in Matthew is John's prediction of what the one coming after him will do. In 3 Nephi neither belongs to a baptism scene at the Jordan: the promise of fire is what the Father does to the person who believes the Son, and the forerunner's forecast has become the Father's own act of attestation.

links.note: “He will visit him with fire, and with the Holy Ghost.” Note the inversion — both KJV verses read “with the Holy Ghost, and with fire”, and the Book of Mormon puts fire first, which is not the order of either source and not the order the Book of Mormon uses elsewhere. Moderate rather than high because the shared phrase is short and the source cannot be narrowed below two verses; the inversion is recorded because it is the kind of departure that shows a writer working from memory rather than from a page.

pericopes.text: and thus will the Father bear record of me; and the Holy Ghost will bear record unto him of the Father and me: for the Father, and I, and the Holy Ghost, are one.
And again I say unto you; ye must repent, and become as a little child, and be baptized in my name, or ye can in nowise receive these things.
And again I say unto you, Ye must repent, and be baptized in my name, and become as a little child, or ye can in nowise inherit the kingdom of God.

links.text: And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.route: Matthew 18:3 + Luke 18:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “become as little children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 18:3; “as a little child” occurs in exactly two, Mark 10:15 and Luke 18:17, of which only Luke reads “shall in no wise enter therein”. mediation-check.py run on Matthew 18:3 against Luke 18:17 returns decisive points in BOTH directions — Matthew's for the verb phrase, Luke's for the singular child and the 'in no wise' — which is the tool's signature for a composite rather than a failure.
provenance.significance: The three synoptic forms of the saying disagree about what the child is for. In Matthew the child is a *conversion*: 'Except ye be converted, and become as little children'. In Mark and Luke the child is a *manner of receiving*: 'whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child'. 3 Nephi 11:37-38 takes Matthew's verb and Mark and Luke's singular noun, and then attaches both to baptism, which none of the three does — 'ye must repent, and become as a little child, and be baptized in my name'. The saying about children becomes a rubric about candidates, and the child that in the Gospels is an image of reception becomes, in a chapter that has just forbidden infant candidates nothing and required repentance of everyone, a description of the baptized adult.

links.note: A clean both-ways mediation result. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's 'become as' with Mark and Luke's 'a little child' (singular, against Matthew's plural 'little children'), Luke's 'in no wise' (1830 'in nowise'), and Paul's 'inherit the kingdom of God' where all three Gospels have 'enter'. Four sources in eighteen words, and no single verse accounts for the sentence. 11:37 gives the same saying with the clauses in a different order ('become as a little child, and be baptized' / 'be baptized … and become as a little child') and is recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than given its own row.

pericopes.text: Verily, verily I say unto you, that this is my doctrine; and whoso buildeth upon this, buildeth upon my rock; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against them.

links.text: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

provenance.other: “gates of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 16:18; “shall not prevail against” occurs in exactly three (Jeremiah 1:19, 15:20, Matthew 16:18). The n-gram stream ranks this the chapter's second candidate, a nine-word run at rarity 4.67.
provenance.significance: Every term of Matthew 16:18 is reassigned. In Matthew the rock is Peter or his confession, the thing built on it is 'my church', and the gates of hell 'shall not prevail against IT' — a singular pronoun with the church as its antecedent. 3 Nephi 11:39 makes the rock Christ's doctrine ('whoso buildeth upon this, buildeth upon my rock'), makes the thing built the individual believer, and reads 'shall not prevail against THEM'. The promise of institutional indefectibility becomes a promise to each person who holds the doctrine, and the church — the only thing Matthew's sentence is about — has disappeared from it.

links.note: Eight of Matthew 16:18's words in order with one pronoun changed, and the source phrase is a KJV singleton. The whole of 11:39-40 is a fusion of the KJV's two rock-building sayings: Matthew 16:18's church on the rock and Matthew 7:24-27's house on rock or sand, which nothing in the Gospels joins. 11:40 carries the second half and is adjudicated separately.
bibliography: Frederick 2016 (index: 3 Nephi 11:30 and 11:39 are discussed in proximity to Matthew 16:18 — co-occurrence in his argument, not a proposed source)

pericopes.text: And whoso shall declare more or less than this, and establish it for my doctrine, the same cometh of evil, and is not built upon my rock, but he buildeth upon a sandy foundation, and the gates of hell standeth open to receive such, when the floods come, and the winds beat upon them.

links.text: And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:

provenance.route: Matthew 7:24-27 + Luke 6:48-49 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sandy foundation” occurs in no KJV verse — it is a fusion of Matthew's 'sand' with Luke 6:49's 'without a foundation'. “The winds blew, and beat” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:25 and 7:27. mediation-check.py run on Matthew 7:26 against Luke 6:49 reports two decisive points for Luke, but both are artefacts of the alignment catching the single word 'foundation' and the single word 'beat'; read whole, the flood and the winds are Matthew's and Luke has neither.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:24-27 is the close of the Sermon on the Mount, and 3 Nephi 12-14 is about to deliver that sermon to this congregation — the parable of the two houses arrives in its own place at 3 Nephi 14:24-27. So the chapter uses the sermon's peroration two chapters before quoting it, and uses it to say something the sermon does not: in Matthew the two builders are distinguished by whether they DO the sayings, and in 3 Nephi 11:40 they are distinguished by whether they 'declare more or less than this' — the doctrinal test replaces the obedience test, and the sandy foundation becomes the fate of anyone who adds to the formula just given.

links.note: Matthew's imagery in Matthew's order with Luke's noun spliced in: 'buildeth upon a sandy foundation' (Matthew's sand, Luke's foundation) and 'when the floods come, and the winds beat upon them' (Matthew 7:27's 'the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house', compressed by a verb). The 1830 reads 'the gates of hell standeth open', corrected to 'stand' in 1920. Recorded at high rather than certain because no clause is reproduced entire — the borrowing is unmistakable but every phrase has been shortened.

pericopes.text: Therefore go forth unto this people, and declare the words which I have spoken, unto the ends of the earth.

And it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words unto Nephi, and to those which had been called, (now the number of them which had been called, and received power and authority to baptize, were twelve,) and behold he stretched forth his hand unto the multitude, and cried unto them saying, Blessed are ye, if ye shall give heed unto the words of these twelve which I have chosen from among you to minister unto you, and to be your servants; and unto them I have given power, that they may baptize you with water; and after that ye are baptized with water, behold I will baptize you with fire and with the Holy Ghost; therefore blessed are ye, if ye shall believe in me, and be baptized, after that ye have seen me, and know that I am.

links.text: Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.

provenance.other: “because thou hast seen me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:29, and its second half “have not seen, and yet have believed” likewise occurs in exactly one. The saying is Thomas's, and it exists nowhere else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: The Sermon at the Temple opens where the Fourth Gospel's resurrection narrative closes, and the setting is the same setting: a risen Christ, a wound-touching multitude (11:14-15), and a beatitude about believing without sight. John 20:29 is spoken to a man who has just been invited to thrust his hand into the side; 3 Nephi 11:14 has issued that invitation to two thousand five hundred people. Recovering John's context turns 12:1-2 from a general encouragement into the Thomas scene enlarged to the size of a nation — and it explains why the blessing has to be split across two verses, because the Nephites, unlike the readers of John, are on the wrong side of it. They have seen.

links.note: “Blessed are ye, if ye shall believe in me, and be baptized, after that ye have seen me, and know that I am.” The first half of John 20:29 — the beatitude qualified by sight — with Thomas's singular made plural and baptism added as the act by which belief is registered. The chapter thus begins on a beatitude that is not one of the eight, and not from Matthew at all: the Sermon on the Mount's opening is delayed two verses while a resurrection saying from John is worked through first. Falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his passages; the case is the rarity of the two clauses and the exactness of the setting.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.1 (John 20:29)

pericopes.text: And again, more blessed are they which shall believe in your words, because that ye shall testify that ye have seen me, and that ye know that I am. Yea, blessed are they which shall believe in your words, and come down into the depths of humility, and be baptized; for they shall be visited with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and shall receive a remission of their sins.

links.text: Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.

provenance.other: “have not seen, and yet have believed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The comparative “more blessed” is not John's; the KJV has “more blessed” once, at Acts 20:35 (“It is more blessed to give than to receive”).
provenance.significance: John 20:29 grades two beliefs and prefers the unseeing one. 3 Nephi 12:1-2 takes the grading seriously enough to make it arithmetic: 12:1 blesses those who believe having seen, 12:2 blesses more those who will believe on the twelve's word. That is a rank the multitude standing in front of Christ cannot win, and the verse says so to their faces. The metalepsis is severe — recover John's context and the audience of the Sermon at the Temple learns, in its second verse, that the readers of the record will be blessed above the eyewitnesses of it.

links.note: “And again, more blessed are they which shall believe in your words, because that ye shall testify that ye have seen me.” The second half of the Thomas beatitude, converted from a statement into a comparative and given a mechanism: testimony by the twelve is how the not-seeing come to believe. Taken with 12:1 the two verses reproduce John 20:29 whole, in John's order, split at the colon. The 1830 “which” for the modern “who” is the KJV relative throughout.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.1 (John 20:29)

pericopes.text: Yea, blessed are the poor in spirit, which cometh unto me, for theirs is the kingdom of Heaven.

links.text: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.other: “poor in spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The phrase has no Old Testament antecedent in the King James English at all.
provenance.significance: The added relative clause is the chapter's programme in five words. Matthew's first beatitude is unconditioned; the Sermon at the Temple attaches a condition — “which cometh unto me” — and that condition governs everything after it, because the same phrase runs through 12:19, 12:20, 12:23 and 12:24, each time replacing a Matthean requirement with a personal one. Matthew's Jesus blesses a class; 3 Nephi's blesses a class defined by its motion toward him.

links.note: “Yea, blessed are the poor in spirit, which cometh unto me, for theirs is the kingdom of Heaven.” Matthew 5:3 verbatim apart from the opening “Yea” and the interpolated relative clause, and the interpolation is the whole interest of the row. 1830 reads “cometh”, a singular verb with a plural antecedent, which 1920 corrected to “come”; the first edition's grammar is the harder reading and it is the running text here.

pericopes.text: And again, blessed are all they that mourn, for they shall be comforted;

links.text: Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.

provenance.other: “they that mourn” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “they shall be comforted” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:4, so the verse's two halves are each a King James singleton.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 61:2 promises “to comfort all that mourn”, and Matthew 5:4 is generally read as its compression. The Sermon at the Temple does not reach past Matthew to Isaiah at any point in the beatitudes: it has Matthew's compression and not Isaiah's clause, which is the pattern the whole chapter will confirm — the route to the Old Testament in 3 Nephi 12 runs through the Gospel, never around it.

links.note: “And again, blessed are all they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Matthew 5:4 with two additions of the same kind, “And again” and “all”, which are the Sermon at the Temple's standing connectives across 12:4-10. Nothing else is altered, and both halves of the KJV verse are phrases that occur nowhere else in the King James Bible.

pericopes.text: and blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.

links.text: Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.

provenance.route: Psalm 37:11 → Matthew 5:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “blessed are the meek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:5. “Shall inherit the earth” occurs in five — Psalm 25:13, Psalm 37:9, 37:11, 37:22 and Matthew 5:5 — and Psalm 37:11 is the one that also has the meek: “But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.”
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's cleanest mediation test and it costs one word. Both candidate sources contain the meek and the inheritance of the earth; only Matthew has the beatitude form, and the Book of Mormon has the beatitude form. Where the psalm makes a promise about a class, the Gospel makes a blessing over them, and 3 Nephi 12:5 blesses. The Old Testament is present here — but at one remove, exactly as Matthew left it.

links.note: “And blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” Matthew 5:5 verbatim, with “And”. Psalm 37:11 is the real source of the sentiment and a reader may reasonably propose it, so the register carries an entry saying why the wording refuses it: the psalm has no beatitude, and the beatitude form is the only King James verse in which the meek are called blessed.

pericopes.text: And blessed are all they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled with the Holy Ghost.

links.text: Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.

provenance.other: “hunger and thirst after righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 “which do hunger” is the King James relative, modernized to “who” in 1920.
provenance.significance: The addition names what the filling is. Matthew leaves “they shall be filled” unqualified and the Gospel never says with what; the Sermon at the Temple supplies “with the Holy Ghost”, which ties the beatitude back to the baptismal promise of 12:1-2 and forward to 19:13, where the disciples are in fact filled. A blessing Matthew leaves open is closed by the book's own narrative, and closed with the element this book has already made its own (3 Nephi 9:20, 11:35).

links.note: “And blessed are all they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled with the Holy Ghost.” Thirteen words of Matthew 5:6 unaltered and then three words that are not in the Gospel. The addition is the kind of variation Hardy's apparatus cross-references throughout this chapter, and it is the strongest sort of evidence for dependence rather than common source: a writer working from a shared oral tradition would not preserve a King James singleton for thirteen words and then finish the sentence differently.

pericopes.text: And blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

links.text: Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.

provenance.other: “blessed are the merciful” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Obtain mercy” occurs in three — Matthew 5:7, Romans 11:31 and Hebrews 4:16 — and only Matthew 5:7 has it as the reward of the merciful.
provenance.significance: One of the four beatitudes the Sermon at the Temple leaves untouched (12:5, 12:7, 12:8, 12:9 — the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers). The set is worth naming because the untouched beatitudes are the ones with no cultic, legal or Judaean content; every beatitude 3 Nephi does alter is altered in the direction of coming to Christ or of removing a Palestinian particular. The silence is as much a pattern as the additions.

links.note: “And blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Matthew 5:7 verbatim but for the connective “And”. Nine of the ten words are the Gospel's in the Gospel's order, and the opening substantive occurs nowhere else in the King James Bible.

pericopes.text: And blessed are all the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

links.text: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.

provenance.other: “pure in heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “shall see God” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:8.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has used this beatitude's substantive before it reaches the Sermon: Jacob 2:10 addresses a congregation as “the pure in heart, and the broken heart”, pairing Matthew 5:8's phrase with Psalm 34:18's. That earlier verse is where the catalogue argues the borrowing; here the phrase returns to its own sentence, in its own beatitude, in the mouth of the speaker to whom Matthew assigns it — which is the rarer event and the reason this row is a full link rather than a cross-reference.

links.note: “And blessed are all the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Matthew 5:8 with “all”. Both halves of the verse are King James singletons, and the Book of Mormon's own earlier use of the first half at Jacob 2:10 makes the phrase demonstrably available to the book as a borrowed unit before this chapter quotes the sentence whole.

pericopes.text: And blessed are all the peace-makers, for they shall he called the children of God.

links.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.

provenance.other: “peacemakers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 edition sets it as two words with a hyphen, “peace-makers”, which is not the King James typography but is the ordinary American compositor's usage of 1830.
provenance.significance: The 1830 typography is worth recording precisely because it is not the KJV's. Where the first edition preserves King James spelling against later correction the fact argues for close copying (CONVENTIONS §8); where, as here, it departs in an accidental of typesetting only, it shows the borrowing running through a compositor's hands rather than a transcriber's eye. The word is still Matthew's and is his alone in the Bible.

links.note: “And blessed are all the peace-makers, for they shall he called the children of God.” Matthew 5:9 with “all”, and with a first-edition misprint — “he called” for “be called” — which 1920 repaired. The substantive occurs in one King James verse only, so the row does not depend on the rest of the clause; “the children of God” by itself occurs in nine.

pericopes.text: And blessed are all they which are persecuted, for my namesake, for theirs is the kingdom of Heaven.

links.text: Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.other: “persecuted for righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:10. The phrase that replaces it, “for my name's sake”, occurs in fifteen.
provenance.significance: The substitution moves the ground of the persecution from an abstraction to a person, and it does so by trading a King James singleton for a King James commonplace — the opposite of what a writer building a pseudo-scriptural cadence would do. It is also the third time in eight verses that this chapter has made the same edit: 12:3 adds “which cometh unto me”, 12:6 fills the blessing with the Holy Ghost, and 12:10 makes the persecution his. Matthew's beatitudes bless qualities; the Sermon at the Temple keeps the qualities and attaches them to Christ.

links.note: “And blessed are all they which are persecuted, for my namesake, for theirs is the kingdom of Heaven.” The frame of Matthew 5:10 exactly, with its distinctive middle term replaced. 1830 sets “namesake” as one word without the apostrophe, corrected in 1920 to “name's sake” — the first edition's form obscures the KJV idiom it is reaching for, and is evidence that the phrase entered the text by ear rather than by copying.

pericopes.text: And blessed are ye when men shall revile you, and persecute, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake,

links.text: Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.

provenance.other: “say all manner of evil against you falsely” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “revile you” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:11.
provenance.significance: The one deletion is grammatical rather than theological: Matthew's “persecute you” loses its object, leaving “revile you, and persecute, and shall say”. That is a slip of the sort that a copying process produces and a composing process does not, and it sits in the middle of a twenty-word stretch otherwise identical to the King James verse. The catalogue records it because the direction of the error — toward ungrammaticality, away from the source — is the kind of evidence 1830 exists to preserve.

links.note: “And blessed are ye when men shall revile you, and persecute, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.” Matthew 5:11 whole, minus one pronoun. The longest continuous run shared with the KJV here is thirteen words, and the verse contains two phrases that occur nowhere else in the King James Bible.

pericopes.text: for ye shall have great joy and be exceeding glad, for great shall be your reward in Heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

links.text: Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

provenance.other: “be exceeding glad” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “so persecuted they the prophets” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:12. “Great is your reward in heaven” likewise occurs in exactly one.
provenance.significance: Three King James singletons in one sentence, and the only change is that Matthew's imperative “Rejoice” becomes a promise, “for ye shall have great joy”. The alteration is small and it converts a command into a prediction, which is what the Sermon at the Temple does at 12:6 as well. Matthew tells the persecuted how to behave; 3 Nephi tells them what will happen to them.

links.note: “For ye shall have great joy and be exceeding glad, for great shall be your reward in Heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.” Fourteen unbroken words of Matthew 5:12 in the second half, and the KJV's “is” becomes “shall be” to agree with the new future frame. Three phrases in the verse occur in one King James verse each, which places dependence beyond argument.

pericopes.text: Verily, verily I say unto you, I give unto you to be the salt of the earth; but if the salt shall lose its savor, wherewith shall the earth be salted? The salt shall be thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.

links.text: Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.

provenance.other: “salt of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “thenceforth good for nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “trodden under foot of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. All three are Matthew 5:13.
provenance.significance: Matthew's “Ye ARE the salt of the earth” is a statement about the hearers; 3 Nephi's “I give unto you to be the salt of the earth” makes it a conferral, and pairs it with the identical construction at 12:14. Read against 12:1, where the twelve have just been given “power and authority to baptize”, the Sermon at the Temple is organizing itself as a series of grants of office rather than descriptions of a condition — and the reason the salt can lose its savour then becomes a matter of a commission forfeited.

links.note: “Verily, verily I say unto you, I give unto you to be the salt of the earth; but if the salt shall lose its savor, wherewith shall the earth be salted?” A seventeen-word run against Matthew 5:13 in the second half of the verse, with three King James singletons in it. Two edits are worth naming: the KJV's “his savour” becomes “its savor”, replacing a King James possessive that modern ears misread; and “wherewith shall IT be salted” becomes “wherewith shall THE EARTH be salted”, supplying the antecedent Matthew leaves to inference.

pericopes.text: Verily, verily I say unto you, I give unto you to be the light of this people. A city that is set on a hill cannot be hid.

links.text: Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.

provenance.other: “set on an hill” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Light of the world” occurs in three — Matthew 5:14, John 8:12 and John 9:5 — and in the two Johannine verses it is Christ's title, not the disciples'.
provenance.significance: Matthew's disciples are the light of the world; the Nephite disciples are the light of this people. The narrowing is the Book of Mormon's most consistent editorial habit in this chapter and it runs alongside the removal of Jerusalem at 12:35: a sermon delivered in the New World is being scrubbed of the Old World's scope. What makes the substitution more than housekeeping is that “light of the world” is elsewhere in the KJV Christ's own self-description, so surrendering it to a smaller sphere leaves the larger title where John puts it.

links.note: “Verily, verily I say unto you, I give unto you to be the light of this people. A city that is set on a hill cannot be hid.” The second sentence is Matthew 5:14 verbatim but for the article, and its central phrase occurs in one King James verse only. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 5:14 at exactly this verse — as it does at every other point in this chapter where the Sermon at the Temple departs from the Gospel, and at none where it does not.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.14 (Matthew 5:14)

pericopes.text: Behold, do men light a candle and put it under a bushel? Nay, but on a candlestick, and it giveth light to all that are in the house;

links.text: Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.

provenance.other: “giveth light unto all that are in the house” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Under a bushel” occurs in three, Matthew 5:15, Mark 4:21 and Luke 11:33, and only Matthew has the candlestick and the house in the same clause.
provenance.significance: The conversion of Matthew's flat “Neither do men light a candle” into a question — “Behold, do men light a candle … ? Nay, but on a candlestick” — is the one homiletic gesture the Sermon at the Temple adds to this paragraph, and it recurs at 12:26 with the senine. In both places a Matthean statement becomes a question put to the audience and answered for them. That is a preacher's alteration and not a translator's, and it is worth having on the record as a class.

links.note: “Behold, do men light a candle and put it under a bushel? Nay, but on a candlestick, and it giveth light to all that are in the house.” Eleven-word runs on either side of the inserted question, and the closing clause occurs in one King James verse only. The KJV's “unto all” becomes “to all” — the sole word of difference in the last nine.

pericopes.text: therefore let your light so shine before this people, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in Heaven.

links.text: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

provenance.other: “let your light so shine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “glorify your Father which is in heaven” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:16.
provenance.significance: “Before men” becomes “before this people”, the same narrowing made two verses earlier at 12:14, and made with the same word. Taken together the two edits are a consistent editorial policy rather than a pair of accidents: wherever Matthew's Sermon addresses the world at large, the Sermon at the Temple addresses the congregation standing at Bountiful. The Father who is glorified is left in heaven and untouched.

links.note: “Therefore let your light so shine before this people, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in Heaven.” A fifteen-word unbroken run and two King James singletons, with one substitution. The 1830 “which is in Heaven” preserves the King James relative that 1920 modernized to “who”.

pericopes.text: Think not that I am come to destroy the law or the prophets. I am not come to destroy but to fulfil:

links.text: Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.

provenance.other: “destroy the law or the prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:17, which is also the only King James verse in which anyone denies an intention to destroy the law.
provenance.significance: This verse and the next are where the Sermon at the Temple's stake is highest, because a risen Christ in the New World says he has not come to destroy the law and then, in the following sentence, says the law is already fulfilled in him — which is not what Matthew's Jesus says. 12:17 is reproduced word for word so that 12:18 can contradict its Gospel sequel. The borrowing is being used to buy the authority to change the doctrine, and the exactness of the borrowing here is what makes the departure at 12:18 legible as a departure.

links.note: “Think not that I am come to destroy the law or the prophets. I am not come to destroy but to fulfil.” A twenty-two word run, effectively the whole of Matthew 5:17 with the punctuation redistributed and the King James comma before “or” removed. This is the longest verbatim agreement in the chapter's first half and it clears Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though the passage is not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: for verily I say unto you, one jot nor one tittle hath not passed away from the law, but in me it hath all been fulfilled.

links.text: For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.

provenance.other: “one jot or one tittle” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Tittle” itself occurs in exactly two, Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17, and “jot” occurs in exactly one.
provenance.significance: Matthew's law stands till heaven and earth pass and till all be fulfilled; 3 Nephi's has already all been fulfilled, in him, in the past tense. The clause the Sermon at the Temple deletes — “Till heaven and earth pass … in no wise pass from the law” — is precisely the clause that would keep the law standing after the crucifixion, and the whole of 3 Nephi 15 is about that deletion. This is the clearest case in the chapter of a borrowing edited against its source's plain sense, and Matthew supplies both the vocabulary of the edit and the doctrine being edited.

links.note: “For verily I say unto you, one jot nor one tittle hath not passed away from the law, but in me it hath all been fulfilled.” Matthew's two rarest words survive, the negative is doubled to “nor … not”, and the verse's temporal logic is reversed: the KJV's “till all be fulfilled” becomes “in me it hath all been fulfilled”. The run is short, so this is catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation, but the confidence is not in doubt — “jot” occurs in exactly one King James verse and “one jot or one tittle” in exactly one, and no other text in English could have supplied the pair.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.18 (Matthew 5:18)

pericopes.text: And behold I have given unto you the law and the commandments of my Father, that ye shall believe in me, and that ye shall repent of your sins, and come unto me with a broken heart and a contrite spirit. Behold, ye have the commandments before you, and the law is fulfilled;

therefore come unto me and be ye saved; for verily I say unto you, that except ye shall keep my commandments, which I have commanded you at this time, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.

links.text: For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.other: “in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the clause it replaces, “except your righteousness shall exceed”, occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:20.
provenance.significance: Matthew's condition is comparative and Judaean — a righteousness exceeding that of the scribes and Pharisees — and there are no scribes and Pharisees at Bountiful. The Sermon at the Temple substitutes “except ye shall keep my commandments, which I have commanded you at this time”, which is not a comparison at all but a reference to the twenty verses just delivered. The removal is of a piece with 12:14, 12:23 and 12:35: every party, institution and place belonging to first-century Judaea is edited out, and what replaces them is always the speaker himself.

links.note: “Therefore come unto me and be ye saved; for verily I say unto you, that except ye shall keep my commandments, which I have commanded you at this time, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven.” The frame of Matthew 5:20 — “except … ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven” — kept intact around a wholly new middle. The closing eight words occur in one King James verse only, so the dependence is not weakened by the substitution; it is displayed by it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.20 (Matthew 5:20)

pericopes.text: Ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, and it is also written before you, that thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill, shall be in danger of the judgement of God.

links.text: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment:

provenance.route: Exodus 20:13 / Deuteronomy 5:17 → Matthew 5:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “In danger of the judgment” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 5:21 and 5:22, and nowhere in the Old Testament. “By them of old time” occurs in exactly three, all of them in Matthew 5 — verses 21, 27 and 33 — and the Sermon at the Temple uses the phrase at exactly those three points, 12:21, 12:27 and 12:33.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's flagship mediation result and the tool settles it in one move. Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17 read, in full, “Thou shalt not kill”; every other word in 3 Nephi 12:21 — the frame “Ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time”, and the sanction “and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment” — exists only in Matthew. The Decalogue reaches the Book of Mormon through the Gospel of Matthew's quotation of it, in Matthew's King James English, complete with a Greek juridical term the Hebrew commandment does not have.

links.note: “Ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, and it is also written before you, that thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill, shall be in danger of the judgement of God.” Fourteen words of Matthew 5:21 in one run. Two additions matter. “And it is also written before you” is the Sermon at the Temple's acknowledgment that this audience possesses the commandment in writing — the plates of brass contain Exodus, which Matthew's audience did not need to be told. And the sanction is referred to God: “in danger of the judgement of God”, where Matthew has the bare “the judgment”, a court. The 1830 “judgement” with the medial e is the spelling of the first edition throughout the chapter and was normalized in 1920.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.21 (Exodus 20:13, Deuteronomy 5:17)

pericopes.text: But I say unto you, that whosoever is angry with his brother, shall be in danger of his judgement. And whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council; and whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell-fire;

links.text: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

provenance.other: “Raca” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “in danger of the council” occurs in exactly one; “danger of hell fire” occurs in exactly one. All three are Matthew 5:22, which is also one of only two King James verses containing “in danger of the judgment”.
provenance.significance: The famous omission of “without a cause” is the best-known variation in the Sermon at the Temple and the Book of Mormon is on the side later textual criticism took: the words are absent from the earliest Greek witnesses and are bracketed or dropped in modern critical editions. That convergence is real and it should be stated exactly. It shows the Book of Mormon agreeing with a reading no English Bible available in 1829 carried; it does not show how, and the catalogue makes no claim about how. What is certain is that the rest of the verse is the King James verse — three of its phrases occur in the King James Bible only here — so whatever produced the omission produced it inside a text that is otherwise Matthew's word for word.

links.note: “But I say unto you, that whosoever is angry with his brother, shall be in danger of his judgement.” Matthew 5:22 entire, with two words gone and one changed. “Without a cause” — the KJV's rendering of an eis, absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus — is not here; and Matthew's “the judgment” becomes “his judgement”, referring the sanction to the brother wronged rather than to a court, which is the same personalizing move the previous verse made in the opposite direction. Raca and the council survive untranslated and unexplained in a sermon preached in the New World, which is itself worth noticing beside the removal of Jerusalem at 12:35.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.22 (Matthew 5:22)

pericopes.text: therefore, if ye shall come unto me, or shall desire to come unto me, and rememberest that thy brother hath aught against thee,

links.text: Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee;

provenance.other: “Thy brother hath ought against thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 edition spells it “aught”, which is not the King James spelling; 1920 kept “aught”.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:23-24 is a temple instruction — bring thy gift to the altar, leave it there, be reconciled, then come and offer thy gift — and the Sermon at the Temple, delivered at a temple, removes the altar and the gift entirely. Three chapters earlier the risen Christ had ended sacrifice outright: “ye shall offer up unto me no more the shedding of blood … your sacrifices and your burnt offerings shall be done away” (3 Nephi 9:19). The edit at 12:23-24 is that abolition being enforced on the Gospel text. What replaces the altar is the speaker: “if ye shall come unto me, or shall desire to come unto me”. It is the neatest instance in the chapter of a borrowing altered to agree with the borrowing book's own narrative.

links.note: “Therefore, if ye shall come unto me, or shall desire to come unto me, and rememberest that thy brother hath aught against thee.” The Matthean skeleton — “Therefore if … and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee” — with the altar and the gift excised, and the clause that survives is one that occurs in exactly one King James verse. The stranded second-person singular “rememberest” after a plural “ye shall come” is the seam where the excision was made.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.23 (Matthew 5:23)

pericopes.text: go thy way unto thy brother, and first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come unto me with full purpose of heart, and I will receive you.

links.text: Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.

provenance.other: “Be reconciled to thy brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “leave there thy gift before the altar” — the clause 3 Nephi drops — occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:24.
provenance.significance: Matthew's sequence is: leave the gift, go, be reconciled, come back and offer the gift. The Sermon at the Temple keeps the going and the reconciling and replaces both ends: nothing is left at an altar, and the return is not to an offering but to Christ, “and then come unto me with full purpose of heart, and I will receive you”. The offering that Matthew makes the object of the whole exercise has become the person of the speaker, and the promise “I will receive you” is what the gift was for.

links.note: “Go thy way unto thy brother, and first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come unto me with full purpose of heart, and I will receive you.” Matthew 5:24's middle preserved word for word — “go thy way … first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come” — with the altar clauses at either end replaced. “Full purpose of heart” is not Matthew's; it is the Book of Mormon's own recurring formula (2 Nephi 31:13, Jacob 6:5, Mosiah 7:33), and its appearance here is the book's idiom closing a Matthean sentence.

pericopes.text: Agree with thine adversary quickly, while thou art in the way with him, lest at any time he shall get thee, and thou shalt be cast into prison.

links.text: Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.

provenance.other: “Agree with thine adversary quickly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Thine adversary” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 5:25 and 1 Samuel 29:4.
provenance.significance: Matthew's parable has three officials in it — an adversary who delivers thee to the judge, and a judge who delivers thee to the officer — and 3 Nephi has none: “lest at any time he shall get thee, and thou shalt be cast into prison”. The Judaean legal apparatus goes the way of the scribes and Pharisees at 12:20 and Jerusalem at 12:35. What is left is a creditor and a prison, which is the minimum the following verse needs.

links.note: “Agree with thine adversary quickly, while thou art in the way with him, lest at any time he shall get thee, and thou shalt be cast into prison.” The KJV's opening five words exactly, and its closing five, with the judicial machinery between them collapsed into one clause. 1830's “while” for the King James “whiles” is the one lexical modernization; the opening phrase occurs in one King James verse only.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.25 (Matthew 5:25)

pericopes.text: Verily, verily I say unto thee, thou shalt by no means come out thence, until thou hast paid the uttermost senine.— And while ye are in prison, can ye pay even one senine? Verily, verily I say unto you, Nay.

links.text: Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing.

provenance.other: “Uttermost farthing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Farthing” occurs in three — Matthew 5:26, Matthew 10:29 and Mark 12:42 — and “senine”, the word substituted for it, occurs in none, being the Nephite coin defined at Alma 11:3-19.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's one substitution of a Book of Mormon realia for a biblical one, and it is done twice in a sentence. A Roman quadrans is replaced by a Nephite senine, a unit the book had already defined a hundred and thirty pages earlier as a day's wage for a judge — which makes the substitution not merely local colour but an argument that the parable's arithmetic works in this economy too. Then, as at 12:15, the statement is turned into a question and answered: “And while ye are in prison, can ye pay even one senine? Verily, verily I say unto you, Nay.” Matthew's Jesus leaves the debt unpayable by implication; 3 Nephi's says so.

links.note: “Verily, verily I say unto thee, thou shalt by no means come out thence, until thou hast paid the uttermost senine.” Thirteen unbroken words of Matthew 5:26 with one noun exchanged, the KJV's “till” modernized to “until”, and the doubled “verily, verily” that the Sermon at the Temple uses throughout where Matthew has one. The retained phrase “paid the uttermost” belongs to the King James Bible's single occurrence of “uttermost farthing”, so the borrowed frame is identifiable even at the point where the borrowing is most obviously localized.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.26 (Matthew 5:26)

pericopes.text: Behold, it is written by them of old time, that thou shalt not commit adultery;

links.text: Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:

provenance.route: Exodus 20:14 / Deuteronomy 5:18 → Matthew 5:27 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “By them of old time” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 5:21, 5:27 and 5:33, and in no Old Testament verse. Exodus 20:14 reads “Thou shalt not commit adultery” and Deuteronomy 5:18 “Neither shalt thou commit adultery”; the Book of Mormon has Exodus's form, which is also Matthew's.
provenance.significance: Run on its own this verse cannot settle its own mediation — the tool reports no decisive divergence, because the four words the Book of Mormon reproduces from the commandment are identical in Exodus and in Matthew's quotation of it. What decides it is the frame. “By them of old time” is a Matthean formula found in three King James verses and no others, and the Sermon at the Temple deploys it at all three of the points where Matthew does. A writer working from the Decalogue would have no occasion to say “by them of old time” at all, and no source in the Old Testament from which to take the phrase.

links.note: “Behold, it is written by them of old time, that thou shalt not commit adultery.” The commandment in its Exodus rather than its Deuteronomy form, inside a frame that exists in the King James Bible only in Matthew 5. Matthew's “Ye have heard that it was said” becomes “it is written”, the same adjustment made at 12:21 (“and it is also written before you”) and 12:31 and 12:38 — this audience has the law on the plates of brass and is told so each time the formula recurs. Mediation is argued from the frame rather than from the commandment, since the commandment itself is worded identically in both candidates.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.27 (Exodus 20:14, Deuteronomy 5:18)

pericopes.text: but I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman, to lust after her, hath committed adultery already in his heart.

links.text: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.

provenance.other: “Looketh on a woman” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “to lust after her” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:28.
provenance.significance: The single deletion is “with her”. Matthew has “hath committed adultery WITH HER already in his heart”, which makes the woman a party to an act she has not performed; 3 Nephi has “hath committed adultery already in his heart”, which leaves the offence entirely with the man who looked. Whatever produced the reading, its effect is to remove the one clause in the verse that implicates the person looked at, and it is the same kind of surgical two-word excision as “without a cause” six verses earlier.

links.note: “But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman, to lust after her, hath committed adultery already in his heart.” An eighteen-word agreement with Matthew 5:28 broken only by the absence of two words, and containing two phrases that occur in one King James verse each. The verse clears Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; it is not among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: Behold, I give unto you a commandment, that ye suffer none of these things to enter into your heart:
for it is better that ye should deny yourselves of these things, wherein ye will take up your cross, than that ye should be cast into hell.

links.text: And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.

provenance.route: Matthew 5:29-30 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Matthew 16:24 supplying the replacement image
provenance.other: “cast into hell” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, of which Matthew 5:29 and 5:30 are two. “take up his cross” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 16:24, Mark 8:34 and Luke 9:23 — and in each it stands beside “let him deny himself”, which is the pairing 3 Nephi 12:30 has.
provenance.significance: The Sermon at the Temple declines Matthew's most violent image. Where Matthew twice says pluck out the eye and cut off the hand, 3 Nephi says “deny yourselves of these things, wherein ye will take up your cross” — and the substitution is not invented, it is imported from Matthew 16:24, where denial of self and the taking up of the cross already stand together. Two Matthean passages have been fused, and the fusion is doctrinally directed: self-denial replaces self-mutilation, and the cross, which in Matthew 5 has not yet been mentioned, arrives in a sermon delivered by a Christ who has already been crucified.

links.note: “For it is better that ye should deny yourselves of these things, wherein ye will take up your cross, than that ye should be cast into hell.” The frame of Matthew 5:29-30 survives — “it is better … than that thy whole body should be cast into hell” — with the amputations removed and Matthew 16:24's self-denial and cross put in their place. The verbal contact with either source is thin, which is why this is catalogued as an allusion and the confidence held at high rather than certain; the case is the retained comparative frame plus the exact Matthew 16:24 pairing of denial with the cross.
links.whyNot: The shared vocabulary with Matthew 5:29-30 amounts to the comparative construction and the phrase “cast into hell”, which occurs in six King James verses; a reader could reasonably say that 12:30 simply is not a rendering of those verses but a different saying occupying their position in the sequence. The answer is positional as much as verbal — the sentence sits exactly where Matthew's pair sits, between the adultery saying and the divorce saying, and does the same work of naming a cost worth paying to avoid hell.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.30 (Matthew 5:29-30)

pericopes.text: It hath been written, That whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement.

links.text: It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement:

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 24:1 → Matthew 5:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Writing of divorcement” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 5:31 and Mark 10:4; the Old Testament's phrase is “bill of divorcement”, which occurs in three, Deuteronomy 24:1, Deuteronomy 24:3 and Jeremiah 3:8. The Book of Mormon has the New Testament noun.
provenance.significance: A one-word mediation test with a clean answer. Deuteronomy 24:1 is a long conditional about uncleanness found in a wife, and it says “let him WRITE her a BILL of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house”. Matthew compresses that to “let him GIVE her a WRITING of divorcement”, and 3 Nephi has Matthew's verb, Matthew's noun, Matthew's compression and Matthew's opening formula, with none of Deuteronomy's conditions. The mediation tool returns four decisive points, all of them for Matthew and none for Deuteronomy. The law of Moses is present in this chapter only as Matthew quotes it.

links.note: “It hath been written, That whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement.” A fourteen-word run against Matthew 5:31 whose only change is that the KJV's “It hath been said” becomes “It hath been written” — the same adjustment for a literate audience made at 12:21, 12:27 and 12:38. The distinguishing noun is the New Testament's: the King James Old Testament never calls it a writing.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.31 (Deuteronomy 24:1-4)

pericopes.text: Verily, verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery; and whoso shall marry her who is divorced, committeth adultery.

links.text: But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.

provenance.other: “Cause of fornication” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:32; the exception is worded differently at Matthew 19:9 (“except it be for fornication”) and is absent from Mark 10:11 and Luke 16:18.
provenance.significance: Of the four New Testament forms of the divorce saying, only Matthew 5:32 reads “saving for the cause of fornication”, and that is the form 3 Nephi has. The Book of Mormon is therefore not following a harmonized or generic version of the saying but one Gospel verse in particular, which is what makes the whole Sermon at the Temple testable in the first place: it tracks Matthew's text and not the tradition behind it.

links.note: “Verily, verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery; and whoso shall marry her who is divorced, committeth adultery.” A twenty-three word run — the longest continuous agreement so far in the chapter and well past Skousen's threshold, though not one of his passages. The changes are two: Matthew's “But I say unto you” becomes the chapter's standing “Verily, verily I say unto you”, and “whosoever … her that is divorced” becomes “whoso … her who is divorced”, the only place in the chapter where the 1830 text modernizes a King James relative rather than preserving it.

pericopes.text: And again it is written, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths.

links.text: Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths:

provenance.route: Leviticus 19:12 / Numbers 30:2 → Matthew 5:33 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Forswear” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:33. Leviticus 19:12 has “ye shall not swear by my name falsely” and Numbers 30:2 “he shall not break his word”; neither has the word the Book of Mormon uses, and neither has “oaths”.
provenance.significance: The strongest mediation result in the chapter, because the decisive word exists in one King James verse in the entire Bible and it is the New Testament one. The mediation tool returns four decisive points for Matthew and none for either Old Testament candidate: “Again” against Leviticus's “And”, “forswear thyself but” against “swear by my name falsely neither”, “perform unto” against “thou profane the name of thy God”, and “thine oaths”, which Leviticus does not have at all. Whatever oath-law stood behind this verse, what reached the Book of Mormon was Matthew's summary of it in Matthew's English.

links.note: “And again it is written, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths.” Thirteen unbroken words of Matthew 5:33, including a verb that occurs in exactly one King James verse. Matthew's own frame, “ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time”, is replaced by “it is written” — the fourth time this chapter has made that substitution — but the “again” with which Matthew opens the verse survives as “And again”, which is why the mediation tool can score even the connective.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.33 (Leviticus 19:12, Numbers 30:2)

pericopes.text: But verily, verily I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by Heaven, for it is God’s throne;

links.text: But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne:

provenance.route: Isaiah 66:1 → Matthew 5:34 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Swear not at all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “God's throne” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:34. Isaiah 66:1, which supplies the image, reads “The heaven is MY throne”, in the first person and without the possessive noun.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 66:1 is the source of the throne and the footstool, and the mediation tool finds three decisive points against it and none for it: the Book of Mormon has Matthew's frame, Matthew's third-person “God's” for Isaiah's “my”, and none of Isaiah's continuation about the house and the place of rest. The prophet's oracle reaches this chapter only in the compressed form a Gospel gave it, which is the same result the tool returns at 12:21, 12:31, 12:33 and 12:43 — five Old Testament sources in one chapter, five times mediated by Matthew.

links.note: “But verily, verily I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by Heaven, for it is God's throne.” Matthew 5:34 entire, with the doubled “verily” this chapter substitutes for Matthew's single “But I say unto you”. Seventeen words run together and two of the verse's phrases occur in one King James verse each.

pericopes.text: nor by the earth, for it his footstool;

links.text: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King.

provenance.route: Isaiah 66:1 → Matthew 5:35 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “For it is his footstool” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:35. Isaiah 66:1 has “the earth is MY footstool”, first person; “his footstool” by itself occurs in five King James verses.
provenance.significance: Here the chapter removes Jerusalem. Matthew forbids swearing by heaven, by the earth and by Jerusalem, “for it is the city of the great King”; the Sermon at the Temple stops after the earth. The deletion belongs with “light of this people” at 12:14, the scribes and Pharisees at 12:20, and the judge and officer at 12:25 — every Judaean particular in the Sermon is removed except the two that are untranslatable, Raca and the council at 12:22. Note what the removal costs: the missing clause is the only place in the Sermon on the Mount that calls Christ's city the city of the great King, and a book much occupied with the New Jerusalem (3 Nephi 20-21) drops it here.

links.note: “Nor by the earth, for it his footstool.” Matthew 5:35's first clause word for word, and the possessive settles the mediation on its own — Isaiah's oracle has “my footstool”, spoken by God, while Matthew's report has “his”, spoken about God, and the Book of Mormon has “his”. The 1830 edition omits the verb, reading “for it his footstool”, which 1920 repaired to “for it is his footstool”; the first edition's slip is at exactly the point where the King James phrase that occurs in one verse only begins.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.35 (Matthew 5:35)

pericopes.text: neither shalt thou swear by the head, because thou canst not make one hair black or white;

links.text: Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.

provenance.other: “Not make one hair” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the full King James phrase is “one hair white or black”, which likewise occurs in exactly one. The Book of Mormon reverses the colours: “black or white”.
provenance.significance: Two small changes and both go the same way. Matthew's “swear by THY head” becomes “swear by THE head”, dropping the possessive that makes the oath personal; and the colours are transposed. Neither alteration changes the sense, and that is what makes them evidence: they are the residue a text leaves when it is being reproduced from memory or by dictation rather than copied by eye, and they cluster in this chapter at exactly the points where nothing doctrinal is at stake.

links.note: “Neither shalt thou swear by the head, because thou canst not make one hair black or white.” Matthew 5:36 with the article for the possessive and the two colours transposed. “Not make one hair” occurs in one King James verse only, so the identification does not turn on the order of the adjectives; the order is worth recording because it is the kind of variation that survives no editorial correction — 1920 left it standing.

pericopes.text: but let your communication be Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever cometh of more than these are evil.

links.text: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.

provenance.other: “Let your communication be” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:37.
provenance.significance: The chapter's clearest case of a King James sentence reassembled with its parts in the wrong sockets. Matthew: “for whatsoever IS MORE THAN THESE COMETH OF evil.” 3 Nephi: “for whatsoever COMETH OF MORE THAN THESE ARE evil.” Every word is Matthew's and the syntax is not; “cometh of” has migrated across the clause and the number of the verb has been pulled to the nearest noun. A reader who wanted to see how this chapter's text was produced could do worse than start here, because the error is of a kind that copying does not make and recitation does.

links.note: “But let your communication be Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever cometh of more than these are evil.” Eleven words of Matthew 5:37 exactly, opening with a phrase that occurs in one King James verse only, and then a scrambled second clause using Matthew's whole vocabulary in a different order. 1830's “are evil” was corrected to “is evil” in 1920 — a change back toward grammar and away from the first edition, and the same kind of tidying 1920 performed on “tender mercies … is over all” at 1 Nephi 1:20 (CONVENTIONS §8).
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.37 (Matthew 5:37)

pericopes.text: And behold, it is written, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.

links.text: Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth:

provenance.route: Exodus 21:24 / Leviticus 24:20 / Deuteronomy 19:21 → Matthew 5:38 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “An eye for an eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:38. The Old Testament's form is articleless and conjunctionless — “eye for eye, tooth for tooth”, which occurs in three verses, Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. Every article and the connective “and” in 3 Nephi 12:38 belong to Matthew alone.
provenance.significance: The most economical mediation result in the chapter: the whole test is four indefinite articles and one conjunction. The lex talionis stands in three places in the King James Old Testament and in all three it is stripped bare, “eye for eye, tooth for tooth”; Matthew alone writes “An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth”, and that is a King James singleton. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's form exactly. Note for anyone re-running this: tools/mediation-check.py reports the divergences as pointing both ways here, because its aligner treats the stray articles as unmatched rather than as Matthean, and the raw phrase count overturns that reading. The tool found the ambiguity; the rarity count resolved it.

links.note: “And behold, it is written, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.” Eleven words of Matthew 5:38 with the frame changed from “Ye have heard that it hath been said” to “it is written”, which is this chapter's standing substitution for a people who hold the law in writing. Hardy's apparatus cross-references the three Pentateuchal statements of the talion at this verse; the wording is Matthew's, so the link sits on Matthew and the register sends a reader from the Old Testament rows to here.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.38 (Exodus 21:23-24, Leviticus 24:19-20, Deuteronomy 19:21)

pericopes.text: But I say unto you, That ye shall not resist evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

links.text: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

provenance.other: “Smite thee on thy right cheek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “resist not evil” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:39. Luke's parallel at 6:29 has neither, reading “unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek”.
provenance.significance: The one alteration is a change of mood. Matthew's “that ye resist not evil” is a subordinate clause describing a state; 3 Nephi's “that ye shall not resist evil” is a commandment. The chapter has made this conversion before — the imperative “Rejoice” became the promise “ye shall have great joy” at 12:12 — and it goes both directions, but it always ends with the Sermon at the Temple speaking in the future indicative of a lawgiver. Nothing else in the verse moves; the right cheek and the other are Matthew's, against Luke's unspecified one.

links.note: “But I say unto you, That ye shall not resist evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.” A sixteen-word run to the end of the verse, with two King James singletons in it, and a single interpolated “shall”. Where Matthew and Luke diverge — Matthew's right cheek against Luke's one cheek — the Book of Mormon is with Matthew, as it is at every point in this chapter where the Synoptics offer a choice.

pericopes.text: And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also.

links.text: And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also.

provenance.other: “Sue thee at the law” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:40. Luke 6:29's parallel has no lawsuit in it at all: “him that taketh away thy cloke forbid not to take thy coat also”, with the two garments in the opposite order.
provenance.significance: A whole verse of Matthew reproduced without a single change, at the centre of a paragraph the chapter has otherwise been editing steadily. Where the Sermon at the Temple removes Judaean particulars it removes institutions — the scribes and Pharisees, the altar and the gift, the judge and the officer, Jerusalem — and it leaves Roman and legal particulars alone: the lawsuit here, the compelled mile at 12:41, the prison at 12:25. That distinction is consistent enough across the chapter to be a policy rather than an accident.

links.note: “And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also.” Twenty-one words, the entire verse, identical to Matthew 5:40 but for the spelling of “cloak” for the KJV's “cloke”. The opening clause occurs in one King James verse only. This is one of the chapter's few whole-verse quotations and it clears Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though the passage is not among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.

links.text: And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.

provenance.other: “Compel thee to go a mile” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does “go with him twain”; both are Matthew 5:41, which has no Lukan parallel at all.
provenance.significance: The verse with no parallel outside Matthew is reproduced entire, including the Roman mile and the archaic “twain”. Every element of it is foreign to the setting — a Roman unit of distance, an angaria the Nephites have no institution of, and a numeral the Book of Mormon uses nowhere else in this sense — and the Sermon at the Temple, which has been busy removing Jerusalem and the Pharisees, keeps all three. The chapter's editing is doctrinal and cultic; it is not an attempt to make the sermon plausible in its new setting.

links.note: “And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.” Thirteen words, the whole of Matthew 5:41, without a word changed, and containing two phrases that each occur in one King James verse only. Matthew 5:41 is unique to Matthew among the Gospels, which makes this the chapter's cleanest single demonstration that the source is the First Gospel's text rather than a Synoptic tradition.
