pericopes.text: Give to him that asketh thee, and to him that would borrow of thee, turn thou not away.

links.text: Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.

provenance.other: “Him that would borrow of thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:42.
provenance.significance: 1830 reads “and TO him that would borrow of thee”, where the King James has “and FROM him that would borrow of thee”, and 1920 restored the preposition to the King James one. The direction of that change is the point (CONVENTIONS §8): a later edition moving the Book of Mormon's text back toward the King James reading is evidence about the editors, not about the original — and it means a reader of the modern text sees a verbatim quotation where the first edition shows a departure.

links.note: “Give to him that asketh thee, and to him that would borrow of thee, turn thou not away.” Matthew 5:42 with one preposition different and the closing three words transposed — the KJV has “turn not thou away”, 1830 “turn thou not away”. The central clause occurs in one King James verse only. Both of the first edition's departures were corrected in 1920, in each case toward the King James wording, which is why this row's argument is only visible in the running text the catalogue uses.

pericopes.text: And behold, it is written also, That thou shalt love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy:

links.text: Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy.

provenance.route: Leviticus 19:18 → Matthew 5:43 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Hate thine enemy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:43, and in no Old Testament verse whatever. “Love thy neighbour” occurs in eight, of which Leviticus 19:18 is one.
provenance.significance: This is the cleanest of the chapter's five mediation tests because the decisive half of the sentence exists nowhere in the Old Testament. Leviticus 19:18 says “thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD” — no commandment to hate an enemy is anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, and Matthew's second clause has been the subject of a long argument about what he was quoting. Whatever the answer to that question, the Book of Mormon has Matthew's version of the maxim, hatred and all, and not Leviticus's; the mediation tool's one decisive point is exactly this clause.

links.note: “And behold, it is written also, That thou shalt love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy.” Matthew 5:43's saying entire, with the frame changed to “it is written” as at 12:27, 12:31 and 12:38. The second clause occurs in one King James verse only and has no Old Testament source at all, so this verse settles its own mediation without needing the first clause: what the Nephites are told is written is a proposition that stands in the Bible only in the Gospel of Matthew.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.43 (Leviticus 19:18)

pericopes.text: but behold I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you and persecute you,

links.text: But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;

provenance.other: “Bless them that curse you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 5:44 and Luke 6:28, and “pray for them which despitefully use you” occurs in exactly two, the same pair. Only Matthew 5:44 holds all four clauses — love, bless, do good, pray — in one verse.
provenance.significance: Thirty consecutive words, the longest agreement in the chapter and one of the longest in the Book of Mormon outside the transcribed Isaiah blocks. Luke 6:27-28 has the same four commands distributed across two verses and in a different order; the Book of Mormon has Matthew's single verse in Matthew's order. Where the parallel tradition offers an alternative arrangement, this chapter takes Matthew's — the same result as at 12:39 with the right cheek and 12:40 with the coat and the cloak.

links.note: “But behold I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you and persecute you.” A thirty-word unbroken run against Matthew 5:44 with one interpolated “behold”, and the 1830 “which” preserving the King James relative that 1920 modernized. Well past Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though not one of his thirty-six passages.

pericopes.text: that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good;

links.text: That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.

provenance.other: “Children of your Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “maketh his sun to rise” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:45. The clause the Book of Mormon drops, “sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust”, likewise occurs in exactly one.
provenance.significance: Matthew's verse balances two impartialities, sun and rain, and 3 Nephi keeps only the sun. What is lost is not decorative: the rain clause carries the antithesis “the just and on the unjust”, which is the sharper of the two and the one later English proverbializes. The deletion belongs to the same class as the Jerusalem clause at 12:35 and the judge and officer at 12:25 — the Sermon at the Temple regularly stops a King James verse short at its second member, and the truncation is the commonest single form its editing takes.

links.note: “That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.” A twenty-seven word run, the whole of Matthew 5:45 up to the rain, with two King James singletons in it and nothing changed. The 1830 “which is in heaven” preserves the King James relative.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.45 (Matthew 5:45)

pericopes.text: therefore those things which were of old time, which were under the law in me, are all fulfilled.—
Old things are done away, and all things have become new;

links.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.

provenance.other: “Old things are passed away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “all things are become new” occurs in exactly one; both are 2 Corinthians 5:17, and the two clauses stand there consecutively as they do here.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most striking substitution and it is a substitution of one biblical text for another. Matthew 5:46-47 asks what reward the publicans have and what the hearers do more than others; 3 Nephi has no parallel to either verse and puts in their place a sentence of Paul's about the new creation in Christ. The effect is to answer the question the Sermon at the Temple has been raising since 12:18 — what happened to the law — with Paul's formula rather than Matthew's, and to do it in the two clauses of 2 Corinthians 5:17 that are each unique in the King James Bible. A sermon that has been Matthew's for thirty verses turns Pauline at the one point where Matthew's own text would have been unusable in the New World, and the seam is where the publicans should be.

links.note: “Old things are done away, and all things have become new.” 2 Corinthians 5:17's two clauses in Paul's order, with the KJV's “passed away” exchanged for “done away” and “are become” for “have become”. Both source clauses occur in one King James verse each, which is what identifies Paul as the source despite the changed verbs; and 12:46 has just used “done away” of the law itself, so the substituted verb is the Book of Mormon's own word for what the law of Moses has undergone (3 Nephi 9:17, 15:2-8). Hardy's apparatus cross-references both Matthew 5:46-47 and 2 Corinthians 5:17 at this verse, which is the right pairing: Matthew's verses are what is missing and Paul's is what is present.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 12.47 (Matthew 5:46-47, 2 Corinthians 5:17)

pericopes.text: therefore I would that ye should be perfect even as I, or your Father which is in Heaven is perfect.

links.text: Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.

provenance.other: “Even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “be ye therefore perfect” occurs in exactly one; both are Matthew 5:48.
provenance.significance: The insertion of two words changes who the standard is. Matthew's Jesus points past himself to the Father; 3 Nephi's inserts himself into the comparison — “perfect even as I, OR your Father which is in Heaven is perfect” — and the disjunction makes the two equivalent as models. This is the last and largest instance of the chapter's governing edit, the one first made at 12:3 with “which cometh unto me”: wherever Matthew's Sermon names a quality, a reward or a standard, the Sermon at the Temple attaches it to the speaker. The chapter that began by blessing those who come to him ends by offering him as the measure of perfection.

links.note: “Therefore I would that ye should be perfect even as I, or your Father which is in Heaven is perfect.” Matthew 5:48 with the imperative softened to “I would that ye should be” and the speaker inserted into the comparison. The nine-word tail is a King James singleton and settles the source; the two words that are not Matthew's are the whole argument of the row. Note that the parallel at 3 Nephi 27:27 (“even as I am”) and the risen Christ's inclusion of himself here are what a later reader has to reconcile with Matthew's Father-only formula.

pericopes.text: Verily, verily, I say that I would that ye should do alms unto the poor; but take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.

links.text: Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.

provenance.significance: The added frame is doing two things at once. It converts a caution into a commandment, which is how the whole Sermon at the Temple treats the Sermon on the Mount — as legislation for a covenant people rather than as instruction to a crowd. And it introduces Matthew's material in the idiom of a different evangelist: “Verily, verily, I say” occurs in exactly twenty-five KJV verses and every one of them is in the Gospel of John. So the Matthean sermon is opened with the Johannine double amen, which is the seam where the two Gospels the Book of Mormon leans on hardest are stitched together. See the exclusion register at 13:1 for why the catalogue declines to make that a link of its own. 3 Nephi 13 is a continuous transcription of Matthew 6 into the Sermon at the Temple, and the transcription itself is not the finding — the departures are. This chapter has four kinds: an added Nephite frame (13:1, 13:25), two petitions of the Lord's Prayer dropped (13:9, 13:10), a clause of Matthew 6:32 dropped (13:31), and a handful of small rewordings that change the sense (13:5, 13:30, 13:34). Each is argued at its own verse.

links.note: From “take heed” to the end this is Matthew 6:1 word for word. “do not your alms” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “to be seen of them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:1. What is not Matthew is the clause the Nephite text sets in front of it: “Verily, verily, I say that I would that ye should do alms unto the poor; but …”. That addition changes the illocution of the whole paragraph. Matthew 6:1 is a warning about a practice it assumes; 3 Nephi 13:1 first commands the practice, and names its object — the poor — which Matthew never does anywhere in the chapter. The 1830 keeps the KJV's “your Father which is in heaven”; 1920 reads “who is in heaven”, so the first edition shows the borrowing a shade more plainly than the current text.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: Therefore, when ye shall do your alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as will hypocrites do in the synagogues, and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily, I say unto you, They have their reward.

links.text: Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.

provenance.significance: “As will hypocrites do” is not a KJV reading, not a modernization, and not obviously English: it survives unchanged into the 1920 edition and the current text, so it is not a first-edition slip that was later cleaned up. Read as a Yorkshire-ish dialectal habitual (‘as hypocrites will do’) it makes sense; read as a compositor's misreading of ‘as the’ it makes sense too. The catalogue records it as the one place in this chapter where the Nephite text departs from the KJV in a direction no editor has been willing to correct.

links.note: Verbatim apart from three small changes: KJV “when thou doest thine alms” becomes “when ye shall do your alms” (Matthew's singular turned plural and future, consistent with 13:1's plural command), “before thee” becomes “before you” to match, and — the oddity of the verse — KJV “as the hypocrites do” becomes “as will hypocrites do”. “sound a trumpet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is this one. Nothing else in the King James Bible has anybody sounding a trumpet before himself to advertise a gift.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth;

links.text: But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:

provenance.significance: The number-switching is the quiet evidence for how this text was produced. A writer paraphrasing from memory smooths person and number; a text being copied keeps the source's alternation even when it is awkward. 3 Nephi 13:2–4 is plural, then singular, then singular, in Matthew's own order, and the one place it does depart (13:2) is the place where 13:1's added Nephite frame had already committed the passage to the plural.

links.note: Verbatim; the only change is the KJV's terminal colon for a semicolon. “left hand know what thy right hand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The clause is one of the most distinctive sentences in the Gospels and it is reproduced without a word altered, including the archaic “doeth”, which the 1830 keeps and later editions kept as well. Note also that 13:2 has just turned Matthew's singular into a plural and 13:3 turns it straight back to “thou”, exactly where Matthew does — the transcription is following its source's grammatical number, not imposing one.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: that thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret, himself shall reward thee openly.

links.text: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.

provenance.significance: “Reward thee openly” is textually interesting quite apart from the Book of Mormon: “openly” at Matthew 6:4, 6:6 and 6:18 renders a phrase absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and is dropped by every modern critical edition. The Nephite text has it three times. That is the same phenomenon as the doxology at 13:13, and it is what makes this chapter one of the strongest kjvSpecific cases in the whole catalogue: the Book of Mormon does not merely follow Matthew, it follows the received Greek text behind the King James Version, including at points where that text is no longer thought original.

links.note: Verbatim. “seeth in secret” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 6:4, 6:6 and 6:18 — and the Nephite chapter reproduces all three, at 13:4, 13:6 and 13:18, in Matthew's order and with Matthew's own small variation between them (6:4 alone has “himself shall reward thee openly”, and 13:4 alone has “himself”). Reproducing a source's internal inconsistencies is stronger evidence of copying than reproducing its consistencies.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: And when thou prayest, thou shalt not do as the hypocrites: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues, and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily, I say unto you, They have their reward.

links.text: And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.

provenance.significance: This is the chapter's second-clearest instance of a systematic, not accidental, redirection. Matthew 6 alternates between 'be not' and 'do not'; where it says 'be', 3 Nephi 13 twice says 'do' (13:5 here, and 13:1's 'I would that ye should do alms'). Whether that is a translator's habit or a redactor's programme is beyond what the wording can settle, but the direction is consistent and it is worth a reader knowing that the departure at 13:5 is not isolated.

links.note: Verbatim but for one substitution, and it is the substitution that carries the verse: KJV “thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are” becomes “thou shalt not do as the hypocrites”. “corners of the streets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is this one. The change is not stylistic. Matthew forbids being a certain kind of person; the Nephite text forbids doing a certain thing, which is the same shift 13:1 made when it turned a warning into a command about almsgiving. Twice in five verses the Sermon's ethic of character is re-pointed as an ethic of practice.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.

links.text: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.

provenance.significance: Isaiah 26:20 — ‘Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee’ — is the standing Old Testament background proposed for Matthew 6:6, and it is worth a reader knowing that the catalogue looked at it and declined it; see the exclusion register at 13:6. The Nephite text has Matthew's ‘closet’ and Matthew's singular ‘door’, not Isaiah's ‘chambers’ and plural ‘doors’, so whatever route Matthew took to Isaiah, 3 Nephi took to Matthew.

links.note: Verbatim. Two absolute rarities inside one sentence: “enter into thy closet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “shut thy door” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:6. The 1830 preserves the KJV's “thy Father which is in secret” and “thy Father, which seeth in secret”; 1920 changed both relatives to “who”, so the first edition again reads closer to the source than the current text does.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.

links.text: But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.

provenance.significance: The verse is a small demonstration of the whole thesis in miniature. A Nephite congregation in the first century is warned against a fault named with a two-word English phrase invented by the Jacobean translators, in a sentence whose other rare collocation is also unique to their rendering of the same verse. The metaleptic reading is uncomfortable but it is the honest one: what is being reproduced here is not a teaching but a page.

links.note: Verbatim but for the elided verb: KJV “as the heathen do” becomes “as the heathen”, the same ellipsis 13:16 will make at Matthew 6:16. “vain repetitions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “much speaking” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:7. ‘Vain repetitions’ is in fact a King James coinage for a single Greek verb, which makes it about as sharp a test of English-version dependence as this catalogue can ask for: no wording behind the KJV supplies the phrase, and no modern version keeps it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of before ye ask him.

links.text: Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.

provenance.significance: Keeping 6:8 while dropping 6:11 produces a small strain the Nephite text does not resolve. Matthew's logic runs: your Father already knows what you need, therefore pray like this, and the model prayer then asks for bread. 3 Nephi keeps the premise and removes the request for daily bread, which arguably tightens the argument — a prayer that asks for nothing material sits better after 6:8 than Matthew's does. Whether that is design or accident, the omission at 13:10 is the only one of the two that leaves the surrounding argument better than it found it.

links.note: Verbatim; the KJV's comma after “need of” is dropped, which is the whole difference. “knoweth what things ye have need of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The sentence is also the hinge of the paragraph — it is the reason given for the prayer that follows — and 3 Nephi keeps it in place even though the prayer it introduces will lose two of its six petitions in the next two verses.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.

links.text: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 11:2: one decisive divergence, and it favours Matthew — the Book of Mormon has “After this manner therefore”, not Luke's “And he said unto them, When ye”.
provenance.significance: Two of the Lord's Prayer's petitions are missing from the Nephite version, and they are the two that would be strangest on the lips of a resurrected Christ standing in the temple courtyard at Bountiful: the petition for the kingdom's coming, and the petition for daily bread, addressed to a crowd that has just been fed. A catalogue of borrowings has to record an omission as carefully as a quotation, because an omission from a transcribed block is a decision, and this one is the clearest evidence in the chapter that the transcription is being read rather than merely copied.

links.note: Verbatim, and the boundary is the point. “Hallowed be thy name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:9 and Luke 11:2, and the mediation test settles which is in view: Matthew opens “After this manner therefore pray ye”, Luke opens “And he said unto them, When ye pray, say”, and 3 Nephi 13:9 has Matthew's opening word for word. What the Nephite verse then does not have is Matthew 6:10's first petition: the KJV verse continues “Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done…” and 3 Nephi 13:10 begins at “Thy will be done”. Hardy's cross-reference apparatus keys Matthew 6:10 to this verse for exactly that reason, and his note records the omission of ‘thy kingdom come’ and offers a reading of it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.9 (note a: the omission of “thy kingdom come” from Mt 6.10)

pericopes.text: Thy will be done in earth as it is in heaven.

links.text: Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 11:2: decisive for Matthew — the Book of Mormon lacks Luke's “as in heaven, so” and has Matthew's “as it is in heaven”.
provenance.significance: The second omission sits at this verse's other end: Matthew 6:11, “Give us this day our daily bread”, is simply not there, and 3 Nephi 13:11 goes straight to the forgiveness of debts. Hardy keys Matthew 6:11 here and his note names the omission. Taken with 13:9, the Nephite Lord's Prayer is the Matthean prayer with its two petitions of request removed, leaving address, submission, forgiveness, deliverance and doxology — a prayer that asks God for nothing except forgiveness and rescue.

links.note: The verse is Matthew 6:10 minus its first petition, and its wording is a KJV singleton: “Thy will be done in earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 reads “in earth” with Matthew; the reading was changed to “on earth” in a later edition, and Hardy's textual note records the 1830 “in earth (= Mt 6.10)” against the 1837 “on earth”. This is CONVENTIONS §8 in its purest form: the current Book of Mormon text no longer preserves the KJV reading, and the borrowing is visible in the first edition and invisible in the modern one. The mediation test rules Luke out here as well — KJV Luke 11:2 reads “as in heaven, so in earth”, and 3 Nephi has Matthew's order.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.10 (note b: “P, 1830 in earth (= Mt 6.10); 1837 on earth”; note c: the omission of “give us this day our daily bread” from Mt 6.11)

pericopes.text: And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.

links.text: And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 11:4: three decisive divergences, all favouring Matthew — “debts as” not “sins for”, no “also”, and “our debtors” not “every one that is indebted to us”.
provenance.significance: ‘Debts’ and ‘debtors’ rather than ‘sins’ and ‘those indebted’ is the reading English liturgy took from Matthew, and it is the reading in front of the Nephites. It matters for the chapter's argument because the omissions at 13:9 and 13:10 might otherwise suggest a Lukan form of the prayer standing behind the Nephite one — Luke's version is the shorter of the two, and a reader who noticed two missing petitions would reasonably reach for it. The mediation test closes that door: the shortening is not Lukan, it is done to Matthew.

links.note: Verbatim. “forgive us our debts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “as we forgive our debtors” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:12. This is the petition on which the two Gospel forms of the prayer differ most sharply — Luke 11:4 reads “forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us” — so the verse is a clean mediation test, and it returns Matthew at every point of divergence.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

links.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 11:4; the single ‘decisive’ point it returns for Luke is produced by the Nephite verse break at the doxology and is discounted.
provenance.significance: Worth recording that tools/mediation-check.py, run on this verse alone against Luke 11:4, reports one decisive point in Luke's favour — the Book of Mormon lacks the doxology that Matthew 6:13 carries and Luke does not. That is a versification artifact, not a finding: the doxology is present, one verse later. The case is a good illustration of why CONVENTIONS §7 says decide rather than default, and why a mechanical mediation result has to be read against the verse division of the text being tested rather than trusted on its own.

links.note: The first half of Matthew 6:13, verbatim, with the KJV's colon turned to a full stop so that the doxology can become a verse of its own at 13:13. “lead us not into temptation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:13 and Luke 11:4, and “deliver us from evil” occurs in exactly two, the same pair; the verse cannot settle its own mediation and does not need to, because 13:11 and 13:13 settle it on either side.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

links.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

provenance.other: “thine is the kingdom” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:13 and 1 Chronicles 29:11 (“Thine, O LORD is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty”). The Book of Mormon has Matthew's selection and Matthew's order, not the Chronicler's fivefold list.
provenance.significance: Recover the doxology's own background and the borrowing gains a second floor. The only other KJV verse with “thine is the kingdom” and “the power, and the glory” is 1 Chronicles 29:11 — David's blessing of the LORD before the whole congregation as he hands over the materials for a temple he will not build. That is where the Church's liturgical ending came from, and it is the reason it is a doxology at all. So the Nephite prayer, spoken in a temple courtyard by the one who will not need it built, closes with the words David used at the founding of the first temple — by way of a Greek scribe's marginal addition and an English translation of it. Neither text says this; the chain says it. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the meaning is in the unstated correspondence, and here the unstated correspondence runs through a stage of transmission that ought not to exist.

links.note: The second half of Matthew 6:13, verbatim, given its own verse. “thine is the kingdom” occurs in exactly two KJV verses and “the power, and the glory” occurs in exactly two, and in both counts the pair is Matthew 6:13 and 1 Chronicles 29:11. The 1830 reads “for ever” as two words with the KJV; 1920 prints “forever”. This is the strongest single kjvSpecific datum in the chapter, and it is a textual one rather than a verbal one: the doxology is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts of Matthew, is bracketed or relegated to a footnote by every modern critical edition, and is generally held to have entered the text from liturgical use. The Nephite record has it, in the King James wording, in a sermon delivered before any of those manuscripts existed.

pericopes.text: For, if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you:

links.text: For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you:

provenance.significance: Matthew 6:14–15 exists to expand the fifth petition of the prayer, and 3 Nephi keeps the expansion intact while cutting the second and fourth petitions. The forgiveness clause is therefore the one part of the Lord's Prayer the Nephite text treats as needing more, not less, which is consistent with where the Sermon at the Temple puts its weight elsewhere.

links.note: Verbatim, with an added comma after “For”. “forgive men their trespasses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The verse pair 13:14–15 reproduces Matthew's own doubling — the positive and then its exact negative — without abridging it, which is notable in a chapter that has just abridged the prayer these verses gloss.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: but if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

links.text: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

provenance.significance: The asymmetry is the evidence. Matthew 6:14 has ‘your heavenly Father’ and 6:15 has ‘your Father’, for no discernible reason; 3 Nephi 13:14–15 has exactly the same pair in the same order. Reproducing a source's unmotivated variation is the signature of transcription rather than recollection, and this chapter does it at least three times (here, at 13:4/13:6/13:18's ‘himself’, and at 13:19/13:20's ‘and thieves’ against ‘and where thieves’).

links.note: Verbatim. Matthew's “But if ye forgive not” becomes “but if ye forgive not” only because 13:14–15 are punctuated as one sentence in the 1830. The pairing with 13:14 reproduces the KJV's characteristic construction — the same clause negated, with “your heavenly Father” in the first limb and “your Father” in the second — including that small asymmetry, which a paraphraser would have levelled. “if ye forgive not men their trespasses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “neither will your Father forgive your trespasses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:15.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: Moreover, when ye fast, be not as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily, I say unto you, They have their reward.

links.text: Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.

provenance.significance: The fasting paragraph is the least adapted stretch of the chapter: 13:16–18 reproduces Matthew 6:16–18 with no substantive change of any kind, in a sermon otherwise willing to add a frame, drop two petitions and re-point an imperative. Where a transcription leaves a paragraph entirely alone, that is worth noticing too — it marks the boundary of whatever editorial hand is at work in 13:1, 13:5, 13:9–10 and 13:30.

links.note: Verbatim but for one ellipsis: KJV “be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance” becomes “be not as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance”, dropping a comma rather than a word. “of a sad countenance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “disfigure their faces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:16. Two absolute rarities in one clause, and ‘disfigure’ appears nowhere else in the King James Bible at all.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thy head, and wash thy face;

links.text: But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face;

provenance.significance: Psalm 23:5's ‘thou anointest my head with oil’ is the parallel a reader is most likely to reach for and it is the wrong one — see the exclusion register at 13:17. Matthew's point is cosmetic normality, the ordinary grooming of a man who is not fasting; the Psalm's is honour at a host's table. The shared noun and verb are the whole of the contact.

links.note: Verbatim but for one word: KJV “anoint thine head” becomes “anoint thy head”, a modernization of the pre-vocalic possessive of the kind the 1830 makes elsewhere. “when thou fastest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The pairing of anointing and washing as the marks of a concealed fast is Matthew's alone; no Old Testament fasting text puts them together, which is why the verse cannot be got from anywhere else.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: that thou appear not unto men, to fast, but unto thy Father, which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.

links.text: That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.

provenance.significance: The refrain is the structural spine of Matthew 6:1–18 — three practices, three secrecies, three identical rewards — and 3 Nephi keeps the structure whole. It also keeps ‘shall reward thee openly’, which as at 13:4 renders a Greek phrase absent from the earliest manuscripts. Three occurrences of a textually secondary KJV reading in one chapter is not a coincidence one can absorb; it is the chapter's cumulative case for kjvSpecific.

links.note: Verbatim, with the KJV's two commas around “which is in secret” normalized. “seeth in secret” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 6:4, 6:6 and 6:18, and 3 Nephi 13 reproduces all three in order at 13:4, 13:6 and 13:18. The 1830 keeps “which” in both relatives; 1920 reads “who”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and thieves break through and steal:

links.text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:

provenance.significance: James 5:2–3 — ‘your garments are motheaten; your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you’ — is the New Testament's other treasure-and-corrosion passage and the one a reader may think of here; the exclusion register at 13:19 says why it is not in play. The decisive point is that James has no thieves and no heaven, and 3 Nephi has Matthew's whole antithesis intact across two verses.

links.note: Verbatim but for one word: KJV “and where thieves break through and steal” becomes “and thieves break through and steal”, while 13:20 keeps the “where” in the answering clause — reproducing an asymmetry the KJV itself has only in one direction. “moth and rust” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “break through and steal” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:19.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal.

links.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:

provenance.significance: Luke 12:33 gives the same teaching in wholly different English — ‘provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not’ — so the Matthean form here is not merely the more familiar one, it is the only one the Nephite wording can have come from.

links.note: Verbatim; the KJV's terminal colon becomes a full stop. “treasures in heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The verse completes Matthew's antithesis word for word, including the shift from “moth and rust” to “neither moth nor rust” and from “break through and steal” to “break through nor steal”, which is a pattern of negation the KJV performs and a paraphrase would flatten.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

links.text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 12:34: the KJV wording is identical in both, so no divergence exists to test. Assigned to Matthew on the sequence of the surrounding block.
provenance.significance: A verse whose parallel is word-for-word identical is exactly the case where a mediation test returns nothing and the adjudicator has to decide from context (CONVENTIONS §7). The catalogue records the failure of the test rather than hiding it: tools/mediation-check.py reports ‘identical wording — no test available here’, and the assignment to Matthew rests on sequence, not on wording.

links.note: Verbatim. “where your treasure is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:21 and Luke 12:34, and the two are identical in the King James Version, so this verse alone cannot say which Gospel is in view. It is placed with Matthew on the strength of its neighbours: 13:19–20 are Matthean against Luke 12:33 at every word, and 13:22 onward continues in Matthew's order.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.

links.text: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.

provenance.other: Matthew 6:22 vs Luke 11:34, checked by eye and against tools/mediation-check.py: the Book of Mormon has Matthew's “if therefore… shall be full of light” rather than Luke's “therefore when… also is full of light”.
provenance.significance: The eye saying is one of the few places in this block where Matthew and Luke are close enough to be confused and different enough to be told apart, so it is worth stating that the test was run and what it returned. Every point of divergence in the two KJV verses falls to Matthew.

links.note: Verbatim; only the KJV's punctuation of “if therefore” differs. “the light of the body is the eye” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:22 and Luke 11:34, and the two diverge immediately afterwards — Matthew has “if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light”, Luke has “therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light”. 3 Nephi 13:22 has Matthew's conditional, Matthew's “whole body” without Luke's “also”, and Matthew's “shall be” for Luke's “is”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!

links.text: But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!

provenance.other: tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 11:34 returns no decisive divergence, because the two verses are too dissimilar for the diff to align; the identity with Matthew 6:23 is verbatim and was confirmed by eye.
provenance.significance: This is a verse where the mechanical mediation check returns nothing usable — the two candidates diverge so completely that the differ cannot align them, and it reports ‘neither’ at every point. Read by eye the answer is unambiguous: 3 Nephi 13:23 is Matthew 6:23 without a word changed. CONVENTIONS §9's warning about the machine streams applies to the mediation tool as well as to the n-gram stream — a null result is a null result, not a negative one.

links.note: Verbatim, including the exclamation. Luke 11:34–35 has the same image but not this sentence: Luke's second limb reads “thy body also is full of darkness” and then “take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness”, where Matthew has “thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!” — an exclamation Luke does not have at all. “full of darkness” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Matthew 6:23, Luke 11:34, Revelation 16:10); the closing exclamation is Matthew's alone.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.

links.text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.

provenance.other: Matthew 6:24 vs Luke 16:13 differ in one word: “No man” against “No servant”. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's. tools/mediation-check.py reports ‘no decisive divergence’ because its common-word filter suppresses the test; the reading was taken by eye.
provenance.significance: This is the cleanest single-word mediation datum in the chapter and the machine could not find it. tools/mediation-check.py deliberately ignores divergences turning on a very common word, to keep its false-positive rate down, and ‘man’ is common enough to be filtered — so it reports ‘neither’ at the one point where the answer lies and then declares no decisive divergence. ADJUDICATING §4 warns about exactly this class of miss. The verse is decided by eye, and it decides for Matthew.

links.note: Verbatim — every word of Matthew 6:24, including “mammon”. “no man can serve two masters” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “God and mammon” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13. Luke's version of the saying is otherwise identical to Matthew's and differs in precisely one word, its first noun: Luke reads “No servant can serve two masters” where Matthew reads “No man”. 3 Nephi 13:24 reads “No man”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.1–24 (printed under the heading “Sincere Piety (Matthew 6.1–24)”)

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words, he looked upon the twelve whom he had chosen, and saith unto them, Remember the words which I have spoken. For behold, ye are they which I have chosen to minister unto this people. Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

links.text: Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 12:22: two decisive divergences, both favouring Matthew — the Book of Mormon has “or what ye shall drink; nor yet” where Luke has only “neither”, and it has Matthew's closing “Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?”, which Luke lacks.
provenance.significance: The frame does real work: it narrows the audience. Matthew 6:25–34 is addressed to the crowd on the mountain; 3 Nephi 13:25 turns it, mid-sermon, into private instruction to the twelve Jesus has just chosen, and Hardy's own section heading for the block reads ‘Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance’. The teaching that follows is thereby converted from a general counsel against anxiety into something closer to a missionary charge — which is how 3 Nephi 13:25–34 has been read in the tradition, and it is the frame, not the Matthean material, that licenses the reading.

links.note: Matthew 6:25 entire, prefixed by the chapter's second Nephite frame: “And now it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words, he looked upon the twelve whom he had chosen, and saith unto them, Remember the words which I have spoken. For behold, ye are they which I have chosen to minister unto this people.” From “Therefore I say unto you” the verse is Matthew word for word. “more than meat” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:25 and Luke 12:23, and the mediation test is decisive for Matthew at two points. The 1830 reads “saith unto them” and “they which I have chosen”; 1920 modernized both to “said” and “whom”, erasing two KJV idioms the first edition kept.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?

links.text: Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 12:24: decisive for Matthew, on the whole of the verse after “Behold the fowls”.
provenance.significance: Psalm 147:9 and Job 38:41 are the Old Testament's God-feeds-the-birds texts and both are about ravens, which is where Luke's version gets them; Matthew's generalization to ‘the fowls of the air’ loses the scriptural allusion. The Nephite text follows Matthew, and so inherits the loss — a small instance of a general pattern in this chapter, where what 3 Nephi reproduces is not the tradition behind Matthew but Matthew's own particular handling of it.

links.note: Verbatim. “gather into barns” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke's form of the saying (12:24) is not merely worded differently but is about different birds — “Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn” — so the Nephite “fowls of the air… sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them” is Matthean at every element, including ‘heavenly’, which Luke does not have.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?

links.text: Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?

provenance.other: Matthew 6:27 vs Luke 12:25: “by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature” against “with taking thought can add to his stature one cubit”. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's.
provenance.significance: A one-verse borrowing whose whole distinctiveness lies in word order rather than word choice, which is a useful reminder that this catalogue's evidence is not only lexical. The n-gram stream missed this verse entirely — it produced no candidate for it — because its window is scoring rare vocabulary, and the vocabulary here is shared with the very verse it needed to be distinguished from.

links.note: Verbatim. “one cubit unto his stature” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 12:25 reads “And which of you with taking thought can add to his stature one cubit?” — the same clause with a different word order and ‘with’ for ‘by’ — so the verse is a mediation test even though its vocabulary is shared, and 3 Nephi has Matthew's order and Matthew's preposition.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin;

links.text: And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 12:27: two decisive divergences, both favouring Matthew — the opening “And why take ye thought for raiment”, which Luke lacks, and the absence of Luke's run-on into the Solomon saying.
provenance.significance: The Nephite chapter's most famous sentence is also one of its most precisely Matthean. Two decisive divergences from Luke fall to Matthew, and the phrase that has passed into English by way of this verse — ‘the lilies of the field’ — is one that exists in exactly one verse of the King James Bible and nowhere in Luke.

links.note: Verbatim; the KJV's comma after “field” is dropped and its terminal colon becomes a semicolon. “lilies of the field” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 12:27 reads “Consider the lilies how they grow”, without ‘of the field’ and without the introductory question ‘And why take ye thought for raiment?’, both of which 3 Nephi has.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: and yet I say unto you, That even Solomon, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these.

links.text: And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.

provenance.significance: Recover Solomon's glory from where the phrase does not occur and the saying gains its edge. The King James Bible never uses ‘in all his glory’ of Solomon outside these two Gospel verses; what it gives instead is 1 Kings 10:4–7 and 2 Chronicles 9:3–6, the queen of Sheba's inventory of his house, his table, his servants, his apparel and his ascent to the temple, at the end of which ‘there was no more spirit in her’. That is the wardrobe a wildflower is here said to outdress — and in 3 Nephi the saying is spoken by one who is himself standing at a temple, to twelve men he has just told to take no thought for their raiment. The register at 13:29 records why the Kings and Chronicles passages are not catalogued as links.

links.note: Verbatim but for punctuation: the 1830 sets “Solomon, in all his glory,” between commas where the KJV does not. “in all his glory” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:29 and Luke 12:27, and the Lukan form of the saying is fused into the previous verse there — so the Nephite text's verse division follows Matthew's as well as its wording.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to-day is, and to-morrow is cast into the oven, even so will he clothe you, if ye are not of little faith.

links.text: Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?

provenance.other: tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 12:28 returns no decisive divergence — an artifact of the 1830 hyphenation and of the closing departure, which leaves the diff nothing it can align. Read by eye, the first half of the verse has Matthew's “the grass of the field, which to day is” against Luke's “the grass, which is to day in the field”.
provenance.significance: The change turns a rebuke into a condition, and it is the theologically loaded departure of the chapter. Matthew's clause is an aside of exasperation addressed to men who already have little faith; the Nephite clause makes the clothing contingent on their not having it. The promise is the same and its ground is not: one is generosity in spite of the hearers, the other is a covenant with terms. Read alongside 13:1's ‘I would that ye should do alms’ and 13:5's ‘thou shalt not do as the hypocrites’, this is the third place in the chapter where the Sermon's grammar of grace is rewritten as a grammar of requirement. Note also that the 1830's hyphenated ‘to-day’ and ‘to-morrow’, modernized in 1920, defeat the mediation tool's tokenizer here; the Matthean word order was confirmed by eye.

links.note: The verse tracks Matthew 6:30 exactly — “Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to-day is, and to-morrow is cast into the oven” — and then departs at its close. Matthew reads “shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?”; 3 Nephi reads “even so will he clothe you, if ye are not of little faith”. Hardy's note flags the divergence, printing what Matthew 6:30 reads against the Nephite text. “cast into the oven” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:30 and Luke 12:28, and the first half of the verse is Matthew's rather than Luke's: Luke reads “the grass, which is to day in the field” where Matthew and 3 Nephi read “the grass of the field, which to day is”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.30 (note a: “Mt 6.30 reads ‘O ye of little faith.’”)

pericopes.text: Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, what shall we drink? or, wherewithal shall we be clothed?

links.text: Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?

provenance.significance: Unlike the two omissions from the Lord's Prayer, this one has an obvious motive on the text's own terms: the clause distinguishes the hearers from Gentiles, and the audience at Bountiful is a remnant of Israel to whom the Gentile/Jew contrast of Matthew's Galilee has no application — 3 Nephi elsewhere uses ‘Gentiles’ for a people yet to come, not for the neighbours of the hearers. The three omissions in the chapter are therefore not of a kind: 13:9 and 13:10 remove petitions, and 13:31 removes an ethnography.

links.note: Verbatim. “wherewithal shall we be clothed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What follows is the chapter's third omission: Matthew 6:32 opens “(For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:)” and 3 Nephi 13:32 begins at “for your heavenly Father knoweth”. Hardy keys Matthew 6:32 to this verse and his note names the omission.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.31 (note b: the omission of “for after all these things do the Gentiles seek” from Mt 6.32)

pericopes.text: For your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.—

links.text: (For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.

provenance.significance: The verse is a doublet of 13:8, which reproduced Matthew 6:8's ‘your Father knoweth what things ye have need of’; Matthew's own repetition frames the whole of 6:8–32, and 3 Nephi keeps both ends of the frame even though it has shortened what stands between them. The catalogue records this as a fresh link rather than a recurrence because the wording differs — ‘heavenly Father’ here, plain ‘Father’ at 13:8 — and the difference is Matthew's own.

links.note: Matthew 6:32 minus its parenthesis, and the remainder is verbatim. “your heavenly Father knoweth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 closes the verse with a dash, which is the first edition's mark for the resumption of Matthew's argument after the excised clause.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.

links.text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.

provenance.other: Mediation tested with tools/mediation-check.py against Luke 12:31: decisive for Matthew — the Book of Mormon lacks Luke's “rather”, and it has Matthew's “first” and “and his righteousness”, neither of which Luke has.
provenance.significance: This is the sentence the Sermon at the Temple has been building toward and the Nephite text does not touch it. In a chapter that adds a frame, drops three clauses and re-points three imperatives, the injunction to seek the kingdom first arrives with every KJV word intact, including the ‘first’ that Luke lacks and that makes the sentence a priority rather than a preference.

links.note: Verbatim; the KJV's semicolon before “and all these things” becomes a comma. “seek ye first the kingdom of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 12:31 reads “But rather seek ye the kingdom of God” — without ‘first’, without ‘and his righteousness’, and with ‘rather’ — so the verse is a mediation test and it returns Matthew.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient is the day unto the evil thereof.

links.text: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.

provenance.significance: It is worth being plain that the transposed clause is hard to construe. The KJV means ‘each day has trouble enough of its own’; ‘Sufficient is the day unto the evil thereof’ inverts subject and complement and yields, at best, ‘the day is enough for its own trouble’ — which is nearly the same thought arrived at backwards, and which no editor has amended in two centuries. The catalogue records it as a departure rather than an improvement, and notes that it falls at the very end of the transcribed block, where a copyist's attention is likeliest to lapse. Against that: 13:2's ‘as will hypocrites do’ is the same kind of anomaly and falls at the block's beginning, so fatigue will not explain both.

links.note: The verse is Matthew 6:34 word for word until its last clause, where the KJV's “Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” becomes “Sufficient is the day unto the evil thereof”. “no thought for the morrow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, “the things of itself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “sufficient unto the day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the first two are reproduced and the third is the one that is transposed. The transposition survives into the 1920 edition and the current text, so it is not an 1830 slip later corrected.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 13.25–34 (printed under the heading “Jesus Instructs the Twelve to Rely on God for Sustenance (Matthew 6.25–34)”)

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words, he turned again to the multitude, and did open his mouth unto them again, saying, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Judge not, that ye be not judged.

provenance.significance: Recover the context and Matthew 7:1 is not the head of a discourse but the hinge of one: the Sermon on the Mount runs unbroken from Matthew 5:3 to 7:27, and the chapter break at 7:1 is a printer's convenience of the thirteenth century, not a joint in the text. 3 Nephi divides its Sermon at exactly the same three places — 12, 13, 14 for Matthew 5, 6, 7. The Book of Mormon's Sermon at the Temple therefore reproduces not only the Authorized Version's English but the Authorized Version's chapter divisions, which is a fact about the printed page rather than about a discourse delivered in Galilee.
provenance.other: “Judge not” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses, of which only Matthew 7:1 and Luke 6:37 govern judgement of one's neighbour; the rest (2 Chronicles 19:6, Isaiah 1:23, Jeremiah 5:28, John 7:24, 1 Corinthians 4:3) are about magistrates or about Paul.

links.note: The Sermon resumes where Matthew 7 begins, and the saying is reproduced entire: “that ye be not judged” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The synoptic alternative is Luke 6:37, “Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned”; 3 Nephi has Matthew's purpose clause and none of Luke's three-part expansion, and that choice holds without a single lapse through all twenty-seven verses of this chapter. What is added is not Lukan either: the frame sentence, and the Johannine “Verily, verily, I say unto you”, which stands in Matthew's mouth nowhere in the Gospels.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Judge not, that ye be not judged.
And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying,

provenance.other: “opened his mouth” occurs in exactly five KJV verses (Matthew 5:2, Matthew 17:27, Acts 8:35, Acts 10:34, Revelation 13:6); only Matthew 5:2 is the opening of a discourse to a multitude.
provenance.significance: The word that carries the argument is “again”. In Matthew the gesture happens once, at 5:2, and never recurs; here it is said to happen a second time. But the Book of Mormon's own opening of the Sermon, at 3 Nephi 12:1, has Jesus “stretch forth his hand unto the multitude, and cry unto them saying” — he does not open his mouth there. So the antecedent of “again” is not in the Book of Mormon at all. It is in Matthew 5:2, a chapter the Nephite Sermon paraphrases but at this point does not reproduce. The narrator is counting a gesture his own text never recorded, which is what it looks like when a frame is written around a source the writer has in view and the reader does not.

links.note: “He turned again to the multitude, and did open his mouth unto them again, saying.” Neither half of the frame is in Matthew 7, and both halves are doing repair work on the transposition. “Turned again to the multitude” answers 3 Nephi 13:25, where the Nephite Sermon inserts a turn toward the twelve that Matthew 6:25 does not have; “open his mouth” reaches back past that insertion to the gesture with which Matthew 5:2 began the whole discourse. The seam is visible because the repair is visible.

pericopes.text: For with what judgement ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.

provenance.significance: The 1830 reads “judgement” and 1920 corrected it to the KJV's “judgment” — one of the two places in this chapter where a later edition moved the Book of Mormon toward its source rather than away from it (compare 14:13–14). CONVENTIONS §8: the direction of an editorial change is itself evidence, and here the direction is restorative.
provenance.other: Luke 6:38's clause is embedded in the giving saying (“good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over”), none of which is here.

links.note: Word for word Matthew 7:2, and the mediation test is decisive at three points. Luke 6:38 carries the same saying — “for with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again” — and 3 Nephi has Matthew's “what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged, and with what” against Luke's “the same”, lacks Luke's “that”, and lacks Luke's “withal”. “measured to you again” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and those two are precisely Matthew 7:2 and Luke 6:38, so the phrase alone could not have chosen between them; the surrounding clause does.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.

pericopes.text: And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?

provenance.significance: This is the cleanest single-word mediation in the chapter and it is worth stating as a rule rather than a curiosity: wherever Matthew and Luke preserve the same saying in different English, 3 Nephi has Matthew's English. A discourse delivered independently in the New World has no reason to prefer one first-century Greek redaction's Jacobean translation over another's at the level of a synonym.
provenance.other: “the beam” occurs in exactly six KJV verses; two of them (Judges 16:14, Habakkuk 2:11) are literal timbers and the other four are this saying in its two forms.

links.note: Identical to Matthew 7:3, and the single word that separates Matthew from Luke is the word the Book of Mormon has. Luke 6:41 is otherwise the same sentence — “And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye” — but reads “perceivest not the beam” where Matthew reads “considerest not the beam”. 3 Nephi reads “considerest”. “the mote” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, three in Matthew 7 and two in Luke 6, so the noun is no help; the verb settles it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?

pericopes.text: Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and behold, a beam is in thine own eye?

provenance.significance: The strongest 1830 evidence in the chapter sits here. The first edition reads “Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye”, which is the King James wording exactly, awkward doubled preposition and all; the 1920 edition removed the first “out” and the current text still reads “Let me pull the mote out of thine eye”. The borrowing is therefore plainer in the running text of this catalogue than in any Book of Mormon a reader is likely to own, and the editorial change ran away from the source, not toward it (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.other: “thou hypocrite”, which the next verse carries, occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Matthew 7:5, Luke 6:42, Luke 13:15).

links.note: Matthew 7:4 entire. Luke 6:42 tells the same joke at greater length and diverges at three testable points: Luke has “Either how canst thou say”, Matthew “Or how wilt thou say”; Luke “the mote that is in thine eye”, Matthew “the mote out of thine eye”; and Luke runs verses 4 and 5 together into one sentence. 3 Nephi has Matthew at every point, including the verse division.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam is in thine own eye?

pericopes.text: Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye.

provenance.significance: Three of the four editorial deletions in this chapter fall in verses 4 and 5, and all three delete the same word from the same construction. Whoever prepared the 1920 text was smoothing a Jacobean idiom he found redundant, and in doing so he removed the clearest verbal fingerprint the mote-and-beam passage carries. It is a small demonstration of why the 1830 wording is this catalogue's running text.
provenance.other: The saying's vocabulary is confined to these five verses in the whole KJV: “the mote” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and “the beam” in exactly six, and outside Matthew 7 and Luke 6 the only “beam” verses are a weaver's beam and a beam in a wall.

links.note: Matthew 7:5 entire, and the second half of the 1830 finding: the first edition twice reads “cast out the beam out of” and “cast out the mote out of”, both of which are the KJV's, and 1920 deleted both instances of “out”. Luke 6:42's version of the same clause reverses the adverb (“cast out first the beam”) and substitutes “pull out” for the second “cast out”; 3 Nephi has neither.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye.

pericopes.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

provenance.significance: Matthew 7:6 is one of the Book of Mormon's most heavily worked biblical phrases, and this is where it is finally quoted whole. The catalogue already carries seven links to it before this chapter — 1 Nephi 19:7, Mosiah 29:22, Alma 5:53, Alma 60:33, Helaman 4:22, 6:39 and 12:2 — spread across five books and four narrators, every one of them using “trample under their feet” for contempt of the holy. A phrase that has been the Book of Mormon's own idiom for a thousand years of its internal chronology is here handed back to Jesus as a quotation. That is metalepsis running in an unusual direction: the source arrives last, and the reader who has met the idiom seven times meets its warrant on the eighth.
provenance.other: “that which is holy” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:6 and Proverbs 20:25, the latter about rash vows and consecrated food; “unto the dogs” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:6 and Mark 7:27.

links.note: Matthew 7:6 without a variation of any kind, and it is built out of three King James singletons: “pearls before swine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, “trample them under their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “turn again and rend you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. No synoptic parallel exists — the saying is Matthean special material — so mediation is settled by the absence of an alternative rather than by a divergence.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

pericopes.text: Ask, and it shall be given unto you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:

provenance.significance: The triad returns at 3 Nephi 27:29 in Jesus' own summary — “ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you” — compressed to two members and re-worded, which is what the Book of Mormon normally does with a Matthean saying. Chapter 14 is the exception that shows the rule: everywhere else the Sermon is paraphrased, and here alone it is transcribed.

links.note: Matthew 7:7 with one word added: the 1830 reads “Ask, and it shall be given unto you” where both Matthew 7:7 and Luke 11:9 read “given you”. The addition is not Lukan and it was never edited out — 1920 and the current text keep it — so it is a Book of Mormon reading rather than an 1830 printer's slip, most likely assimilation to “opened unto you” at the end of the same sentence, where “unto” is the KJV's own. The mediation is still decisive for Matthew: “and it shall be opened unto you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:7 and Luke 11:9, and Luke prefixes “And I say unto you”, which 3 Nephi does not have.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:

pericopes.text: for every one that asketh, receiveth; and he that seeketh, findeth; and to him that knocketh, it shall be opened.

provenance.significance: Worth recording precisely because it is negative. A chapter that agrees with Matthew against Luke twenty times running is not thereby shown to agree with Matthew here; it is shown that the question does not arise here. Hays's criterion of Volume has nothing to measure when the two candidate sources are identical, and honesty about that is what makes the twenty positive results worth something.
provenance.alternative: Luke 11:10, which is verbally identical in the KJV and cannot be excluded on wording.

links.note: Matthew 7:8 exactly. This is one of the few verses in the chapter that cannot settle its own mediation: Luke 11:10 reproduces Matthew 7:8 word for word in the KJV, so there is no point of divergence to test. “every one that asketh” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and they are those two. The verse is assigned to Matthew on the company it keeps — the verse before it and the verse after it are both decisively Matthean — not on evidence of its own.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

pericopes.text: Or what man is there of you, whom, if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?

provenance.significance: The 1830 preserves the KJV's “whom” and its resumptive “will he give him a stone”; the 1920 edition changed “whom” to “who” and deleted the “he”, producing “who, if his son ask bread, will give him a stone”, which is in no King James verse. Two words of grammatical tidying, and the sentence stops being a quotation.

links.note: Matthew 7:9 entire, and the divergence from Luke is structural rather than lexical. Luke 11:11 recasts the question — “If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone? or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent?” — folding the next verse into this one and dropping Matthew's opening. 3 Nephi keeps Matthew's “Or what man is there of you”, keeps the verse boundary, and keeps “whom, if his son ask bread”: “his son ask bread” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?

pericopes.text: Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent?

provenance.significance: Versification is not usually evidence, and here it is. The Book of Mormon's chapter and verse divisions are modern, but the units of thought they divide follow Matthew's, including at the two places (verses 9–10, verses 4–5) where Luke's arrangement would have produced a different join.

links.note: Matthew 7:10 exactly. Like verse 8 this one carries no decisive divergence of its own — “ask a fish” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:10 and Luke 11:11 — but the verse division does the work instead: Luke has no separate fish verse, having folded the clause into 11:11. 3 Nephi has Matthew's two verses where Luke has one sentence.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Or if he ask a fish, will he give him a serpent?

pericopes.text: If ye then being evil know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?

provenance.significance: This is the one verse in the chapter where preferring Matthew changes the sense rather than the phrasing. A risen Christ instructing a people he has just baptized with fire and the Holy Ghost (3 Nephi 12:1) has, in Luke's form of the saying, an obvious reason to promise the Spirit; the Book of Mormon takes the form that promises “good things” instead. Whatever else is going on, the chapter is not selecting its synoptic readings for their fit with its own narrative.
provenance.other: “give good gifts” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:11 and Luke 11:13, which is the shared half of the saying; every word on which they differ goes Matthew's way here. Note that tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive point for this verse — the divergences are adjacent and the matcher scores them “neither” — and the reading above is by eye against the two printed verses.

links.note: Matthew 7:11 entire, and the sharpest doctrinal divergence between the two synoptic forms falls exactly here. Matthew's Father gives “good things to them that ask him”; Luke 11:13's heavenly Father gives “the Holy Spirit to them that ask him”. 3 Nephi has “good things”, and it also has Matthew's “your Father which is in heaven” against Luke's “your heavenly Father”. “good things to them that ask him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “which is in heaven give” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is Matthew 7:11 both times.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?

pericopes.text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
