provenance.significance: The closing clause is the interesting one. “This is the law and the prophets” is a claim about the Hebrew scriptures, and it is spoken here to a people who have just been told, and will be told again at 3 Nephi 15:4–5, that the law of Moses is fulfilled and has an end. The Book of Mormon takes the clause over unchanged and then spends the next chapter explaining it away; at 15:10 Jesus reuses the phrase with a different referent, “this is the law and the prophets, for they truly testified of me”. The quotation creates the problem that the following chapter exists to solve.
provenance.other: “the law and the prophets” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, so the phrase is not distinctive on its own; what identifies the source is that Matthew 7:12 is the only one of the six attached to the golden rule.

links.note: The golden rule in Matthew's form, entire. Luke 6:31 has the same rule in half the words — “And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise” — and the test is decisive twice: 3 Nephi has Matthew's opening “Therefore all things whatsoever” against Luke's “And as”, and Matthew's closing “for this is the law and the prophets” against Luke's “likewise”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.

pericopes.text: Enter ye in at the straight gate; for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:

provenance.significance: The 1830 reads “straight gate”, not the KJV's “strait gate”, and so does every other Book of Mormon occurrence of the phrase in the first edition — Jacob 6:11, 3 Nephi 14:14, 3 Nephi 27:33, and the cognate “straightness of the path” at 2 Nephi 31:9. The 1920 edition restored “strait”. Two things follow. First, the substitution is of a homophone, not a synonym: “straight” and “strait” sound identical and mean opposite things here, since the point of the gate is that it is narrow, not that it is direct. Second, it is consistent across four books, which makes it the Book of Mormon's own orthography rather than a compositor's slip. A borrowing that arrives spelled by ear is evidence about how it arrived. The same verse then shows the opposite editorial motion: 1830's “that leadeth to destruction” and “many there be which go in thereat” are the KJV's relative pronouns, and 1920 changed both to “which” and “who”, away from the source. One verse, one restoration and two erasures.
provenance.other: We considered treating this verse as mediated by the Book of Mormon's own earlier use — Jacob 6:11 is already catalogued as a quotation of Matthew 7:13–14 and shares the “straight” spelling — and declined it: everything in the verse except the spelling follows Matthew word for word, including the two clauses Jacob 6:11 does not have, so the proximate model is the King James page and the spelling is the Book of Mormon's habit imposed on it.

links.note: Matthew 7:13, and three of its phrases are King James singletons: “enter ye in at the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, “wide is the gate” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “go in thereat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Lukan alternative, Luke 13:24, shares only “strait gate” and is decisively excluded at four points: it reads “Strive to enter in”, it has no wide gate, no broad way, no destruction, and no “thereat”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:

pericopes.text: because, straight is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

provenance.significance: The pair 13–14 is the single most productive passage of Matthew 7 in the Book of Mormon before this chapter: the catalogue already carries it at 1 Nephi 8:20 and 12:17 (the strait and narrow path of Lehi's dream), 2 Nephi 9:41, 2 Nephi 31:9, Jacob 6:11 and Helaman 3:29. When Jesus quotes it here he is quoting the verse out of which the Book of Mormon's most famous image was built five hundred years earlier in its own chronology. At 3 Nephi 27:33 he returns to it a third time and rearranges it, putting the narrow gate first and the wide gate second.

links.note: Matthew 7:14 entire: “strait is the gate” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “few there be that find it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, so the verse identifies its own source twice over. The 1830's “straight” for “strait” is the same homophone as in verse 13 and was likewise restored in 1920.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 27.33, cross-referencing 3 Ne 14.13–14 (Mt 7.13–14) and noting that there “v. 13 is split and v. 14 is inserted”
links.text: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

pericopes.text: Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.

provenance.significance: Three singletons in seventeen words is the highest concentration of King James-specific vocabulary in the chapter, and it is the kind of row that needs no argument at all. It is worth noticing what the Book of Mormon does with the saying elsewhere: at Alma 5:60 the figure is inverted — the good shepherd calls, and “if a wolf entereth” he drives it out — and at 4 Nephi 1:34 the phrase “false prophets” returns in the account of the church's decay a century after this sermon was preached.

links.note: Matthew 7:15 entire, and it is three King James singletons end to end: “beware of false prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, “in sheep's clothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “ravening wolves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthean special material; Luke has no parallel.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.

pericopes.text: Ye shall know them by their fruits: Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?

provenance.significance: Luke's version reverses which fruit goes with which plant. Matthew asks whether men gather grapes of thorns or figs of thistles; Luke asks whether they gather figs of thorns or grapes of a bramble. A tradition transmitted independently to another hemisphere might be expected to preserve the sense; this one preserves the pairing, which is the part of the saying that carries no meaning at all.

links.note: Matthew 7:16 entire. “grapes of thorns” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “figs of thistles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 6:44 has the same proverb with different plants and a different frame — “For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes” — and the test is decisive at four points, including the bramble bush, which 3 Nephi does not have.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?

pericopes.text: Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.—

provenance.significance: The good-tree saying reaches the Book of Mormon three times independently of this chapter — Jacob's allegory of the olive tree, Alma 5, Helaman 14 — and every one of those uses the Matthew 7:19 formula about hewing down rather than this verse's contrast. Chapter 14 supplies the two verses of the paragraph the rest of the Book of Mormon never quotes.
provenance.other: “corrupt tree” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 7:17, Matthew 7:18 and Luke 6:43.

links.note: Matthew 7:17 entire. “bringeth forth evil fruit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 6:43 states the same principle negatively and with “corrupt fruit” for Matthew's “evil fruit”; the Book of Mormon has Matthew's positive form and Matthew's adjective.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.

pericopes.text: A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.

provenance.significance: The deleted “can” is the only word this chapter loses from Matthew, and it costs the sentence its parallelism without changing its sense. Set beside the added “unto” at verse 7, it gives the measure of the whole chapter's divergence from its source: across twenty-seven verses and something over six hundred words, one word added, one word dropped, one spelling changed, and one “whoso” for “whosoever”.

links.note: Matthew 7:18 with one deletion: the KJV reads “neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit” and the 1830 reads “neither a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit”, dropping the auxiliary. No edition has restored it. “cannot bring forth evil fruit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the deletion leaves that singleton intact. The Lukan alternative is excluded twice over: Luke 6:43 reads “bringeth not forth” where Matthew and 3 Nephi read “cannot bring forth”, and Luke reads “corrupt fruit” where Matthew and 3 Nephi read “evil fruit”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.

pericopes.text: Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.significance: This is the Book of Mormon's single most reused sentence from Matthew 7 — Jacob 5:26 and 5:42, Jacob 6:7, Alma 5:52, Helaman 14:18, and again from Jesus' own mouth at 3 Nephi 27:11 and 27:17. Alma 5:52 is the instructive one: it quotes the saying with the axe clause attached (“the axe is laid at the root of the tree”), which is to say it quotes the Baptist's form, from Matthew 3:10 or Luke 3:9. Here, four hundred years later in the narrative, Jesus quotes the Sermon's form without the axe. The Book of Mormon distinguishes between the two King James settings of one sentence.

links.note: Matthew 7:19 entire, and the choice among the KJV's three forms of the saying is testable. “hewn down, and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9 — but the first and third belong to John the Baptist and both prefix “the axe is laid unto the root of the trees”, which is not here. The remaining discriminator is the relative pronoun: “every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, because Matthew 3:10 reads “which bringeth not” and Luke 3:9 reads “every tree therefore which”. 3 Nephi reads “that”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, by their fruits ye shall know them.

provenance.significance: Moroni quotes this verse at the end of the book and changes one word: “I remember the word of God, which saith, By their works ye shall know them” (Moroni 7:5). Fruits become works, and a saying about discerning false prophets becomes a saying about judging whether a deed is good — which is the argument of Moroni 7 as a whole. It is the same kind of substitution the Book of Mormon makes constantly outside this chapter, and its absence inside the chapter is what makes chapter 14 anomalous.

links.note: Matthew 7:20, the inclusio that closes the fruits paragraph. “by their fruits” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and both are this paragraph's frame, Matthew 7:16 and 7:20; Luke's version of the saying (6:44) reads “every tree is known by his own fruit” and has no such repetition.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
Hardy MSI at Moro 7.5, cross-referencing 3 Ne 14.20 and Mt 7.20
links.text: Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.

pericopes.text: Not every one that saith unto me Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.

provenance.significance: “The kingdom of heaven” is a Matthean expression: it occurs in exactly 32 KJV verses and every one of them is in Matthew, where the other evangelists write “the kingdom of God”. So the phrase in a Nephite Jesus' mouth is not merely biblical, it is specific to one Gospel's editorial habit, and that habit is a fact about Greek redaction rather than about anything said aloud.
provenance.other: “will of my Father” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:21 and Matthew 12:50.

links.note: Matthew 7:21 entire. “doeth the will of my Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Lukan counterpart, Luke 6:46, is a bare rebuke — “And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — with no kingdom, no entering, and no Father; the test is decisive at three points, all of them Matthew's.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.

pericopes.text: Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?

provenance.significance: Three of the verse's clauses turn on “in thy name”, and the people being addressed are, in the Book of Mormon's own narrative, people who have just been baptized in that name by the twelve Jesus named eight chapters earlier. The saying warns against a confidence that the surrounding chapters are in the act of creating.

links.note: Matthew 7:22 entire, punctuation apart. “in that day, Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, “have we not prophesied” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “many wonderful works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthean special material in this form; Luke 13:26's nearest equivalent is “We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets”, which shares nothing.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?

pericopes.text: And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.

provenance.significance: Mosiah 26:27 puts this sentence in God's mouth four hundred years before Jesus speaks it here, and puts it there in Matthew's wording, not the Psalm's. So the chapter's quotation of Matthew 7:23 is the second time the catalogue has met the verse in the Book of Mormon and the first time it is presented as a quotation.

links.note: Matthew 7:23 entire. “I never knew you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “depart from me, ye that work iniquity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The saying exists in the KJV in three forms and 3 Nephi has Matthew's at every testable point (see the separate row on Psalm 6:8 below): against Luke 13:27 it reads “profess unto them” not “tell you”, “never knew” not “know”, and “ye that work iniquity” not “all ye workers of iniquity”.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.
Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity; for the LORD hath heard the voice of my weeping.

provenance.route: Psalm 6:8 → Matthew 7:23 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “workers of iniquity” occurs in exactly 21 KJV verses, overwhelmingly in the Psalms; Psalm 6:8 is the one that pairs it with “Depart from me”, and Luke 13:27 quotes it in that form. Matthew 7:23 does not: he writes “ye that work iniquity”.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's one Old Testament source, and it does not arrive from the Old Testament. Psalm 6:8 reads “Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity”; Luke 13:27 keeps the Psalm's noun phrase; Matthew 7:23 breaks it into a relative clause, “ye that work iniquity”. 3 Nephi 14:23 has Matthew's relative clause, lacks the Psalm's “all”, and carries Matthew's preface “And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you”, which is in neither the Psalm nor Luke. Three decisive points, all Matthean. Recover what the borrowing suppresses and the metalepsis is sharp: in the Psalm the speaker is a man dismissing his enemies because God has heard his weeping; in Matthew, and here, the speaker is the judge and the dismissal is final. The Book of Mormon inherits the Psalm's sentence only after the First Gospel has reassigned the speaker.

links.note: The Old Testament stands behind Matthew 7:23 and the mediation test settles which route it took. Psalm 6:8 is the source of “depart from me” plus “iniquity”, and tools/mediation-check.py returns three decisive points for Matthew against the Psalm: the Book of Mormon has Matthew's whole first clause, lacks the Psalm's “all”, and reads “that work” rather than “workers of”. The same three points exclude Luke 13:27, which follows the Psalm's wording here. The verse therefore reaches 3 Nephi through the New Testament, not from the Psalter that a Nephite record claims to carry on the plates of brass.

pericopes.text: Therefore, whoso heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:

provenance.significance: Jesus applies this parable to himself twice in the surrounding chapters, and both times in the Book of Mormon's own words rather than Matthew's: at 3 Nephi 11:39–40, “whoso buildeth upon this, buildeth upon my rock … but he buildeth upon a sandy foundation”, and again at 18:13. Both use “sandy foundation”, which is in no KJV verse, and both arrive before the parable itself is quoted. The paraphrase precedes the quotation by three chapters.

links.note: Matthew 7:24 with one substitution: the KJV reads “whosoever heareth these sayings of mine” and 3 Nephi reads “whoso heareth”, the Book of Mormon's ordinary form (compare 3 Nephi 15:1, “whoso remembereth these sayings of mine”). Everything else is Matthew's: “wise man, which built” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 6:47–48 tells the parable with a different builder — a man who “digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock” — and no likening formula at all.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:

pericopes.text: and the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.

provenance.significance: The triad rain-floods-winds is what the Book of Mormon actually carries away from this parable. Helaman 5:12 has “the mighty storm … his hail and his mighty storm shall beat upon you”; 3 Nephi 18:13 has “when the rain descends, and the floods come, and the winds blow, and beat upon them”, which is this verse's three agents in this verse's order with the tenses shifted. The order is arbitrary and it survives every retelling.

links.note: Matthew 7:25 entire, and the mediation is decisive at four points. Luke 6:48 has one water and no wind — “when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house” — where Matthew has three agents in a fixed order: rain, floods, winds. 3 Nephi has Matthew's three, in Matthew's order, and lacks Luke's “vehemently”. “founded upon a rock” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:25 and, in a different construction, Luke 6:48.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.

pericopes.text: And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:

provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon reached this verse long before it quoted it: 1 Nephi 8:26 and 12:18 build the great and spacious building of Lehi's dream on it, and 2 Nephi 28:28 warns against the man “built upon a sandy foundation”. Nephi's dream turns a parable about two houses into a landscape with one, and the building that stands “as it were in the air” is the foolish builder's house with the sand removed.
provenance.other: “upon the sand” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:26 and Revelation 13:1, where John stands upon the sand of the sea.

links.note: Matthew 7:26 entire. “shall be likened unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “these sayings of mine” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 7:24 and 7:26, the two halves of this parable. Luke 6:49's foolish builder “built an house upon the earth without a foundation”; the sand is Matthew's.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
links.text: And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:

pericopes.text: and the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it.

provenance.significance: This clause is the most widely distributed sentence of Matthew 7 in the Book of Mormon and the catalogue has met it repeatedly before now: 1 Nephi 8:26 and 11:36 (“the fall thereof was exceeding great”), 1 Nephi 22:14 (“that great and abominable church shall tumble to the dust, and great shall be the fall of it”), 2 Nephi 28:18, Helaman 5:12. In every one of those the falling thing is a building or a church, and in every one the wording is adapted. Here alone it is Matthew's, unaltered, and the falling thing is a house in a parable. Read across the whole book, chapter 14 is the source arriving after four hundred pages of its own echoes — which is the shape of the finding the catalogue keeps making, and the reason a chapter that is 'only' a transcription is worth twenty-seven rows.

links.note: Matthew 7:27 entire, and the last verse of the Nephite Sermon. “great was the fall of it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Luke 6:49 ends “and the ruin of that house was great”, which the Book of Mormon does not have anywhere; every one of its eight uses of the clause is built on Matthew's noun. Matthew 7:28–29, the crowd's astonishment, is not carried over — 3 Nephi 15:1 substitutes its own frame.
bibliography: Hardy MSI, section heading at 3 Ne 14: “Parables of Discipleship (Matthew 7.1–27)”
Hardy MSI note at 3 Ne 14.27: “This concludes the Nephite version of the Sermon on the Mount. Note that 3 Ne 14 reproduces Mt 7 almost exactly.”
links.text: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when Jesus had ended these sayings, he cast his eyes round about on the multitude, and saith unto them, Behold, ye have heard the things which I have taught before I ascended to my Father; therefore whoso remembereth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, him will I raise up at the last day.

links.text: And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine:

provenance.other: “when Jesus had ended these sayings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “these sayings of mine, and doeth them” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 7:24 and 7:26, both of which the Book of Mormon has already reproduced at 3 Nephi 14:24 and 14:26. One Book of Mormon sentence therefore closes the sermon with Matthew's closing formula and summarises it with Matthew's peroration.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:28's suppressed continuation is the crowd's reaction and its ground: “the people were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes” (7:29). 3 Nephi 15 is that unstated clause turned into an argument. The chapter's whole business is the authority by which a speaker can declare the law of Moses at an end, and it answers in the first person what Matthew reports as a crowd's impression: “I am he that gave the law, and I am he which covenanted with my people Israel” (15:5). Matthew's audience infers the authority; this one is told its source.

links.note: The Sermon at the Temple ends at 3 Nephi 14:27, and 15:1 opens with the clause the King James Bible uses to close the Sermon on the Mount, in the identical structural position — “when Jesus had ended these sayings”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What follows diverges: Matthew turns to the crowd's astonishment, and the Book of Mormon instead reaches back four verses in the same chapter to the parable of the two builders, so that “these sayings of mine, and doeth them” — two KJV verses, Matthew 7:24 and 7:26 — arrives with the wise man's house replaced by a promise of resurrection. The sentence is a seam, and both halves of it are Matthew 7.

links.text: No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.

provenance.other: “raise him up at the last day” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, John 6:40, 6:44 and 6:54, all in one discourse; the Book of Mormon inverts the word order to “him will I raise up at the last day”. “at the last day” occurs in exactly five, four of them in the same chapter of John.
provenance.significance: The reward clause is not a decoration. John 6's refrain sits inside an argument about the Father's giving and drawing — “all that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (6:37), “except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (6:44) — and that is the note this chapter closes on twenty-three verses later: “ye are numbered among them which the Father hath given me” (15:24). The chapter opens and shuts on the same Johannine premise, that the audience in front of the speaker is an audience the Father assigned him, which is exactly the premise 15:13-21 needs in order to explain why there was a second flock at all.

links.note: “Therefore whoso remembereth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, him will I raise up at the last day.” The protasis is Matthew 7:24; the apodosis is not. Matthew promises the wise builder a house that stands, and this verse promises resurrection in the refrain of John 6, where “raise him up at the last day” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and nowhere else in the Bible. The chapter's first sentence therefore welds the end of the Sermon on the Mount to the Bread of Life discourse, which is a fair announcement of what the next twenty-three verses do: the Matthaean material is expounded, and it is expounded in John's vocabulary throughout.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had said these words, he perceived that there were some among them which marvelled, and wondered wat he would concerning the law of Moses: for they understood not the saying, That old things had passed away, and that all things had become new.

links.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.

provenance.other: Two King James singletons in one verse: “old things are passed away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “all things are become new” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse. tools/mediation-check.py against Isaiah 43:18 (“Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old”) returns three decisive points for Paul at every place the two differ: the Book of Mormon has “old things” and “all things ... new”, not Isaiah's “former things” and “things of old”. The apocalyptic commonplace reaches this chapter in its Pauline form only.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about a person — “if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature” — and the old things that pass away are the old man's. 3 Nephi 15 hears it as a statement about a legal dispensation, and the next six verses are spent forcing that reading: the old thing that has passed away is the law of Moses, and the marvelling is at the transfer. The catalogue's interest is that the transfer is unannounced. Nothing in 15:2 marks the words as a quotation; they are simply the saying the hearers cannot construe, and the reader who recovers 2 Corinthians 5:17 finds a soteriological formula being used as a periodisation.

links.note: “They understood not the saying, That old things had passed away, and that all things had become new.” This is 2 Corinthians 5:17 with one change, and the change is grammatical rather than substantive: the King James present (“are passed away ... are become new”) becomes a pluperfect because the clause is being reported rather than uttered. That shift is why the machine never proposed it — an n-gram stream reading contiguous windows loses the run at the verb, and it ranked Luke 2:50 first in this verse instead (CONVENTIONS §9). Both halves of Paul's sentence are King James singletons, and both are here, in order, and the verse says outright that they were said before and misunderstood, which is a claim only a quotation can make.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 15.2 (2 Corinthians 5:17)

links.text: And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them.

provenance.other: “understood not the saying” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The looser formula “they understood not” occurs in exactly six — Mark 9:32, Luke 2:50, Luke 9:45, John 8:27, John 10:6 and Acts 7:25 — and only Luke 2:50 has the definite article with the singular noun.
provenance.significance: Recover Luke 2:50's setting and it is the boy Jesus in the temple, and the saying his parents cannot understand is “wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?” 3 Nephi 15 is also set at a temple, its hearers also fail to understand a saying, and by 15:18 the thing they cannot understand has become specifically a matter of what the Father has and has not commanded him to say. The one King James verse about a saying of Jesus not understood is a verse about a saying concerning the Father, which is the subject this chapter drives toward.

links.note: The machine ranked this first in the verse and it is not the verse's source — 2 Corinthians 5:17 is — but it is not therefore nothing. “Understood not the saying” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon has it with the article and the singular intact, introducing a quotation the hearers cannot place. Catalogued at moderate confidence as a plausible second layer on a verse whose primary borrowing is secure.
links.whyNot: The contact is four words of an idiom the King James Bible has in looser form six times over and the Book of Mormon uses constantly, and this chapter's own three later formulas for incomprehension (15:18, 15:22, 15:23) are worded differently, which is what one expects of a narrator's habit rather than a borrowing. Nothing else of Luke 2 is present.

pericopes.text: And he saith unto them, Marvel not that I said unto you, that old things had passed away, and that all things had become new.

links.text: Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.

provenance.other: “Marvel not that I said unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's only change is thee → you, which the setting requires: John's Jesus is answering one man, this one a multitude that “marvelled, and wondered” (15:2).
provenance.significance: John 3:7's suppressed remainder is “Ye must be born again”, and its addressee is a master of Israel who cannot construe a saying about newness because he keeps hearing it as a statement about the old order — how can a man enter the second time into his mother's womb. 3 Nephi 15:2-3 is the same exchange with the terms made explicit: the hearers marvel “concerning the law of Moses”, and what they cannot construe is “that old things had passed away, and that all things had become new”. The King James Bible has exactly one rebuke of the form “Marvel not that I said unto”, and it is addressed to a teacher of the law who cannot hear that his order is finished. That is precisely this chapter's audience and precisely this chapter's subject, and neither text says so.

links.note: “And he saith unto them, Marvel not that I said unto you, that old things had passed away.” Five words that occur together in one King James verse, deployed to do the same work: to stop an audience marvelling at a saying about newness and then to explain the saying. The two halves of 15:3 are drawn from different books — John 3:7 supplies the rebuke, 2 Corinthians 5:17 the saying rebuked — and the join is invisible in the running text, which is the usual shape of this chapter's borrowing.

pericopes.text: Behold I say unto you, That the law is fulfilled that was given unto Moses.
Behold, I am he that gave the law, and I am he which covenanted with my people Israel; therefore, the law in me is fulfilled: for I have come to fulfil the law; therefore, it hath an end.

links.text: For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.

provenance.other: “the end of the law” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The bare phrase “hath an end” also occurs in exactly one — Mark 3:26, of Satan's divided kingdom — which is an accident of English and not a source; the contact is with Romans 10:4's noun phrase, which the Book of Mormon converts into a predicate.
provenance.significance: Paul's τέλος is famously undecidable between terminus and goal, and the King James “end” preserves the ambiguity exactly. 3 Nephi 15:5 and 15:8 resolve it, and resolve it temporally: the law “hath an end”, the covenant with Israel does not (15:8), and the prophets are not destroyed because their referents are still future (15:6-7). What Paul leaves as a christological claim — Christ is the law's end for righteousness to everyone who believes — becomes a chronological one, and the qualifying clauses that carry Paul's whole soteriology (“for righteousness to every one that believeth”) are the part not taken over.

links.note: “Therefore, the law in me is fulfilled: for I have come to fulfil the law; therefore, it hath an end.” The King James Bible speaks of the end of the law once, at Romans 10:4, and the Book of Mormon says of the law in the first person what Paul says of Christ in the third, keeping the noun and dropping the qualifications. The 1830 text repeats the predicate three verses later — “the law which was given unto Moses, hath an end in me” (15:8) — and the two together are the chapter's thesis about the law of Moses; the surrounding verses run “fulfil” and “fulfilled” six times in five verses, which is Matthew 5:17's verb, so the sentence is Pauline in its noun and Matthaean in its verb.

links.text: For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.

provenance.route: John 1:17 (with Haggai 2:5) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the law was given by Moses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. For the second clause, “covenanted” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — 2 Chronicles 7:18, Haggai 2:5, Matthew 26:15 and Luke 22:5 — and Haggai 2:5 is the only one where God is the subject and Israel at the exodus the object: “the word that I covenanted with you when ye came out of Egypt”.
provenance.significance: The Johannine Prologue's one sentence about the law divides agency between two names: the law came by Moses, grace and truth by Jesus Christ. This verse refuses the division and keeps both for the speaker, and the refusal is the premise of the chapter — he can end the law because he gave it, and he can say the covenant is unfinished (15:8) because he made it. Note that 3 Nephi has already built the risen Christ's self-declaration out of the Prologue at 9:15-18, so the Prologue is a text this book is demonstrably working in when it reaches this claim.

links.note: “Behold, I am he that gave the law, and I am he which covenanted with my people Israel.” Two self-identifications in one sentence, and the first stands directly against the King James Bible's only statement about who gave the law: John 1:17's “the law was given by Moses”, against 15:4's “the law ... that was given unto Moses” and 15:5's “I am he that gave the law”. The Book of Mormon is not reproducing John 1:17; it is reversing its preposition, and doing so in a book that has already drawn its christology from the same twelve verses of John. The second clause reaches for Haggai 2:5, the one place in the King James Bible where God says he covenanted with Israel at the exodus.
links.whyNot: The contact with John 1:17 is a reversal of agency and a shared subject rather than reproduced wording: “gave the law” is not John's phrase, and the assertion that Christ gave the law of Moses is a standing Book of Mormon position (3 Nephi 15:5 is not its first statement) which could be reached without John. Catalogued at moderate because the reversal is exact and because the Prologue is demonstrably in this book's hands six chapters earlier, not because the words match.

pericopes.text: Behold, I do not destroy the prophets: for as many as have not been fulfilled in me, verily, I say unto you, shall all be fulfilled.

links.text: Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.

provenance.other: “destroy the law” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reproduced Matthew 5:17 entire three chapters earlier, at 3 Nephi 12:17, inside the Sermon at the Temple.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:17 holds “the law” and “the prophets” together under one verb and one denial, and leaves them together. 3 Nephi 15:4-8 prises them apart and gives each a different answer: the law is fulfilled and “hath an end”, but “I do not destroy the prophets”, because prophecy still has referents that have not arrived (15:7, “things which is to come”). The exposition therefore uses Matthew's own denial — not come to destroy — to license a distinction Matthew does not draw, and the suppressed half of the source, “I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil”, supplies the verb the passage runs on: “fulfil” or “fulfilled” appears six times in 15:4-8.

links.note: “Behold, I do not destroy the prophets: for as many as have not been fulfilled in me ... shall all be fulfilled.” The saying was given whole at 3 Nephi 12:17 as part of the sermon, and this is not the narrator recurring to his own formula but the exposition returning to its text — the case ADJUDICATING §4 ratified at Mosiah 29:2, where a phrase's second use is the argument because the passage it first translated is the passage now being answered. Here the answering is a division: Matthew's single clause about the law and the prophets is split down the middle, and only half of it survives the fulfilment. Recorded as a link rather than a repeat for that reason, and because a reader who meets 15:6 with nothing attached has been told the chapter is not expounding Matthew 5:17, which is the one thing it is unmistakably doing.

pericopes.text: And because I said unto you, That old things hath passed away, I do not destroy that which hath been spoken concerning things which is to come.
For behold, the covenant which I have made with my people, is not all fulfilled; but the law which was given unto Moses, hath an end in me.
Behold, I am the law, and the light: Look unto me, and endure to the end, and ye shall live: for unto him that endureth to the end, will I give eternal life.

links.text: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.

provenance.route: Isaiah 45:22 (with Amos 5:4) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Look unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “and ye shall live” occurs in exactly five, of which Amos 5:4 and 5:6 are the two where it answers an imperative God addresses to the house of Israel (“Seek ye me, and ye shall live”); the other three are the dry bones of Ezekiel 37. “remnant of Joseph” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 5:15.
provenance.significance: The Amos context keeps paying three verses later. Amos 5 threatens that the LORD will “break out like fire in the house of Joseph” (5:6) and hopes he “will be gracious unto the remnant of Joseph” (5:15), and 3 Nephi 15:12 addresses these hearers as “a remnant of the house of Joseph”. So an imperative-plus-promise borrowed from Amos's summons to Israel is followed, within four verses, by Amos's own name for the survivors. Neither text draws the line; the sequence does.

links.note: “Look unto me, and endure to the end, and ye shall live.” The imperative is a King James singleton, and its interest here is that this book has used Isaiah 45:22 once already, at 3 Nephi 9:22, where the same speaker kept Isaiah's addressees and changed the verb — “repent, and come unto me ye ends of the earth, and be saved.” Six chapters later he restores Isaiah's verb exactly and changes the other half instead, and the substitute is Amos's: “and ye shall live”, the promise attached to God's imperative to the house of Israel at Amos 5:4 and 5:6. The catalogue records both uses because the pair is the evidence: a source used twice with complementary substitutions is being handled, not remembered.
links.whyNot: “Look unto me” is three words, and Isaiah 45:22 is already established as a text this book draws on, so the second use could be the speaker's own idiom rather than a fresh borrowing. The Amos half rests on a five-verse phrase and a thematic cluster rather than on a run of words, and “endure to the end”, which sits between the two halves, is Book of Mormon boilerplate from 1 Nephi onward.

links.text: And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:22 (with John 10:28) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:22 (Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13 read “endure unto the end”). “I give unto them eternal life” occurs in exactly one, John 10:28.
provenance.significance: The apodosis is the finding. 3 Nephi 27:6 has Matthew's own consequence — “endureth to the end, the same shall be saved” — so the Book of Mormon knows the King James clause and can reproduce it when it wants to. Here it does not: the reward is John 10:28's, from six verses before the “other sheep” saying this chapter is about to quote twice. Recover that context and the promise is one Jesus makes specifically to his sheep, in the discourse whose unfinished business fills 15:13-24 — “I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand”, followed at 10:29 by “My Father, which gave them me”, which is where 15:24 ends up.

links.note: “For unto him that endureth to the end, will I give eternal life.” The protasis is a King James singleton and Matthew's; the apodosis is not Matthew's. Matthew 10:22 promises that the endurer “shall be saved”, and the Book of Mormon can and does say exactly that elsewhere (3 Nephi 27:6). What it substitutes here is John 10:28's promise to the sheep, in a chapter that quotes John 10:16 twice — so the substitution runs in the direction the whole chapter runs, from the Synoptic saying to the Johannine discourse behind it.

pericopes.text: Behold, I have given unto you the commandments; therefore keep my commandments. And this is the law and the prophets: for they truly testified of me.

links.text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.

provenance.other: “this is the law and the prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the looser “the law and the prophets” occurs in exactly six. “they are they which testify of me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:39.
provenance.significance: John 5:39's suppressed setting is an accusation: it is said to people who search the scriptures for eternal life and will not come to the one the scriptures testify of. 3 Nephi 15 has just spent six verses on hearers who cannot let go of the law of Moses, and it closes the exposition by stating as settled fact (“for they truly testified of me”) what John 5 states as a charge against an audience. The word “truly” is doing the work: it converts a disputed claim into a summary.

links.note: Matthew's tag for the sum of scripture returns, three verses after being reproduced at 3 Nephi 14:12 in its Matthaean place as the coda to the golden rule, and it returns detached — attached now to “the commandments” the speaker has just given, and then glossed by a second source: “for they truly testified of me.” That gloss is John 5:39's, the King James Bible's one sentence in which the antecedent of “they” is the scriptures and the predicate is testimony to Christ. The effect of the fusion is a quiet shift of antecedent — Matthew's “this” summarises a commandment, John's “they” are the scriptures — and the sentence ends up claiming that law and prophets alike were always testimony, which is the conclusion 15:4-9 has been building toward.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words, he said unto those twelve whom he had chosen,
Ye are my disciples; and ye are a light unto this people, which are a remnant of the house of Joseph.

links.text: Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.

provenance.route: Matthew 5:14 → KJV → 3 Nephi 12:14 → 3 Nephi 15:12. FLAGGED: the `mediation` vocabulary has no value for an NT source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage — `OT-via-earlier-BoM` names the Old Testament case only — so the field is recorded as `uncertain` and the route is given here in full. This needs Wilson's ruling (CONVENTIONS §7).
provenance.other: “the light of the world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 5:14, John 8:12 and John 9:5, and 3 Nephi 15:12 has none of them: its phrase is “a light unto this people”, and “light of this people” occurs in no KJV verse at all. The wording therefore follows 3 Nephi 12:14 (“I give unto you to be the light of this people”), not Matthew directly. “ye are my disciples” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 13:35.
provenance.significance: The narrowing is the point. At 12:14 the saying was addressed to the whole multitude and its “world” had already been localised to “this people”; here Matthew's own “Ye are” is restored, the localisation is kept, and the addressee shrinks to the twelve alone (15:11). Everything that follows — the land of inheritance, the withheld disclosure at Jerusalem, the identification of the other sheep — is private teaching, and it opens by telling twelve men that they, and not the crowd they were standing in, are the light of this people. John 13:35's “ye are my disciples” belongs to the same manoeuvre: it too is said to the twelve alone, after a public ministry has ended.

links.note: “Ye are my disciples; and ye are a light unto this people, which are a remnant of the house of Joseph.” Two King James formulas in one clause, and neither is taken in its King James form. “The light of the world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and this verse has none of them; what it has is the sermon's own localisation from 3 Nephi 12:14, with Matthew's “Ye are” put back and the audience cut down from a multitude to twelve. Catalogued at moderate because the proximate model is a Book of Mormon verse rather than the King James text, which is a route the schema's mediation values cannot express — see provenance.route.

pericopes.text: And behold, this is the land of your inheritance; and the Father hath given it unto you.—
And not at any time hath the Father given me commandment that I should tell it unto your brethren at Jerusalem;

links.text: For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.

provenance.other: “gave me a commandment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's negative form, “given me commandment”, occurs in no KJV verse, which is what one expects of a construction being reused rather than copied.
provenance.significance: John 12:49-50 is the last sentence of Jesus's public ministry in that Gospel, and the disclosure 3 Nephi 15:14-16 says was withheld is the “other sheep” saying of John 10:16 — the one place in John where Jesus mentions hearers outside the fold and then says nothing further about them. So the chapter takes the Fourth Gospel's own reticence about the other sheep and gives it a cause, using the Fourth Gospel's own rule for why Jesus says anything at all. The metalepsis runs both ways: John 12:49 explains 3 Nephi 15:14, and 3 Nephi 15:14 purports to explain the silence after John 10:16.

links.note: “And not at any time hath the Father given me commandment that I should tell it unto your brethren at Jerusalem.” Six verses of this chapter turn on a principle the New Testament states once, and states only in John: that Jesus speaks what the Father commanded him to speak and nothing else. “For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” The Book of Mormon's contribution is to run the rule negatively — 15:14 and 15:15 say what he was not commanded to tell, 15:16 what he was, 15:18 that he was commanded to stop, 15:19 that he is now commanded to tell it here. John's rule accounts for what Jesus said; 3 Nephi 15 uses it to account for what he did not.

pericopes.text: neither at any time hath the Father given me commandment, that I should tell unto them concerning the other tribes of the house of Israel, which the Father hath led away out of the land.—
This much did the Father command me, That I should tell unto them,
that other sheep I have, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.

links.text: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.

provenance.other: A thirty-word verbatim reproduction, well above Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold, though this passage is not one of his thirty-six (CONVENTIONS §2). Five of its phrases are King James singletons on their own: “other sheep”, “not of this fold”, “them also I must bring”, “they shall hear my voice” and “and there shall be one fold” each occur in exactly one KJV verse. The only departures are the loss of the opening “And”, which the Book of Mormon's framing clause displaces, and a semicolon for the King James colon. On mediation: the shepherd oracle behind John is Ezekiel's, and “one shepherd” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Ecclesiastes 12:11, Ezekiel 34:23, Ezekiel 37:24 and John 10:16. tools/mediation-check.py against Ezekiel 37:24 returns four decisive points for John at every place the two candidates differ: the Book of Mormon has “other sheep I have, which are not of this fold” and “one fold”, and none of Ezekiel's David, servant, king, judgments or statutes. The oracle reaches this chapter in its Johannine form only.
provenance.significance: Everything this chapter does afterwards depends on a feature of the King James wording rather than of the Greek. John's second noun is ποίμνη, a flock, distinct from the αὐλή, the fold, of the first half of the verse; the English tradition renders both as “fold”, following the Vulgate's *unum ovile*, and modern versions separate them again as “one flock, one shepherd”. The Book of Mormon reproduces the conflation, and reproduces it twice (15:17, 15:21). It matters because the argument of 15:17-24 is about two enclosures becoming one — sheep who are “not of this fold” being brought so that there is “one fold” — and that is a reading the King James “fold” supports and the Greek does not.

links.note: The verse the whole chapter has been approaching, quoted entire and without a seam. It arrives inside 15:16's frame — “This much did the Father command me, That I should tell unto them” — so it is presented not as scripture cited but as the speaker's own earlier words repeated, which is exactly what John 10:16 is. Five phrases of it are King James singletons, and there is no other candidate: the Ezekiel shepherd oracles behind John share only the two words “one shepherd” and none of the wording the Book of Mormon actually reproduces. What CONVENTIONS §4 calls the KJV-specific claim is unusually sharp here, because the conflation of flock and fold in the English tradition is what makes 15:17-24's argument about two folds becoming one available at all.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 15.17 (John 10:16)

pericopes.text: And now because of stiffneckedness and unbelief, they understood not my word; therefore I was commanded to say no more of the Father concerning this thing unto them.

links.text: This parable spake Jesus unto them: but they understood not what things they were which he spake unto them.

provenance.route: John 10:6 (with John 8:27) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “they understood not” occurs in exactly six KJV verses: Mark 9:32, Luke 2:50, Luke 9:45, John 8:27, John 10:6 and Acts 7:25. Two of the six are the ones that matter here — John 10:6, ten verses before the saying 15:17 has just quoted, and John 8:27, “They understood not that he spake to them of the Father”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and shares this verse's object.
provenance.significance: John 10:6 records the incomprehension and does not explain it: “This parable spake Jesus unto them: but they understood not what things they were which he spake unto them.” 3 Nephi 15:18 supplies both a cause (“stiffneckedness and unbelief”) and a consequence John does not record — that the discourse was therefore cut short, and that everything the reader might have wanted John 10 to say about the other sheep was withheld for that reason. The chapter is reading a gap in the Fourth Gospel as deliberate.

links.note: “And now because of stiffneckedness and unbelief, they understood not my word; therefore I was commanded to say no more of the Father concerning this thing unto them.” The verse that reports the failure of the Good Shepherd discourse in John is John 10:6, ten verses before the saying just quoted, and its verb is the one used here. The second clause pulls in John 8:27, the King James Bible's one sentence about people not understanding that Jesus “spake to them of the Father” — which is the precise thing 15:18 says he stopped doing. Catalogued at moderate: the argument is the coincidence of a common formula with the specific discourse under discussion, not the wording.
links.whyNot: “They understood not” is a two-word formula the King James Bible has six times and the Book of Mormon has constantly, and 15:22-23 uses a differently-worded variant three times over, which suggests a narrator's habit rather than a borrowing. Nothing else of John 10:6 or John 8:27 is reproduced, and the case would collapse entirely if the chapter were not already quoting John 10:16 verbatim one verse earlier.

pericopes.text: But, verily, I say unto you, that the Father hath commanded me, and I tell it unto you, that ye were separated from among them because of their iniquity; therefore it is because of their iniquity, that they know not of you.
And verily, I say unto you again, That the other tribes hath the father separated from them; and it is because of their iniquity, that they know not of them.

And verily, I say unto you, That ye are they of which I said, other sheep I have, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.

links.text: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.

provenance.other: The second full reproduction in five verses: “other sheep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the rest of the rarity evidence is set out at 15:17 and not repeated here. The 1830 reads “ye are they of which I said” where 1920 has “of whom I said” — the first edition keeps the King James relative, which is the relative of the source clause itself (“other sheep I have, which are not of this fold”), and 1920's correction to the personal “whom” moves the sentence away from its model even as it improves the grammar. CONVENTIONS §8's second case exactly.
provenance.significance: John 10:16 is one of the Fourth Gospel's genuinely unresolved sentences — commentators divide over whether the other sheep are Diaspora Jews, Gentiles, or a later generation of Christians — and it resolves nothing itself. 3 Nephi 15:21 does the one thing the source refuses to do: it names them, and it names them in the second person, to twelve men standing in front of the speaker. The two verses that follow then rule out the reading the Jerusalem hearers are said to have taken (the Gentiles, 15:22) and explain why the Gentiles cannot be meant (they will not hear his voice, 15:23). The quotation is thus not decoration but the premise of an exegesis, and the repetition is what makes the exegesis possible: 15:17 gives the words as spoken at Jerusalem, 15:21 gives them again as fulfilled here.

links.note: John 10:16 quoted a second time, and catalogued rather than filed as a repeat because the repetition is the argument — the case ADJUDICATING §4 ratified at Mosiah 29:2. At 15:17 the words are reported as what the Father commanded him to say at Jerusalem; at 15:21 the same words return with an identification prefixed, “ye are they of which I said”, which is the interpretive act the whole chapter exists to perform. A reader who met 15:21 with a bare cross-reference back to 15:17 would be told that the second occurrence carries nothing new, and it carries the point.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: n. 70 — quotes 3 Nephi 15:21-22 as the Book of Mormon's own confirmation that the “other sheep” of John 10:16 are the Nephites. His argument in that passage is about the allusion to John 10:16 in D&C 10:59-62, and the Book of Mormon verses appear in a footnote as evidence for it; he proposes no source apparatus for 3 Nephi.

pericopes.text: And they understood me not, for they supposed it had been the Gentiles: for they understood not that the Gentiles should be converted through their preaching;

and they understood me not that I said they shall hear my voice; and they understood me not that the Gentiles should not at any time hear my voice; that I should not manifest myself unto them, save it were by the Holy Ghost.

links.text: He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.

provenance.other: “manifest myself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:21, and the verse immediately following it is the disciples' question about precisely the restriction 3 Nephi 15:23 describes: “Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?”
provenance.significance: John 14 never answers Judas's question directly. It answers obliquely and at length, by promising “the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive” (14:17) and who “shall teach you all things” (14:26) — so the mode of the restricted manifestation is the Comforter, and John leaves the reader to assemble that. 3 Nephi 15:23 assembles it in one clause: “that I should not manifest myself unto them, save it were by the Holy Ghost.” The Book of Mormon supplies the missing apodosis of John 14:22, and supplies it in John 14's own terms. Note that this is the second time in ten verses the chapter takes a Johannine silence as its subject — 15:14-18 explains what Jesus was not commanded to say, and 15:23 explains to whom he would not appear. Read together they turn the Fourth Gospel's reticence into a doctrine.

links.note: “That I should not manifest myself unto them, save it were by the Holy Ghost.” The King James Bible uses “manifest myself” once, and the next verse of that same chapter asks the question this sentence answers: how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world? The Book of Mormon has the reflexive verb, the restriction, and the excepted mode, and John 14 has the verb, the restriction, and — spread over ten verses rather than one clause — the mode. The borrowing is small in volume and exact in function, which is the shape CONVENTIONS §3a calls thematic coherence doing the work that vocabulary cannot.

pericopes.text: But behold, ye have both heard my voice, and seen me; and ye are my sheep, and ye are numbered among them which the Father hath given me.

links.text: But I have greater witness than that of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me.

provenance.other: “the Father hath given me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:36, where the thing given is works rather than people; the Book of Mormon transfers the phrase to persons, which is John 6:37 and 17:6's usage but not their wording. “nor seen his shape” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:37, the verse immediately before it. The chapter's characteristic adverbial “at any time” (15:14, 15:15, 15:23) is John 5:37's too; “at any time” occurs in exactly eighteen KJV verses.
provenance.significance: John 5:36-39 is a single continuous argument about witness — the works the Father gave, the Father's voice never heard, the scriptures that testify — and this chapter draws on all three parts of it: 15:10 takes John 5:39's “testify of me”, and 15:24 takes 5:36 and reverses 5:37. The metalepsis is the reversal. What John 5 lists as the Jerusalem hearers' disqualifications is what 3 Nephi 15:24 lists as the Nephite twelve's credentials, and the chapter has just spent ten verses (15:14-23) explaining exactly why the two audiences differ. The closing sentence is therefore not a benediction but the conclusion of the argument, and it is made of the same paragraph of John that the argument's opening was made of.

links.note: “But behold, ye have both heard my voice, and seen me; and ye are my sheep, and ye are numbered among them which the Father hath given me.” Two adjacent verses of John stand behind one sentence, and the first is inverted. John 5:37 is a charge against Jerusalem — “Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape” — and here the “neither ... nor” becomes “both ... and”, with the object moved from the Father's voice and shape to the speaker's own. The second clause then takes John 5:36's phrase, a King James singleton, and applies “given me” to persons instead of works. The 1830 reads “them which the Father hath given me” against 1920's “those whom”, so the first edition preserves the King James relative here as it does at 15:21; the modernisation quietly removes the last word-for-word contact with John 5:36 (CONVENTIONS §8).

pericopes.text: And verily, verily, I say unto you, That I have other sheep, which are not of this land; neither of the land of Jerusalem; neither in any parts of that land round about, whither I have been to minister.

links.text: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.

provenance.other: 'One fold, and one shepherd' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:16, and is reproduced intact at 16:3. The clause reworked here, 'which are not of this fold', is likewise John's and no other verse's.
provenance.significance: The interesting thing at 16:1 is the substitution, not the borrowing. The discourse has already given John 10:16 twice, verbatim both times, at 15:17 and 15:21, where the Nephites are identified as the other sheep. Now the same sentence is spoken again with one word changed — 'not of this fold' becomes 'not of this land' — and the change is what licenses a third group. A fold cannot be subdivided without dissolving John's figure, since the whole point of 10:16 is that there is finally one of them; a land can, and the verse goes on to distinguish this land, the land of Jerusalem, and 'any parts of that land round about'. The Book of Mormon has converted an ecclesial metaphor into a geography so that it can be applied twice, and then at 16:3 restores the metaphor unaltered — 'that there may be one fold, and one shepherd' — once the geographical work is done.

links.note: 'I have other sheep, which are not of this land.' Ten of the twelve words are John 10:16's and one of the two that are not is doing all the work: 'land' for 'fold'. The verse is the third use of John 10:16 in as many chapters and the first that alters it, and the alteration is systematic — 16:1 divides the world by land, 16:3 reunites it by fold. Note also that the KJV's inverted 'other sheep I have', preserved exactly at 15:17 and 15:21, is here normalized to 'I have other sheep', which is what a writer does when he is rephrasing rather than citing. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations.

pericopes.text: For they of which I speak, are they which have not as yet heard my voice; neither have I at any time manifested myself unto them.

But I have received a commandment of the Father, That I shall go unto them, and that they shall hear my voice, and shall be numbered among my sheep, that there may be one fold, and one shepherd; therefore I go to shew myself unto them.

And I command you that ye shall write these sayings, after that I am gone, that if it so be that my people at Jerusalem, they which have seen me, and been with me in my ministry, do not ask the Father in my name, that they may receive a knowledge of you by the Holy Ghost, and also of the other tribes which they know not of, that these sayings which ye shall write, shall be kept, and shall be manifested unto the Gentiles, that through the fulness of the Gentiles, the remnant of their seed which shall be scattered forth upon the face of the earth, because of their unbelief, may be brought in, or may be brought to a knowledge of me, their Redeemer.

links.text: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.

provenance.other: 'Fulness of the Gentiles' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:25. 'Because of unbelief' occurs in exactly three, Romans 11:20, Hebrews 3:19 and Hebrews 4:6; only Romans 11:20 is about Israel.
provenance.significance: The whole of Romans 11:20-25 is compressed into one sentence and in Paul's order. Israel does not ask (blindness in part is happened to Israel); the remnant is scattered 'because of their unbelief' (11:20, 'because of unbelief they were broken off'); the Gentiles receive the record; and the remnant 'may be brought in' through 'the fulness of the Gentiles' (11:25, 'until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in'). Recover Paul's context and the metalepsis is severe: Romans 11:25 makes the Gentile fulness a terminus after which 'all Israel shall be saved', and it is addressed to Gentiles precisely to stop them boasting. 3 Nephi 16 takes the same clause and builds the next six verses out of the warning attached to it — the Gentiles who are lifted up in pride have the gospel taken from among them (16:10), which is Romans 11:21-22's severity. The book that Paul wrote against Gentile presumption is being used, in Christ's mouth, to threaten it.

links.note: 'That through the fulness of the Gentiles, the remnant of their seed which shall be scattered forth upon the face of the earth, because of their unbelief, may be brought in.' A KJV singleton and a three-word rarity from the same Pauline paragraph, arriving together and in Paul's sequence. The argument for Romans 11:25 as the source was made at 1 Nephi 15:13 and is not restated; the row is written here rather than deferred because this is a new book, a new speaker, and — unlike 1 Nephi 15 — a passage that goes on to develop Paul's warning as well as his promise.

links.text: And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

provenance.other: 'Ask the Father in my name' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 16:23. John 15:16 has the nearest rival, 'whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name', with the preposition the Book of Mormon does not have.
provenance.significance: John 16:23 is a promise with no failure condition — 'whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you' — and 3 Nephi 16:4 turns it into a hypothesis about non-asking: if the disciples at Jerusalem 'do not ask the Father in my name', a whole dispensation of record-keeping is set in motion to compensate. The clause that in John guarantees an answer is here the clause whose omission produces the Book of Mormon. Worth noting that the same KJV verse also carries the 'Verily, verily, I say unto you' with which this chapter opens at 16:1 and repeats at 16:9 and 16:16; the discourse is speaking in the register of John 16 throughout.

links.note: A five-word KJV singleton, and the surrounding sentence is Johannine at every joint — the double amen, the Father asked in the Son's name, the Holy Ghost as the giver of knowledge (John 16:13). Held at moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and because the Book of Mormon's use is negated, which weakens the sequence evidence: the borrowing is a formula being reversed rather than a clause being carried over.

pericopes.text: And then will I gather them in from the four quarters of the earth; and then will I fulfil the covenant which the Father hath made unto all the people of the house of Israel.
And blessed are the Gentiles, because of their belief in me, in and of the Holy Ghost, which witness unto them of me and of the Father.

Behold, because of their belief in me, saith the Father, and because of the unbelief of you, O house of Israel, in the latter day shall the truth come unto the Gentiles, that the fulness of these things shall be made known unto them.

But Wo, saith the Father, unto the unbelieving of the Gentiles: for notwithstanding that they have come forth upon the face of this land, and have scattered my people, which are of the house of Israel; and my people which are of the house of Israel, have been cast out from among them, and have been trodden under feet by them;

and because of the mercies of the Father unto the Gentiles, and also the judgements of the Father upon my people, which are of the house of Israel, verily, verily, I say unto you, That after all this, and I have caused my people which are of the house of Israel, to be smitten, and to be afflicted, and to be slain, and to be cast out from among them, and to become hated by them, and to become a hiss and a by-word among them.

links.text: Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have hallowed for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people:

provenance.other: 'A hiss and a byword' is not a KJV phrase; it is 1 Kings 9:7's 'a proverb and a byword' with 9:8's 'shall hiss' put in place of 'proverb'. 'A proverb and a byword' occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Deuteronomy 28:37, 1 Kings 9:7 and 2 Chronicles 7:20 — and only the 1 Kings/2 Chronicles pair also supplies the hissing.
provenance.significance: The compound was adjudicated at 1 Nephi 19:14 and the argument is not restated. What 3 Nephi 16:9 adds is the other half of 1 Kings 9:7. Nephi took only the byword; here the verse arrives with its neighbouring clause attached — Israel 'cast out from among them' answers 'will I cast out of my sight', and the two stand in the same order as in 1 Kings. The verbal case is therefore better here than at its first adjudication, which is why the row is written rather than excluded. The metalepsis runs into the next verses: 1 Kings 9:7 opens 'Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them', and two verses later 3 Nephi 16:11 answers with Leviticus 26:42's 'then will I remember my covenant'. The same first-person 'Then will I' formula that pronounces the sentence is the one that revokes it.

links.note: 'To be smitten, and to be afflicted, and to be slain, and to be cast out from among them, and to become hated by them, and to become a hiss and a by-word among them.' The distinctive pairing and the casting-out are both 1 Kings 9:7's, in its order. 1830's hyphenated 'by-word' is the KJV's word regularized by 1920 to 'byword'; the hyphen is the compositor's, not a variant reading. Moderate rather than high because what is reproduced is a pairing spliced from two verses rather than a continuous clause.

pericopes.text: And thus commandeth the Father that I should say unto you at that day, When the Gentiles shall sin against my Gospel, and shall reject the fulness of my Gospel, and shall be lifted up in the pride of their hearts above all nations, and above all the people of the whole earth, and shall be filled with all manner of lyings, and of deceits, and of mischiefs, and all manner of hypocrisy, and murders, and priestcrafts, and whoredoms, and of secret abominations; and if they shall do all these things, and shall reject the fulness of my Gospel, behold, saith the Father, I will bring the fulness of my Gospel from among them;

links.text: Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity; but toward thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off.

provenance.alternative: 'Lifted up in the pride of their hearts' is a standing Book of Mormon formula (Jacob 2:13, Alma 4:8, Helaman 3:33 and many more) and carries no Pauline wording; the structural match may be a common inference from the same premise rather than a borrowing.
provenance.significance: Paul's grafted branch is warned that its standing is conditional — 'be not highminded, but fear', 'otherwise thou also shalt be cut off' — and 3 Nephi 16:10 states exactly that condition with exactly that consequence, in the same position in the same argument: the Gentiles are lifted up above all nations, and the fulness of the gospel is taken 'from among them'. The Book of Mormon's version withdraws the gospel rather than the branch, which is the substitution that matters: for Paul the Gentile can be cut off from the olive tree, for 3 Nephi 16 the gospel can be cut off from the Gentile, and the difference is precisely the one a nineteenth-century restorationist argument needs.

links.note: The verse follows 16:4's Romans 11:25 by exactly the interval Paul's own warning follows his promise, and it says what Romans 11:21-22 says: Gentile presumption forfeits Gentile privilege. Recorded because the sequence evidence is strong even where the vocabulary is nil — 16:4 takes the singleton from Romans 11:25 and 16:10 takes the argument from three verses above it. See CONVENTIONS §0a: the row is proposed, not asserted.
links.whyNot: There is no shared distinctive wording at all. 'Lifted up in the pride of their hearts' is the Book of Mormon's own idiom and none of Paul's four load-bearing terms — highminded, boast, graffed, cut off — appears. A reader who declines this row is declining a structural argument, not a verbal one, and the catalogue's own rule is that a bare cross-reference is not a link; what carries it here is that the adjacent verse 16:4 has already established Romans 11 as the passage in use.

pericopes.text: and then will I remember my covenant which I have made unto my people, O house of Israel, and I will bring my Gospel unto them;

links.text: Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land.

provenance.other: 'Then will I remember my covenant' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 26:42. Ezekiel 16:60's 'I will remember my covenant with thee' is the nearest rival and lacks the 'then'.
provenance.significance: The word that carries this is 'then'. In Leviticus 26 it is a hinge: the chapter has spent nine verses on the curse — scattered among the heathen, the land desolate, the cities waste, pining away in the enemies' land — and at v. 40 the confession of iniquity turns it, so that v. 42's 'then will I remember my covenant' is the first mercy in the chapter. 3 Nephi 16:8-11 reproduces that shape exactly and at the same length: the scattering, the treading down, the smiting and the byword occupy 16:8-9, the mercies and judgements are weighed at 16:9, and 16:11 opens 'and then will I remember my covenant'. The Book of Mormon is not quoting a covenant formula out of the air; it is running Leviticus 26's own sequence and taking the hinge verse at the hinge.

links.note: A six-word KJV singleton arriving at the structural position it occupies in its source. The substitution is instructive: Leviticus remembers the covenant 'with Jacob … Isaac … Abraham', naming patriarchs, while 3 Nephi 16:11 remembers it 'which I have made unto my people, O house of Israel', naming the nation — the covenant has been transposed from ancestors to a scattered remnant, which is the transposition the whole chapter is for.

pericopes.text: and I will shew unto thee, O house of Israel, that the Gentiles shall not have power over you, but I will remember my covenant unto you, O house of Israel, and ye shall come unto the knowledge of the fulness of my Gospel.

links.text: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

provenance.other: 'Come unto the knowledge' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 2:4. 2 Timothy 3:7's 'come to the knowledge of the truth' and Hebrews 10:26's 'received the knowledge of the truth' are the near neighbours and neither has the Book of Mormon's preposition.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 2:4 is the New Testament's most compact statement that God's saving intention has no national boundary, and three verses later Paul names himself 'a teacher of the Gentiles'. 3 Nephi 16:12 puts the phrase in the mouth of the God who has just promised that 'the Gentiles shall not have power over you' — the universalism is retained and the direction reversed, so that the object of the knowledge is not 'the truth' but 'the fulness of my Gospel', and the ones brought to it are the house of Israel rather than the nations.

links.note: A four-word KJV singleton, and the substitution at its end is the argument: 1 Timothy's 'knowledge of the truth' becomes 'the knowledge of the fulness of my Gospel', which is this chapter's governing phrase (16:4, 16:7, 16:10 twice, 16:12).
