links.note: ‘As I have prayed among you, even so shall ye pray … I have set an example for you.’ The KJV’s sentence has two limbs — the example given, and ‘that ye should do as I have done to you’ — and 3 Nephi 18 uses both, the second limb ten verses earlier at 18:6 (‘this shall ye always observe to do, even as I have done’) and again at 18:24 (‘that which ye have seen me do’). The Book of Mormon changes ‘given’ to ‘set’, which is not the KJV’s verb for it and is the reason the phrase drops below the n-gram threshold. What is transferred is John 13:15’s logic: an act performed by Jesus in front of disciples, then commanded as a standing ordinance on the ground that they saw him do it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had spake these words unto his disciples, he turned again unto the mnltitude, and saith unto them,
Behold, verily, verily I say unto you, ye must watch and pray always, lest ye enter into temptation; for satan desireth to have you, that he may sift you as wheat;

links.text: And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:

provenance.route: Luke 22:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with the watch-and-pray clause from Matthew 26:41 / Mark 14:38
provenance.other: “sift you as wheat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 22:31. “lest ye enter into temptation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 14:38 and Luke 22:46; Matthew 26:41 has ‘that ye enter not into temptation’. “watch and pray” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 26:41 and Mark 13:33 — Mark 14:38 reads ‘Watch ye and pray’. So the Book of Mormon’s sentence takes its first clause from Matthew’s form and its second from Mark’s.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter’s clearest evidence that Luke 22 is being followed as a sequence and not merely quarried. Luke gives the institution at 22:19-20 and the sifting of Simon at 22:31; 3 Nephi 18 gives the institution at 18:7-11 and the sifting at 18:18, twelve verses apart in one and eleven in the other. Recover Luke’s context and the recipient changes everything: in Luke the sifting is addressed to one man who will deny Jesus that night, and Jesus’ answer is ‘I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not’ (22:32). 3 Nephi 18 turns the second person singular into a plural addressed to a whole multitude, and replaces Jesus’ intercession with a standing command that they pray for themselves — which is what 18:19-21 then legislates, down to praying in families.

links.note: ‘Ye must watch and pray always, lest ye enter into temptation; for satan desireth to have you, that he may sift you as wheat.’ Ten consecutive words of Luke 22:31 with one change of tense: ‘hath desired’ becomes ‘desireth’. The phrase is a KJV singleton and the surrounding sentence is welded to the Gethsemane command, which itself appears in both its Matthean and Markan forms across 18:15 and 18:18. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and therefore not one of his thirty-six, but a reproduced clause from an identifiable single source, which is what CONVENTIONS §2 calls a quotation.

pericopes.text: therefore ye must always pray unto the Father in my name;
and whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is right, believing that ye shall receive, and behold it shall be given unto you.

links.text: And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

provenance.route: John 16:23 + Matthew 21:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 16:23; John 15:16 has ‘whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name’, with the preposition, which the Book of Mormon does not have. “believing, ye shall receive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:22.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons fused in one sentence, from two Gospels, and the seam is where the Book of Mormon inserts its own qualification: ‘which is right’. John 16:23 promises without condition and Matthew 21:22 conditions only on believing; the Book of Mormon adds a condition on the petition itself, and then makes the whole thing a standing law of prayer for a church (18:19-21). Recovering John 16:23’s context sharpens it further — ‘in that day’ is the day after Jesus goes to the Father, which is exactly what he announces at 18:27 and 18:35 and performs at 18:39.

links.note: ‘Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, which is right, believing that ye shall receive, and behold it shall be given unto you.’ Nine words of John 16:23 in order, then four of Matthew 21:22, then John’s apodosis restored in the passive. Both halves are KJV singletons and the machine found the first without the second, which is the usual pattern: the n-gram stream cannot see a source whose contribution begins after a clause boundary. The same John 16:23 promise stands behind 3 Nephi 16:4, where only the bare ‘ask the Father in my name’ survives; here the whole clause is present, so the row is written fresh.

pericopes.text: Pray in your families unto the Father, always in my name, that your wives and your children may be blessed.
And behold, ye shall meet together oft, and ye shall not forbid any man from coming unto you when ye shall meet together, but suffer them that they may come unto you, and forbid them not;

links.text: But Jesus said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.route: Matthew 19:14 / Mark 10:14 / Luke 18:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “forbid them not” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 19:14, Mark 10:14 and Luke 18:16 — the three Synoptic tellings of one incident and nothing else. All three pair it with ‘suffer’ and ‘come unto me’, and 3 Nephi 18:22 has all three words: ‘suffer them that they may come unto you, and forbid them not’.
provenance.significance: The chapter before this one is the blessing of the children (3 Nephi 17:11-24), so the KJV verse being borrowed is the one the narrative has just enacted. What 18:22 does with it is the finding: the words Jesus uses in the Gospels to stop disciples turning away children are turned into a general law of assembly forbidding the disciples to turn away anyone at all. ‘Come unto me’ becomes ‘come unto you’ — the object of the welcome shifts from Christ to the church, and the sentence becomes church order rather than a rebuke.

links.note: ‘Ye shall not forbid any man from coming unto you … but suffer them that they may come unto you, and forbid them not.’ Three distinctive words of a KJV three-verse phrase, in the KJV’s own construction, with the pronoun moved from Christ to the disciples. The n-gram stream instead ranked Ezekiel 16:33 first here on ‘that they may come unto’, which is registered as an exclusion. Mark 10:14 is already adjudicated at 3 Nephi 9:22 for a different clause of the same verse (‘of such is the kingdom’), so the recurrence is noted rather than argued again.

pericopes.text: but ye shall pray for them, and shall not cast them out; and if it so be that they come unto you oft, ye shall pray for them unto the Father, in my name;

links.text: All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.

provenance.other: “in no wise cast out” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:37, and “him that cometh to me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The pairing of coming to Christ with not being cast out is unique to it.
provenance.significance: Three times in ten verses the chapter forbids casting out — 18:23 of those who come, 18:30 of the unworthy, 18:32 out of the synagogues — and it is the same prohibition each time. John 6:37 is the promise; John’s Gospel is also the book in which being cast out of the synagogue is the standing penalty for confessing Christ (9:22, 9:34, 12:42, 16:2, ‘They shall put you out of the synagogues’). 3 Nephi 18:32 names the synagogue explicitly. Read together, the chapter takes the one thing John’s Jesus promises he will never do, and the one thing John’s opponents habitually do, and makes the first a binding rule against the second.

links.note: ‘But ye shall pray for them, and shall not cast them out; and if it so be that they come unto you oft, ye shall pray for them.’ The two elements of John 6:37 — coming, and not being cast out — in that order, with the Book of Mormon’s usual transfer of the pronoun from Christ to the disciples. The verbal contact is a construction rather than a run of words, which is why no machine stream proposed it; ‘cast them out’ by itself occurs in sixteen KJV verses and identifies nothing. What identifies John 6:37 is that it is the only verse where the two halves stand together, and that the rest of the chapter (18:25, 18:29) is demonstrably working through John 6.

pericopes.text: therefore hold up your light, that it may shine unto the world. Behold I am the light which ye shall hold up—that which ye have seen me do. Behold ye see that I have prayed unto the Father, and ye all have witnessed;

and ye see that I have commanded that none of you should go away, but rather have commanded that ye should come unto me, that ye might feel and see; even so shall ye do unto the world; and whosoever breaketh this commandment, suffereth himself to be lead into temptation.

links.text: Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away?

provenance.other: “Will ye also go away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:67. In John it follows immediately on 6:66, ‘From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him’ — the desertion caused by the flesh-and-blood saying of 6:53-56, which 3 Nephi 18:29 borrows four verses later.
provenance.significance: John 6 runs feeding (6:11-13) → come to me and I will not cast you out (6:37) → eat my flesh and drink my blood (6:53-56) → many go away (6:66-67). 3 Nephi 18 runs feeding and filling (18:2-9) → come unto you, do not cast out (18:22-23) → go away / come unto me (18:25) → eateth my flesh and blood (18:29) → do not cast him out (18:30-32). The elements are John 6’s and so, nearly, is the order; the difference is that John 6 ends in desertion and 3 Nephi 18 ends by legislating against it. Where John’s Jesus watches disciples walk away and asks the twelve whether they will too, this Jesus says he has commanded that none of them should go away.

links.note: ‘Ye see that I have commanded that none of you should go away, but rather have commanded that ye should come unto me, that ye might feel and see.’ The two verbs are John 6:67’s ‘go away’ and John 6:37’s ‘come to me’, set against each other as they are in John, and the sentence is a flat denial of the Johannine outcome. Taken alone the contact is thin — ‘go away’ occurs in twelve KJV verses. It is proposed because of what stands around it: 18:23 has John 6:37’s not-casting-out, 18:29 has John 6:54’s eating of flesh, and the chapter’s opening has John 6’s feeding. The row records the sequence, not the two words.
links.whyNot: The verbal evidence at this verse is two ordinary words, and ‘feel and see’ points at 3 Nephi 11:14-15 rather than at John. If the John 6 sequence elsewhere in the chapter is judged coincidental, nothing here survives on its own.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when Jesus had spoken these words, he turned his eyes again upon the disciples whom he had chosen, and saith unto them,
behold, verily, verily I say unto you, I give unto you another commandment, and then I must go unto my Father, that I may fulfil other commandments which he hath given me.
And now behold, this is the commandment which I give unto you, that ye shall not suffer any one, knowingly, to partake of my flesh and blood unworthily, when ye shall minister it:

For whoso eateth and drinketh my flesh and blood unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to his soul; therefore if ye know that a man is unworthy to eat and drink of my flesh and blood, ye shall forbid him;

links.text: For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 fused with John 6:53-54 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “damnation to himself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 11:29. “unworthily” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 11:27 and 11:29, and nowhere else in the Bible; 3 Nephi uses it twice in two verses (18:28, 18:29) and ‘unworthy’ once more. “eateth and drinketh” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 2:16 and 1 Corinthians 11:29. From the other side, “whoso eateth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:54, ‘Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood’.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 11:27 alone, if ‘my flesh and blood’ is read as the Book of Mormon’s own idiom rather than as John’s.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter’s densest verse and it is a weld. Paul supplies the warning — the adverb, the doubled verb, the damnation — and Paul never says ‘flesh’: at 11:27 his phrase is ‘the body and blood of the Lord’, a KJV singleton. John supplies ‘whoso eateth’ and the flesh-and-blood pair, and John’s discourse contains no warning about unworthiness at all. The New Testament’s two eucharistic hard sayings are on opposite sides of the canon and address opposite problems; 3 Nephi 18:29 is a single sentence containing both. Note also what the fusion costs: ‘flesh and blood’ as a unit occurs in five KJV verses, and in every one of them it means human nature, not sacramental food.

links.note: ‘For whoso eateth and drinketh my flesh and blood unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to his soul.’ Paul’s clause is reproduced almost intact — the doubled ‘eateth and drinketh’ on both sides of the adverb, the adverb itself, and the damnation — with one substitution: ‘to himself’ becomes ‘to his soul’. The object of the eating is John’s, not Paul’s, and the opening ‘whoso eateth’ is John 6:54’s own first two words. Paul’s explanatory tag, ‘not discerning the Lord’s body’, is dropped and replaced by an administrative rule (18:28-30): the disciples are to know who is unworthy and forbid him. That converts Paul’s self-examination into a gatekeeping duty, which is the pastoral question the rest of the chapter answers.

pericopes.text: nevertheless ye shall not cast him out from among you, but ye shall minister unto him, and shall pray for him unto the Father, in my name. and if it so be that he repenteth, and is babtized in my name, then shall ye receive him, and shall minister unto him of my flesh and blood;
but if he repenteth not, he shall not be numbered among my people, that he may not destroy my people: For behold I know my sheep, and they are numbered;

links.text: I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.

provenance.other: “know my sheep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:14.
provenance.significance: John 10:14’s knowing is mutual and is the ground of the shepherd’s laying down his life for the flock; here it is cited as the ground for keeping a man out of it — ‘he shall not be numbered among my people, that he may not destroy my people: for behold I know my sheep’. The Book of Mormon then adds a word John does not have: ‘and they are numbered’. Numbering sheep is a shepherd’s act nowhere in John 10 and is what makes the sentence an argument about membership rolls rather than about intimacy. The other-sheep verse of the same discourse, John 10:16, is already at work at 3 Nephi 15:21 and 16:1, so this chapter’s shepherd language is continuous with the discourse the visit has been quoting for three chapters.

links.note: ‘He shall not be numbered among my people, that he may not destroy my people: for behold I know my sheep, and they are numbered.’ Three words of a KJV singleton, in the first person, in a speech that has been drawing on John 10 since 15:21. The verse turns the shepherd’s knowledge into an audit — the same verb, ‘numbered’, governs both the excluded man and the sheep, so that being known and being counted are made one thing. Note that 18:32 immediately reverses direction and forbids casting the man out of the synagogues, so the exclusion of 18:31 is from the roll and not from the assembly.

pericopes.text: nevertheless ye shall not cast him out of your synagogues, or your places of worship, for unto such shall ye continue to minister; for ye know not but what they will return and repent, and come unto me with full purpose of heart, and I shall heal them, and ye shall be the means of bringing salvation unto them.
Therefore keep these sayings which I have commanded you, that ye come not under condemnation: For wo unto him whom the Father condemneth.

links.text: And if any man hunger, let him eat at home; that ye come not together unto condemnation. And the rest will I set in order when I come.

provenance.other: “unto condemnation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 11:34, and “come not together unto condemnation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon reads ‘that ye come not under condemnation’ — one preposition apart.
provenance.significance: The sequence is the finding. 1 Corinthians 11 gives the institution (11:23-25), then the unworthy eating and its damnation (11:27-29), then closes the instruction with ‘that ye come not together unto condemnation’ (11:34). 3 Nephi 18 gives the institution (18:3-11), then the unworthy eating and its damnation (18:28-29), then closes with ‘that ye come not under condemnation’ (18:33). Two chapters, the same three moves, the same two rare words at the same point in the sequence. Whatever else the chapter is doing, at 18:28-34 it is following the shape of 1 Corinthians 11 from the warning to the sign-off.

links.note: ‘Therefore keep these sayings which I have commanded you, that ye come not under condemnation.’ The KJV’s phrase is unique to 1 Corinthians 11:34 and the substitution of ‘under’ for ‘together unto’ is exactly the kind of change that hides a borrowing from an n-gram search — nothing proposed this verse, and it is one of the two or three strongest in the chapter. Paul’s ‘together’ is doing work the Book of Mormon does not need, since his condemnation attaches to the assembly convening badly; here it attaches to individual disobedience, and the phrase is generalised accordingly.

pericopes.text: And I give you these commandments, because of the disputations which hath been among you beforetime. And blessed are ye if ye have no disputations among you.

links.text: For first of all, when ye come together in the church, I hear that there be divisions among you; and I partly believe it.

provenance.other: “divisions among you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 1:10 and 1 Corinthians 11:18; “no divisions among you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 1:10. The Book of Mormon’s word is ‘disputations’, which is not the KJV’s word here at all.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 11 gives its sacrament instruction because of divisions in the assembly (11:18-19), and closes it so that they may not come together unto condemnation (11:34). 3 Nephi 18 gives its sacrament commandments ‘because of the disputations which hath been among you’ (18:34), immediately after ‘that ye come not under condemnation’ (18:33). Both the motive and the sign-off are in Paul’s order. That the Book of Mormon reaches for its own word rather than Paul’s is what keeps this at moderate; that it reaches for it at Paul’s point in Paul’s argument is why the row exists.

links.note: ‘I give you these commandments, because of the disputations which hath been among you beforetime. And blessed are ye if ye have no disputations among you.’ The second sentence has 1 Corinthians 1:10’s construction — that there be no divisions among you — with a different noun, and the first has 1 Corinthians 11:18’s function: the divisions are the reason the sacrament instruction is being given. The link is structural rather than verbal and is proposed as such. The 1830 ‘hath been among you beforetime’ keeps a KJV word (‘beforetime’) that 1920 simply deleted.
links.whyNot: ‘Disputations’ is the Book of Mormon’s own term and 3 Nephi 11:28-29 has already forbidden disputations twice, without any Pauline framing, so 18:34 may be looking back to 11:28 and not to Corinth. There is no shared distinctive word: the argument is entirely from the position of the sentence in a sequence, and a reader who declines the 1 Corinthians 11 sequence at 18:29 and 18:33 should decline this too.

pericopes.text: And now I go unto the Father, because it is expedient that I should go unto the Father, for your sakes.

links.text: Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you.

provenance.other: “it is expedient” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 11:50 and John 16:7. The n-gram stream instead proposed John 14:28 here, on ‘I go unto the Father’, which is the phrase’s home but carries no expediency.
provenance.significance: Both KJV occurrences are in John and both are about a departure that benefits others, and the other one is Caiaphas: ‘it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people’ (John 11:50), which the catalogue has already met at 1 Nephi 4:13. So the King James Bible uses this construction twice, once for the death of Jesus as political calculation and once for his going to the Father as gift, and 3 Nephi 18:35 has the second with the first standing behind it. The metalepsis is available whether or not it was intended: the expediency that killed him and the expediency that takes him to the Father are the same word.
provenance.alternative: John 14:28 for ‘I go unto the Father’, which the Book of Mormon also has — but 14:28 has no expediency clause and no ‘for your sakes’.

links.note: ‘And now I go unto the Father, because it is expedient that I should go unto the Father, for your sakes.’ John 16:7’s three elements are all present — the going, the expediency of the going, and the benefit to the hearers — in John’s order, with ‘for your sakes’ for John’s ‘for you’ and ‘unto the Father’ for John’s ‘away’ (which John himself supplies at 16:10 and 14:28). What John gives as the reason — that the Comforter cannot come while he stays — is not stated here but is performed: the last thing Jesus does before departing is give the disciples power to bestow the Holy Ghost (18:36-37).

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had made an end of these sayings, he touched with his hand the disciples whom he had chosen, one by one, even until he had touched them all, and spake unto them as he touched them;

and the multitude heard not the words which he spake, therefore they did not bear record; but the disciples bear record that he gave them power to give the Holy Ghost. And I will shew unto you hereafter that this record is true.

links.text: Saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “he may receive the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:19, and “the Holy Ghost was given” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:18. Acts 8:14-19 is the King James Bible’s only passage in which a power to confer the Holy Ghost by touch is spoken of as a transferable thing.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing acquires an edge the Book of Mormon does not comment on. The KJV’s one account of a power to give the Holy Ghost is the account of a man who tries to buy it — Simon offers the apostles money, and Peter answers ‘Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money’ (Acts 8:20). 3 Nephi 18:37 confers exactly that power, by touch, on twelve men, and immediately withholds the words — ‘the multitude heard not the words which he spake’. The one thing the KJV says about this power is that it is not for sale and not for onlookers; this chapter gives it in silence, in front of a crowd that cannot hear.

links.note: ‘The disciples bear record that he gave them power to give the Holy Ghost.’ Two of the three content words — power, and the giving of the Holy Ghost — with the touching of the disciples one by one at 18:36 supplying the third, which in Acts 8 is the laying on of hands. The whole verse is constructed on a passage no machine stream proposed, since ‘give the Holy Ghost’ as a string occurs in no KJV verse at all: the KJV always writes it as the Holy Ghost being received or given, never as a person giving it. The 1830 has ‘bear record’ twice where 1920 reads ‘bare’, and ‘shew’ where 1920 reads ‘show’.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had touched them all, there came a cloud and overshadowed the multitude, that they could not see Jesus.

links.text: While he thus spake, there came a cloud, and overshadowed them: and they feared as they entered into the cloud.

provenance.route: Luke 9:34 → KJV → Book of Mormon, doing the work of Acts 1:9
provenance.other: “there came a cloud” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 9:34; Matthew 17:5 has ‘a bright cloud overshadowed them’ and Mark 9:7 ‘there was a cloud that overshadowed them’. For the departure, “a cloud received him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:9, and “carried up into heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:51.
provenance.significance: The KJV has two clouds around Jesus and they do opposite things. At the Transfiguration the cloud comes down and the disciples enter it and hear the Father’s voice; at the Ascension the cloud takes him up and out of sight. 3 Nephi 18:38-39 uses the Transfiguration’s wording to do the Ascension’s work: ‘there came a cloud and overshadowed the multitude, that they could not see Jesus … he departed from them, and ascended into Heaven’. The transfer is legible because this book has already used the other end of Luke 9 — 3 Nephi 11:7 quotes the voice out of the cloud. So the visit closes with the cloud that opened it, turned from a theophany the disciples walk into to a screen they are left behind.

links.note: ‘There came a cloud and overshadowed the multitude, that they could not see Jesus.’ Six words of a KJV singleton, with the object changed from the disciples to the multitude and a purpose clause added that Luke has no room for. The purpose clause is the Ascension’s: Acts 1:9’s cloud receives him ‘out of their sight’, which is the only reason a cloud is ever said in the Bible to prevent seeing Jesus. Luke 24:51’s ‘parted from them, and carried up into heaven’ stands behind 18:39’s ‘departed from them, and ascended into Heaven’ at one remove, since the Book of Mormon uses ‘ascended’, which is John’s verb (John 20:17) rather than Luke’s.

pericopes.text: And while they were overshadowed, he departed from them, and ascended into Heaven.— And the disciples saw and did bear record that he ascended again into Heaven.
And now it came to pass that when Jesus had ascended into Heaven, the multitude did disperse, and every man did take his wife and his children, and did return to his own home.

And it was noised abroad among the people immediately, before it was yet dark, that the multitude had seen Jesus, and that he had ministered unto them, and that he would also show himself on the morrow unto the multitude;

links.text: Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.

provenance.other: “noised abroad” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 1:65 and Acts 2:6; the Book of Mormon uses it twice in two verses here (19:2, 19:3). Within Acts 2:6 the phrase is immediately followed by “the multitude came together”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and 19:4 opens “when the multitude was gathered together”. Luke 1:65's setting is the naming of John the Baptist, and it has no second element in common.
provenance.alternative: Luke 1:65, “all these sayings were noised abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea”, is the other occurrence and is a closer match for the sense of news travelling overnight through a countryside. Nothing but the Pentecost sequence chooses between them.
provenance.significance: Read as a whole, 19:1-14 is Acts 2 with the order of its parts kept: a report noised abroad (19:2-3, Acts 2:6), a multitude assembling in consequence (19:4, Acts 2:6), and then the descent of the Holy Ghost with fire on the assembled disciples while the crowd looks on and testifies (19:13-14, Acts 2:3-4). The Nephite twelve receive at their own Pentecost what the Jerusalem twelve received at theirs, and the KJV phrase that opens the Jerusalem account is the phrase that opens this one. Two words is thin evidence for that reading on its own, which is why it is graded moderate; the argument is the sequence, not the phrase.

links.note: “And it was noised abroad among the people immediately … yea, and even all the night it was noised abroad concerning Jesus.” Two words, from a two-verse KJV phrase, but placed at the head of a chapter that then reproduces Acts 2's sequence — assembly, Holy Ghost, fire, witnessing multitude — in Acts 2's order. Proposed under CONVENTIONS §0a as worth putting on the table; a reader who declines the verbal link is still owed the observation about the sequence.
links.whyNot: “Noised abroad” is the natural King James English for a rumour spreading and the Book of Mormon writer had two verses to have picked it up from. Nothing else of Acts 2:6 — the confounding, the languages — is present, and the assembling verb at 19:4 is “gathered together”, not Acts's “came together”.

pericopes.text: yea, and even all the night it was noised abroad concerning Jesus; and insomuch did they send forth unto the people, that there were many, yea, an exceeding great number did labor exceedingly all that night, that they might be on the morrow in the place where Jesus should shew himself unto the multitude.

And it came to pass that on the morrow, when the multitude was gathered together, behold Nephi and his brother, whom he had raised from the dead, whose name was Timothy, and also his son, whose name was Jonas, and also Mathoni, and Mathonihah, his brother, and Kumen, and Kumenonhi, and Jeremiah, and Shemnon, and Jonas, and Zedekiah, and Isaiah: Now these were the names of the disciples whom Jesus had chosen. And it came to pass that they went forth and stood in the midst of the multitude.
And behold, the multitude was so great, that they did cause that they should be separated into twelve bodies.
And the twelve did teach the multitude; and behold, they did cause that the multitude should kneel down upon the face of the earth, and should pray unto the Father, in the name of Jesus.
And the disciples did pray unto the Father also, in the name of Jesus. And it came to pass that they arose and ministered unto the people.
And when they had ministered those same words which Jesus had spoken—nothing varying from the words which Jesus had spoken—behold, they knelt again, and prayed to the Father in the name of Jesus;
and they did pray for that which they most desired; and they desired that the Holy Ghost should be given unto them.
And when they had thus prayed, they went down unto the water’s edge, and the multitude followed them.
And it came to pass that Nephi went down into the water, and was baptized.
And he came up out of the water, and began to baptize. And he baptized all they whom Jesus had chosen.

links.text: And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way rejoicing.

provenance.other: “come up out of the water” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:39. The only other KJV description of anyone emerging from a baptism is Mark 1:10's “coming up out of the water”, and Matthew 3:16's “went up straightway out of the water”; the Book of Mormon has the participle of neither but the perfect of Acts — 19:12 “he came up out of the water”, 19:13 “had come up out of the water”. tools/mediation-check.py finds no divergence the Book of Mormon reproduces except the absent clauses of Mark, so the case rests on the verbal form.
provenance.significance: Acts 8:39 is the KJV's one verse about a man coming up out of the water and the Spirit acting immediately: Philip is caught away, and the eunuch goes on his way rejoicing. 3 Nephi 19:12-13 keeps the sequence and redirects the Spirit — the men who come up out of the water are not left behind by the Holy Ghost but filled with it. The other candidate, Mark 1:10, would make Nephi's baptism the Lord's own; that reading is available and the wording does not support it.

links.note: “And he came up out of the water, and began to baptize.” Five words matching the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, in the chapter's one narrated baptism, and the very next verse repeats it. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass when they were all baptized, and had come up out of the water, the Holy Ghost did fall upon them, and they were filled with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.

links.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.route: Matthew 3:11 (or Luke 3:16) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the Holy Ghost, and with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16 — the Baptist's promise in each synoptic. tools/mediation-check.py finds no point at which those two diverge that 3 Nephi 19:13 reproduces, so the synoptic cannot be chosen and the mediation is recorded as direct-NT without a gospel. Two further phrases sit alongside it: “filled with the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, all Lukan (Luke 1:15, 1:41, 1:67; Acts 2:4, 4:8, 4:31, 9:17, 13:9), and Acts 10:44's “the Holy Ghost fell on” is the KJV's one idiom for the Spirit descending on a group unbidden (with Acts 11:15).
provenance.significance: This is the verse where the Baptist's promise is reported as kept, and the report is assembled out of the KJV's own vocabulary for that keeping. John says the coming one “shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire”; Acts 2 is where the fire arrives and Luke's phrase “filled with the Holy Ghost” is coined for it; Acts 10:44 supplies the falling. 3 Nephi 19:13 has all three in one sentence — fell upon them, filled, and with fire — so the Nephite disciples receive, in a single clause, what the Bible distributes across the promise, the Pentecost, and the Gentile Pentecost. Note also what is absent: no tongues. Acts 2:4's other half, “began to speak with other tongues”, is exactly the element 19:32-34 will replace with words that cannot be uttered at all.

links.note: “The Holy Ghost did fall upon them, and they were filled with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.” The last six words are the Baptist's promise verbatim, from a phrase in only two KJV verses; “fall upon” and “filled with” are Luke's own Acts idioms for its fulfilment. The 1830 and the current text are identical here.

pericopes.text: And behold, they were encircled about as if it were fire; and it came down from heaven, and the multitude did witness it, and do bear record; and angels did come down out of heaven, and did minister unto them.
And it came to pass that while the angels were ministering unto the disciples, behold, Jesus came and stood in the midst, and ministered unto them.

links.text: Then the same day at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.

provenance.other: “came Jesus and stood in the midst” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:19; John 20:26 has the same clause split by an interposed phrase (“then came Jesus, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst”). The bare “stood in the midst” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, of which three are resurrection appearances (Luke 24:36, John 20:19, 20:26) — so the phrase alone is not decisive and the finite verb before the name is what makes it so.
provenance.alternative: Luke 24:36, “Jesus himself stood in the midst of them”, is the source this catalogue adopted at 3 Nephi 11:8, where the Book of Mormon has “stood in the midst of them” with the pronoun. 19:15 drops the pronoun, which is John's form and not Luke's.
provenance.significance: This verse and 19:18 walk John 20 in John's order. At 20:19 Jesus comes and stands in the midst; at 20:26 he does it a second time, eight days later, for Thomas; at 20:28 Thomas answers “My Lord and my God.” 3 Nephi 19:15 is the coming and standing, 19:16-17 the interval, and 19:18 the confession — except that the confession is made by all twelve, and made in prayer rather than in astonishment. The metalepsis is in what John 20 supplies and 3 Nephi does not repeat: the doors shut for fear of the Jews. The Nephite disciples are in an open place before a multitude, and the same appearance that consoled a frightened remnant here inaugurates a public church.

links.note: “Behold, Jesus came and stood in the midst, and ministered unto them.” John 20:19's clause with the word order inverted, at precisely the corresponding narrative moment — the risen Christ arriving unannounced among gathered disciples. The catalogue has already given 3 Nephi 11:8 to Luke 24:36 on the strength of “of them”; that pronoun is absent here, which is what moves this verse to John.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he spake unto the multitude, and commanded them that they should kneel down again upon the earth, and also that his disciples should kneel down upon the earth.
And it came to pass that when they had all knelt down upon the earth, he commanded his disciples that they should pray.
And behold, they began to pray; and they did pray unto Jesus, calling him their Lord and their God.

links.text: And Thomas answered and said unto him, My LORD and my God.

provenance.other: “my Lord and my God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:28. It is the only place in the King James Bible where a disciple addresses Jesus as God, and it is the last thing said to him in the Fourth Gospel before its first ending.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 19:18 takes Thomas's exclamation and makes it a liturgy: “they did pray unto Jesus, calling him their Lord and their God” — first person singular to third person plural, an outburst to a practice. That conversion is what the chapter then has to defend, and it does defend it: at 19:22 Christ tells the Father “they pray unto me because I am with them”, which is an answer to an objection the text never states. So the one KJV verse in which Christ is called God by a disciple becomes, in the Book of Mormon, the warrant for prayer addressed to Christ — with a warrant of its own supplied four verses later, and withdrawn again by the argument's own logic, since the reason given is presence. Recovering John 20's context sharpens it further: Thomas says it because he has touched the wounds, and Jesus immediately answers “blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.”

links.note: “And they did pray unto Jesus, calling him their Lord and their God.” Five words of a KJV singleton, and the singleton is Thomas's confession — the chapter having already put the twelve in John 20's room at 19:15. The Book of Mormon converts the vocative into a description of what the disciples call him, which is why this is an allusion and not a quotation.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Jesus departed out of the midst of them, and went a little way off from them and bowed himself to the earth, and he saith,

links.text: And he went a little farther, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.

provenance.other: The frame is Matthew's and it is built of KJV singletons. “went a little farther” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (Matthew 26:39); “he cometh unto the disciples” in exactly one (26:40); “he came and found them asleep again” in exactly one (26:43); “the third time, saying the same words” in exactly one (26:44). Mark 14:35 has “went forward a little, and fell on the ground”; Luke 22:41 has “was withdrawn from them about a stone's cast, and kneeled down”. tools/mediation-check.py returns divergences pointing both ways between Matthew and Mark, which is the expected signature of a composite: the Book of Mormon's “went a little way off” is neither gospel's exact wording, and “bowed himself to the earth” is neither Matthew's “fell on his face” nor Mark's “fell on the ground”.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 33:3's “bowed himself to the ground” is a KJV singleton and the closest match for the posture clause; it is registered as an exclusion at this verse, because Jacob approaching Esau has nothing else to do with the scene.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's governing borrowing and it runs to 19:35. Gethsemane's shape is: Jesus withdraws a little way and prays (26:39); he returns to the disciples and finds them asleep, and says watch and pray (26:40-41); he goes away a second time and prays (26:42); he returns and finds them asleep again (26:43); he goes away and prays the third time, saying the same words (26:44); he comes to them a third time and speaks (26:45). 3 Nephi 19 keeps every joint of it — 19:19 (withdraws), 19:24 (returns), 19:27 (second withdrawal), 19:30 (returns), 19:31 (third withdrawal), 19:35 (returns and speaks) — and changes exactly one thing. Each time he returns, the disciples are not asleep. 19:24: “they did still continue, without ceasing, to pray unto him”; 19:30: “they did pray steadfastly, without ceasing”. So the command that Gethsemane's disciples failed, “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation”, is kept here, and 19:26's “Pray on” answers 26:45's “Sleep on now, and take your rest” word for word in form and opposite in sense. Matthew 26:44 supplies one more inversion: there the third prayer is “the same words”, here (19:32) the third prayer is words that cannot be written or spoken at all. This is Gethsemane run again with the disciples awake — and the chapter's whole doctrinal payload, prayer offered to Christ, is placed inside the one gospel scene in which Christ prays alone and is not attended.

links.note: “Jesus departed out of the midst of them, and went a little way off from them and bowed himself to the earth, and he saith.” On its own the verse is a modest echo: “a little” is shared with Matthew and Mark, the posture with neither. The link is graded high on the structure rather than the wording, because 19:19, 19:24, 19:27, 19:30, 19:31 and 19:35 reproduce Matthew 26:39-45's six movements in order and without omission, and the one systematic departure — the disciples pray instead of sleeping — is legible only against that source. 1830 reads “he saith”, changed to “said” in 1920.
links.whyNot: There is no long verbal run anywhere in the sequence, and a scene of a man repeatedly withdrawing to pray needs no literary source. A reader who thinks three withdrawals is simply what earnest prayer looks like will not be moved by “a little”, and the argument then rests entirely on the count and the order.

pericopes.text: Father, I thank thee that thou hast given the Holy Ghost unto these whom I have chosen; and it is because of their belief in me, that I have chosen them out of the world.

links.text: Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me.

provenance.route: John 11:41 + John 15:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Father, I thank thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 11:41, and so does the fuller “Father, I thank thee that thou hast”. The verse's closing clause is a second singleton: “I have chosen you out of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 15:19. Both prayers in this chapter open with the Lazarus formula (19:20 and 19:28).
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's Christ opens his prayer with the only words in the King James Bible by which Jesus thanks the Father — and they are the words spoken over an open tomb, immediately before Lazarus is called out. Recover that context and the thanksgiving is not general: John 11:42 explains it as spoken aloud “because of the people which stand by, that they may believe that thou hast sent me.” 3 Nephi 19:20 is likewise a prayer prayed within earshot of a watching multitude and about their believing. The closing clause then reaches to John 15:19, where being chosen out of the world is the reason the world hates the disciples; here it is the reason they have received the Holy Ghost.

links.note: “Father, I thank thee that thou hast given the Holy Ghost unto these whom I have chosen … I have chosen them out of the world.” Two KJV singletons bracketing one verse, both Johannine, both from prayers or farewell discourse. Nine words matching John 11:41 at the head and eight matching John 15:19 at the foot — below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold in each half, and not one of his passages.

pericopes.text: Father, I pray thee that thou wilt give the Holy Ghost unto all them that shall believe in their words.

Father, thou hast given them the Holy Ghost, because they believe in me, and thou seest that they believe in me, because thou hearest them, and they pray unto me; and they pray unto me because I am with them.
And now Father, I pray unto thee for them, and also for all they which shall believe on their words, that they may believe in me, that I may be in them as thou, Father, art in me, that we may be one.

links.text: That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.

provenance.other: “as thou, Father, art in me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 17:21, and “which shall believe on me through their word” occurs in exactly one, John 17:20. 3 Nephi 19:23 has the first verbatim and the second with one substitution: “which shall believe on their words”, dropping “on me through” and pluralising “word”. 1830 reads “all they which shall believe”, modernised to “all those who shall believe” in 1920, which moves the clause further from John.
provenance.significance: This is the hinge of the whole prayer and the substitution is where the argument lives. John 17:20 prays for those who will believe on Jesus through the apostles' word; 3 Nephi 19:23 prays for those who will believe on the apostles' words, and then adds the clause John does not have — “that they may believe in me”. Belief in the messengers is made the antecedent of belief in Christ rather than its synonym, which is a claim about the standing of a text and its witnesses, made inside a prayer about unity. The suppressed half of John 17:21 is the purpose clause: “that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.” The Book of Mormon stops at “that we may be one” and leaves the world out of it, which 19:29 will then make explicit by importing John 17:9's “I pray not for the world”.

links.note: “That I may be in them as thou, Father, art in me, that we may be one.” Six words of John 17:21 verbatim, from a clause in that one KJV verse, inside a sentence that has already reworked John 17:20. Hardy cross-references John 17:20-22 at this verse.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 19.23 (cross-references John 17:20-22)

pericopes.text: And it came to pass, that when Jesus had thus prayed unto the Father, he came unto his disciples, and behold they did still continue, without ceasing, to pray unto him; and they did not multiply many words, for it was given unto them what they should pray, and they were filled with desire.

links.text: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

provenance.other: “what we should pray for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:26. The other half of 3 Nephi 19:24's clause, “it was given unto them what they should pray”, is the shape of Matthew 10:19, where “it shall be given you in that same hour” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. For the first half of the verse the source is not the Bible directly: “much speaking” and “vain repetitions” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:7, and 3 Nephi 13:7 has already reproduced that verse whole.
provenance.significance: Romans 8:26 says the Spirit supplies what a praying man does not know how to ask, and it says so with a phrase — “groanings which cannot be uttered” — that this chapter picks up again at 19:32-34, where Christ's own third prayer cannot be written or uttered by man. So the same Pauline verse underwrites both halves of the chapter's theory of prayer: what the disciples pray is given them, and what Christ prays cannot be said. And the disciples' restraint is obedience to a sermon this book has already reported: at 13:7, the Nephite Sermon on the Mount, they were told not to be heard for their much speaking. 19:24's “they did not multiply many words” is the narrator certifying that the congregation kept the rule.

links.note: “They did not multiply many words, for it was given unto them what they should pray.” Three strands, none of them a long run: Matthew 6:7's prohibition, already given to these hearers at 3 Nephi 13:7 and here reported as kept; Matthew 10:19's promise that what to say will be given in the hour; and Romans 8:26, the KJV's only verse about not knowing what one should pray for. Graded moderate because no single strand would carry the verse alone.
links.whyNot: The Book of Mormon's actual words — “multiply many words” — are in no KJV verse; “multiply words” occurs in none. The link is to the ideas of three verses and to one four-word run from Romans, and a reader who wants a verbal case will find only the run.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Jesus blessed them, as they did pray unto him, and his countenance did smile upon them, and the light of his countenance did shine upon them, and behold they were as white as the countenance, and also the garments of Jesus; and behold the whiteness thereof did exceed all the whiteness, yea, even there could be nothing upon earth so white as the whiteness thereof.

links.text: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee:

provenance.other: Numbers 6:25 has “make his face shine upon thee” and 6:26 “lift up his countenance upon thee”; the Book of Mormon has both elements fused — “his countenance did smile upon them, and the light of his countenance did shine upon them”. The word Numbers lacks is “light”: “the light of thy countenance” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Psalm 4:6, 44:3, 89:15 and 90:8, all Psalms. tools/mediation-check.py finds no divergence between Numbers 6:25 and Psalm 4:6 that this verse reproduces — both elements are present — so the composite is recorded rather than a choice made.
provenance.significance: The verse opens “Jesus blessed them”, and what follows is the priestly blessing being performed rather than recited. Numbers 6:23 tells Aaron and his sons “On this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel”, and the wise is: face shine upon thee, countenance lifted upon thee, peace. Here the blessing has no words at all — it is a smile and a shining — and the recipients become what the blessing describes, white as the face and garments of the one blessing them. The Aaronic formula's grammar is petition (“The LORD make his face shine”); 3 Nephi 19:25 reports it in the indicative, with the LORD present and doing it. That is what a study edition's cross-reference to Numbers 6:22-27 gestures at, and it is worth spelling out.

links.note: “Jesus blessed them … his countenance did smile upon them, and the light of his countenance did shine upon them.” The blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 enacted rather than spoken, with the Psalms' “light of thy countenance” supplying the noun Numbers does not use. Hardy cross-references Numbers 6:22-27 at this verse.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 19.25 (cross-references Numbers 6:22-27)

links.text: And his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them.

provenance.route: Mark 9:3 + Matthew 17:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “no fuller on earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 9:3, and it is the King James Bible's only whiteness superlative bounded by the earth. 3 Nephi 19:25 closes “there could be nothing upon earth so white as the whiteness thereof”. Matthew 17:2 supplies the other element — “his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light” — matching the Book of Mormon's pairing of a shining countenance with white garments. Luke 9:29 has “white and glistering” and no earth-clause. tools/mediation-check.py finds Matthew 17:2's form where it and Daniel 7:9 diverge, on “did shine”.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 19:25 is a transfiguration, and the person transfigured is not Jesus. The KJV's two transfiguration accounts are ransacked for their two distinctive details — Matthew's shining face, Mark's superlative that no earthly fuller could match the white — and both are transferred to the disciples: “they were as white as the countenance, and also the garments of Jesus.” Mark's fuller is the point of the metalepsis. His clause exists to say the whiteness was not produced by any human process, and the Book of Mormon keeps the disclaimer and drops the fuller, leaving “nothing upon earth so white”. What Mark says of Christ's clothes on the mountain, 3 Nephi says of praying men on a plain — and 19:30 completes it, “they were white, even as Jesus.”

links.note: “There could be nothing upon earth so white as the whiteness thereof.” Mark 9:3's earth-bounded superlative, from the KJV's only verse that contains one, joined to Matthew 17:2's shining countenance — and applied to the disciples rather than to Christ. Note that the surrounding words are the Book of Mormon's own; the borrowing is the figure, not a run.

pericopes.text: And Jesus saith unto them, Pray on, nevertheless they did not cease to pray.
And he turned from them again, and went a little way off, and bowed himself to the earth; and he prayed again unto the Father, saying:

Father, I thank thee that thou hast purified those which I have chosen, because of their faith, and I pray for them, and also for them which shall believe on their words, that they may be purified in me, through faith on their words, even as they are purified in me.

links.text: And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth.

provenance.other: “sanctify them through thy truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 17:17, and John 17:19 repeats the verb twice more. The Book of Mormon does not use the word: 19:28 says “purified” four times where John says “sanctify/sanctified” three times, in the same position in the same prayer. That substitution is what holds kjvSpecific at uncertain — the sentence tracks John's structure closely and its distinctive verb not at all. The verse also reopens with John 11:41's formula, “Father, I thank thee that thou hast”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: John 17:17-19 is the petition of the high-priestly prayer that asks for the disciples' consecration on the ground of Christ's own; 3 Nephi 19:28 asks for the same thing on the ground of the disciples' faith, and says so three times — “because of their faith … through faith on their words … even as they are purified in me.” Faith replaces truth as the medium of sanctification. That is a substantive change to what the prayer asks for, and it is made without disturbing a single joint of the sentence it is made in.

links.note: “Father, I thank thee that thou hast purified those which I have chosen, because of their faith … that they may be purified in me.” The second prayer opens with John 11:41's formula for the second time and then reproduces the movement of John 17:17-20 with “purified” standing throughout where John has “sanctified”. Frederick reads 3 Nephi 19 as “a lengthy variation of the intercessory prayer” and singles out verses 28-29 as “alluding in particular to John 17”; his interest is in what a nineteenth-century reader would hear, not in identifying a source verse, and he names none.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: 5

pericopes.text: Father, I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given unto me out of the world, because of their faith, that they may be purified in me, that I may be in them as thou, Father, art in me, that we may be one, that I may be glorified in them.

links.text: I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.

provenance.other: “I pray not for the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 17:9, and the Book of Mormon reproduces the whole of its second clause — thirteen consecutive words, “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given” — interrupted only by the 1830's added “unto” before “me”, which 1920 deleted, moving the text back toward John. The verse then closes with two more singletons: “as thou, Father, art in me” (John 17:21) and “I am glorified in them” (John 17:10). 1830's “them which” was changed to “those whom” in 1920.
provenance.significance: This is the one place in the chapter where the borrowing is long enough to be a quotation on any definition, and it is the place where the prayer's logic is most changed. John 17:9's ground for the restriction is possession — “for they are thine”. 3 Nephi 19:29's ground is merit: “because of their faith”, the third time in two verses. And John 17:10's “I am glorified in them” is a statement of fact in the indicative; here it becomes a petition, “that I may be glorified in them”. So the Book of Mormon takes the high-priestly prayer's most exclusive sentence, keeps it word for word, and shifts both its warrant and its mood. The 1830 reading is the sharper witness to the borrowing in one respect and the weaker in another: “given unto me” is not John's, and the 1920 correction quietly restored John's phrase.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 60:21 ends “that I may be glorified”, which is where the n-gram stream pointed; John 17:10's “I am glorified in them” supplies the prepositional phrase Isaiah lacks and is registered as the source.

links.note: “Father, I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given unto me out of the world … that I may be glorified in them.” A thirteen-word run from John 17:9 — still below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and not one of his 36 passages — plus two further KJV singletons from John 17:10 and 17:21. Hardy cross-references John 17:6-9 at this verse; Frederick quotes 19:28-29 whole and describes them as alluding in particular to John 17.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 19.29 (cross-references John 17:6-9)
Frederick 2016: 5

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had spake these words, he came again unto his disciples, and behold they did pray steadfastly, without ceasing, unto him; and he did smile upon then again; and behold they were white, even as Jesus.
And it came to pass that he went again a little way off, and prayed unto the Father;
and tongue cannot speak the words which he prayed, neither can be written by man the words which he prayed.
And the multitude did hear, and do bear record, and their hearts were open, and they did understand in their hearts the words which he prayed.

links.text: For this people’s heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears, and should understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.

provenance.route: Isaiah 6:10, in one of its New Testament forms (Matthew 13:15, John 12:40, Acts 28:27) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “understand with their heart” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Isaiah 6:10 and its three New Testament quotations, Matthew 13:15, John 12:40 and Acts 28:27. Every one of them is negative: the phrase exists in the King James Bible only inside the prophecy that this people will NOT understand with their heart. 3 Nephi 19:33 reads “they did understand in their hearts”, with the preposition and the number both changed. Separately, “whose heart the Lord opened” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 16:14, and 19:33 has “their hearts were open”.
provenance.significance: The mediation cannot be settled and the reason is itself worth recording. tools/mediation-check.py, run on Isaiah 6:10 against Matthew 13:15, returns no divergence that 3 Nephi 19:33 reproduces: the phrase is identical in the Hebrew prophet and in Matthew's quotation of him, so the Book of Mormon's four words cannot say which page they came from. What can be said is the reversal. Isaiah 6:10 is the commission to make a people's heart fat so that they shall not understand; the Book of Mormon takes its one distinctive clause and reports it fulfilled in the affirmative — hearts open, hearts understanding — over a multitude that has just heard words no man can write. If Matthew's is the form in view, the reversal is pointed, because the same chapter of Matthew supplies 19:35 (13:58) and 19:36 (13:17), and 13:16-17 is precisely where Matthew turns from the unhearing crowd to the disciples whose eyes are blessed because they see.
provenance.alternative: Acts 16:14's opened heart is the closer match for “their hearts were open” and has nothing else in common with the verse; it is recorded here as the other half of the composite rather than as the source.

links.note: “Their hearts were open, and they did understand in their hearts the words which he prayed.” Four words from a phrase the King James Bible uses only in the Isaiah 6:10 hardening oracle and its three New Testament citations, here inverted into a report that the hearing did occur. Graded moderate: the contact is real and rare, the wording is altered at two points, and the mediation is undecidable on the evidence of this verse.
links.whyNot: “Understand with their heart” is not an unusual thing for an English writer to say about comprehension, and its KJV rarity may be an accident of the one oracle that happens to phrase it that way. If the reversal is not deliberate the link is nothing.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, so great and marvellous were the words which he prayed, that they cannot be written, neither can they be uttered by man.

links.text: How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.

provenance.other: “unspeakable words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “not lawful for a man to utter” occurs in exactly one, both 2 Corinthians 12:4. It is the King James Bible's only account of words heard and not repeatable. The Book of Mormon's clause at 19:34 is “neither can they be uttered by man”, and at 19:32 “tongue cannot speak the words which he prayed, neither can be written by man”. Romans 8:26's “groanings which cannot be uttered” is the KJV's one other unutterable speech and is the verse this catalogue records at 19:24.
provenance.significance: The change is from prohibition to incapacity, and it is the whole point. Paul's words are unutterable because it is not lawful — a restriction laid on the hearer, who could speak them and may not. 3 Nephi 19:32-34 makes it a limit of the instrument: tongue cannot speak them, they cannot be written, they cannot be uttered by man. Read against Matthew 26:44, which the chapter has been following since 19:19, this is where the Gethsemane frame breaks: Matthew's third prayer is reported as “the same words”, and the third prayer here has no words that can be reported at all. And it completes the pair with 19:24 — the disciples are given what they should pray, and what Christ prays cannot be given to anyone.

links.note: “So great and marvellous were the words which he prayed, that they cannot be written, neither can they be uttered by man.” Both distinctive elements of 2 Corinthians 12:4 are present — the unutterability and the agent “man” — with the ground moved from law to possibility. 1830 keeps the KJV spelling “marvellous”, modernised to “marvelous” in 1920.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had made an end of praying, he came again to the disciples, and saith unto them, So great faith have I never seen among all the Jews; wherefore I could not shew unto them so great miracles, because of their unbelief.

links.text: When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.

provenance.route: Matthew 8:10 (or Luke 7:9) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “so great faith” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 8:10 and Luke 7:9, which are the same saying about the centurion; so does its completion, “no, not in Israel”. tools/mediation-check.py finds no divergence between the two that 3 Nephi 19:35 reproduces — the Book of Mormon keeps only the words the synoptics share — so the gospel cannot be chosen and the mediation is recorded as direct-NT without one.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible has exactly one measurement of faith by comparison with Israel, and it is Jesus marvelling at a Gentile soldier: I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel. 3 Nephi 19:35 reuses the measurement with the terms enlarged — “So great faith have I never seen among all the Jews” — so a comparison Jesus once made between one centurion and his own nation is now made between a whole people and that nation. The metalepsis cuts against the borrower: the centurion's faith consisted in not needing Christ to come under his roof, and these disciples have had Christ standing bodily in the midst of them for two days.

links.note: “So great faith have I never seen among all the Jews.” Three words from a phrase in only two KJV verses, both the centurion pericope, with the comparison term changed from “in Israel” to “among all the Jews” and the verb from “found” to “seen”. The reordering is what keeps this an allusion rather than a quotation.

links.text: And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

provenance.route: Matthew 13:58 + Mark 6:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “because of their unbelief” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 13:58 and Mark 6:6, both in the Nazareth episode. tools/mediation-check.py, run against Mark 6:5, returns divergences pointing both ways: the Book of Mormon has Mark's modal, “could not”, against Matthew's flat “did not many”, and Matthew's cause clause, “because of their unbelief”, against Mark's “save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk”. “could there do no mighty work” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (Mark 6:5) and “he did not many mighty works there” in exactly one (Matthew 13:58). The verse's opening frame is a third singleton: “Jesus had made an end of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:1, where the completed activity is commanding his twelve disciples and here it is praying.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 19:35-36 is built out of Matthew 13 — 13:58 here and 13:17 in the next verse — and Matthew 13:58 is the closing sentence of that chapter, the verdict on Christ's own countrymen. The Book of Mormon has Christ deliver that verdict himself, in the first person, as an unfavourable comparison with the people in front of him: he could not shew the Jews so great miracles, and these have seen greater. Recover Matthew's context and the sentence is about Nazareth, his home town, where “a prophet is not without honour, save in his own country” — so the failure being reported is not the Jews' in general but the failure of the people who knew him. Note the composite's shape: the modal is Mark's and the causal clause is Matthew's, which is the ordinary signature of a writer working from a memory of both synoptics rather than from one page.

links.note: “Wherefore I could not shew unto them so great miracles, because of their unbelief.” Mark 6:5's “could not” fused with Matthew 13:58's “because of their unbelief”, in a verse whose narrative frame — “when Jesus had made an end of” — is itself a KJV singleton from Matthew 11:1. The 1830's “shew” is the KJV spelling; 1920 modernised it to “show”, which obscures the register.

pericopes.text: Verily I say unto you, there are none of them that have seen so great things as ye have seen; neither have they heard so great things as ye have heard.

links.text: For verily I say unto you, That many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them; and to hear those things which ye hear, and have not heard them.

provenance.other: “which ye see, and have not seen them” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 13:17 and Luke 10:24, which are the same beatitude on the disciples' eyes. tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point and it favours Matthew: 3 Nephi 19:36 opens “Verily I say unto you”, which is Matthew 13:17's “For verily I say unto you”; Luke 10:24 reads “For I tell you”. Matthew's other distinctive term, “righteous men”, against Luke's “kings”, is not reproduced.
provenance.significance: Matthew 13:16-17 blesses the disciples' eyes and ears against the prophets and righteous men who desired to see and hear and did not. 3 Nephi 19:36 keeps the seeing-and-hearing antithesis and changes the losing party from the prophets of the past to the Jews of the present — “there are none of them that have seen so great things as ye have seen”. That completes what 19:35 began, and it means the chapter closes with three separate contacts with Matthew 13: the hardening oracle at 19:33 (13:15), the Nazareth verdict at 19:35 (13:58), and this beatitude. Matthew 13 is the gospel chapter about who is given to understand and who is not, and 3 Nephi 19 answers it verse by verse in the affirmative — these hearts understood, these eyes have seen — which is a considerable claim to have made out of borrowed clauses.

links.note: “There are none of them that have seen so great things as ye have seen; neither have they heard so great things as ye have heard.” The antithesis and the verily-formula of Matthew 13:17, with the mediation settled by the opening words against the Lukan parallel. Frederick quotes this verse and reads it as hinting at the superiority of the Book of Mormon apostles and people to those of the Old World; that is a claim about its rhetorical effect, not an identification of a source, and he names no verse.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: 5-6

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he commanded the multitude that they should cease to pray, and also his disciples. And he commanded them that they should not cease to pray in their hearts.
And he commanded them that they should arise and stand up upon their feet. And they arose up and stood upon their feet.
And it came to pass that he break bread again, and blessed it, and gave to the disciples to eat.
And when they had eat, he commanded them that they should break bread, and give unto the multitude.
And when they had given unto the multitude, he also gave them wine to drink, and commanded them that they should give unto the multitude.
Now there had been no bread, neither wine, brought by the disciples, neither by the multitude;
but he truly gave unto them bread to eat, and also wine to drink;

and he saith unto them, He that eatheth this bread, eatheth of my body to their soul, and he that drinketh of this wine, drinketh of my blood to their soul, and their soul shall never hunger nor thirst, but shall be filled.

links.text: And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.

provenance.other: “never hunger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:35, where it stands in the same pair with “never thirst” that 3 Nephi 20:8 compresses into “never hunger nor thirst”. “drinketh my blood” occurs in exactly two, John 6:54 and John 6:56, and both couple it with eating, as this verse does. Revelation 7:16, “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more”, is the other candidate for the hunger-and-thirst clause and is displaced (see the exclusion register): it lacks the eating and drinking that occupy the first two thirds of the verse.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 26:26-27 supplies the narrative frame of verses 3-5 — took bread, blessed it, brake it, gave to the disciples — but not this verse's saying, which has no synoptic parallel. The Last Supper words are 'this is my body'; John 6's are 'he that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood'. 3 Nephi 20:8 has the second construction, not the first.
provenance.significance: The Fourth Gospel keeps its eucharistic discourse and its Last Supper apart: John 6 is preached in the synagogue at Capernaum a year early and John's supper narrative has no institution at all. 3 Nephi 20 puts them back together — the bread is broken and passed in verses 3-5, and then the Capernaum saying is spoken over it in verse 8. Recover John 6's context and what is recovered is the offence: 'This is an hard saying; who can hear it?' and 'from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him'. The saying that emptied the synagogue is here the saying over a meal at which the multitude is filled and cries out with one voice. The borrowing reverses the reception.

links.note: Not a quotation — no clause of John 6 is reproduced intact, and the verse falls far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold. The case is the collocation: eating a bread that is a body, drinking a drink that is blood, and a consequent hungering and thirsting no more, in that order, within one sentence. John 6 is the only KJV chapter where those three sit together. The 1830 reading is worth noticing on its own account: it reads 'eateth of my body to their soul … to their soul, and their soul shall never hunger', with a plural pronoun after the singular 'he that eateth', and 1920 regularized all three to 'his'. The first edition's grammar is looser than John's and than its own successor's.

pericopes.text: Now when the multitude had all eat and drank, behold they were filled with the spirit, and they did cry out with one voice, and gave glory to Jesus, whom they both saw and heard.

And it came to pass that when they had all given glory unto Jesus, he saith unto them, Behold now I finish the commandment which the Father hath commanded me concerning this people, which are a remnant of the house of Israel.
Ye remember that I spake unto you, and said that when the words of Isaiah should be fulfilled: Behold they are written, ye have them before you; therefore search them.
And verily, verily I say unto you, that when they shall be fulfilled, then is the fulfilling of the covenant which the Father hath made unto his people. O house of Israel,

and then shall the remnants which shall be scattered abroad upon the face of the earth, be gathered in from the east, and from the west, and from the south, and from the north; and they shall be brought to the knowledge of the Lord their God, who hath redeemed them.

links.text: And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south.

provenance.other: “from the east and from the west” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 107:3 and Luke 13:29. Psalm 107:3 is a gathering — 'And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south' — and 3 Nephi 20:13 is a gathering: 'shall the remnants … be gathered in from the east, and from the west, and from the south, and from the north'. Luke 13:29 is a banquet: those who 'come from the east, and from the west' sit down in the kingdom of God. The verb decides between them and it decides for the Psalm.
provenance.alternative: Luke 13:29 ranked first in the machine stream for this verse on a ten-word run and is filed in the exclusion register. Isaiah 43:5-6 has the same four quarters and the same gathering, but distributes them across two verses and four separate clauses ('I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west'), which is not this verse's shape.
provenance.significance: Whichever verse is in view, neither has the Book of Mormon's order. Psalm 107:3 and Luke 13:29 both run east, west, north, south; 3 Nephi 20:13 runs east, west, south, north. The transposition is the reason this row is moderate and not high, and it is worth recording rather than smoothing over, because the four-quarters gathering is a formula the Book of Mormon uses in its own right and a formula does not need a source.

links.note: A deliberately cautious row. The four compass points are common property and the catalogue does not claim otherwise; what makes the Psalm worth naming is that the pairing of the four quarters with the verb 'gather' is not common property — it is Psalm 107:3, and 3 Nephi 20:13 has both halves. Recorded at moderate so that a reader who arrives at this verse with Luke 13:29 in hand (as the machine did) is told which of the two verses actually shares the sense.
links.whyNot: The order of the quarters matches neither candidate, and 'gathered in from the four quarters' is a standing Book of Mormon idiom by this point in the text; the verse can be accounted for without any KJV verse at all.

pericopes.text: And the Father hath commanded me that I should give unto you this land, for your inheritance.
And I say unto you, that if the Gentiles do not repent after the blessing which they shall receive, after that they have scattered my people,

then shall ye which are a remnant of the house of Jacob, go forth among them; and ye shall be in the midst of them, which shall be many; and ye shall be among them, as a lion among the beasts of the forest, and as a young lion among the flocks of sheep, who, if he goeth through, both treadeth down and teareth in pieces, and none can deliver.

links.text: And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles in the midst of many people as a lion among the beasts of the forest, as a young lion among the flocks of sheep: who, if he go through, both treadeth down, and teareth in pieces, and none can deliver.

provenance.other: “as a lion among the” and “none can deliver” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:8. “beasts of the forest” occurs in exactly two (Psalm 104:20, Micah 5:8) and “flocks of sheep” in exactly three (Genesis 29:2, Joel 1:18, Micah 5:8); only Micah 5:8 holds all four phrases, and 3 Nephi 20:16 has all four in Micah's order.
provenance.significance: The departures are all of one kind: Micah's third-person report becomes a second-person commission. Micah writes 'the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles'; the risen Christ says 'then shall ye, who are a remnant of the house of Jacob, go forth among them'. Micah's remnant is simply there among the nations, a lion by nature; 3 Nephi's is sent, and sent conditionally — verse 15 makes the whole sentence the apodosis of 'if the Gentiles do not repent'. So the one KJV verse in which Israel's remnant is a lion among the nations is here turned into a threat that repentance can still avert.
