Chapter 16 had already reached for this verse and reached for it in the negative (16:14-15, 'I will not suffer my people … to go through among them, and tread them down'); this is where the same verse is quoted almost whole.

links.note: Fifty-odd words tracking Micah 5:8 clause by clause, with four departures that all serve the change of person: 'the remnant of Jacob shall be' → 'ye, who are a remnant of the house of Jacob, go forth'; 'the Gentiles' → 'them' (Hardy's apparatus notes the substitution at this verse); 'in the midst of many people' → 'in the midst of them who shall be many'; and 'go through' → 'goeth through'. From 'as a lion' to 'none can deliver' — twenty-eight words — the verse is the King James Bible with one inserted conjunction. Well above Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though whether he counts it cannot be checked. Hardy hangs the citation for the whole span on the last verse of it, 20:17; the catalogue writes a link at each verse so that Micah 5:8 and 5:9 can be seen doing different work.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.16 (Mic 5.8)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.17 (Mic 5.8-9)

pericopes.text: Thy hand shall be lifted up upon thine adversaries, and all thine enemies shall be cut off.

links.text: Thine hand shall be lifted up upon thine adversaries, and all thine enemies shall be cut off.

provenance.other: “lifted up upon thine adversaries” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:9. The verse is reproduced in full with a single word changed: the King James 'Thine hand' becomes 'Thy hand'. Everything after it — 'shall be lifted up upon thine adversaries, and all thine enemies shall be cut off' — is verbatim, and 'thine' survives twice in that stretch, so the change at the head of the verse is not a systematic modernization.
provenance.significance: The verse matters out of proportion to its length because of the two words at the end. 'Cut off' returns six verses later at 20:23, where it displaces Acts 3:23's 'destroyed' in the prophet-like-unto-Moses oracle, and Hardy's apparatus at 3 Nephi 21:11 observes that the term connects Deuteronomy 18:19 with Micah 5:8-15. The catalogue's own reading is that 3 Nephi 20 puts the connection into practice: it quotes Micah's cutting off here, and then, when it comes to Peter's sermon, it rewrites Peter with Micah's verb. The chapter's two great blocks of borrowing are stitched together at one word.

links.note: A sixteen-word verbatim reproduction, exactly at Skousen's threshold and therefore worth flagging for a reader collating this catalogue against his list; whether he counts it cannot be checked (PLAN §4.1). Hardy keys 'Verses 16-17 quote Mic 5.8-9' to this verse, which is his convention of hanging a multi-verse citation on the last member of the span; the wording of Micah 5:9 is genuinely here and nowhere else in the chapter.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.17 (Mic 5.8-9)

pericopes.text: And I will gather my people together, as a man gathereth his sheaves into the floor:

links.text: But they know not the thoughts of the LORD, neither understand they his counsel: for he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor.

provenance.other: “sheaves into the floor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 4:12 — 'for he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor'. The threshing-floor image is common in the KJV; this particular collocation of sheaves with a floor and a gathering is not.
provenance.significance: Micah's simile has no agent inside it. 'He shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor' leaves the sheaves to arrive as sheaves do, and the point of the verse is that the nations gathered against Zion do not know they are being harvested. 3 Nephi supplies the missing farmer — 'as a man gathereth his sheaves into the floor' — and in doing so changes who is gathered. In Micah the sheaves are the hostile nations, brought in for threshing by the daughter of Zion in the next verse; in 3 Nephi 20:18 they are 'my people', gathered by their own God. The image survives the transfer intact and its referent is inverted, which is the same operation the chapter performs on Isaiah 52 twenty verses later.

links.note: Six shared words and one KJV singleton, which is what carries it; the departures are larger than the agreement. Catalogued at high rather than certain because the sentence is a paraphrase, not a quotation, and because a threshing-floor is available to any writer. What is not available to any writer is the sheaves-into-the-floor phrasing followed immediately, in the next verse, by the iron horn and brass hoofs of Micah 4:13 — the two verses arrive together and in Micah's order. Hardy keys 'Verses 18-19 quote Mic 4.12-13' to 20:19; this row puts the 4:12 half at the verse whose words it is.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.19 (Mic 4.12-13)

pericopes.text: for I will make my people with whom the Father hath covenanted, yea, I will make thy horn iron, and I will make thy hoops [hoofs] brass. And thou shalt beat in pieces many people; and I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord, and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth. And behold, I am he which doeth it.

links.text: Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion: for I will make thine horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass: and thou shalt beat in pieces many people: and I will consecrate their gain unto the LORD, and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth.

provenance.other: “thy hoofs brass”, “beat in pieces many people” and “consecrate their gain” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 4:13. “the Lord of the whole earth” occurs in exactly three (Psalm 97:5, Micah 4:13, Zechariah 4:14), and only Micah 4:13 has it in the same sentence as the other three. From 'I will make thy horn iron' to 'the Lord of the whole earth' the reproduction is verbatim but for 'thine horn' → 'thy horn'.
provenance.significance: What is dropped is the addressee. Micah 4:13 opens 'Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion' — Hardy's apparatus notes the missing clause — and 3 Nephi replaces it with 'I will make my people with whom the Father hath covenanted'. The daughter of Zion is displaced by a covenant people, and with her goes the imperative: Micah commands, 3 Nephi promises. The closing addition works the same way. Micah 4:13 ends with the substance consecrated to the Lord of the whole earth and no speaker named; 3 Nephi adds 'And behold, I am he who doeth it', which claims the whole oracle for the risen Christ standing in front of the crowd. Micah's verse is about what will be done; this one is about who is doing it.

links.note: Forty words of Micah 4:13, three KJV singletons among them, comfortably past Skousen's threshold. The 1830 running text carries a compositor's slip worth recording: it sets 'I will make thy hoops brass' where the King James reads 'hoofs', and later editions restore the source's word. The direction of that correction is the one CONVENTIONS §8 asks to be noticed — a later edition moving the Book of Mormon back toward the King James Bible rather than away from it — and it happens twice more in this chapter, at 20:42 and 20:45.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.19 (Mic 4.13)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.19 (Mic 4.12-13)

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass, saith the Father, That the sword of my justice shalt hang over them at that day; and except they repent, it shall fall upon them, saith the Father, yea, even upon all the nations of the Gentiles.—
And it shall come to pass that I will establish my people, O house of Israel.

And behold, this people will I establish in this land, unto the fulfilling of the covenant which I made with your Father Jacob; and it shall be a new Jerusalem. And the powers of heaven shall be in the midst of this people; yea, even I will be in the midst of you.

links.text: And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.

provenance.other: “new Jerusalem” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 3:12 and Revelation 21:2, and in no Old Testament verse at all. Revelation 21:2 also supplies 'the holy city', which 3 Nephi 20 has fourteen verses later at 20:36 in its Isaiah 52:1 quotation — so both halves of Revelation's phrase are in this chapter, from two different directions.
provenance.alternative: Luke 21:26, 'the powers of heaven shall be shaken', is the only KJV verse containing 'powers of heaven' and therefore the highest-scoring candidate a rarity search returns for this verse. It is displaced in the exclusion register: Luke's powers are shaken in judgment and 3 Nephi's are present in blessing.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's New Jerusalem is not John's. Revelation 21:2 sees the city 'coming down from God out of heaven'; 3 Nephi 20:22 promises 'this people will I establish in this land … and it shall be a New Jerusalem', which locates it on the ground the audience is standing on. The borrowed phrase brings the whole eschatological weight of Revelation 21 with it and then spends that weight on a piece of American geography — the move the chapter has been making since verse 14, 'the Father hath commanded me that I should give unto you this land'.

links.note: Two words, and they would not be worth a row if they were two ordinary words. 'New Jerusalem' is a coinage of Revelation with no Old Testament ancestor, and a text purporting to be spoken by the risen Christ in the New World in the first century uses it as a known term needing no gloss. Recorded at moderate because the phrase is short enough to have been transmitted through ordinary nineteenth-century religious speech rather than off the page of Revelation, which is the standing difficulty with famous phrases. The rest of the verse — 'the powers of heaven shall be in the midst of this people; yea, even I will be in the midst of you' — has no verbal source the catalogue can identify; the nearest sense is Ezekiel 37:26-27 and Zechariah 2:10-11, and neither shares wording.

pericopes.text: Behold, I am he of whom Moses spake, saying: A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me: him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you. And it shall come to pass that every soul which will not hear that prophet, shall be cut off from among the people.

links.text: For Moses truly said unto the fathers, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you.

provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 18:15 — 'The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken.' Deuteronomy 18:19 — 'whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.'
provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15-19 → Acts 3:22-23 → KJV → Book of Mormon (with 1 Nephi 22:20 in between)
provenance.other: “raise up unto you of your brethren” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 3:22 and Acts 7:37, and in no Old Testament verse at all. mediation-check.py against Deuteronomy 18:15 and Acts 3:22 returns one decisive point and it is a sixteen-word one: the clause 'him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you' exists in Acts and not in Deuteronomy, and the Book of Mormon has it entire. Against Deuteronomy 18:19 and Acts 3:23 it returns two more, both decisive for Acts: 'every soul which' for Deuteronomy's 'whosoever', and 'hear that prophet' for Deuteronomy's 'hearken unto my words which he shall speak'. Acts 7:37 is displaced in the exclusion register — it stops at 'him shall ye hear' and cannot account for the twelve words that follow. The word order ('A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you') and the pronoun ('your God', not 'thy God') are Acts's throughout.
provenance.alternative: The one point at which this verse leaves Acts is its last verb: Acts 3:23 reads 'destroyed from among the people' and 3 Nephi 20:23 reads 'cut off from among the people'. That is precisely the departure 1 Nephi 22:20 had already made, in the same clause, five hundred pages earlier — so the proximate model for this one word is plausibly the earlier Book of Mormon rather than the King James Bible. It cannot be the model for the rest of the verse: 1 Nephi 22:20 omits 'of your brethren', and 3 Nephi 20:23 has it, which means the fuller Acts wording is independently in view. The schema carries a single mediation value and this row wants two; 'OT-via-NT' is recorded as the dominant route and the Book-of-Mormon-internal layer is stated here. FLAGGED for Wilson: a row with a genuinely double route has no clean representation in the field as defined.
provenance.significance: 'Cut off from among the people' occurs in no KJV verse. 'Cut off from among' occurs in eleven, and they are almost all Levitical: the karet formula, 'that soul shall be cut off from among his people', by which a violator is severed from Israel. So the substitution does not merely soften Peter's 'destroyed' — it exchanges an apostolic word for a priestly one, and re-files the penalty for refusing the prophet under the law of excommunication rather than of destruction. Hardy's apparatus observes at 3 Nephi 21:11 that 'cut off' is the term connecting Deuteronomy 18:19 with Micah 5:8-15; this chapter has just quoted Micah 5:9's 'all thine enemies shall be cut off' at 20:17, six verses back, which is where the catalogue thinks the verb was picked up.

links.note: A thirty-word run of Acts 3:22 followed by a seventeen-word run of Acts 3:23, with two departures: the introduction ('Behold, I am he of whom Moses spake, saying' for 'For Moses truly said unto the fathers') and the sanction ('cut off' for 'destroyed'). The first is the chapter's characteristic move — Peter's report of Moses becomes the speech of the one Moses spoke of, exactly as verses 24 and 26 turn Peter's 'these days' and 'his Son Jesus' into 'me'. The mediation is the same one the pilot got at 1 Nephi 22:20 and it is not close: the prophet-like-unto-Moses oracle reaches the Book of Mormon in Peter's wording, not Moses's. Well above Skousen's threshold; whether he counts it cannot be checked. Hardy cross-references Acts 3:23 and Deuteronomy 18:15, 18-19 here and notes both that Acts reads 'destroyed' and that 1 Nephi 22:20 also uses 'cut off'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.23 (Acts 3.23; Deut 18.15, 18-19)

pericopes.text: Verily, I say unto you, Yea; and all the prophets from Samuel, and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have testified of me.

links.text: Yea, and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days.

provenance.other: “all the prophets from Samuel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:24. Eighteen consecutive words are reproduced without change — 'and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken' — and the verse departs only at its last five.
provenance.significance: Peter, preaching at Solomon's porch, says the prophets 'have likewise foretold of these days'; the speaker here says they 'have testified of me'. The change is small and it moves the referent of the entire prophetic tradition from an epoch to a person standing in front of the audience — and the person is the one Peter was preaching about. Verse 26 does the identical thing to Acts 3:26, where Peter's 'God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him' becomes 'the Father having raised me up … and sent me'. Read together, the three verses 23, 24 and 26 convert a sermon about Jesus into a sermon by him without altering the sermon.

links.note: The catalogue's claim here is narrow and checkable: eighteen words of Acts 3:24 in order, including a KJV singleton, with the closing clause replaced. Hardy cross-references Acts 3:24 at this verse and notes the divergent ending. Above Skousen's sixteen-word threshold on the unaltered stretch alone.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.24 (Acts 3.24)

pericopes.text: And behold, ye are the children of the prophets; and ye are of the house of Israel; and ye are of the covenant which the Father made with your fathers, saying: Unto Abraham, and in thy seed, shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed:

links.text: Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.

provenance.mt: Genesis 22:18 — 'And in thy seed shall all the NATIONS of the earth be blessed; BECAUSE THOU HAST OBEYED MY VOICE.'
provenance.route: Genesis 22:18 → Acts 3:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “kindreds of the earth be blessed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:25. mediation-check.py against Genesis 22:18 returns two decisive points, both for Acts: the Book of Mormon has 'kindreds', not Genesis's 'nations', and it stops where Acts stops, without Genesis's 'because thou hast obeyed my voice'. 'Children of the prophets' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 9:1 and Acts 3:25, and only Acts's are addressed to a congregation.
provenance.significance: The pronoun is the finding. Peter says the covenant was made 'with our fathers' — he is a Jew addressing Jews and includes himself. The speaker here says 'with your fathers', and the single letter changed is the whole difference between an Israelite preacher and the God of the covenant addressing Israel from outside the family. The same verse also converts Acts's 'God made' to 'the Father made', which is the substitution Hardy names as running through this discourse and which the Isaiah block at 20:32-35 performs on 'the LORD'. The catalogue's observation is that it begins here, eight verses earlier than the Isaiah quotation where it is usually noticed.

links.note: Seventeen consecutive words of Acts 3:25 at the close of the verse, and the Abrahamic promise reaches the Book of Mormon in Peter's form: 'kindreds', which is Acts's word for what Genesis calls nations. This is the fourth passage in the corpus to take Genesis 22:18 through Acts 3:25 rather than from Genesis (1 Nephi 15:18 and 22:9 are the earlier two, and 20:27 below is the second in this chapter), which makes Peter's sermon at Solomon's porch one of the most heavily used chapters in the New Testament for this text. Hardy cross-references Genesis 22:18 at this verse; the catalogue puts the link at Acts because that is the wording present.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.25 (Gen 22.18)

pericopes.text: the Father having raised me up unto you first, and sent me to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities; and this because ye are the children of the covenant.—

links.text: Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities.

provenance.other: “turning away every one of you from his iniquities” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:26, and 3 Nephi 20:26 reproduces it word for word — thirteen consecutive words — along with 'unto you first', 'raised', 'sent' and 'to bless you' in Acts's order.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest instance in the chapter of a borrowing that is also a reattribution. Acts 3:26 is Peter speaking about a third party in the third person: 'Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you.' 3 Nephi 20:26 keeps every content word and moves the speaker: 'the Father having raised me up unto you first, and sent me to bless you.' God becomes the Father, his Son Jesus becomes me, and him becomes me — three substitutions, one operation. Nothing else in the sentence changes, which is why the operation is visible: the sermon is intact and only the person preaching it has moved.

links.note: A thirteen-word verbatim run inside a verse whose every other clause is Acts 3:26 recast into the first person. Below Skousen's threshold on the unaltered stretch, and that is the right way to read it — the length of the untouched clause is not the point, the systematic pronoun conversion is. Note that the conversion is not available to Peter and is not a paraphrase: it is the claim that the sermon Acts reports second-hand is here being delivered at first hand.

pericopes.text: And after that ye were blessed, then fulfilleth the Father the covenant which he made with Abraham, saying: In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed, unto the pouring out of the Holy Ghost, through me upon the Gentiles, which blessing upon the Gentiles, shall make them mighty above all, unto the scattering of my people, O house of Israel;

links.text: Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.

provenance.route: Genesis 22:18 → Acts 3:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “kindreds of the earth be blessed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:25. mediation-check.py at this verse returns the same two decisive points as at 20:25: 'kindreds' for Genesis's 'nations', and the absence of Genesis's closing 'because thou hast obeyed my voice'. The promise is quoted here as a twelve-word run, 'In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed'.
provenance.significance: A second citation of the same clause two verses after the first is not a narrator reusing his own formula, which is the case ADJUDICATING §4 sends to the exclusion register; it is a speaker quoting a text twice in order to argue from it twice. At 20:25 the promise establishes who the audience is — 'ye are of the covenant which the Father made with your fathers'. At 20:27 the same words are made to run forward instead of backward: 'after that ye were blessed, then fulfilleth the Father the covenant … unto the pouring out of the Holy Ghost through me upon the Gentiles.' The seed in which all kindreds are blessed is first the audience's ancestry and then, on the second reading, the mechanism by which the blessing leaves them for the Gentiles and returns as a scourge. Abraham's promise is the hinge of the chapter's whole argument about scattering and gathering, and it is quoted twice because it has to face both ways.

links.note: The row is written rather than sent to the exclusion register as a within-book repeat because the repetition is the argument, in the sense ADJUDICATING §4 ratified at Mosiah 29:2 — the second use answers the first rather than reiterating it. The wording is Acts's, not Genesis's, on the same two tests that decided 20:25.

pericopes.text: and they shall be a scourge unto the people of this land. Nevertheless, when they shall have received the fulness of my Gospel, then if they shall harden their hearts against me, I will return their iniquities upon their own heads, saith the Father.

And I will remember the covenant which I have made with my people: and I have covenanted with them, that I would gather them together in mine own due time; that I would give unto them again the land of their fathers, for their inheritance, which is the land of Jerusalem, which is the promised land unto them forever, saith the Father.
And it shall come to pass that the time cometh, when the fulness of my gospel shall be preached unto them,
and they shall believe in me, that I am Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and shall pray unto the Father in my name.
Then shall their watchmen lift up their voice; and with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye.

links.text: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion.

provenance.other: “see eye to eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:8. The middle of the verse — 'with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye' — is verbatim; the frame is rewritten at both ends. Isaiah's 'Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice' becomes 'Then shall their watchmen lift up their voice', and Isaiah's closing 'when the LORD shall bring again Zion' is dropped and replaced by the whole of the next verse.
provenance.alternative: This is the fourth time the corpus quotes Isaiah 52:8 (Mosiah 12:22, Mosiah 15:29, 3 Nephi 16:18) and the possibility of an OT-via-earlier-BoM mediation has to be taken seriously, because 'their voice' agrees with Mosiah 15:29 against Isaiah 52:8, Mosiah 12:22 and 3 Nephi 16:18, which all read 'the voice'. Two things hold the catalogue back from recording that route. First, 3 Nephi 20:32 recasts the whole verse into the third person ('their watchmen', 'Then shall'), and once the watchmen are theirs the voice follows without any need of a model. Second, Hardy's apparatus records a possible reading 'the voice' at this verse and at Mosiah 15:29 alike — so the single word on which the earlier-Book-of-Mormon case rests is textually unsettled at both ends of the comparison. The mediation is recorded as direct-OT and the condition that would overturn it is stated: if 'their' is the reading at both places, this row should become OT-via-earlier-BoM.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's watchmen sing when the LORD brings again Zion; the clause is the reason they sing. 3 Nephi cuts it and replaces it with 'Then will the Father gather them together again, and give unto them Jerusalem' (20:33) — which keeps Isaiah's 'again' and exchanges Zion for Jerusalem and the LORD for the Father. Chapter 16 had quoted this verse whole and unaltered eight chapters earlier. Setting 16:18 beside 20:32 gives the clearest single view in the Book of Mormon of the difference between transcribing Isaiah and interpreting him, because the same speaker does both to the same verse.

links.note: Fourteen verbatim words of Isaiah 52:8 inside a verse whose opening and closing clauses are rewritten. Below Skousen's threshold on the unbroken run, and the row is not about length: Hardy's own note at 20:35 is that this second quotation carries 'interpretive variations' where the earlier one at 3 Nephi 16:18-20 was very close to the King James Bible, and the point of cataloguing all four members of the block at 20:32-35 separately is to let each variation be seen. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:8 at this verse and records a possible reading 'the voice' for the text's 'their voice'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.32 (Isa 52.8)

pericopes.text: Then will the Father gather them together again, and give unto them Jerusalem for the land of their inheritance.

links.text: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion.

provenance.other: No phrase of Isaiah 52:8 survives here except the adverb. Isaiah's clause is 'when the LORD shall bring again Zion'; this verse is 'Then will the Father gather them together again, and give unto them Jerusalem for the land of their inheritance'. Of Isaiah's six words, one is retained — 'again' — and it is retained in a different construction.
provenance.significance: The verse is the clearest place in the chapter to watch the substitution Hardy names operating on more than a divine title. Three things change at once: the LORD becomes the Father, bringing again becomes gathering together again, and Zion becomes Jerusalem given as a land of inheritance. The third is the substantive one. Isaiah's clause is about a city restored to itself; 3 Nephi's is about a people restored to a territory, which is the vocabulary the chapter has used since verse 14 ('this land, for your inheritance') and will use again at its last words in verse 46 ('it shall be the land of their inheritance'). Isaiah's closing clause is not dropped; it is translated into the chapter's own idiom of covenant land.

links.note: Recorded at high confidence and low verbal scores, which is the shape CONVENTIONS §3 exists to allow: the dependence is not seriously deniable, because this verse occupies exactly the position in the Isaiah 52:8-10 sequence that the excised clause vacated, and yet almost no wording is shared. Hardy attaches Isaiah 52:8 to this verse with the note that Isaiah reads 'when the Lord shall bring again Zion' — that is, he records the reference precisely as a replacement, which is how the catalogue reads it too.
links.whyNot: One shared word. Anybody proposing this link from verbal evidence alone would be wrong to; it rests entirely on sequence and on the clause it displaces.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.33 (Isa 52.8)

pericopes.text: Then shall they break forth into joy—sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the Father hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.

links.text: Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the LORD hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “break forth into joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:9, and so does “waste places of Jerusalem”. From 'sing together' to 'he hath redeemed Jerusalem' the verse is verbatim but for one word: 'the LORD hath comforted his people' becomes 'the Father hath comforted his people'.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 49:13, 'break forth into singing, O mountains: for the LORD hath comforted his people', is the other KJV verse joining a breaking forth to that clause and is displaced in the exclusion register; it has neither the joy nor the waste places.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:9 is an imperative addressed to ruins: break forth, sing, because the comforting has already happened. 3 Nephi turns the first half into a prediction — 'Then shall they break forth into joy' — and leaves the second half as Isaiah's imperative, so the verse is half foretold and half commanded, and the seam falls exactly where the chapter's own frame ends and the quotation begins. The comforting is then reassigned: the LORD who comforted his people in Isaiah is the Father here, which is the substitution running through 20:32-35 and, as 20:25 shows, through the Acts block before it. Compare 3 Nephi 16:19, where the same verse stands with no alteration at all.

links.note: Twenty-two words of Isaiah 52:9 with a single word replaced, past Skousen's threshold on the unbroken stretch. The value of the row is comparative: the catalogue already holds this verse unaltered at 3 Nephi 16:19 and at Mosiah 12:23 and 15:30, so the one word changed here is measurable against three earlier copies rather than only against the King James Bible.

pericopes.text: The Father hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of the Father; and the Father and I are one.—

links.text: The LORD hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

provenance.other: “made bare his holy arm”, “in the eyes of all the nations” and “ends of the earth shall see” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:10 — three singletons in twenty-five words. The two departures are both at the divine names: 'The LORD hath made bare' → 'The Father hath made bare', and 'the salvation of our God' → 'the salvation of the Father'. “I and my Father are one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:30, and the appended clause 'and the Father and I are one' is that verse with its two terms reversed.
provenance.significance: Chapter 16 removed a word here and chapter 20 fills the hole. At 3 Nephi 16:20 Isaiah's 'the salvation of our God' was quoted as 'the salvation of God', with the possessive simply deleted and nothing put in its place; here the possessive is supplied, and supplied as 'the Father'. Then the sentence does not stop where Isaiah stops. It adds 'and the Father and I are one', which is John 10:30 inverted, and the addition is what makes the whole substitution legible: if the Father and the speaker are one, then replacing Isaiah's LORD with the Father through four verses has changed the reference of nothing. The chapter rewrites Isaiah's divine name and then, in five words, argues that the rewriting was not a change. Hardy directs the reader to 3 Nephi 11:27 at this point, where the same unity is stated of Father, Son and Holy Ghost.

links.note: Twenty-five words of Isaiah 52:10 carrying three KJV singletons, two divine-name substitutions, and a five-word Johannine addition. Well past Skousen's threshold. Hardy hangs 'Verses 32-35 quote Isa 52.8-10' on this verse, notes that this is the second time the speaker quotes the passage, and observes that the earlier wording at 3 Nephi 16:18-20 was very close to the King James Bible whereas here the original Lord is replaced by Father throughout — which is the sentence that governs how this whole block has been adjudicated. The catalogue writes four links rather than one so that the replacement can be counted verse by verse.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.35 (Isa 52.8-10)

pericopes.text: And then shall be brought to pass that which is writen: Awake, awake again, and put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.

links.text: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.

provenance.other: “put on thy beautiful garments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:1, and so does “the uncircumcised and the unclean”. Apart from two inserted words the verse is reproduced entire — thirty consecutive words from 'put on thy strength, O Zion' to 'the uncircumcised and the unclean'. The insertion is 'again, and': 'Awake, awake again, and put on thy strength'.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 52:1-2 had already been quoted in the corpus at 2 Nephi 8:24-25, inside the Isaiah 51-52 block, and an OT-via-earlier-BoM route has to be weighed. At this verse it is not supported: 2 Nephi 8:24 reads 'Awake, awake, put on thy strength' with the King James Bible, and 3 Nephi 20:36's 'again, and' is this verse's own. The following verse, 20:37, gives a different answer.
provenance.significance: 'Awake, awake again' is not a stutter. Isaiah 52:1 is itself a second awakening — it answers Isaiah 51:9's 'Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD' and 51:17's 'Awake, awake, stand up, O Jerusalem', so the chapter opens by waking a city that has been told to wake twice already. The inserted 'again' says out loud what Isaiah's arrangement implies, which is a small but real piece of interpretation performed inside a quotation. Note also where the quotation begins: this chapter reached Isaiah 52 at verse 8 first (20:32, and 3 Nephi 16:18 before that), and only now goes back for the opening. The frame is quoted after the middle, which is why the verse order of the block runs 8-10, 1-3, 6-7, 11-15.

links.note: A thirty-word verbatim run, comfortably past Skousen's threshold, in a verse the corpus has quoted once before. Hardy keys 'Verses 36-38 quote Isa 52.1-3' to 20:38 and notes that Isaiah 52:1-2 was also quoted at 2 Nephi 8:24-25; the catalogue writes a link at each of 36, 37 and 38 because the three verses stand in three different relations to the earlier Book of Mormon quotation.

pericopes.text: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.

links.text: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:2 → KJV → 2 Nephi 8:25 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “captive daughter of Zion” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:2, and so does “the bands of thy neck”. The verse is otherwise reproduced entire, seventeen consecutive words at the end of it, with exactly one departure from the King James Bible: Isaiah reads 'arise, AND sit down, O Jerusalem' and 3 Nephi 20:37 reads 'arise, sit down, O Jerusalem'.
provenance.alternative: A dropped conjunction is thin evidence for a route on its own, and two writers could drop it independently. What makes it worth recording is that it is the ONLY departure in either passage: 2 Nephi 8:25 reproduces Isaiah 52:2 word for word except for the same missing 'and', and 3 Nephi 20:37 reproduces it word for word except for the same missing 'and'. Two verbatim quotations of one verse, made hundreds of pages apart, agreeing in their single deviation. Both readings hold in the 1830, 1920 and current editions, so this is not an artifact of the running text chosen. Compare 20:36, where 2 Nephi 8:24 and 3 Nephi 20:36 do NOT agree — 3 Nephi adds 'again, and' where 2 Nephi has the King James text — which is the control that keeps this from being a claim about the block as a whole.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's cleanest instance of the route CONVENTIONS §7 predicted would appear from 2 Nephi onward: a Book of Mormon passage whose proximate model is an earlier Book of Mormon passage rather than the Bible. The evidence is a single conjunction, which is exactly the kind of evidence a mediation test is built to use — the pilot's sixteen OT-via-NT rows each turned on one word. The metaleptic payoff is that the chapter is quoting a text its audience's own scriptures already contained: Nephi had read Isaiah 52:1-2 to this people's ancestors six centuries earlier, and the risen Christ gives it back to them in the form their own record preserved.

links.note: Seventeen words verbatim and one conjunction missing, and the missing conjunction carries the row. Past Skousen's threshold on run length. The mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM with its evidence stated in full above so that a reader who thinks one dropped 'and' is too little can see exactly what the claim rests on and decline it. Hardy notes at 20:38 that Isaiah 52:1-2 was also quoted at 2 Nephi 8:24-25; the collation of the two Book of Mormon passages against each other, and the finding, are the catalogue's own.
links.whyNot: One word, and a function word at that. If 2 Nephi 8:25's omission and 3 Nephi 20:37's omission are independent — and a light conjunction is the likeliest word in the verse to drop by accident twice — the route collapses to direct-OT and nothing else in the verse would notice.

pericopes.text: For thus saith the Lord, Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.

links.text: For thus saith the LORD, Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.

provenance.other: “sold yourselves for nought” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:3, and so does “redeemed without money”. The verse is reproduced without a single substantive change — eighteen consecutive words — the only difference being the printing of 'the Lord' for the King James small-capital 'LORD', which is a compositor's choice and not a reading.
provenance.significance: The verse is worth its row precisely because nothing happens to it. Isaiah 52 reaches this chapter under continuous alteration — the LORD becomes the Father at 20:34 and 20:35, the watchmen change person at 20:32, an 'again' is inserted at 20:36, a conjunction is dropped at 20:37 — and then verse 3 arrives untouched. It is also the one verse of the quoted portion that speaks of a redemption without payment, which the chapter has no need to reassign, since the speaker is the redeemer. Where the substitutions stop is as much a fact about the discourse as where they occur.

links.note: Eighteen words verbatim, two KJV singletons, above Skousen's threshold. The 1830 sets 'nought', the King James spelling, where later editions read 'naught' — one of three places in this chapter (with 'hoofs' at 20:19 and 'rereward' at 20:42) where the first edition preserves the source's orthography and a later edition modernizes it. CONVENTIONS §8's first bullet, three times in one chapter. Hardy keys 'Verses 36-38 quote Isa 52.1-3' to this verse.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.38 (Isa 52.1-3)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.38 (Isa 52.1-2)

pericopes.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, That my people shall know my name; yea, in that day they shall know that I am he that doth speak.

links.text: Therefore my people shall know my name: therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I.

provenance.other: “he that doth speak” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:6. The shared material is substantial — 'my people shall know my name', 'they shall know', 'in that day', 'that I am he that doth speak' — but reordered: Isaiah has 'they shall know in that day that I am he', and 3 Nephi has 'in that day they shall know that I am he'. Isaiah's two 'therefore's are replaced by 'Verily, verily, I say unto you' and 'yea', and Isaiah's closing three words are dropped.
provenance.significance: What is dropped is the point. Isaiah 52:6 ends 'behold, it is I' — a self-identification deferred to a future day when the people will at last know the name. The speaker of 3 Nephi 20 removes it, and he removes it because he has just supplied it in person: the chapter opened with the multitude giving glory to Jesus 'whom they both saw and heard' (20:9). Isaiah's promise that one day they will know that I am he that doth speak is quoted by the one speaking, to people who are looking at him. The excision is the fulfilment. Hardy's apparatus records the missing clause without comment; the reading of it is the catalogue's.

links.note: Substantial verbal agreement with one KJV singleton, but the clause order is rearranged and the verse is framed by the Book of Mormon's own 'Verily, verily, I say unto you', so it falls below Skousen's threshold on any single unbroken run. Certain nonetheless: Isaiah 52:6 is the only verse in the Bible with this combination, and it arrives in the exact sequential position between the block's 52:3 and 52:7. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:6 here and quotes the omitted words.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.39 (Isa 52.6)

pericopes.text: And then shall they say, How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings unto them, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings unto them of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “how beautiful upon the mountains” and “Thy God reigneth” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:7; “that publisheth peace” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15. mediation-check.py against Romans 10:15 and Nahum 1:15 returns seven decisive points and every one favours Isaiah: the Book of Mormon has 'How beautiful' where Nahum has 'Behold', keeps 'that publisheth salvation … Thy God reigneth' which Nahum lacks entirely, and keeps 'bringeth good tidings, that publisheth' where Romans reads 'preach the gospel of'. The only departure from Isaiah is a twice-inserted 'unto them' after 'good tidings'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:7 is the most quoted verse of this chapter in the New Testament — Paul cites it at Romans 10:15 to argue that the gospel must be preached before it can be believed — and the mediation test is decisive that it does not reach 3 Nephi through Paul. That is worth stating because the context here is Paul's context: verse 30 has just promised that 'the fulness of my gospel shall be preached unto them', which is Romans 10's argument exactly, and the quotation that follows is still Isaiah's wording and not Paul's. The doubled 'unto them' is the interpretive addition: Isaiah's herald brings good tidings to nobody in particular, and here the tidings have an addressee — the scattered Israel of verse 29 to whom the gospel is to be preached.

links.note: Thirty-odd words tracking Isaiah 52:7 clause for clause with two identical two-word insertions, well past Skousen's threshold on the unbroken stretches. The verse has been quoted twice before in the corpus, at Mosiah 12:21 and in Abinadi's exposition at Mosiah 15:14-18, neither of which has the doubled 'unto them'; so unlike 20:37, this verse gives no evidence of an earlier-Book-of-Mormon route. Hardy keys 'Verses 39-40 quote Isa 52.6-7' to this verse and notes the Mosiah quotations.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.40 (Isa 52.6-7)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.40 (Isa 52.7)

pericopes.text: And then shall a cry go forth, Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch not that which is unclean; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the Lord.

links.text: Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD.

provenance.other: “bear the vessels of the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:11. The verse is otherwise reproduced whole, eighteen consecutive words from 'go ye out of the midst of her' to the end, with one clause rephrased: Isaiah's 'touch no unclean thing' becomes 'touch not that which is unclean'.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 6:17 quotes this verse — 'come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing' — and the Book of Mormon's 'touch not' agrees with Paul's negative against Isaiah's 'touch no'. mediation-check.py nonetheless returns three decisive points for Isaiah and none for Paul: the Book of Mormon has 'Depart ye, depart ye, go ye' where Paul has 'Wherefore come', keeps 'from thence' which Paul lacks, and keeps the whole of 'go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the Lord', for which Paul substitutes 'and I will receive you'. The mediation is direct-OT; the rephrased clause is filed in the exclusion register so that a reader who notices the agreement with Paul is told the catalogue noticed it too.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:11 is addressed to the priests carrying the temple vessels out of Babylon, and the uncleanness it forbids is the ritual kind — a thing, an object one might handle on the road. 'Touch not that which is unclean' loosens the object into a category, which is the direction 2 Corinthians 6:17 had already taken the verse when Paul made it about company rather than cargo. So the departure moves with the New Testament's reading without adopting the New Testament's words — the sense is Pauline and the vocabulary is Isaian. That combination is worth recording precisely because the mediation test says it is not a case of borrowing from Paul.

links.note: Eighteen words verbatim, past Skousen's threshold, inside a verse whose only alteration is a four-word rephrasing and an added frame ('And then shall a cry go forth'). Hardy keys 'Verses 41-45 quote Isa 52.11-15' to 20:45, his convention of hanging the citation on the last verse of a span; the catalogue writes a link at each of the five so that the very different amounts of alteration in them can be seen. He also notes at 3 Nephi 21:29 that the speaker there returns to Isaiah 52:11 and to this verse.

pericopes.text: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the Lord will go before you; and the God of Israel shall be your rereward.

links.text: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the LORD will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward.

provenance.other: “nor go by flight” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:12, and “will be your rereward” in exactly one, the same verse. The whole verse is reproduced — twenty-four consecutive words — with a single word changed: 'the God of Israel WILL be your rereward' becomes 'SHALL be your rereward'.
provenance.significance: One auxiliary verb, and it is the same auxiliary the chapter has been putting into Isaiah since verse 32. Isaiah's futures are statements about what God will do; 3 Nephi's are promises inside a covenant being enacted in front of an audience, and 'shall' is the covenanting form. The metalepsis is in what Isaiah 52:12 is doing when it says it: the verse contrasts the return from Babylon with the Exodus, where Israel DID go out in haste (Exodus 12:11, 'ye shall eat it in haste'). Quoted here, the promise of an unhurried departure with God before and behind is addressed to a people whose founding story in this book is a hurried flight from Jerusalem.

links.note: Twenty-four words verbatim with one auxiliary changed, past Skousen's threshold. The 1830 keeps the King James spelling 'rereward' — an archaic form of rearguard, which Hardy has to gloss for his own readers — and 1920 modernizes it to 'rearward'. The first edition therefore shows the borrowing on the page in a way the current text does not, which is the whole reason CONVENTIONS §8 makes the 1830 the running text.

pericopes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high.

links.text: Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high.

provenance.other: “exalted and extolled” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:13, as do “deal prudently” and “my servant shall deal”. The verse is reproduced entire and without any change whatever — sixteen consecutive words, the whole verse.
provenance.significance: This is where the Book of Mormon's most consequential piece of Isaiah interpretation begins, and it begins by changing nothing. Isaiah 52:13-15 opens the fourth Servant Song, which runs on into Isaiah 53; the speaker here quotes its first three verses verbatim at 20:43-45 and then, in the next chapter, takes them up as a prophecy of a latter-day servant and of a book (21:8-11, where Hardy notes that the 'marred' of Isaiah 52:14 is applied to a named individual). So the exact reproduction here is the precondition for the reading there: the text has to be given whole before it can be reapplied.

links.note: A sixteen-word verbatim reproduction of an entire verse, three KJV singletons in it, and exactly at Skousen's threshold — worth flagging for anyone collating this catalogue against his list of long quotations, though whether he counts it cannot be checked (PLAN §4.1). Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:13-14 and this verse at 3 Nephi 21:10, which is where the servant passage is put to work.

pericopes.text: As many were astonished at thee; (his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men:)

links.text: As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men:

provenance.other: “his visage was so marred” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:14. Twenty consecutive words are reproduced from 'his visage' to 'the sons of men'. The single departure is the opening participle: Isaiah reads 'As many were ASTONIED at thee', and 3 Nephi 20:44 reads 'astonished'.
provenance.alternative: “astonished at thee” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Ezekiel 26:16, 27:35 and 28:19 — and Isaiah 52:14 is not among them, so a rarity search on the Book of Mormon's own wording lands on the oracles against Tyre rather than on the Servant Song. That is a trap and it is filed in the exclusion register. Nothing else in the verse is Ezekiel's, and the twenty words after the participle are Isaiah's alone.
provenance.significance: 'Astonied' is the King James Bible's older form and it occurs in ten of its verses; 'astonished' is the form that displaced it, and every edition of the Book of Mormon from 1830 onward has the modern word. It is the only place in this chapter's whole Isaiah block where the Book of Mormon reads a modernization of the King James vocabulary rather than preserving it — and it stands three verses after 'rereward', which the 1830 preserves and 1920 modernizes. The two words pull in opposite directions within a single page, which is a useful caution against treating the first edition's relation to the King James Bible as uniform.

links.note: Twenty words verbatim past a single modernized participle, well above Skousen's threshold. The one substituted word is the row's whole interest, because it is a substitution of exactly the kind CONVENTIONS §8 says to watch for and it runs the other way from the chapter's other three. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:13-14 at 3 Nephi 21:10.

pericopes.text: so shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.

links.text: So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.

provenance.other: “sprinkle many nations” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:15, and so does “shut their mouths”. The verse is reproduced entire. In the current and 1920 texts there is no departure at all; in the 1830 running text there is exactly one, and it is an omitted negative.
provenance.significance: The 1830 sets 'for that which had been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider', dropping the 'not' from the first clause and keeping it in the second. Isaiah's couplet depends on both negatives — kings fall silent because what was never reported to them is now in front of their eyes — and without the first one the line says the opposite of what the second says, which is why later editions restore it. This is CONVENTIONS §8's second pattern and the clearest instance the catalogue has met: a first-edition reading that departs from the King James Bible, and a later edition correcting the Book of Mormon back TOWARD its source. The chapter contains three such corrections — 'hoops' to 'hoofs' at 20:19, this omitted negative, and, running the other way, 'rereward' to 'rearward' at 20:42.

links.note: A complete verbatim verse in the modern text, past Skousen's threshold; the finding is in the 1830. The missing negative also matters downstream, because 3 Nephi 21:8 quotes the second half of this verse again — 'kings shall shut their mouths; for that which had not been told them shall they see' — and the 1830 prints the 'not' there, so the first edition disagrees with itself about the same clause one chapter apart. Hardy keys 'Verses 41-45 quote Isa 52.11-15' to this verse and cross-references 20:45 from 21:8.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.45 (Isa 52.11-15)

pericopes.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, All these things shall surely come, even as the Father hath commanded me. Then shall this covenant which the Father hath covenanted with his people, be fulfilled; and then shall Jerusalem be inhabited again with my people: and it shall be the land of their inheritance.

links.text: In that day will I make the governors of Judah like an hearth of fire among the wood, and like a torch of fire in a sheaf; and they shall devour all the people round about, on the right hand and on the left: and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again in her own place, even in Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “inhabited again” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Zechariah 12:6 — 'and Jerusalem shall be inhabited again in her own place, even in Jerusalem'. 3 Nephi 20:46 reads 'then shall Jerusalem be inhabited again with my people'. The shared material is 'Jerusalem … be inhabited again', four words plus the name, and the name is in both clauses in the same syntactic slot. “shall be inhabited” occurs in exactly four KJV verses and only Zechariah 12:6 has the adverb.
provenance.significance: Zechariah 12 is the chapter in which Jerusalem is besieged by all nations and delivered, and its reinhabitation is the reward for a siege survived. 3 Nephi 20 ends on the same note and reaches it by an entirely different route — through a covenant with Abraham, a scattering by the Gentiles and a gathering by the Father. The borrowed adverb carries Zechariah's premise with it: 'again' presumes an emptying, and the chapter has spent forty-five verses describing one. Note too what the chapter does with 'in her own place'. Zechariah insists the restored city is the old city on the old ground; 3 Nephi 20:46 replaces that clause with 'with my people … and it shall be the land of their inheritance', which is the covenant-land vocabulary of 20:14 and 20:33.

links.note: A row the machine did not propose and that a reader could reasonably decline. Four shared words is very little, and 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited' is a thought a writer on the restoration of Israel might have without a source. What lifts it to moderate is that the adverb is a KJV singleton and that it is the operative word in both sentences — in Zechariah because the city was emptied, here because the people were scattered. Recorded under CONVENTIONS §0a as a connection worth gesturing at; declining it costs the catalogue nothing and it is offered on that understanding.
links.whyNot: Four words, one of them a proper noun. There is no syntactic agreement beyond the phrase itself, no second point of contact anywhere in the verse, and the wider contexts share a topic rather than a text.

pericopes.text: And verily, I say unto you, I give unto you a sign, that ye may know the time when these things shall be about to take place, that I shall gather in from their long dispersion, my people, O house of Israel, and shall establish again among them my Zion.

And behold, this is the thing which I will give unto you for a sign: for verily, I say unto you, That when these things which I declare unto you, and which I shall declare unto you hereafter of myself, and by the power of the Holy Ghost, which shall be given unto you of the Father, shall be made known unto the Gentiles, that they may know concerning this people which are a remnant of the house of Jacob, and concerning this my people which shall be scattered by them;
verily, verily, I say unto you, When these things shall be made known unto them of the Father, and shall come forth of the Father from them unto you:

for it is wisdom in the Father that they should be established in this land, and be set up as a free people by the power of the Father, that these things might come forth from them unto a remnant of your seed, that the covenant of the Father may be fulfilled which he hath covenanted with his people, O house of Israel;
therefore, when these works, and the works which shall be wrought among you hereafter, shall come forth from the Gentiles unto your seed, which shall dwindle in unbelief because of iniquity:

for thus it behooveth the Father that it should come forth from the Gentiles, that he may shew forth his power unto the Gentiles, for this cause, that the Gentiles, if they will not harden their hearts, that they may repent and come unto me, and be baptized in my name, and know of the true points of my doctrine, that they may be numbered among my people, O house of Israel;

and when these things come to pass, that thy seed shall begin to know these things, it shall be a sign unto them, that they may know that the work of the Father hath already commenced unto the fulfilling of the covenant which he hath made unto the people which are of the house of Israel.

links.text: In that day shall thy mouth be opened to him which is escaped, and thou shalt speak, and be no more dumb: and thou shalt be a sign unto them; and they shall know that I am the LORD.

provenance.other: “a sign unto them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 24:27, and in exactly one Book of Mormon verse, this one — the corpus never uses the phrase again.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 24:27 is the hinge of Ezekiel's commission: the prophet's mouth is opened on the day the fugitive arrives from the fallen city, and the prophet himself becomes the sign that Israel is meant to read. 3 Nephi 21:7 asks the same of a record rather than a man — the coming forth of a book is the sign, and the thing to be known from it is that the Father's work has begun. The borrowed clause carries Ezekiel's grammar of signs intact: a sign given to a scattered people, whose content is not information but the identity of the one acting.

links.note: “It shall be a sign unto them, that they may know that the work of the Father hath already commenced.” The phrase “a sign unto them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 24:27, where it is followed by exactly the same purpose clause — “and they shall know that I am the LORD” answering “that they may know that the work of the Father hath already commenced.” Sign plus knowledge-clause is a small unit of two elements, and it is well below any quotation threshold; what recommends it is that the Book of Mormon uses the phrase once in 6,000 verses and the KJV uses it once in 31,000, and that both uses do the same work in the same order.

pericopes.text: And when that day shall come, it shall come to pass that kings shall shut their mouths: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.

links.text: So shall he sprinkle many nations; the kings shall shut their mouths at him: for that which had not been told them shall they see; and that which they had not heard shall they consider.

provenance.other: “kings shall shut their mouths” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The twenty-one words from “for that which had not been told them” to “shall they consider” are reproduced without a single change, which is above Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold for a long quotation — though whether he counts this passage among his thirty-six cannot be checked, since the itemized list is unobtainable (PLAN §4.1).
provenance.significance: Christ has already quoted Isaiah 52:15 nine verses earlier, at 3 Nephi 20:45, inside the continuous Isaiah 52:11-15 block. Here he quotes it again and re-times it: “And when that day shall come” replaces Isaiah's “So shall he sprinkle many nations”, and the silenced kings are relocated from the servant's exaltation to the coming forth of a record among the Gentiles. Dropping “at him” is what makes the move possible — with the servant removed from the clause, the kings fall silent before a thing seen and heard rather than before a person.

links.note: Three departures from the KJV, all at the head: Isaiah's “So shall he sprinkle many nations” is replaced by “And when that day shall come, it shall come to pass”; “the kings” loses its article; and “at him” is dropped. What follows is twenty-one words verbatim. The 1830 reading is itself the evidence here (CONVENTIONS §8): at 3 Nephi 20:45 the first edition prints “for that which had been told them shall they see”, dropping the KJV's “not” and inverting the sense, and 1920 restored it. The first edition therefore contains one defective and one exact citation of the same verse nine verses apart, and this is the exact one — a first-edition fact that the modern text, having repaired 20:45, no longer shows.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.8 (Isa 52.15; cf. 3 Ne 20.45)

pericopes.text: For in that day, for my sake shall the Father work a work, which shall be a great and a marvellous work among them; and there shall be among them which will not believe it, although a man shall declare it unto them.

links.text: Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you.

provenance.mt: Habakkuk 1:5 — 'for I WILL WORK A WORK in your days WHICH YE WILL NOT BELIEVE, THOUGH IT BE TOLD YOU.'
provenance.route: Habakkuk 1:5 → Acts 13:41 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “work a work” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Habakkuk 1:5 and Acts 13:41 — the prophecy and Paul's citation of it at Antioch. The two diverge at the end of the sentence, and tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point: Habakkuk has “though it be told you”, Acts has “though a man declare it unto you”, and the Book of Mormon has “although a man shall declare it unto them”. Every other divergence between the two is a place where 3 Nephi reads with neither.
provenance.significance: This is a mediation result of the kind CONVENTIONS §7 exists for, and it turns on one word: 'a man'. Habakkuk's unbelieved work is told; Acts's unbelieved work is declared by a man, and 3 Nephi's is too. Recover the context of the New Testament form and the borrowing acquires a target — Acts 13:41 is the closing threat of Paul's synagogue sermon, quoted against hearers who are about to reject the message and so hand it to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46, 'lo, we turn to the Gentiles'). 3 Nephi 21 is doing the reverse motion with the same verse: a work brought forth by the Gentiles, disbelieved by some among them, which will be the sign that the covenant with Israel is resuming. Hardy's apparatus glosses the 'man' of this verse as Joseph Smith Jr.; it cites no biblical source at the verse.

links.note: “For my sake shall the Father work a work … and there shall be among them which will not believe it, although a man shall declare it unto them.” Three elements of Acts 13:41 survive in Acts's order — working a work, not believing it, and a man declaring it — and the third is the one that decides the source. The Old Testament verse behind Acts, Habakkuk 1:5, has no man in it at all: the work there is simply 'told'. So the Book of Mormon has the sermon's wording, not the prophet's, in a chapter whose whole subject is a message rejected by its first hearers and carried to the Gentiles. The shared run is short and the case rests on the collocation plus the single decisive substitution, not on length.

links.text: Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid.

provenance.other: “a marvellous work among” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:14 — 'I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder'. 3 Nephi 21:9 reads 'a marvellous work among them'. Note what is NOT borrowed: “great and marvellous” is the Book of Mormon's own settled formula, used twenty-four times from 1 Nephi 1:14 onward, where it is taken from Revelation 15:3; here it is prefixed to Isaiah's noun phrase rather than drawn from Revelation afresh.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29 is the chapter the Book of Mormon has already mined twice at length (2 Nephi 27 quotes it entire, around the sealed book that the learned cannot read), and Isaiah 29:14's marvellous work is glossed in its own verse as the perishing of 'the wisdom of their wise men'. 3 Nephi 21:9-10 then does exactly that: it announces the marvellous work and immediately says 'I will shew unto them that my wisdom is greater than the cunning of the Devil'. The wisdom contest is Isaiah's, recovered from the half of the verse that is not quoted.

links.note: Isaiah 29:14's “marvellous work” arrives here fused with the Book of Mormon's own habitual intensifier. The KJV singleton is precise — “a marvellous work among” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the object is the same in both: a people among whom God will do something they will not be able to account for. The Isaiah half of this verse and the Acts 13:41 half are two sources in one clause, which is why both are catalogued: 'work a work' is Acts's, 'a marvellous work among them' is Isaiah's, and the sentence needs both to be what it is.

pericopes.text: But behold, the life of my servant shall be in my hand; therefore they shall not hurt him, although he shall be marred because of them. Yet I will heal him, for I will shew unto them that my wisdom is greater than the cunning of the Devil.

links.text: As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men:

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:13-14 → KJV → Book of Mormon (via the block quoted at 3 Nephi 20:43-44)
provenance.other: “marred” occurs in five KJV verses; three are potters' and vintners' spoilage (Jeremiah 13:7, 18:4, Nahum 2:2), one is a wineskin (Mark 2:22), and only Isaiah 52:14 marrs a person. 'My servant' opens Isaiah 52:13, the verse quoted at 3 Nephi 20:43. The verse's one distinctive word is decisive on its own: “marred more than” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:14.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis in the strict sense. Thirteen verses earlier Christ quoted Isaiah 52:13-14 of himself: 'Behold, my servant shall deal prudently … his visage was so marred more than any man.' Here the same two words — 'my servant', 'marred' — are transferred to a different figure, and the transfer is what the verse is for: this servant is marred but not killed, and unlike Isaiah's he is healed. Isaiah 52:13-53:12 never heals its servant; the healing in that poem happens to other people, by his stripes. 3 Nephi 21:10 detaches the marring from the atoning death and gives it a survivor. Recovering the suppressed context is exactly what makes the sentence legible: the latter-day servant is being placed inside the Servant Song without being made the Servant.

links.note: “The life of my servant shall be in my hand; therefore they shall not hurt him, although he shall be marred because of them. Yet I will heal him.” Two words carry the link, and both were on the page a few minutes earlier in the discourse: 'my servant' from Isaiah 52:13 and 'marred' from Isaiah 52:14, quoted at 3 Nephi 20:43-44. There is no continuous run and the verbal contact is thin, which is why this is catalogued as an allusion and not a quotation; what makes it high confidence is that the source was quoted verbatim by the same speaker in the same sermon, so availability, in the ordinary sense, is not in question here even though it is for the corpus at large (CONVENTIONS §3a).
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.10 (compare Isa 52.13-14; 3 Ne 20.43-44)

pericopes.text: Therefore it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not believe in my words, which am Jesus Christ, which the Father shall cause him to bring forth unto the Gentiles, and shall give unto him power that he shall bring them forth unto the Gentiles, (it shall be done even as Moses said,) they shall be cut off from among my people which are of the covenant;

links.text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.

provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 18:19 — 'And it shall come to pass, that WHOSOEVER WILL NOT HEARKEN UNTO MY WORDS which he shall speak in my name, I WILL REQUIRE IT OF HIM.' Acts 3:23 — 'And it shall come to pass, that EVERY SOUL, WHICH WILL NOT HEAR THAT PROPHET, SHALL BE DESTROYED FROM AMONG THE PEOPLE.'
provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:19 → Acts 3:23 → 1 Nephi 22:20 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points, both for Deuteronomy: the Book of Mormon has “whosoever” where Acts has “every soul, which”, and “not believe in my words” against Deuteronomy's “not hearken unto my words” where Acts has “not hear that prophet”. The apodosis belongs to neither: Deuteronomy has “I will require it of him”, Acts has “shall be destroyed from among the people”, and 3 Nephi has “they shall be cut off from among my people”. “Cut off” for “destroyed” is the Book of Mormon's own reading, introduced at 1 Nephi 22:20 and repeated at 3 Nephi 20:23. Note also that “hearken unto my words”, the phrase Deuteronomy 18:19 supplies and this verse negates as “believe in my words”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse — that verse — which is why 21:22's positive restatement is catalogued too.
provenance.significance: This is the OT-via-earlier-BoM case CONVENTIONS §7 anticipates, and it is unusually clean because the same sentence appears twice in the same sermon in two different forms. At 3 Nephi 20:23 Christ quotes the Mosaic prophecy in Acts 3:22-23's wording — 'every soul which will not hear that prophet' — as 1 Nephi 22:20 had. Thirty-four verses later he quotes it again and the protasis has reverted to Deuteronomy 18:19: 'whosoever will not … my words'. What does not revert is the verb. Both citations read 'cut off', which is in neither biblical source and is the reading 1 Nephi 22:20 established. So the proximate model here is not the Bible on either side; it is the Book of Mormon's own settled form of the sanction, with a fresh Deuteronomic protasis fitted to it. The substitution that makes the verse do its work is orthogonal to all of this: 'will not hearken unto my words' becomes 'will not believe in my words, which am Jesus Christ' — the Mosaic prophet's words are identified as the Book of Mormon, and refusing the book is made the disqualifying act.

links.note: “Whosoever will not believe in my words … they shall be cut off from among my people which are of the covenant.” The mediation test is decisive twice over and it points two ways at once. Against Acts 3:23 the protasis is Deuteronomy's; against Deuteronomy 18:19 the apodosis has a 'from among the people' clause Deuteronomy does not have. The reading that reconciles them is that neither Bible verse is the proximate source: 1 Nephi 22:20 fused Acts 3:22-23's sermon-form with 'cut off' for 'destroyed', 3 Nephi 20:23 repeated that fusion, and 21:11 inherits the fused apodosis while going back to Deuteronomy for the front of the sentence. Hardy's apparatus reaches the same chain by a different route, cross-referencing Deuteronomy 18:19 with Acts 3:23 and 1 Nephi 22:20 at this verse and observing that the term 'cut off' is what ties the Mosaic sanction to the Micah oracle beginning in the next verse, where it recurs six times. The parenthesis '(it shall be done even as Moses said)' is the text saying so itself.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.11n (Deut 18.19; cf. Acts 3.23; cf. 1 Ne 22.20)
Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 20.23n (Acts 3.23 reads “destroyed”)

pericopes.text: and my people which are a remnant of Jacob, shall be among the Gentiles, yea, in the midst of them, as a lion among the beasts of the forest, as a young lion among the flocks of sheep, who, if he go through, both treadeth down and teareth in pieces, and none can deliver.

links.text: And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles in the midst of many people as a lion among the beasts of the forest, as a young lion among the flocks of sheep: who, if he go through, both treadeth down, and teareth in pieces, and none can deliver.

provenance.other: Three separate phrases of this verse are KJV singletons: “young lion among the flocks” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, “teareth in pieces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “none can deliver” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — all three of them Micah 5:8.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 21:12-18 and 21:21 reproduce Micah 5:8-15 continuously, the longest Micah quotation anywhere in the Bible or the Book of Mormon. The quotation is not the finding; the substitutions are. Two run through the whole block: 'saith the LORD' becomes 'saith the Father' (21:14), and the second-person address of Micah's oracle is converted into third-person description of the Gentiles. Recover Micah's context and the reversal is the point — Micah 5:10-15 is a threat against Israel's own war-machine and idolatry, spoken to Israel; in 3 Nephi the same words are turned outward and spoken against the Gentiles, with the remnant of Jacob standing where Micah's God stands. This verse is also the third and closest of three passes at Micah 5:8 in 3 Nephi, and the sequence is the argument. At 16:14 the verse enters as a threat withheld, with only its two verbs ('go through', 'tread down') and no lion. At 20:16 the lion appears but the subject is converted to direct address — 'ye shall be among them, as a lion'. Only here is Micah's own subject restored: 'my people which are a remnant of Jacob, shall be among the Gentiles'. The quotation moves toward its source as the discourse proceeds, which is the opposite of what a fading formula does.

links.note: A thirty-four word run against Micah 5:8 with two changes: Micah's 'the remnant of Jacob' becomes 'my people which are a remnant of Jacob', and 'in the midst of many people' becomes 'yea, in the midst of them'. Everything from 'as a lion among the beasts of the forest' to 'and none can deliver' is verbatim, and three of its phrases occur nowhere else in the King James Bible. This is the fullest of the book's three uses of the verse and it is not the first: 3 Nephi 16:14 and 20:16 precede it. Under ADJUDICATING §4 a repeat within a book is normally recorded rather than re-linked, but the rule's own exception applies — the phrase is not recurring, it is returning to its source, and it arrives here more nearly Micah's than at either earlier stop. Hardy sets this verse and the eleven that follow under the heading 'Jesus Quotes Micah 5.8-15'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.13n (Mic 5.8-9, noting the same verses were quoted at 3 Ne 20.16-17)

pericopes.text: Their hand shall be lifted up upon their adversaries, and all their enemies shall be cut off.

links.text: Thine hand shall be lifted up upon thine adversaries, and all thine enemies shall be cut off.

provenance.other: “hand shall be lifted up upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:9.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 21:12-18 and 21:21 reproduce Micah 5:8-15 continuously, the longest Micah quotation anywhere in the Bible or the Book of Mormon. The quotation is not the finding; the substitutions are. Two run through the whole block: 'saith the LORD' becomes 'saith the Father' (21:14), and the second-person address of Micah's oracle is converted into third-person description of the Gentiles. Recover Micah's context and the reversal is the point — Micah 5:10-15 is a threat against Israel's own war-machine and idolatry, spoken to Israel; in 3 Nephi the same words are turned outward and spoken against the Gentiles, with the remnant of Jacob standing where Micah's God stands. Here the direction of drift is the reverse of 21:12's: 3 Nephi 20:17 reproduced Micah 5:9 with its pronouns nearly intact ('Thy hand … thine adversaries … thine enemies'), and this citation converts all three to 'their'. That is not carelessness but consistency — 21:12 had already replaced Micah's addressee with a described third party, so the oracle spoken TO the remnant at 20:17 is now spoken ABOUT it.

links.note: Fourteen of Micah 5:9's seventeen words, with the second-person pronouns — its only other content — turned to third person throughout: 'Their hand … their adversaries … all their enemies'. The KJV construction 'hand shall be lifted up upon' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The verse also supplies the first of the six occurrences of 'cut off' that run through the rest of the quoted block, and it is the same verb the previous verse used for the Mosaic sanction — which is why 21:11 and 21:12-18 read as one argument rather than two quotations laid end to end.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.13n (Mic 5.8-9)

pericopes.text: Yea, wo be unto the Gentiles, except they repent: for it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Father, that I will cut off thy horses out of the midst of thee, and I will destroy thy chariots,

links.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD, that I will cut off thy horses out of the midst of thee, and I will destroy thy chariots:

provenance.other: “cut off thy horses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:10.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 21:12-18 and 21:21 reproduce Micah 5:8-15 continuously, the longest Micah quotation anywhere in the Bible or the Book of Mormon. The quotation is not the finding; the substitutions are.
