Two run through the whole block: 'saith the LORD' becomes 'saith the Father' (21:14), and the second-person address of Micah's oracle is converted into third-person description of the Gentiles. Recover Micah's context and the reversal is the point — Micah 5:10-15 is a threat against Israel's own war-machine and idolatry, spoken to Israel; in 3 Nephi the same words are turned outward and spoken against the Gentiles, with the remnant of Jacob standing where Micah's God stands.

links.note: Nineteen words verbatim from 'that I will cut off thy horses' to 'and I will destroy thy chariots', with one substitution and one addition. The substitution is the one that governs the whole block: Micah's “saith the LORD” becomes “saith the Father”, and it is repeated at 21:20. The addition is the head of the verse, “Yea, wo be unto the Gentiles, except they repent”, which redirects an oracle Micah aimed at Israel's own cavalry onto the Gentiles and makes it conditional on repentance — the condition is not in Micah, where the disarming is announced flat. “cut off thy horses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.

pericopes.text: and I will cut off the cities of thy land, and throw down all thy strong holds;

links.text: And I will cut off the cities of thy land, and throw down all thy strong holds:

provenance.other: “throw down all thy strong holds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:11. The 1830 reading “strong holds” is the KJV's two-word form; 1920 and the current text read “strongholds”.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 21:12-18 and 21:21 reproduce Micah 5:8-15 continuously, the longest Micah quotation anywhere in the Bible or the Book of Mormon. The quotation is not the finding; the substitutions are. Two run through the whole block: 'saith the LORD' becomes 'saith the Father' (21:14), and the second-person address of Micah's oracle is converted into third-person description of the Gentiles. Recover Micah's context and the reversal is the point — Micah 5:10-15 is a threat against Israel's own war-machine and idolatry, spoken to Israel; in 3 Nephi the same words are turned outward and spoken against the Gentiles, with the remnant of Jacob standing where Micah's God stands.

links.note: Seventeen words reproduced without a single change of wording. The only thing that moves is the punctuation and, later, the spelling: the 1830 prints “strong holds” as two words, which is the King James Bible's own form, and 1920 closed it to “strongholds” (CONVENTIONS §8). The first edition therefore shows the borrowing at this verse in a way the modern text no longer does. “throw down all thy strong holds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.

pericopes.text: and I will cut off witchcrafts out of thy hand, and thou shalt have no more soothsayers:

links.text: And I will cut off witchcrafts out of thine hand; and thou shalt have no more soothsayers:

provenance.other: “cut off witchcrafts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:12. 1830 and the Printer's Manuscript read “out of thy hand” with Micah; 1920 and the current text read “out of thy land”.
provenance.significance: 3 Nephi 21:12-18 and 21:21 reproduce Micah 5:8-15 continuously, the longest Micah quotation anywhere in the Bible or the Book of Mormon. links.note: Micah 5:12 entire, with 'thine hand' modernized to 'thy hand' and nothing else altered. This is the chapter's best first-edition reading (CONVENTIONS §8): the 1830 prints “out of thy hand”, which is Micah's noun, and 1920 changed it to “out of thy land”, which is not — so a later edition moved the text AWAY from its source, the opposite of the correction seen at 3 Nephi 20:45. Hardy's apparatus records the Printer's Manuscript and 1830 reading and marks it as agreeing with Micah 5:12. “cut off witchcrafts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.

pericopes.text: thy graven images I will also cut off, and thy standing images out of the midst of thee; and thou shalt no more worship the works of thy hands;

links.text: Thy graven images also will I cut off, and thy standing images out of the midst of thee; and thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands.

provenance.other: “standing images” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:13, and “no more worship” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, also Micah 5:13.

Micah's inverted 'Thy graven images also will I cut off' is regularized to 'thy graven images I will also cut off', and 'the work of thine hands' is pluralized to 'the works of thy hands'. “standing images” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “no more worship” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both of them this one, so the verse is identifiable from either half alone.

pericopes.text: and I will pluck up thy groves out of the midst of thee; so will I destroy thy cities.

links.text: And I will pluck up thy groves out of the midst of thee: so will I destroy thy cities.

provenance.other: “pluck up thy groves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Micah 5:14.

links.note: Micah 5:14 reproduced word for word, nineteen words, the only alteration being the colon to a semicolon. “pluck up thy groves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The verse carries the block's one piece of dead vocabulary intact — the KJV's 'groves' translates the Asherah poles of the Hebrew, an institution with no plausible referent in the world the surrounding chapter describes, and the text keeps it rather than adapt it, which is what a transcription does and a paraphrase does not.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass that all lyings, and deceivings, and envyings, and strifes, and priestcrafts, and whoredoms, shall be done away.
For it shall come to pass, saith the Father, that at that day, whosoever will not repent and come unto my beloved Son, them will I cut off from among my people, O house of Israel;
and I will execute vengeance and fury upon them, even as upon the heathen, such as they have not heard.

The quotation is not the finding; the substitutions are. Two run through the whole block: 'saith the LORD' becomes 'saith the Father' (21:14), and the second-person address of Micah's oracle is converted into third-person description of the Gentiles. Recover Micah's context and the reversal is the point — Micah 5:10-15 is a threat against Israel's own war-machine and idolatry, spoken to Israel; in 3 Nephi the same words are turned outward and spoken against the Gentiles, with the remnant of Jacob standing where Micah's God stands. Micah 5:15 closes the oracle by turning outward: having disarmed and de-idolized his own people through verses 10-14, God executes vengeance 'upon the heathen'. 3 Nephi keeps the closing verse but has already spent verses 14-18 aiming the disarming at the Gentiles, so the final clause has to be re-pointed — 'upon them, even as upon the heathen'. The heathen become the measure of a punishment rather than its object, and the Gentiles take the place Israel held in Micah.

links.note: Micah 5:15 with two departures, and the first is the one that carries the argument: Micah reads 'I will execute vengeance in anger and fury upon the heathen', and 3 Nephi drops 'in anger and' and inserts 'upon them, even as' before 'upon the heathen'. The comparison is new; in Micah the heathen ARE the recipients. Hardy's apparatus flags the omission at this verse, noting that Micah 5:15 reads 'execute vengeance in anger and fury'. Nine words run continuously from 'upon the heathen, such as they have not heard', and 'such as they have not heard' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. This is the last verse of the Micah 5:8-15 block; the two verses before it, 21:19-20, are the Book of Mormon's own insertion into the middle of the quotation.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.21n (Mic 5.15 reads “execute vengeance in anger and fury”)

pericopes.text: But if they will repent, and hearken unto my words, and harden not their hearts, I will establish my church among them, and they shall come in unto the covenant, and be numbered among this the remnant of Jacob, unto whom I have given this land for their inheritance,

links.text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.

provenance.other: “hearken unto my words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 18:19. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twelve times, from 1 Nephi 2:18 onward, so it is a corpus formula and not a fresh borrowing on its own.
provenance.significance: What makes this worth a row is position, not vocabulary. Eleven verses earlier the same chapter quoted Deuteronomy 18:19 outright, in its negative form: 'whosoever will not believe in my words … shall be cut off'. Here the formula returns in the positive — 'if they will repent, and hearken unto my words' — and the promise attached is admission to the covenant rather than excision from it. The Mosaic sanction and its reversal frame the Micah quotation between them, and the frame is built out of the same verse.

links.note: “But if they will repent, and hearken unto my words, and harden not their hearts, I will establish my church among them.” The phrase 'hearken unto my words' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 18:19 — the sanction clause of the prophet-like-unto-Moses oracle — and 21:11 has just quoted that verse, in its negative form, as the condition of being cut off. This verse is its apodosis inverted. The case is recorded at moderate confidence because the vocabulary alone would not support it.
links.whyNot: 'Hearken unto my words' is a Book of Mormon formula used twelve times across five books, and its KJV singleton status is very likely the reason the corpus adopted it in the first place rather than evidence that this particular occurrence reaches back to Deuteronomy. Strip the context and this is 3 Nephi speaking its own idiom. The row rests entirely on the proximity of 21:11's explicit quotation of the same verse; a reader who thinks eleven verses is too far apart to count should decline it.

pericopes.text: and they shall assist my people, the remnant of Jacob; and also, as many of the house of Israel as shall come, that they may build a city, which shall be called the New Jerusalem;

links.text: Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name.

provenance.other: “new Jerusalem” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 3:12 and Revelation 21:2, and in both it descends from heaven rather than being built. Of the two, 3:12 is the closer formal match here, because it alone frames the phrase as a name conferred on a city — 'the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem' against 'a city, which shall be called the New Jerusalem'.
provenance.significance: The reversal is the finding. In both Revelation verses the new Jerusalem comes down out of heaven, finished; the city is received, not constructed. In 3 Nephi 21:23 it is a building project with a labour force — Gentile converts assisting the remnant of Jacob, and the house of Israel arriving to help. The name is John's and the verb is not. Ether 13:3 will later restore Revelation's own verb ('which should come down out of Heaven'), so the corpus holds both readings, and this verse is where the descending city is put on the ground and given builders.

links.note: “That they may build a city, which shall be called the New Jerusalem.” The name occurs in exactly two KJV verses. This is not the first occurrence in the discourse — 3 Nephi 20:22 has already said of this land 'it shall be a new Jerusalem', and the catalogue keys that verse to Revelation 21:2, the descending city — but 21:23 is where the city is named as a city and given a construction, and the naming formula tracks Revelation 3:12's rather than 21:2's: 'the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem' against 'a city, which shall be called the New Jerusalem'. The two rows are keyed to the two Revelation verses deliberately, because the discourse uses them for two different things. Recorded at moderate confidence because a two-word proper name is thin evidence of dependence on one of two verses, and because the phrase is by this point established in the discourse.

pericopes.text: and then shall they assist my people that they may be gathered in, which are scattered upon all the face of the land, in unto the New Jerusalem.
And then shall the power of heaven come down among them; and I also will be in the midst:

and then shall the work of the Father commence, at that day even when this Gospel shall be preached among the remnant of this people. Verily, I say unto you, At that day shall the work of the Father commence among all the dispersed of my people; yea, even the tribes which have been lost, which the Father hath led away out of Jerusalem.

links.text: And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

provenance.other: “the dispersed of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:12 — 'gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth'. 3 Nephi 21:26 and 21:27 read 'all the dispersed of my people'; the only other Book of Mormon verse with the construction is 2 Nephi 21:12, which is the transcription of Isaiah 11:12 itself and so reads 'the dispersed of Judah'. Isaiah 11 has already been transcribed whole into the corpus at 2 Nephi 21, so the KJV wording was available to this chapter by two routes and no test distinguishes them.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:12 is the gathering verse — the ensign for the nations, the outcasts assembled, the dispersed collected from the four corners — and it is the verse the Book of Mormon's whole gathering programme is built on. 3 Nephi 21:26 takes its distinctive noun phrase and does two things to it: 'of Judah' becomes 'of my people', which widens the gathering past the tribe Isaiah names, and the agent changes. In Isaiah God sets up an ensign and the nations do the assembling; here 'the work of the Father shall commence', and the ensign is a preached gospel. The chapter's opening promise, 'I shall gather in from their long dispersion' (21:1), is the same verse in paraphrase before it is used in Isaiah's own words here.

links.note: “At that day shall the work of the Father commence among all the dispersed of my people; yea, even the tribes which have been lost.” The construction 'the dispersed of [X]' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The chapter uses it twice, at 21:26 and 21:27, and the corpus's only other instance is the verbatim Isaiah transcription at 2 Nephi 21:12; 21:1's 'gather in from their long dispersion' anticipates it in the chapter's first sentence, so the whole chapter is framed by a verse it quotes only once and only partially. Recorded at moderate confidence: three words is little, and Isaiah 11 is transcribed whole at 2 Nephi 21, which means the phrase was already inside the corpus and this may be the corpus quoting itself.

pericopes.text: Yea, the work shall commence among all the dispersed of my people, with the Father, to prepare the way whereby they may come unto me, that they may call on the Father in my name;

links.text: And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man’s work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear:

provenance.other: “call on the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 1:17 — 'And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work'. The Book of Mormon has it twice, here and at Moroni 2:2. The commoner biblical idiom is 'call on the name of the Lord' or 'call upon God'; addressing the invocation to the Father specifically is what makes the phrase rare.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest piece of metalepsis in the chapter, and it depends on where 1 Peter 1:17 sits. The letter is addressed 'to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia' (1 Peter 1:1) — that is, to a dispersion — and 1:17 tells those addressees to call on the Father and to 'pass the time of your sojourning here in fear'. 3 Nephi 21:27 has, in one sentence, precisely those two elements: 'all the dispersed of my people' and 'that they may call on the Father in my name'. The one KJV verse that instructs a scattered people to call on the Father is quoted in the one Book of Mormon verse about a scattered people being taught to call on the Father. Neither text says the other is in view; the collocation says it.

links.note: “The work shall commence among all the dispersed of my people, with the Father, to prepare the way whereby they may come unto me, that they may call on the Father in my name.” Four words, but 'call on the Father' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse belongs to a letter written to the diaspora — which is the subject of this sentence. What the Book of Mormon adds is the mediating clause: 1 Peter's readers call on the Father directly, and here they do it 'in my name', with Christ as the way prepared. Moderate confidence: the run is short, and the phrase could be assembled from ordinary devotional English without 1 Peter. The rarity count and the shared addressee are what carry it.

pericopes.text: yea, and then shall the work commence, with the Father, among all nations, in preparing the way whereby his people may be gathered home to the land of their inheritance.
And they shall go out from all nations; and they shall not go out in haste, nor go by flight: for I will go before them, saith the Father, and I will be their rereward.

links.text: For ye shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight: for the LORD will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward.

provenance.other: “nor go by flight” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:12. The 1830 spells the closing word “rereward”, which is the KJV's spelling and which occurs in six KJV verses; 1920 and the current text modernize it to “rearward”, a spelling in no King James verse (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:12 is the second-Exodus verse — the departure from Babylon that is not to be a flight, because unlike the first Exodus it is not a rout. Christ quoted it verbatim at 3 Nephi 20:42, inside the Isaiah 52:11-15 block, in the second person: 'ye shall not go out with haste … the Lord will go before you'. Here he quotes it a second time and converts every pronoun to the third person, so that the verse describes the gathering rather than commanding it — and, in the process, the speaker changes. Isaiah's 'the LORD will go before you; and the God of Israel will be your rereward' has two divine titles for one figure; 3 Nephi has 'I will go before them, saith the Father, and I will be their rereward', collapsing both onto the Father and putting the sentence in his mouth. The chapter that began by promising a sign ends with the Father as the rearguard of his own gathering.

links.note: Isaiah 52:12 with the pronouns turned and one preposition changed: 'ye shall not go out with haste' becomes 'they shall not go out in haste'. 'Nor go by flight' is verbatim and occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 reading is the evidence here (CONVENTIONS §8): it prints 'rereward', the King James Bible's archaic spelling of the rearguard, and 1920 modernized it to 'rearward' — so the first edition displays the borrowing in a word the modern text has silently normalized out of visibility. Christ has already quoted this verse at 3 Nephi 20:42; that citation kept Isaiah's second person and Isaiah's 'the Lord'. This one does not, and both changes point the same way, at a Father who speaks in the first person throughout the chapter.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.29n (Isa 52.12, with significant changes; cf. 3 Ne 20.42)

links.text: Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing; go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the LORD.

provenance.other: 'Go out' and 'go ye out' are common KJV idiom and no rarity count supports this row; what supports it is sequence. Isaiah 52:11 and 52:12 are consecutive, and 3 Nephi 21:29 places 'they shall go out from all nations' immediately before its quotation of 52:12, in Isaiah's order.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:11's departure is a departure from somewhere — 'go ye out from thence … go ye out of the midst of her' — and the somewhere is Babylon, with the vessels of the Lord carried out by clean hands. 3 Nephi 21:29 has 'they shall go out from all nations', which universalizes the exit: every nation is now the Babylon being left. That reading depends on recovering Isaiah's antecedent, which the Book of Mormon verse deliberately does not supply.

links.note: “And they shall go out from all nations” — the clause that introduces the Isaiah 52:12 quotation, and it appears to reach back one verse. Christ quoted Isaiah 52:11 at 3 Nephi 20:41 ('Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence'), and here the same verb reappears in the same position relative to 52:12, with 'from thence' replaced by 'from all nations'. Hardy's apparatus makes the same connection at this verse. Catalogued as an echo at moderate confidence because the verbal contact is two very common words; the case is one of sequence and of the speaker having quoted the source verse thirty-four verses earlier in the same sermon.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 21.29n (compare Isa 52.11; 3 Ne 20.41)

pericopes.text: And now behold I say unto you, That ye had ought to search these things. Yea, a commandment I give unto you, that ye search these things diligently: for great is the words of Isaiah.

links.text: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.

provenance.other: “commandment I give unto you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 13:34, and “I give unto you that ye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The formula is used twice in the whole Book of Mormon, at Jacob 3:9 and here.
provenance.significance: John 13:34 is spoken at the last supper, to the Twelve, hours before the passion, and its content is the one commandment the Fourth Gospel calls new: love one another. 3 Nephi 23:1 puts the identical frame in the risen Christ's mouth to the Nephite twelve and fills it with a different object — not love one another but search these things diligently. The substitution is the reading. A farewell commandment about how the disciples are to treat each other becomes a farewell commandment about how they are to read, and it is issued four verses before the demonstration that their own book was defective.

links.note: 'Yea, a commandment I give unto you, that ye search these things diligently.' Two King James singletons in one clause and both belong to John 13:34: the six-word run “commandment I give unto you” and the frame “I give unto you that ye”, which in the KJV introduces the new commandment and nothing else. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, so it is catalogued as an allusion and is not one of his long quotations. The Book of Mormon has used the formula once before, at Jacob 3:9, where the content is likewise supplied by the local argument rather than by John; that is its only other occurrence, and a fresh row is given here because a new book is a new hand.

links.text: Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that should come unto you:

provenance.other: “searched diligently” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 1:10. The Book of Mormon's 'search these things' is in no KJV verse and appears nowhere else in the Book of Mormon.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 1:10-12 is the New Testament's one paragraph in which prophecy is described as a reading problem: the prophets 'enquired and searched diligently', the Spirit in them 'testified beforehand', and what they found was ministered not to themselves but to a later audience. Every one of those three moves is made across 3 Nephi 23:1-5 — search diligently (23:1), Isaiah's words 'hath been, and shall be' (23:3), and 'Search the prophets: for many there be that testify of these things' addressed to a Gentile future (23:4-5). If the echo holds it explains a choice the next rows have to account for anyway: why the imperative at 23:5 is 'Search the prophets' and not John 5:39's 'Search the scriptures'. Peter's paragraph is about prophets specifically.

links.note: 'Ye had ought to search these things. Yea, a commandment I give unto you, that ye search these things diligently.' The verbal contact is thin — one verb and one adverb, in different grammatical forms — and the row is written because the paragraph behind it does everything this unit of 3 Nephi does. Proposed under CONVENTIONS §0a as a link worth the risk rather than a demonstration; a reader who wants a source with wording in it should take the John 5:39 row at 23:5 and leave this one.
links.whyNot: The shared lexemes are 'search' and 'diligently' and neither is distinctive on its own; 'search' stands in 46 KJV verses. The constructions differ at every point: 1 Peter reports in the past tense about prophets, 3 Nephi commands in the imperative to disciples, and the participial 'Searching what' of 1 Peter 1:11 has no counterpart here. The coherence is at the level of the paragraph, which is the level at which coincidence is cheapest.

pericopes.text: For surely he spake as touching all things concerning my people which are of the house of Israel; therefore it must needs be that he must speak also to the Gentiles.
And all things that he spake, hath been, and shall be, even according to the words which he spake.
Therefore give heed to my words: write the things which I have told you; and according to the time and the will of the Father, they shall go forth unto the Gentiles.

links.text: Write the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter;

provenance.other: “write the things which” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 1:19, and “which shall be hereafter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. 'Hath been, and shall be' is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Revelation 1:19 is the glorified Christ's commission to a seer to write, and it divides what is to be written into three tenses — what thou hast seen, what is, what shall be hereafter. 3 Nephi sets the same two elements side by side across two verses: 23:3 says of Isaiah's words that they 'hath been, and shall be', and 23:4 says 'write the things which I have told you'. Recover Revelation and the tense-division that 23:3 makes about a prophet's words turns out to be the tense-division Revelation makes about the book its seer is being told to write. The scene that follows in 3 Nephi is then the darker half of the same commission: a risen Christ auditing a written record and finding a required entry missing, which is the anxiety Revelation ends on at 22:18-19.

links.note: 'Therefore give heed to my words: write the things which I have told you.' “Write the things which” is a King James singleton and its one verse is the risen Christ's commission to John on Patmos. The setting agrees at every load-bearing point — a glorified Christ, a seer, an order to commit what has just been said to writing, and a named future audience, 3 Nephi's 'they shall go forth unto the Gentiles' against Revelation's seven churches. The 1830 reads 'hath been' at 23:3 where 1920 reads 'have been'; the singular is the older wording and does not bear on the source, but it is the 1830 text that keeps 23:3 and 23:4 sounding like one sentence.

pericopes.text: And whosoever will hearken unto my words, and repenteth, and is baptized, the same shall be saved. Search the prophets: for many there be that testify of these things.

links.text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.

provenance.alternative: Acts 3:23 quotes Deuteronomy 18:19 and is the form the Book of Mormon follows elsewhere; tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points against it here.
provenance.other: “hearken unto my words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 18:19. Its New Testament quotation does not preserve the phrase: Deuteronomy's 'whosoever ... hearken unto my words which he shall speak' becomes Acts 3:23's 'every soul, which will not hear that prophet'. tools/mediation-check.py finds two decisive divergences between the two and the Book of Mormon has Deuteronomy's form at both — 'whosoever' not 'every soul which', and 'hearken unto my words' not 'hear that prophet'.
provenance.significance: This is a recorded counter-example to the corpus's strongest tendency. Deuteronomy 18 enters the Book of Mormon three times and the other two follow Acts rather than Deuteronomy: 1 Nephi 22:20 reproduces twenty-six continuous words of Acts 3:22-23, and 3 Nephi 20:23 — three chapters earlier in this same discourse — has Acts' 'every soul which will not hear that prophet'. Here, at the one point where Acts does not carry the phrase, the wording is Deuteronomy's own. And the sanction is inverted. Deuteronomy 18:19 is a threat: whosoever will NOT hearken, I will require it of him. 3 Nephi 23:5 is a promise: whosoever WILL hearken, the same shall be saved. Christ has already claimed at 20:23 to be the prophet Deuteronomy 18 promises; three chapters later he takes that prophet's penalty clause, deletes its negative, and reads it as a beatitude.

links.note: 'And whosoever will hearken unto my words, and repenteth, and is baptized, the same shall be saved.' Six words of Deuteronomy 18:19 in Deuteronomy's order with one word removed — 'whosoever will [not] hearken unto my words' — and “hearken unto my words” is a King James singleton. The rest of the sentence is not Deuteronomy's: the condition ('repenteth, and is baptized') and the apodosis ('the same shall be saved') are Mark 16:16's, already adjudicated in this book at 3 Nephi 11:33, so the verse welds the Deuteronomic prophet's sanction onto the Marcan baptismal formula and turns both into a single promise. What makes the row worth its space is the mediation result rather than the volume: this is the one Old Testament verse the Book of Mormon is elsewhere demonstrably taking through Acts, and here it is not.

links.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

provenance.other: “search the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:39, and “they which testify” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “testify of me” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 5:39 and John 15:26.
provenance.significance: The source was adjudicated for this book at 3 Nephi 10:14, where Mormon breaks John's imperative into a relative clause, and used again at 15:10 as a gloss on Matthew 7:12. This verse is catalogued rather than cross-referred because it is the only place in the Book of Mormon that reproduces John 5:39's actual shape — imperative, causal 'for', clause of testimony — and because it alters exactly one word of it. John's object is 'the scriptures'; here it is 'the prophets'. The substitution earns its keep one verse later: 23:6 distinguishes 'the Scriptures ... which they had received' from 'other Scriptures I would that ye should write, that ye have not', and a canon that is about to be found deficient is not the thing to send a reader to. The prophets can be searched when the scriptures are incomplete.

links.note: 'Search the prophets: for many there be that testify of these things.' John 5:39 is the King James Bible's one sentence holding a command to search, a causal clause and a verb of testimony in that order, and both of its distinguishing phrases are singletons. Two changes are made: 'the scriptures' becomes 'the prophets', and the object of the testimony moves from the speaker ('testify of me') to the events under discussion ('testify of these things'). The second change is the one 3 Nephi 10:14-17 also made, so it is the book's settled handling of the verse and not a fresh departure. Written as a link rather than as a within-book repeat under ADJUDICATING §4 because what is borrowed here is the syntax the earlier rows dismantled; a reader who meets this verse and is shown nothing has been told there is no borrowing in it.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when Jesus had said these words, he saith unto them again, after he had expounded all the Scriptures unto them which they had received, he saith unto them, Behold, other Scriptures I would that ye should write, that ye have not.

links.text: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.

provenance.route: Luke 24:27 + Mark 4:34 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “expounded unto them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:27, and “all the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. “expounded all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 4:34. The bare word 'expounded' stands in six KJV verses, of which only these two have Jesus as its subject.
provenance.significance: Luke 24:27 is the risen Christ on the Emmaus road, beginning at Moses and all the prophets and expounding in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. 3 Nephi 23 is that half-verse held open for a whole chapter, with the road replaced by a written record laid before him and his eyes cast upon it. What Luke cannot supply is the audit, and that is what this chapter adds: at 23:6 the expounding is finished and the risen Christ says there are 'other Scriptures I would that ye should write, that ye have not'. Recover Luke 24 and the addition reads as an answer to a gap Luke leaves open, since Luke's Christ expounds a canon and the reader is never told what was in it or whether anything was missing from it.

links.note: 'After he had expounded all the Scriptures unto them which they had received.' The clause lays the King James Bible's only two 'expounded' sentences about Jesus over each other: Luke 24:27's “expounded unto them” and “all the scriptures”, both singletons and both from the Emmaus road, and Mark 4:34's “expounded all”, where Jesus expounds all things privately to his disciples when they are alone. Neither source has the Book of Mormon's word order, and the fusion 'expounded all the Scriptures unto them' is what produces it. The 1830 keeps the historic present 'he saith unto them' twice in this verse where 1920 reads 'said', which is the KJV narrative idiom surviving in the first edition and erased later. The construction returns at 23:14 and again at 3 Nephi 26:1; both are cross-referred here rather than argued again.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he saith unto Nephi, Bring forth the record which ye have kept.
And when Nephi had brought forth the records, and laid them before him, he cast his eyes upon them, and saith,

Verily, I say unto you, I commanded my servant Samuel, the Lamanite, that he should testify unto this people, that at the day that the Father should glorify his name in me, that there were many saints which should arise from the dead, and should appear unto many, and should minister unto them. And he saith unto them, Were it not so?

links.text: And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose,

provenance.other: “appeared unto many” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:53, and “bodies of the saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:52. 'Many saints' is in no KJV verse: it is Helaman 14:25's compression of Matthew's 'many bodies of the saints', and 3 Nephi 23:9 takes it in that compressed form.
provenance.significance: The proximate model is not Matthew but Helaman 14:25, and the chapter says so: Christ states that he commanded Samuel to prophesy this, and Helaman 14:25 is where Samuel does, on two Matthaean singletons. What 3 Nephi then does to Helaman is the finding. Helaman has graves opened, dead yielded up, and many saints appearing unto many; 3 Nephi drops the graves, keeps 'many saints ... appear unto many', and adds a third verb that stands in neither Helaman nor Matthew — 'should minister unto them', repeated at 23:11 and written into the record at 23:13. So the chapter whose entire subject is a record found incomplete supplies, in the very sentence that rebukes the omission, a detail neither of its own sources contains. Matthew's saints walk into the holy city and are seen; the Nephite saints minister.

links.note: 'That there were many saints which should arise from the dead, and should appear unto many, and should minister unto them.' The distinguishing phrase is “appeared unto many”, a King James singleton at Matthew 27:53, and it arrives here already fitted to a Nephite setting by Helaman 14:25 — which is why the mediation is recorded as running through the Book of Mormon's own earlier text and not straight from the gospel. Two departures from Helaman are worth noting: 'arise from the dead' replaces Helaman's 'graves shall be opened, and shall yield up many of their dead', and is nearer Matthew's 'the saints which slept arose' than Helaman was; and 'minister unto them' is new. The 1830 reads 'many saints which should arise' where 1920 reads 'who', keeping Matthew 27:52's own relative pronoun in 'the saints which slept arose'; the 1830 also asks 'Were it not so?' where 1920 asks 'Was it not so?'. The mediation value is filed as OT-via-earlier-BoM, which is the right category under a wrong name — the ultimate source is a New Testament verse. PLAN §7 already has that enum open for a ruling; this row is another instance of it.

links.text: Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.

provenance.route: John 12:28 + John 13:31-32 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “glorify thy name” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Psalm 86:9, Psalm 86:12, John 12:28 and Revelation 15:4 — and only John 12:28 addresses the Father and dates the hour of the passion. “glorified in him” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 13:31 and John 13:32. 'Glorify his name' is in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon dates the resurrection of the saints by a Johannine clock. John 12:23-28 is the hour arriving — 'the hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified' — and ends in the prayer 'Father, glorify thy name'; John 13:31-32 answers that prayer four times over, with God glorified 'in him' and glorifying him 'in himself'. 3 Nephi 23:9 collapses the prayer and its answer into a single time-reference for an event that Matthew 27:53 dates plainly, 'after his resurrection'. The effect is to move the Nephite dead out of Matthew's chronology and into John's hour: what Samuel was commanded to predict is not a date but a glorification.

links.note: 'At the day that the Father should glorify his name in me.' No King James verse reads 'glorify his name', and the clause looks assembled from the two that come nearest: John 12:28's 'Father, glorify thy name', spoken as the hour of the passion arrives, and John 13:31-32's 'God is glorified in him', which supplies the otherwise unaccountable 'in me'. Held at moderate confidence because nothing is quoted — the phrase is built rather than borrowed. What carries the row is that both halves come from two adjacent chapters of one gospel and that the referent of the Book of Mormon's clause, the day of the crucifixion and resurrection, is the referent of both.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that when Jesus had told these things, he expounded them unto the multitude: and he did expound all things unto them, both great and small.

provenance.route: Mark 4:34 (with its Matthean parallel, Matthew 13:34) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “expounded all things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 4:34. The other half of the Book of Mormon's clause, “unto the multitude”, occurs in exactly four KJV verses, and the only one of the four that is about Jesus teaching is Matthew 13:34 — which is Mark 4:34's own Synoptic parallel and shares its second half word for word (“without a parable spake he not unto them”). So both halves of 3 Nephi 26:1 come from the two verses of one Synoptic pair.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is a reversal, and it is the premise of the whole chapter. In Mark 4:34 expounding all things is precisely what Jesus does NOT do for the multitude: they get parables, and the exposition is reserved for the disciples when they are alone. 3 Nephi 26:1 takes that sentence and inverts its economy — here he expounds all things *unto the multitude*, and holds nothing back. The withholding does not disappear; it moves. Five verses later it is Mormon who cannot write a hundredth part (26:6), who is forbidden to write what the babes utter (26:16), and who keeps back a lesser part against the reader's faith (26:8-11). Mark's secret is repositioned from Christ to his abridger.

links.note: 'He expounded them unto the multitude: and he did expound all things unto them, both great and small.' The verb is rare in the King James Bible — six verses — and the phrase “expounded all things” occurs in exactly one of them. That verse is Mark 4:34, where the object of the expounding is the disciples and the multitude are the ones excluded from it; the Book of Mormon keeps the phrase and swaps the audience. Luke 24:27 belongs in the same family and may be the closer situational model, since it is the risen Christ expounding the scriptures 'beginning at Moses and all the prophets', which is what 26:3 goes on to describe ('even from the beginning'). The machine's top candidate here was 2 Chronicles 20:24, a heap of corpses seen from a watchtower; the real source is not in the candidate list at all, which is CONVENTIONS §9's point about the n-gram stream being a recall floor.
links.text: But without a parable spake he not unto them: and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples.

pericopes.text: And he saith, These Scriptures which ye had not with you, the Father commanded that I should give unto you: for it was wisdom in him that they should be given unto future generations.

And he did expound all things, even from the beginning until the time that he should come in his glory; yea, even all things which should come upon the face of the earth, even until the elements should melt with fervent heat, and the earth should be wrapt together as a scroll, and the heavens and the earth should pass away;

provenance.other: “melt with fervent heat” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Peter 3:10 and 2 Peter 3:12, and nowhere else in scripture do the elements melt at all. 2 Peter 3:10 is also the only verse in the Bible that holds both that clause and “the heavens shall pass away” in one sentence; the Book of Mormon reproduces the pair in 2 Peter's order. “shall pass away” occurs in six KJV verses, of which Matthew 24:35, Mark 13:31 and Luke 21:33 supply the fuller 'heaven and earth shall pass away' that the Book of Mormon's 'the heavens and the earth should pass away' actually reads.
provenance.significance: Recover 2 Peter 3 and the borrowed sentence turns out to sit inside an argument about a delayed revelation and a withheld word — which is this chapter's subject and not its imagery. 2 Peter 3 answers scoffers who ask 'Where is the promise of his coming?' by saying the delay is the Lord's longsuffering (3:9); it ends by conceding that in Paul's epistles are 'some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest … unto their own destruction' (3:16). Ten verses later in 3 Nephi, greater things are withheld from those who will not believe 'unto their condemnation' (26:10). The chapter takes 2 Peter's cosmology in verse 3 and, without quoting it again, arrives at 2 Peter's doctrine of who may safely be given more.

links.note: 'Even until the elements should melt with fervent heat … and the heavens and the earth should pass away.' The two clauses are the two halves of 2 Peter 3:10 in 2 Peter's own order, and the first of them has no other home in the King James Bible. The 1830 text reads 'should' throughout where the KJV reads 'shall', which is the tense the surrounding indirect discourse requires ('he did expound … that …') and not a departure from the source.
links.text: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.

provenance.other: “together as a scroll” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 34:4. Revelation 6:14 is the New Testament's use of the same image and reads 'the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together'; mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Isaiah and none for Revelation, because the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's word order (the participle before the noun) and lacks Revelation's trailing 'when it is rolled together' entirely. The Book of Mormon's verb is neither: “wrapt together” occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 34:4 is the collapse of the heavens over Edom, a local judgment written in cosmic terms; Revelation 6:14 had already lifted it out of Edom and made it universal. 3 Nephi 26:3 takes the Isaian form and puts it to the universal use — the pattern of the whole chapter, which reaches for Old Testament wording and New Testament scope.

links.note: 'And the earth should be wrapt together as a scroll.' The image has exactly one Old Testament home and one New Testament reuse, and the mediation test settles it for the Old: the Book of Mormon follows Isaiah's construction rather than Revelation's inverted one. What it does not follow is Isaiah's verb — Isaiah rolls, Revelation rolls, the Book of Mormon wraps, and “wrapt together” is in no King James verse at all. Note also that the subject has moved: in Isaiah it is the heavens that are rolled up and in 3 Nephi it is the earth, with the heavens left for the next clause and 2 Peter's.
links.text: And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree.

provenance.other: “come in his glory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:31. The Synoptic parallels read otherwise — Mark 8:38 'when he cometh in the glory of his Father', Luke 9:26 'in his own glory' — so the Book of Mormon has Matthew's form of the phrase and not the others'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 25:31 is the opening line of the sheep-and-goats judgment, and what the Book of Mormon does with it is to keep reading. 3 Nephi 26:3 borrows the coming; 26:4 supplies the assize — all nations gathered before him, separated as a shepherd divides — and 26:5 supplies the two destinations. The borrowing is not a phrase but a position in a passage: the chapter picks up Matthew 25 at verse 31 and stays with it through to its end.

links.note: 'Even from the beginning until the time that he should come in his glory.' Three words, but they are three words the King James Bible uses once, and the two verses that follow in 3 Nephi walk through the scene that Matthew 25:31 introduces. Held at moderate because the phrase alone would not carry it; the case is the sequence.
links.whyNot: A three-word run is thin, and 'come in his glory' is an obvious enough English rendering of a common idea that independent coinage cannot be excluded. The link rests on 26:4-5 continuing Matthew 25's scene, which is an argument about arrangement rather than wording.
links.text: When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory:

pericopes.text: and even unto the great and last day, when all people, and all kindreds, and all nations and tongues shall stand before God, to be judged of their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil:

provenance.route: Revelation 20:12, with the fourfold formula of Revelation 7:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “stand before God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12. “according to their works” occurs in exactly three, of which two are Revelation 20:12 and 20:13. The list is Revelation's other fixed formula: “nations and kindreds and people and tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 7:9, whose crowd 'stood before the throne' — the Book of Mormon has the same four members and sends them to stand before God rather than the throne.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's key, and it is metaleptic in Hays's strict sense: the point lies in what Revelation 20:12 says and 3 Nephi 26:4 does not repeat. In Revelation the dead stand before God and 'the books were opened', and they are judged 'out of those things which were written in the books'. 3 Nephi borrows the standing and the judging and drops the books — and then spends the next fourteen verses on nothing but books and what may be put in them: a hundredth part cannot be written (26:6), the greater part is on the plates of Nephi (26:7), a lesser part is written to try the reader's faith (26:8-11), the children's words are forbidden to be written (26:16), and what the disciples saw is 'not lawful to be written' (26:18). The verse that founds the judgment on a complete written record is the verse this chapter quotes at the head of an argument for an incomplete one.

links.note: 'All people, and all kindreds, and all nations and tongues shall stand before God, to be judged of their works.' Two rarities converge in one sentence: the fourfold list is Revelation's and occurs in that order in exactly one verse, and “stand before God” occurs in exactly one verse, the great white throne of Revelation 20:12, which also supplies 'according to their works'. The Book of Mormon has fused Revelation's census of the redeemed with Revelation's assize of the dead. Neither is quoted at length; both are unmistakable.
links.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

pericopes.text: if they be good, to the resurrection of everlasting life; and if they be evil, to the resurrection of damnation, being on a parallel, the one on the one hand, and the other on the other hand, according to the mercy, and the justice, and the holiness which is in Christ, which was before the world began.

provenance.route: John 5:29, with Daniel 12:2's adjective restored → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Both halves are KJV singletons in the same verse: “resurrection of life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “resurrection of damnation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is John 5:29 both times. Run against Daniel 12:2 — the Old Testament passage John is reworking — mediation-check.py returns decisive points BOTH ways, which it flags as a composite rather than a bug: the frame ('they that have done good … they that have done evil … unto the resurrection of') is John's, and the adjective 'everlasting' attached to life is Daniel's ('some to everlasting life'), which John does not have.
provenance.significance: The split is worth naming. A writer following John alone would have written 'the resurrection of life'; a writer following Daniel alone would not have reached 'damnation' at all. 3 Nephi 26:5 has John's antithesis with Daniel's adjective inside it — the New Testament verse read back through the Old Testament verse it depends on. Compare the same move at 26:15, where Isaiah's wording is preferred over the Gospel paraphrase of it.

links.note: 'If they be good, to the resurrection of everlasting life; and if they be evil, to the resurrection of damnation.' John 5:29 is the only verse in the King James Bible that puts two resurrections in one antithesis and gives them these names, and the Book of Mormon reproduces the antithesis, the conditional, and both nouns. The one word that is not John's is 'everlasting', which is Daniel 12:2's — the source behind John's own sentence. The 1830 reading 'which was before the world began' (1920: 'who') is preserved in the running text.
links.text: And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.

provenance.other: “before the world began” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Timothy 1:9 and Titus 1:2. Only one of the two attaches it to Christ: “in Christ Jesus before the world began” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 1:9, and the Book of Mormon writes 'which is in Christ, which was before the world began'.
provenance.significance: 2 Timothy 1:9 makes the pre-mundane grace the ground of a calling that is 'not according to our works'. 3 Nephi 26:5 has just said the opposite in Revelation's words — men are judged 'of their works' — and then attaches the pre-mundane clause to mercy, justice and holiness together. Whether the tension is felt or accidental, the verse holds both halves of the New Testament's own difficulty about works and grace in a single sentence.

links.note: 'According to the mercy, and the justice, and the holiness which is in Christ, which was before the world began.' The collocation of Christ with the phrase 'before the world began' has one home in the King James Bible. Held at moderate: the phrase is short, and Titus 1:2 shows it was available without the Christological attachment.
links.whyNot: Four words, and nothing else of 2 Timothy 1 is present. The reason for preferring 2 Timothy 1:9 over Titus 1:2 — the words 'in Christ' immediately preceding — is a matter of two more words, and a reader who thinks the phrase simply idiomatic in this register would not be unreasonable.
links.text: Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,

pericopes.text: And now there cannot be written in this book, even a hundredth part of the things which Jesus did truly teach unto the people;

provenance.other: “things which Jesus did” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Luke 9:43, John 11:45 and John 21:25 — and only John 21:25 is about whether they can be written. “should be written” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 21:25. The Book of Mormon's own fraction is not biblical in this sense: “hundredth part” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 5:11, where it is a rate of interest, and the standing exclusion for that stands at Words of Mormon 1:5.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has recorded this idiom four times already, and this is the occurrence where it comes home. At 1 Nephi 6:3, Words of Mormon 1:5, Helaman 3:14 and 3 Nephi 5:8 the abridger borrows John's apology for omission and applies it to wars, proceedings, records — subjects John 21:25 is not about. Here the subject is the one John 21:25 actually names: the things which Jesus did, which cannot all be written. The phrase has returned to its source (ADJUDICATING §4), and that is why this row is written in full rather than filed as a repeat pointing back to 5:8.

links.note: 'There cannot be written in this book, even a hundredth part of the things which Jesus did truly teach unto the people.' The last sentence of the Fourth Gospel is the King James Bible's one editorial apology for an incomplete record, and the Book of Mormon has used it as such since 1 Nephi. What distinguishes this occurrence from the four before it is that the shared words are now the ones that matter: 'the things which Jesus did' is John 21:25's own subject, and 5:8 shared no such phrase. The verbal contact remains a substitution rather than a reproduction — 'cannot be written in this book' for 'could not contain the books that should be written' — but it is a closer substitution than any of the earlier rows, and it sits in John's situation rather than beside it.
links.text: And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.

pericopes.text: but behold the plates of Nephi do contain the more part of the things which he taught the people;

and these things have I written, which are a lesser part of the things which he taught the people; and I have wrote them to the intent that they may be brought again unto this people, from the Gentiles, according to the words which Jesus hath spoken.—

And when they shall have received this, which is expedient that they should have first, to try their faith: And if it shall so be that they shall believe these things, then shall the greater things be made manifest unto them.
And if it so be that they will not believe these things, then shall the greater things be withheld from them, unto their condemnation.
Behold I were about to write them all which were engraven upon the plates of Nephi, but the Lord forbid it, saying, I will try the faith of my people;
therefore I, Mormon, do write the things which have been commanded me of the Lord. And now I, Mormon, make an end of my sayings, and proceed to write the things which have been commanded me;

therefore I would that ye should behold that the Lord truly did teach the people, for the space of three days; and after that, he did shew himself unto them oft, and did break bread oft, and bless it, and give it unto them.

provenance.other: “blessed it and brake” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 26:26 and Luke 24:30. Of the two, only Luke 24:30 is a post-resurrection meal, and only Luke 24:30 is followed by a verse that turns the act into a mode of recognition — “breaking of bread” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 24:35 and Acts 2:42. Matthew 26:26 supplies the pronoun the Book of Mormon carries ('blessed it', 'gave it'), which Luke 24:30 lacks ('brake, and gave to them'), so the wording is a conflation of the two.
provenance.significance: Luke 24:30-35 is the only place in the King James Bible where a risen Christ breaks bread, and its point is that he 'was known of them in breaking of bread' — a single meal that ends in recognition and immediate disappearance. 3 Nephi 26:13 has the same act with the temporal marker changed: 'he did shew himself unto them oft, and did break bread oft'. The Emmaus moment, which in Luke happens once and is over, becomes here a standing practice. Recognition is not the issue, because these disciples already know him; repetition is.

links.note: 'He did shew himself unto them oft, and did break bread oft, and bless it, and give it unto them.' The three verbs in that order, applied to bread, are the institution formula, and the Book of Mormon reorders them — break, bless, give, against the Gospels' bless, break, give. The 1830 'shew' is the King James spelling and is what makes the borrowing visible; 1920's 'show' obscures it (CONVENTIONS §8). Luke 24:30 is preferred to Matthew 26:26 on the situation rather than the syntax: this is the risen Christ eating with his disciples, which the Last Supper is not. The rest of the verse's setting — teaching, daily bread, and at 26:19 all things in common — is Acts 2:42-46's description of the same community, which is where 26:19's link goes.
links.text: And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he did teach and minister unto the children of the multitude of whom hath been spoken, and he did loose their tongues, and they did speak unto their fathers great and marvellous things, even greater than he had revealed unto the people, and loosed their tongues that they could utter.

provenance.other: “the string of his tongue was loosed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 7:35, and it is the only verse in the Bible in which anyone's tongue is loosed at all. The Book of Mormon writes 'he did loose their tongues … and loosed their tongues that they could utter', which is the same act in the same words minus Mark's 'string'. Isaiah 35:6, the front half of the block Hardy cross-references at 26:15, supplies the Old Testament form: 'the tongue of the dumb sing'.
provenance.significance: Mark 7:35 has two clauses — 'straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed' — and 3 Nephi uses both, in reverse order and across a verse boundary: tongues loosed at 26:14, the ears of the deaf unstopped at 26:15. Mark 7:37 then glosses the healing in Isaiah's own terms ('he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak'), which is exactly the pairing the Book of Mormon has made. Whichever way the dependence runs, the two verses reproduce a nexus — Isaiah 35:5-6 read through Mark 7 — that the King James Bible itself supplies as a unit.

links.note: 'He did loose their tongues, and they did speak unto their fathers great and marvellous things … and loosed their tongues that they could utter.' The verbal contact is two words, 'tongue' and 'loosed', and it would be nothing on its own; what makes it a link is that it is the King James Bible's only instance of the idea, and that the very next verse of 3 Nephi supplies the other clause of the same source verse. The 1830 spelling 'marvellous' is the KJV's and is modernized in 1920. Note that the deafness and dumbness here are not the children's — nothing says they were mute — so the healing formula is being used of an enabling, not a cure.
links.whyNot: Two shared words, and the Book of Mormon drops the distinctive noun ('string'). The case rests almost entirely on the 26:14/26:15 pairing reproducing Mark 7:35's two clauses; a reader who takes 'loose the tongue' to be ordinary English rather than a borrowing has a fair objection, and the phrase does not otherwise occur in the King James Bible in that ordinary sense either way.
links.text: And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after he had ascended into Heaven the second time that he shewed himself unto them, and gone unto the Father, after having healed all their sick, and their lame, and opened the eyes of their blind, and unstopped the ears of the deaf, and even had done all manner of cures among them, and raised a man from the dead, and had shewn forth his power unto them, and had ascended unto the Father,

provenance.other: “unstopped” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 35:5, and “ears of the deaf shall be unstopped” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22 are the New Testament's use of the Isaiah 35 catalogue, and mediation-check.py is decisive for Isaiah: the Book of Mormon reads 'opened the eyes of their blind', which is Isaiah's 'the eyes of the blind shall be opened', not Matthew's 'the blind receive their sight'. “eyes of the blind” by itself occurs in six KJV verses and settles nothing; the participle does.
provenance.significance: The interesting result is that the wording and the list come from different places. The verbs are Isaiah's, decisively; but the Book of Mormon's inventory — sick, lame, blind, deaf, and then 'raised a man from the dead' — is Matthew 11:5's, because Isaiah 35 has no raising of the dead in it and Matthew 11:5 does ('the dead are raised up'). So 26:15 answers John the Baptist's question in Isaiah's vocabulary: the sign-list by which Jesus identified himself to John is here a report of what he had already done among another people, with the Gospel's paraphrase corrected back to the prophet's words.

links.note: 'Opened the eyes of their blind, and unstopped the ears of the deaf.' Nine words of Isaiah 35:5 in Isaiah's order, containing a word the King James Bible uses exactly once. The clause before it, 'their sick, and their lame', reaches Isaiah 35:6 ('then shall the lame man leap as an hart'), which is the verse behind 26:14's loosed tongues as well — so the two verses together work through Isaiah 35:5-6 as a block. This is one of two rows in the chapter that Hardy's apparatus cross-references (Isaiah 35:4-5); the verbal case here is our own and the mediation result against Matthew 11:5 is the part worth having.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 26.15 (Isaiah 35:4-5)
links.text: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.

pericopes.text: behold, it came to pass on the morrow, that the multitude gathered themselves together, and they both saw and heard these children; yea, even babes did open their mouths, and utter marvellous things; and the things which they did utter were forbidden, that there should not any man write them.

provenance.route: Psalm 8:2 as quoted at Matthew 21:15-16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “out of the mouth of babes” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 8:2 and Matthew 21:16, the second quoting the first. mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence, because the Book of Mormon reproduces neither continuation — not the Psalm's 'ordained strength' nor Matthew's 'perfected praise' — so the mediation is argued from setting rather than from wording, as CONVENTIONS §7 allows. The setting is decisively Matthew's: a temple, children uttering what the adults are made to hear, and the adults unable to answer it.
provenance.significance: Matthew 21:15-16 is the only place in the King James Bible where children speak in the temple and their elders have to reckon with it, and Jesus settles the matter by quoting Psalm 8 at them. 3 Nephi 26:16 has the multitude gathered at the temple in Bountiful to hear the babes, and there is no objection at all — the elders come back the next morning specifically to listen. The Gospel's contest is resolved before it starts, and what the children say is then forbidden to be written, which is a suppression Matthew's scene has no equivalent for.

links.note: 'Even babes did open their mouths, and utter marvellous things.' Two words of contact — babes, mouths — and that is the whole verbal case, which is why this is filed as figural rather than as an allusion. What earns it a row is that the King James Bible has exactly one scene of this shape and 3 Nephi 26:14-16 is built on it: children given speech, in the temple, in the hearing of a gathered adult multitude, uttering praise their elders had not expected. The 1830 'marvellous' is the KJV spelling.
links.whyNot: No distinctive phrase is shared, and 'babes' plus 'mouths' will follow from the subject matter without any borrowing at all. The mediation test cannot be run, so the choice of Matthew over the Psalm rests entirely on the temple setting. A reader who declines the whole row is not making an error, and the register would be dishonest if it did not say so.
links.text: And said unto him, Hearest thou what these say? And Jesus saith unto them, Yea; have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise?

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the disciples whom Jesus had chosen, began from that time forth to baptize and to teach as many as did come unto them; and as many as were baptized in the name of Jesus, were filled with the Holy Ghost.

provenance.route: Acts 19:5-6, with the commission of Matthew 28:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 8:16 and Acts 19:5. The Book of Mormon's shorter form, 'baptized in the name of Jesus', occurs in no KJV verse — which is why kjvSpecific is recorded as uncertain here rather than yes. “filled with the Holy Ghost” occurs in eight KJV verses, every one of them in Luke or Acts.
provenance.significance: The two Acts verses that use the formula are a matched pair, and the Book of Mormon's sentence takes a side. Acts 8:16 is the negative case — at Samaria they 'were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus' and the Holy Ghost 'was fallen upon none of them' until the apostles came down. Acts 19:5-6 is the positive case: baptized in that name, and the Holy Ghost came on them. 3 Nephi 26:17 states the positive case as a rule ('as many as were baptized … were filled with the Holy Ghost'), which is precisely what Acts 8:16 exists to deny can be assumed. Note too that the name is the Acts formula and not the trinitarian one Christ gave these same disciples at 3 Nephi 11:25.

links.note: 'The disciples whom Jesus had chosen, began from that time forth to baptize and to teach … and as many as were baptized in the name of Jesus, were filled with the Holy Ghost.' Teaching and baptizing in that pair is the commission of Matthew 28:19-20, and the chapter completes it at 26:20; the baptismal formula and the promise attached to it are Acts's. Held at moderate because no phrase is reproduced exactly: the Book of Mormon says 'in the name of Jesus' where the King James Bible always says 'in the name of the Lord Jesus'.
links.whyNot: Nothing here is a verbatim run. The case is that the sequence — chosen disciples, teaching, baptism in Jesus' name, the Holy Ghost following — is Acts's and occurs in Acts twice; a reader could hold that early-Christian practice as described anywhere would produce the same sentence.
links.text: When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

pericopes.text: And many of them saw and heard unspeakable things, which are not lawful to be written;

provenance.other: “unspeakable words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:4, and “caught up into paradise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The whole of the Book of Mormon's clause is that verse's second half with two substitutions: 'things' for 'words', and 'written' for 'utter'. 'Not lawful' by itself is common — fourteen KJV verses — but thirteen of them are sabbath and legal disputes and none is about a vision.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is the New Testament's charter for a revelation that exists and may not be reported, and it locates the prohibition in speech: a man may not *utter* what he heard. 3 Nephi 26:18 moves it to the page — the things are 'not lawful to be written'. That single substitution is the chapter in miniature. Everything Mormon has said since 26:6 is about the limits of a record rather than the limits of speech: Christ expounded all things aloud to the multitude (26:1), the multitude heard the babes (26:16), and it is only the writing that is forbidden (26:16, 26:18) or deferred (26:9-11). Paul's unspeakable words become Mormon's unwritable ones, and the catalogue's readers are on the wrong side of the substitution by construction.

links.note: 'And many of them saw and heard unspeakable things, which are not lawful to be written.' This is the closest verbal contact in the chapter and rests on a King James singleton. 2 Corinthians 12:4 reads 'heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter'; 3 Nephi 26:18 reads 'saw and heard unspeakable things, which are not lawful to be written'. The clause structure, the adjective, the legal negative and the infinitive of communication all survive; what changes is the verb, and the change is the argument. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and catalogued as an allusion accordingly (CONVENTIONS §2).
links.text: How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.

pericopes.text: and they taught, and did minister one to another; and they had all things common among them, every man dealing justly, one with another.

provenance.other: “had all things common” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 2:44 and Acts 4:32, and nowhere else in scripture. The Book of Mormon's 'they had all things common' matches Acts 4:32's pronoun and clause exactly; Acts 2:44 reads 'and had all things common' without the subject. The phrase enters the Book of Mormon here and returns once, at 4 Nephi 1:3.
provenance.significance: Read on, and Acts 4:32 turns out to be the verse before the Book of Mormon's own problem. Acts 4:32-37 describes the community of goods and names Barnabas, who sold a field and laid the whole price at the apostles' feet; Acts 5:1-2 then names Ananias, who 'kept back part of the price' and died for it. 3 Nephi 26 is a chapter about keeping back part — a hundredth part written, a lesser part given, a greater part withheld (26:6-11) — and it reaches for the community that held all things common as its closing image. We do not claim the writer meant the juxtaposition. But the source passage's next episode is about a withheld portion, and this is the catalogue's business to record.

links.note: 'They had all things common among them, every man dealing justly, one with another.' Four words with two homes in the King James Bible, both in Acts's descriptions of the Jerusalem church, and the surrounding verses of 3 Nephi assemble the rest of that description: teaching and ministering (26:19, cf. Acts 2:42), breaking bread (26:13, cf. Acts 2:46), baptism and the Holy Ghost (26:17, cf. Acts 2:38). The chapter is not borrowing a phrase; it is reproducing Acts 2-4's portrait of a church and using Acts's own words to do it. 'Every man dealing justly' is the Book of Mormon's addition and has no King James parallel.
links.text: And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did do all things, even as Jesus had commanded them.

provenance.route: Mark 11:6 and Matthew 21:6 conflated, in the setting of Matthew 28:20 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Two singletons, one on each side of a Synoptic parallel: “as Jesus had commanded” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 11:6, and “as Jesus commanded them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:6. Both report the same errand, the fetching of the colt. The Book of Mormon reads 'even as Jesus had commanded them', which takes Mark's 'even … had' and Matthew's 'them' — so the mediation test between the two forms does not resolve; the verse has both, and mediation-check.py's one decisive point is an absence rather than a reading.
provenance.significance: The wording comes from the colt-fetching, but the situation is the Great Commission's: “all things whatsoever I have commanded you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 28:20, and 3 Nephi 26:17-20 works through Matthew 28:19-20 in order — chosen disciples, teaching, baptizing, and finally doing all things as commanded. The chapter ends its account of the church with the sentence Matthew ends his Gospel with, in the words two other Gospels use for a small act of obedience whose point the doers could not yet see.

links.note: 'They did do all things, even as Jesus had commanded them.' A short clause, but every part of it is a King James singleton in one Gospel or another, and the Book of Mormon has assembled it from both members of a Synoptic pair rather than following either. Held at moderate: the phrase is the plainest possible statement of obedience and could be written by anyone, and the argument is that the chapter has by this point already reproduced the other two clauses of Matthew 28:19-20.
links.whyNot: 'As Jesus had commanded them' is not a distinctive form of words in the way that 'unstopped' or 'unspeakable words' are — its rarity in the King James Bible is close to arithmetic, since the KJV rarely needs to say it. The conflation argument cuts both ways: a text that matches neither source exactly may be matching neither.
links.text: And they said unto them even as Jesus had commanded: and they let them go.

pericopes.text: And they which were baptized in the name of Jesus, were called the church of Christ.

And it came to pass that as the disciples of Jesus were journeying, and were preaching the things which they had both heard and seen, and were baptizing in the name of Jesus, it came to pass that the disciples were gathered together, and were united in mighty prayer and fasting.

And Jesus again shewed himself unto them: for they were praying unto the Father, in his name; and Jesus came and stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, What will ye that I shall give unto you?

links.text: And Jesus stood still, and called them, and said, What will ye that I shall do unto you?

provenance.other: “what will ye that I shall” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:32. The Book of Mormon changes one word of it, “do” to “give”, and “Ask what I shall give thee” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 3:5 and its doublet 2 Chronicles 1:7 — God to Solomon at Gibeon. The 1830 “saith unto them” for a past narration is retained throughout this chapter and modernised to “said” in 1920.
provenance.significance: In Matthew the question is put to two blind men sitting by the road at Jericho, and the thing asked for is sight. Here it is put to the twelve at the end of forty days of instruction, and the thing asked for is a name for the church. The one KJV substitution is the interesting one: replacing “do” with “give” turns Matthew's roadside question into the formula of the only other place in the KJV where God invites a request open-endedly, God to Solomon in the dream at Gibeon, where the thing asked for is an understanding heart to judge a people and the granting of it founds a temple. A question about what to call a house of worship is asked in the words of the man who built one.

links.note: “What will ye that I shall give unto you?” — six words of Matthew 20:32 with a single substitution, from the only KJV verse that has the clause. The setting supplies the reason for the substitution: nobody here is asking to be healed, and the disciples' answer at 27:3 is a request for instruction rather than a request for a thing. Below any quotation threshold on length; recorded as an allusion because the clause is a KJV singleton and the substitution is legible.

pericopes.text: And they saith unto him, Lord, we will that thou wouldst tell us the name whereby we shall call this church; for there are disputations among the people concerning this matter.
And the Lord said unto them, Verily, verily I say unto you, why is it that the people should murmur and dispute because of this thing?
have they not read the scriptures, which saith ye must take upon you the name of Christ, which is in my name? for by this name shall ye be called at the last day;
and whoso taketh upon him my name, and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved at the last day;

links.text: And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:22 + Matthew 24:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “he that endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:22; “the same shall be saved” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13, which both read “he that shall endure unto the end”. `mediation-check.py` on 3 Nephi 27:6 against Matthew 10:22 and Matthew 24:13 returns one decisive divergence and it falls to Matthew 10:22: the Book of Mormon has “endureth to”, not “shall endure unto”. It then takes “the same shall be saved”, which Matthew 10:22 does not have. The clause as it stands is in no KJV verse.
