provenance.significance: The composite is not decorative; it is doing exactly the work the surrounding verses need. 27:5-7 is an argument that the church must bear Christ's name, and Matthew 10:22 is the KJV's one verse where enduring to the end is set against being hated “for my name's sake” — the endurance saying in its name-bearing form. Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13 carry the same saying but attach it to the abomination of desolation. The Book of Mormon takes the wording of the name verse and the cadence of the eschatological one, and the sentence it builds — “whoso taketh upon him my name, and endureth to the end” — is Matthew 10:22 read as a definition of discipleship rather than a warning about persecution. The suppressed half of Matthew 10:22 is the hatred, which this chapter will not need until 27:32.

links.note: The verse fuses the two Synoptic forms of one saying and takes the diagnostic word from each. Matthew 10:22's “endureth to the end” is a KJV singleton and it is what the Book of Mormon has; Matthew 24:13's “the same shall be saved” is what it appends. Matthew 10:22 was adjudicated at 3 Nephi 15:9 for a different half of the verse, and this is not that borrowing recurring: 15:9 is about endurance under hatred, 27:6 is about endurance under a name, and the fusion with Matthew 24:13 appears only here.

pericopes.text: therefore, whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name; therefore ye shall call the church in my name; and ye shall call upon the Father in my name, that he will bless the church for my sake;

and how be it my church, save it be called in my name? for if a church be called in Moses’ name, then it be Moses’ church: or if it be called in the name of a man, then it be the church of a man; but if it be called in my name, then it is my church, if it so be that they are built upon my Gospel.

Verily I say unto you, that ye are built upon my Gospel; therefore ye shall call whatsoever things ye do call in my name; therefore if ye call upon the Father, for the church, if it be in my name, the Father will hear you;
and if it so be that the church is built upon my Gospel, then will the Father shew forth his own works in it;

but if it be not built upon my Gospel, and is built upon the works of men, or upon the works of the Devil, verily I say unto you, they have joy in their works for a season, and by and by the end cometh, and they are hewn down and cast into the fire, from whence there is no return;

links.text: Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.other: “hewn down and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9 — and in all three the subject is a tree that bears no good fruit. 3 Nephi 14:19 transcribes Matthew 7:19 verbatim as part of the sermon at the temple; the clause returns twice in this chapter, at 27:11 and 27:17, with no tree in either.
provenance.significance: The clause is being re-used against a new subject, and that is the finding. In the three KJV verses the thing hewn down is a fruitless tree, an image with a long agricultural life and no institutional edge to it. Here it is a church — one built on the works of men or the works of the devil — and then at 27:17 an individual who does not endure. The metaphor's vehicle has been discarded and its verdict kept, which is a use of Matthew 7:19 that Matthew 7 does not make: John's axe at Matthew 3:10 is laid to the root of the trees, and the Book of Mormon lays it to the root of a congregation.

links.note: “They are hewn down and cast into the fire, from whence there is no return.” Six words of a clause that stands in exactly three KJV verses, all of the fruitless tree. It is a second use — 3 Nephi 14:19 already reproduced Matthew 7:19 whole — but not the narrator reusing his own formula: the sermon quoted the tree, this verse drops the tree and applies the sentence to a church, and adds a clause no KJV verse has, “from whence there is no return”. Confidence is held at moderate because the clause is short and its distribution across three verses gives no way to pick between Matthew 7:19 and its two parallels; Matthew 7 is named because this chapter is otherwise saturated with it.

pericopes.text: for their works do follow them: for it is because of their works that they are hewn down; therefore remember the things that I have told you.

links.text: And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.

provenance.other: “their works do follow them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:13, and the Book of Mormon has all five words in order. The idiom is not otherwise available in English scripture: the KJV's usual formula for judgement by deeds is “according to their works” (Revelation 20:12, 20:13), which this chapter also uses at 27:14, 27:15 and 27:25.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest inversion and it turns on nothing but context. In Revelation 14:13 the clause is a beatitude, spoken by a voice from heaven and confirmed by the Spirit: the dead who die in the Lord are blessed, they rest from their labours, and their works follow them into that rest as a comfort and a credential. In 3 Nephi 27:12 the same five words are the reason for a sentence of destruction — “for their works do follow them: for it is because of their works that they are hewn down”. Recover Revelation's context and the borrowing reads as a deliberate reversal of its polarity: what follows the blessed dead into rest is what follows the unblessed into the fire, and the difference is not in the following but in the works. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's one phrase for posthumous vindication and made it a phrase for posthumous liability.

links.note: A KJV singleton reproduced exactly, and reproduced with its verdict reversed. Revelation 14:13 says the works of those who die in the Lord follow them; 3 Nephi 27:12 says the works of those built on the works of men follow them, and immediately glosses what following means — “it is because of their works that they are hewn down”. Well below any quotation threshold on length, and catalogued as an allusion on the strength of the singleton and the exactness of the run. Whether the reversal is designed or accidental cannot be shown from the text; that it is a reversal can.

pericopes.text: Behold I have given unto you my Gospel, and this is the Gospel which I have given unto you: That I came into the world to do the will of my Father, because my Father sent me;

links.text: For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.

provenance.other: “to do the will of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 4:34 (“My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work”); “the will of him that sent me” occurs in three, all in John (4:34, 6:38, 6:39). The Book of Mormon writes “to do the will of my Father, because my Father sent me”, which converts John's periphrasis — “him that sent me” — into a named Father and a separate causal clause.
provenance.significance: The definition of the gospel that this chapter is famous for is given in Johannine vocabulary and Johannine sequence, and what it drops is as telling as what it keeps. John 6:38's sentence begins “I came down from heaven”; 3 Nephi 27:13 begins “I came into the world”, which is the formula of 1 Timothy 1:15 and John 18:37 rather than the descent language of John 6, and which suits a speaker who is at that moment standing in a hemisphere the fourth gospel does not know about. John 6:38 also states the will negatively — not mine own — and the Book of Mormon deletes the negation, so that a saying framed in John as a denial of independent agency becomes here a bare statement of commission. The suppressed half is the polemic: in John 6 the sentence is spoken to a murmuring crowd that will not have him, and it is the ground of his refusal to lose any of them, which is the argument this chapter returns to at 27:30-32.

links.note: “I came into the world to do the will of my Father, because my Father sent me.” Three of the four distinctive elements of John 6:38 are present in John's order — coming, doing the will, being sent — and the fourth, the negation, is removed. “To do the will of” is a KJV singleton at John 4:34, which supplies the same clause in the same construction; the fusion is the ordinary Johannine idiom rather than a pointed composite, and the link is written on John 6:38 because it, not 4:34, is a first-person definition of why he came.

pericopes.text: and my Father sent me that I might be lifted up upon the cross; and after that I had been lifted up upon the cross, I might draw all men unto me; that as I have been lifted up by men, even so should men be lifted up by the Father, to stand before me, to be judged of their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil;

links.text: And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.

provenance.other: “draw all men unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:32, and the Book of Mormon has it twice in two verses (27:14, 27:15). John 12:33 is the evangelist's gloss on it: “This he said, signifying what death he should die.”
provenance.significance: This is metalepsis with the gloss written back into the saying. John 12:32 says only “lifted up from the earth”, and the phrase is a riddle the crowd immediately objects to at 12:34; the fourth gospel resolves it in the narrator's aside at 12:33, which tells the reader that the lifting up is a manner of death without naming it. 3 Nephi 27:14 names it — “lifted up upon the cross”, twice in one verse — and so folds John's editorial explanation into the speech John gives it about. It then does something John does not: it makes the figure reciprocal, so that being lifted up by men is answered by men being lifted up by the Father “to stand before me, to be judged of their works”. In John the lifting up draws; here it also weighs, and the same verb carries the crucifixion, the resurrection of the dead and the verdict.

links.note: The one KJV verse with “draw all men unto me”, used twice in consecutive verses and each time expanded. What the expansion supplies is precisely John 12:33 — the death that “lifted up” means — which the fourth gospel keeps outside the saying as a narrator's note. The link is filed at 27:14 because that is where the cross is named and where the figure is turned round; 27:15 repeats the clause at greater length and with a fuller verbal run, and is recorded in `recurrenceRefs` rather than given its own row.

pericopes.text: and for this cause have I been lifted up; therefore, according to the power of the Father, I will draw all men unto me, that they may be judged according to their works.

And it shall come to pass, that whoso repenteth and is baptized in my name, shall be filled; and if he endureth to the end, behold, him will I hold guiltless before my Father, at that day when I shall stand to judge the world.

links.text: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

provenance.other: “hold him guiltless” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:7 and its Deuteronomy 5:11 doublet, and they are word-for-word identical in the relevant clause; `mediation-check.py` on the pair returns “identical wording — no test available here”, so the third commandment can be identified as the source but the Exodus and Deuteronomy forms of it cannot be told apart. The word “guiltless” alone stands in ten KJV verses, of which one more couples it with holding — 1 Kings 2:9, David instructing Solomon to “hold him not guiltless”, which is a sentence of death on Shimei and has nothing to do with a name.
provenance.significance: Both KJV verses that hold a man guiltless do it in the negative, and both do it about the divine name: the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain. This chapter has spent eleven verses on taking the name — 27:5, “ye must take upon you the name of Christ”; 27:6, “whoso taketh upon him my name”; 27:7, everything done and every prayer offered in that name — and it now says “him will I hold guiltless before my Father”. The commandment's clause is repeated with its negation removed and its speaker changed: the Lord who in Exodus will not acquit the man who takes the name emptily here acquits the man who takes it and endures. Reading the source recovers the condition the Book of Mormon has left unstated, which is that a name taken can be taken in vain, and 27:11's church built on the works of men is what that looks like.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Exodus 20:7 at this verse, and the verbal warrant is “hold him guiltless”, which stands in exactly two KJV verses, the third commandment in each of its two forms. The Book of Mormon reverses the polarity of the clause and keeps its subject-matter: Exodus withholds acquittal from a man who misuses the name, 3 Nephi 27:16 grants it to a man who is baptized in it and endures. Which of the two KJV forms is in view cannot be settled from the wording, since they are identical here; “direct-OT” is recorded because neither is quoted in the New Testament and there is no mediating form to test.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 27.16 (cross-references Exodus 20:7)

pericopes.text: And he that endureth not unto the end, the same is he that is also hewn down and cast into the fire, from whence they can no more return, because of the justice of the Father;
and this is the word which he hath given unto the children of men. And for this cause he fulfilleth the words which he hath given, and he lieth not, but fulfilleth all his words;

and no unclean thing can enter into his kingdom; therefore nothing entereth into his rest, save it be those who have washed their garments in my blood, because of their faith, and the repentance of all their sins, and their faithfulness unto the end.

links.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.route: Revelation 7:14 → KJV → Book of Mormon (via a figure already established at 1 Nephi 12:11)
provenance.other: “washed their robes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 7:14; “washed their garments” occurs in none. “Washed us from our sins in his own blood” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 1:5, and is the only KJV verse that puts the washing in the speaker's own blood. The Book of Mormon's clause — “washed their garments in my blood” — has Revelation 7:14's verb and possessive, Revelation 1:5's first-person blood, and a noun from neither.
provenance.significance: Every earlier Book of Mormon use of this figure is third-person and follows Revelation 7:14's grammar: garments made white in the blood of the Lamb (1 Nephi 12:11, Alma 13:11), a robe made white through the blood (Alma 5:21). 3 Nephi 27:19 is the first time the speaker is the Lamb. What in Revelation is a vision explained to a seer by an elder is here said by the one whose blood it is, in the first person, to people who have handled his wounds five chapters earlier. The image loses its apocalyptic frame and gains a speaker.

links.note: The verbal contact is real but narrow — washing, a garment, blood — and it is the possessive that carries it: “washed their” plus blood is Revelation 7:14's construction, and the substitution of “garments” for “robes” matches the form the figure has taken throughout the Book of Mormon since 1 Nephi 12:11. Confidence is moderate rather than high because by this point the phrase is the corpus's own idiom as much as Revelation's, and a reader could reasonably file the borrowing at 1 Nephi 12:11 and count this a later use of it. It is given a row because a new book, a new speaker and the shift to “my blood” change what the figure asserts.

links.text: And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest, but to them that believed not?

provenance.other: “into his rest” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Hebrews 3:18, 4:1 and 4:10, and “enter into his rest” in exactly one, Hebrews 3:18. “Rest” used absolutely for the state the faithful are admitted to is a Hebrews idiom and nowhere else a KJV one.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon puts two entrances in one sentence — “no unclean thing can enter into his kingdom; therefore nothing entereth into his rest” — and only the second is scriptural English. Hebrews 3:18 supplies it, and supplies with it a condition: the wilderness generation was sworn out of the rest for unbelief, “they could not enter in because of unbelief” (3:19). 3 Nephi 27:19 states the condition positively, “because of their faith”, and adds repentance and endurance to it. What is recovered by reading Hebrews 3 is that the rest is something a covenant people can be excluded from after being brought out, which is exactly the anxiety 27:32 will voice about the fourth generation.

links.note: An echo, not more: the shared string is three words and the argument for it is that “his rest” as a destination is Hebrews' vocabulary and not the KJV's generally. It is recorded because the whole clause structure of 27:19 — entry barred, a condition of faith supplied — is Hebrews 3:18-4:1's, and because the same source stands behind Alma 13:6.
links.whyNot: Three words is thin, “rest” for the state of the saved is common Christian English by 1830 quite apart from Hebrews, and the Book of Mormon has used “enter into the rest of the Lord” often enough that this may be its own formula rather than a fresh borrowing. A reader who declines this row loses nothing from the chapter's argument.

pericopes.text: Now this is the commandment: Repent, all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me and be baptized in my name, that ye may be sanctified by the reception of the Holy Ghost, that ye may stand spotless before me at the last day.

Verily, verily I say unto you, this is my Gospel; and ye know the things that ye must do in my church; for the works which ye have seen me do, that shall ye also do; for that which ye have seen me do, even that shall ye do;

links.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father.

provenance.other: “the works that I do shall he do also” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 14:12. The Book of Mormon writes “the works which ye have seen me do, that shall ye also do”, keeping the verb, the object and the “also” and changing the person from singular to plural and the relative clause from believing to having seen. Both this verse and 27:21's second clause open on “Verily, verily I say unto you”, which is John 14:12's own opening.
provenance.significance: The two halves of John 14:12 are split across this chapter and separated by seven verses. 27:21 has the first — the works that I do shall ye do also — and 27:28 has the last, “And now I go unto the Father”, which is the reason John 14:12 gives for the promise. What falls out in between is the clause that stands between them in John: “greater works than these shall he do”. The Book of Mormon promises the same works and not greater ones, and it changes the qualifying condition from believing on him to having seen him, which is available to these hearers and to nobody after them. Recovering John 14 recovers a promise deliberately narrowed.

links.note: “For the works which ye have seen me do, that shall ye also do; for that which ye have seen me do, even that shall ye do.” The construction is John 14:12's, from the only KJV verse that has it, and the doubling for emphasis is the Book of Mormon's own. “What ye have seen me do” is also Judges 9:48, Abimelech at mount Zalmon telling his men to copy him with an axe, which the n-gram stream ranks here; that is a coincidence of a very ordinary English clause and is filed in the register.

pericopes.text: therefore if ye do these things, blessed are ye, for ye shall be lifted up at the last day.
Write the things which ye have seen and heard, save it be those which are forbidden;
write the works of this people, which shall be even as hath been written of that which hath been;
for behold, out of the books which have been written, and which shall be written, shall this people be judged: for by them shall their works be known unto men.

links.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “judged out of those things which were written in the books” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12, and it is the only verse in the Bible where judgement is said to proceed out of books in the plural. 3 Nephi 27:25 has “out of the books which have been written, and which shall be written, shall this people be judged” and 27:26 “out of the books which shall be written, shall the world be judged”; the KJV's governing phrase “according to their works” appears in both, at 27:25 as “their works” and at 27:14, 27:15 and 27:26 in full.
provenance.significance: Revelation 20:12 is a vision of a future assize: the books already exist, they are opened, and the dead are judged from them. 3 Nephi 27:23-26 makes the same books a present writing assignment — “Write the things which ye have seen and heard”, “write the works of this people” — and puts the disciples on the composing end of the volumes John saw opened. That is the metalepsis, and it is unusually consequential: it makes the act of record-keeping that produces the Book of Mormon itself an act of drafting the evidence at the last judgement, and it explains why 27:23 has to carve out an exception for “those which are forbidden”. A book that will be read against the world is a book with things properly left out of it.

links.note: The one KJV verse that judges out of books, reworked into a commission to write them. The link is filed at 27:25, where the phrase “out of the books ... shall this people be judged” first stands, and 27:26 repeats it of the world and is recorded in `recurrenceRefs`. Revelation 20:12 is used elsewhere in the corpus, always of the judgement scene itself (2 Nephi 29:11, Mosiah 16:10, Alma 11:41); this is the only place it is turned round to describe the making of the books.

pericopes.text: And behold, all things are written by the Father; therefore out of the books which shall be written, shall the world be judged.

And know ye that ye shall be judges of this people, according to the judgement which I shall give unto you, which shall be just; therefore what manner of men had ye ought to be?— Verily I say unto you, Even as I am.

links.text: Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness,
variants: 1830 “had ye ought to be” → 1920 “ought ye to be”

provenance.other: “What manner of persons ought ye to be” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 3:11; “what manner of” alone stands in eighteen. The Book of Mormon substitutes “men” for “persons”. The 1830 reading is “what manner of men had ye ought to be”, which is not English of any Bible; 1920 emended it to “what manner of men ought ye to be”.
provenance.significance: The 1830 variant is the evidence here, and it runs the way CONVENTIONS §8 predicts: the first edition has a non-scriptural construction, “had ye ought to be”, and the 1920 correction moves the sentence back toward the KJV verse behind it rather than away from it. The borrowing is plainer in the modern text than in the running text, which is the reverse of the usual pattern and worth recording as such. What 2 Peter 3:11 asks the question about is the dissolution of the elements at the day of the Lord; 3 Nephi 27:27 asks it about sitting as judges of this people, and answers it in a way 2 Peter does not dare — “Even as I am”. Peter's rhetorical question expects holy conversation; this one expects the questioner's own character.

links.note: The interrogative is a KJV singleton in this form and the Book of Mormon changes one noun. What makes the row worth having is the 1830 reading: “had ye ought to be” is the running text, and the 1920 edition's repair of it produces the KJV's exact word order. Confidence is moderate because the 1830 construction is far enough from 2 Peter that a reader could take the resemblance to be the later editors' work rather than the first edition's; on that reading the link belongs to 1920 and not to 1830, which is itself a finding.

pericopes.text: And now I go unto the Father. And verily I say unto you, whatsoever things ye shall ask the Father, in my name, it shall be given unto you;
therefore ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you: for he that asketh, receiveth, and unto him that knocketh, it shall be opened.

links.text: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.

provenance.other: “That asketh receiveth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:8 and Luke 11:10, which are word-for-word identical in the KJV and so cannot be told apart here; “him that knocketh it shall be opened” occurs in the same two and nowhere else. Matthew is named because everything else in this chapter's Sermon material is Matthean and because 3 Nephi 14:7-8 transcribes Matthew 7:7-8 verbatim, seeking and all. 27:29 does not: it drops the seeking clause from both halves, so that a threefold saying becomes twofold, and it replaces “Ask, and it shall be given you” with “ask, and ye shall receive”, which is John 16:24's form and a KJV singleton there. The surviving run — “he that asketh, receiveth, and unto him that knocketh, it shall be opened” — is Matthew 7:8 minus its middle clause, with “unto” added before “him”, a preposition no KJV verse has here.
provenance.significance: The abridgement is the argument. Matthew's saying is a triad and its middle term, seeking and finding, is the one that admits of not having arrived; the Book of Mormon's second pass keeps the two terms that resolve — asking is answered, knocking is opened — and drops the one that searches. Read against 27:30, where the joy is already full and “none of them are lost”, the pruning is consistent: this is a discourse to people who have found.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Matthew 7:7-8 here, and this is the chapter's second engagement with the saying — 3 Nephi 14:7-8 gave it whole. It is written as a fresh link rather than filed as a repeat because the second pass is a reworking and not a copy: the seeking clause is gone from both halves, and the opening imperative has been replaced from John 16:24, which is adjudicated separately at this verse. Below any quotation threshold once the omissions are counted.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 27.29 (cross-references Matthew 7:7-8)

links.text: Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full.

provenance.other: “Ask, and ye shall receive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 16:24; Matthew 7:7 and Luke 11:9 both read “Ask, and it shall be given you”. The Book of Mormon has John's form. “That your joy may be full” occurs in two verses, John 16:24 and 1 John 1:4, and “fulness of joy” in exactly one, Psalm 16:11.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest single finding in the chapter and it depends on reading three verses together. 27:29 substitutes John 16:24's imperative into a Matthew 7 saying — “ask, and ye shall receive” where Matthew has “it shall be given you” — and then 27:30 and 27:31 supply John 16:24's own continuation, which Matthew 7 does not have: “my joy is great, even unto fulness”, “in them I have fulness of joy”. The suppressed half of the borrowed clause has been recovered and written out in the following two verses. That is metalepsis performed rather than implied, and it also reverses the possessive: John's promise is that your joy may be full, and the Book of Mormon's report is that his is.

links.note: The chapter takes the ask-and-receive saying from Matthew 7 but takes its verb from John, and “ask, and ye shall receive” is a KJV singleton at John 16:24. The reason for the substitution appears immediately: John 16:24 ends “that your joy may be full”, and 27:30-31 is about nothing else — fulness of joy, in the Son, in the Father and in the holy angels. The two verses that follow the borrowing are the rest of the verse it was borrowed from.

pericopes.text: And now behold, my joy is great, even unto fulness, because of you, and also this generation; yea, and even the Father rejoiceth, and also all the holy angels, because of you and this generation: for none of them are lost.
Behold, I would that ye should understand; for I mean them which are now alive, of this generation; and none of them are lost; and in them I have fulness of joy.—

But behold, it sorroweth me because of the fourth generation from this generation, for they are led away captive by him, even as was the son of perdition; for they will sell me for silver, and for gold, and for that which moth doth corrupt, and which thieves can break through and steal. And in that day will I visit them, even in turning their works upon their own heads.

links.text: While I was with them in the world, I kept them in thy name: those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition; that the scripture might be fulfilled.
variants: 1830 and 1920 both read “none of them are lost” against the KJV's “is lost”

provenance.other: “None of them is lost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 17:12; “none of them” alone stands in thirteen. “Son of perdition” occurs in exactly two, John 17:12 and 2 Thessalonians 2:3, and only John 17:12 has both. The Book of Mormon reads “none of them are lost”, a plural verb the KJV does not have and that 1920 did not correct — unlike 1 Nephi 1:20's “tender mercies ... is over all”, which 1920 restored to the KJV's “are”.
provenance.significance: One KJV sentence is dismantled across three Book of Mormon verses. John 17:12 reads “none of them is lost, but the son of perdition”, a single clause with a single exception attached; 3 Nephi 27:30 says “none of them are lost”, 27:31 repeats “none of them are lost”, and 27:32 supplies the exception — “even as was the son of perdition” — after an intervening sentence and applies it not to one man but to a generation four removed. The effect is to hold the two halves of Jesus's high-priestly report apart long enough for the reader to feel the first as unqualified before the qualification arrives, and to make the exception corporate. Judas's place in the sentence is filled by the fourth generation of the Nephites, and the chapter that opened by naming the church closes by losing it.

links.note: Hardy cross-references John 17:12 at this verse. The clause “none of them is lost” is a KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon has it twice in the two preceding verses before delivering John's own exception here. The 1830 plural “are lost” is not the KJV's grammar and survived into 1920, which is worth recording alongside the cases where a later edition corrected such an agreement back toward the source. Adjudicated as an extended allusion rather than a quotation because no continuous run of John 17:12 is reproduced — the borrowing is of a sentence's architecture and of two of its rare phrases, taken apart and redistributed.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 27.32 (cross-references John 17:12)

links.text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:

provenance.other: “Thieves break through and steal” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:19. The Book of Mormon transcribed that verse whole at 3 Nephi 13:19 as part of the sermon at the temple, and returns to it here with the clause intact but the object changed: what moth corrupts and thieves steal is no longer a treasure laid up on earth but the price paid for Christ. “Sell me for silver, and for gold” has no KJV parallel; the nearest are Matthew 26:15's covenant for thirty pieces of silver and Amos 2:6's “sold the righteous for silver”.
provenance.significance: This is the second-use case that ADJUDICATING §4 reserves for a phrase returning to its source rather than a narrator repeating his own formula, and the return is what makes the verse. In Matthew 6:19 the corruptible treasure is what a disciple is told not to accumulate; in 3 Nephi 27:32 it is what a disciple's descendants accept in exchange for the speaker. The sermon's warning is being cashed out as a prophecy of betrayal, and the vocabulary that framed it as prudence — moth, thieves, breaking through — now frames it as apostasy. The son of perdition named in the same verse sold him for silver too, and Matthew 6:19 stands between the two acts as the standard both fail.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Matthew 6:19 at this verse. The clause “thieves break through and steal” is a KJV singleton, and this is its second appearance in 3 Nephi — 13:19 has the whole of Matthew 6:19 verbatim. It is written as a link rather than filed as a within-book repeat because the second use is the argument: the treasure that moth corrupts has become the price of the Messiah, and the sermon's own image is turned against the people who heard it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 27.32 (cross-references Matthew 6:19)

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when Jesus had ended these sayings, he saith unto his disciples, Enter ye in at the straight gate: for straight is the gate, and narrow is the way that leads to life, and few there be that find it: But wide is the gate, and broad the way which leads to death, and many there be that traveleth therein, until the night cometh, wherein no man can work.

links.text: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
variants: 1830 “straight gate” / “straight is the gate” → 1920 “strait” in both places
1830 “many there be that traveleth therein” → 1920 “travel therein”

provenance.other: 3 Nephi 14:13-14 transcribes Matthew 7:13-14 in Matthew's order and almost word for word: wide gate first, strait gate second, “leadeth to destruction”, “many there be which go in thereat”. 27:33 reverses the order to put life first, changes “leadeth” to “leads” in both members, changes “destruction” to “death”, and changes “many there be which go in thereat” to “many there be that traveleth therein”. The 1830 spelling is “straight” in both places at 27:33 and at 14:13-14, corrected to the KJV's “strait” in 1920.
provenance.significance: That the second pass is a free reworking and not a copy of the first is the finding, and it is what licenses calling this a fresh borrowing from Matthew rather than the book quoting itself. A writer working from 3 Nephi 14 would have reproduced its order and its “destruction”; this verse reproduces neither, yet keeps Matthew 7:14's rare run “and narrow is the way ... and few there be that find it” intact. Reversing the members also changes the rhetoric: Matthew ends on the narrow way as the thing few find, and 3 Nephi 27:33 ends on the broad way and the crowd travelling it, which sets up the clause from John 9:4 that follows and gives the chapter a close on nightfall rather than on life.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Matthew 7:13-14 here. Both members of the saying are present with their distinctive KJV wording, but in Matthew's reverse order and with three substitutions, none of which comes from the verbatim version the same book gave at 3 Nephi 14:13-14. The 1830 “straight” for “strait” is the KJV's homophone rather than its word and is corrected in 1920; it does not affect the identification, since “straight gate” is not a KJV reading at all.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 27.33 (cross-references Matthew 7:13-14)

links.text: I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.

provenance.other: “The night cometh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 9:4, and “no man can work” in exactly one, the same. The Book of Mormon has both, joined as John joins them: “until the night cometh, wherein no man can work.” The only alteration is “wherein” for “when”.
provenance.significance: Nothing in Matthew 7:13-14 leads to a nightfall; the strait-gate saying ends on the few who find life, and the clause bolted onto it here comes from a different gospel and a different occasion — Jesus before the man born blind, explaining why the works have to be done now. Recover John 9 and the borrowed clause brings its subject with it: the works of him that sent me, which is the phrase this chapter has been circling since 27:13 (“the will of my Father, because my Father sent me”) and 27:21 (“the works which ye have seen me do”). The chapter's last words are therefore a time limit on the works it has spent thirty verses defining, and the broad way full of travellers is where the dark falls. Hardy cross-references John 9:4 at this verse; the pairing with Matthew 7:13 is the Book of Mormon's.

links.note: Two KJV singletons in one clause, both from John 9:4, appended to a Matthew 7 saying that has no such ending. It is the clearest composite in the chapter: the sermon material is Matthean and the sentence that closes it is Johannine, and the join is visible because nothing in Matthew 7 prepares for night. Alma 34:33 uses the same verse for the same purpose — a deadline on labour — in a different book, and is recorded in `recurrenceRefs`.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 27.33 (cross-references John 9:4)

pericopes.text: And it came to pass when Jesus had said these words, he spake unto his disciples, one by one, saying unto them, What is it that ye desire of me, after that I am gone to the Father?

And they all spake, save it were three, saying, We desire that after we have lived unto the age of man, that our ministry, wherein thou hast called us, may have an end, that we may speedily come unto thee, in thy kingdom.

And he saith unto them, Blessed are ye, because ye desired this thing of me; therefore after that ye are seventy and two years old, ye shall come unto me in my kingdom, and with me ye shall find rest.
And when he had spake unto them, he turned himself unto the three, and said unto them, What will ye that I should do unto you, when I am gone unto the Father?

links.text: And he said unto them, What would ye that I should do for you?

provenance.route: Mark 10:35-40, with the wording of Matthew 20:32 and Mark 10:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The King James Bible puts this question three times and never elsewhere. “what will ye that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:32; “that I should do unto” occurs in exactly one, Mark 10:51. 3 Nephi 28:4 reads ‘What will ye that I should do unto you’ — the opening of Matthew 20:32 welded to the closing of Mark 10:51. Mark 10:36, ‘What would ye that I should do for you?’, is the same question asked not of blind beggars but of two disciples, and it is prompted at Mark 10:35 by ‘we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire’ — the verb 3 Nephi 28:1 uses twice, ‘What is it that ye desire of me’.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the whole chapter is Mark 10:35-40 answered the other way. There the two who ask are James and John, the request is for places in the kingdom, and the reply is a refusal: ye know not what ye ask, and to sit on my right hand and on my left is not mine to give. Here twelve are asked what they desire, nine ask for a place in the kingdom and get it (28:3, ‘with me ye shall find rest’), and three ask for something else and are told they are more blessed. Two verses later the disciple whose desire is named as the precedent is John — one of the two who asked in Mark 10:35. The Book of Mormon is not quoting the Zebedee request; it is granting it.

links.note: ‘And when he had spake unto them, he turned himself unto the three, and said unto them, What will ye that I should do unto you, when I am gone unto the Father?’ Eight words that exist in the KJV only as two halves of two Synoptic questions, put in the setting of the third. The frame is set at 28:1, where the question is asked of all twelve with ‘desire’, Mark 10:35’s word; 1830 reads ‘when he had spake’, regularised to ‘spoken’ in 1920. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as an allusion, not a quotation.

pericopes.text: And they sorrowed in their hearts, for they durst not speak unto him the thing which they desired.
And he saith unto them, Behold, I know your thoughts, and ye have desired the thing which John, my beloved, which was with me in my ministry, before that I was lifted up by the Jews, desired of me;

links.text: Jesus saith unto him, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.

provenance.other: “the disciple whom Jesus loved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 21:20, and “if I will that he tarry till I come” occurs in exactly two, John 21:22 and 21:23, which are one sentence reported twice. 3 Nephi 28:6 has ‘John, my beloved, which was with me in my ministry’. The dating clause is traceable too: “lifted up the Son of man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:28, where Jesus says it to the Jews — which is exactly what ‘before that I was lifted up by the Jews’ makes of it. 1830’s relative ‘which’ is modernised to ‘who’ in 1920 at both points in this verse.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is in the half of John 21 the Book of Mormon does not quote. John 21:23 exists to correct a rumour: ‘Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him, He shall not die; but, If I will that he tarry till I come.’ The evangelist is denying the very thing 3 Nephi 28 asserts. So the source text of the three Nephites is the New Testament’s own retraction of the belief that a disciple would not die — and this chapter takes the retracted reading, makes it explicit doctrine (28:7, ‘ye shall never taste of death’), and extends it to three more men. Reading the two together, the Book of Mormon does not merely echo John 21; it overrules its footnote.

links.note: ‘Behold, I know your thoughts, and ye have desired the thing which John, my beloved, which was with me in my ministry, before that I was lifted up by the Jews, desired of me.’ The verse names John, calls him beloved in the epithet the KJV uses of him in one verse only, and refers to a request of his which the Bible reports only at John 21:21-22. Hardy cross-references John 21:20-24 here.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 28.6 (cross-references John 21:20-24)

links.text: Behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me.

provenance.route: Job 21:27 for the wording, the Synoptic thought-reading formula for the situation → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “I know your thoughts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 21:27, and the four words run on identically: ‘Behold, I know your thoughts’. The Gospels have Jesus reading thoughts repeatedly — Matthew 9:4 ‘Jesus knowing their thoughts’, Luke 6:8 ‘he knew their thoughts’, Luke 11:17 ‘he, knowing their thoughts’ — but always as third-person narration and never in his own mouth. The KJV’s only first-person form belongs to Job.
provenance.significance: The split is the finding: the situation is the Gospels’ and the sentence is Job’s. What the Synoptics report about Jesus from outside, 3 Nephi 28:6 has him say about himself, and the only English the King James Bible offers for saying it is a line of Job’s accusing his comforters. Job’s next clause is ‘and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me’; here the thoughts known are a desire too holy to speak aloud (28:5, ‘they durst not speak unto him the thing which they desired’). The borrowed clause is turned from indictment to reassurance by the words that follow it.

links.note: Four consecutive words from the one KJV verse that has them, and the eye-catching ‘Behold’ with them. Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a): the verbal match is absolute and the contextual match is nil, which is the shape of a genuine borrowing of an idiom rather than of a passage.
links.whyNot: Job 21:27 is an accusation and 3 Nephi 28:6 is a disclosure of grace; nothing else of Job 21 is present, and ‘I know your thoughts’ is short enough and ordinary enough in its parts that a writer steeped in the KJV could produce it without reaching for Job. The Synoptic thought-reading scenes account for the idea; only the grammatical person requires Job.

pericopes.text: therefore more blessed are ye, for ye shall never taste of death, but ye shall live to behold all the doings of the Father, unto the children of men, even until all things shall be fulfilled, according to the will of the Father, when I shall come in my glory, with the powers of heaven;

links.text: Then said the Jews unto him, Now we know that thou hast a devil. Abraham is dead, and the prophets; and thou sayest, If a man keep my saying, he shall never taste of death.

provenance.route: John 8:52 for the phrase, Matthew 16:28 / Mark 9:1 / Luke 9:27 for the promise, Luke 21:26-27 for the coming → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “taste of death” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 16:28, Mark 9:1, Luke 9:27 and John 8:52 — and the three Synoptic ones all read ‘shall not taste of death, till’. “never taste of death” occurs in exactly one, John 8:52. 3 Nephi 28:7 has John’s absolute adverb on the Synoptics’ promise. The rest of the sentence keeps counting: “coming in his kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 16:28; “come with power” occurs in exactly one, Mark 9:1; and “the powers of heaven” occurs in exactly one, Luke 21:26, whose next verse has the Son of man ‘coming in a cloud with power and great glory’ against this verse’s ‘when I shall come in my glory, with the powers of heaven’.
provenance.significance: Two suppressed contexts are doing the work. The first is John 8:52, where ‘he shall never taste of death’ is not a promise at all: it is the Jews quoting Jesus back at him as proof that he has a devil, since Abraham is dead and the prophets are dead. The Book of Mormon takes the sceptics’ formulation of the claim and grants it as fact. The second is the Synoptic saying itself, which is the New Testament’s own unfinished business — some standing here shall not taste of death till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom — a promise whose non-fulfilment John 21:23 is already managing. 3 Nephi 28 closes both loops at once by producing three men for whom the saying is literally true, and it does so in the exact words of all four verses.

links.note: ‘Therefore more blessed are ye, for ye shall never taste of death, but ye shall live to behold all the doings of the Father, unto the children of men, even until all things shall be fulfilled, according to the will of the Father, when I shall come in my glory, with the powers of heaven.’ Four KJV singletons converge in one sentence, one from each of the four verses that could supply it. This is the chapter’s densest verse and the one that shows the composition method plainly: the wording is John’s, the promise is Matthew’s and Mark’s, and the parousia clause is Luke’s.

pericopes.text: and ye shall never endure the pains of death; but when I shall come in my glory, ye shall be changed in the twinkling of an eye, from mortality to immortality; and then shall ye be blessed in the kingdom of my Father.—

links.text: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

provenance.other: “twinkling of an eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “we shall be changed” occurs in exactly one, both 1 Corinthians 15:52. The second clause is from the next verse: ‘this mortal must put on immortality’ (15:53) behind ‘from mortality to immortality’. “mortality” itself occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 5:4, so the abstract noun is not Paul’s word here; the Book of Mormon has abstracted it from his adjective, and Mormon 6:21 keeps the adjectival form ‘your mortal must put on immortality’.
provenance.significance: Paul’s sentence is strictly about the last trump: the dead raised incorruptible and the living changed, all at once, at the end. 3 Nephi 28:8 lifts the formula out of the eschaton and applies it to three men in the middle of history, and the text knows it has done so — 28:39 stops to say that ‘this change was not equal to that which should take place at the last day’. So the borrowing carries a qualification the source cannot supply, and 28:37-40 exists to supply it. The chapter borrows the resurrection’s vocabulary for something it then has to argue is not the resurrection.

links.note: ‘And ye shall never endure the pains of death; but when I shall come in my glory, ye shall be changed in the twinkling of an eye, from mortality to immortality.’ A KJV singleton reproduced word for word, with the verb 1 Corinthians 15:52 attaches to it, and the following verse’s antithesis behind the next clause. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold, but there is no question of the source.

pericopes.text: And again, ye shall not have pain while ye shall dwell in the flesh, neither sorrow, save it be for the sins of the world; and all this will I do because of the thing which ye have desired of me: for ye have desired that ye might bring the souls of men unto me, while the world shall stand;

links.text: Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.

provenance.other: “while the world standeth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 8:13. 3 Nephi 28:9 reads ‘while the world shall stand’ — the same idiom with the auxiliary future for the KJV’s present. No other English in the King James Bible measures a personal undertaking by the duration of the world.
provenance.significance: Paul’s one use of the phrase is a vow of permanent renunciation undertaken for somebody else’s sake: ‘I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.’ It is the strongest self-denial in the Pauline letters and its object is one weak brother’s conscience. 3 Nephi 28:9 sets the same measure on the same kind of vow at the largest possible scale — not meat but death forgone, not one brother but ‘the souls of men’ — and the sentence in which it does so is also about pain accepted for others (‘neither sorrow, save it be for the sins of the world’). Recover Paul’s context and the three Nephites’ request is a Corinthian scruple written large.

links.note: ‘And all this will I do because of the thing which ye have desired of me: for ye have desired that ye might bring the souls of men unto me, while the world shall stand.’ A KJV singleton with one auxiliary changed, in a clause whose logic — an indefinite personal cost accepted for the sake of others’ souls — is the logic of the verse it comes from.
links.whyNot: Four common words, and ‘while the world shall stand’ is natural English that a writer could reach independently; nothing else of 1 Corinthians 8 is in the chapter. The case is the absolute rarity plus the coincidence of situation, and a reasonable reader could decline it.

pericopes.text: and for this cause ye shall have fulness of joy; and ye shall sit down in the kingdom of my Father; yea, your joy shall be full, even as the Father hath given me fulness of joy; and ye shall be even as I am; and I am even as the Father; and the Father and I are one;

links.text: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.

provenance.route: Psalm 16:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Luke 13:29 and the Johannine ‘joy full’ formula in the same sentence
provenance.other: “fulness of joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 16:11, and 3 Nephi 28:10 has it twice. “sit down in the kingdom” occurs in exactly one, Luke 13:29 (Matthew 8:11 has ‘shall sit down with Abraham… in the kingdom of heaven’), against this verse’s ‘ye shall sit down in the kingdom of my Father’. “joy might be full” occurs in exactly one, John 15:11, and John 16:24 has ‘that your joy may be full’ against ‘your joy shall be full’ here. The closing chain — ‘ye shall be even as I am; and I am even as the Father; and the Father and I are one’ — is the John 17:21-22 unity language this catalogue adjudicates at 3 Nephi 19:23 and 19:29, and the phrase enters 3 Nephi at 27:31.
provenance.significance: Psalm 16:11 is a resurrection psalm in the New Testament’s own reading of it, and its ‘fulness of joy’ is located ‘in thy presence’ — a joy that consists in being where God is. 3 Nephi 28:10 keeps the location and makes it reciprocal: the Father has given Christ fulness of joy, Christ gives it to the three, and the giving ends in the unity formula of John 17. The Psalm supplies the noun, the Fourth Gospel supplies the mechanism by which it is transmitted, and Luke supplies the furniture of the kingdom the recipients sit down in.

links.note: ‘And for this cause ye shall have fulness of joy; and ye shall sit down in the kingdom of my Father; yea, your joy shall be full, even as the Father hath given me fulness of joy.’ Three KJV singletons in one sentence, from a Psalm, from Luke and from John. The mediation is genuinely undecided and is recorded as such: Psalm 16:11 is quoted at Acts 2:28, and tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence here because the Book of Mormon verse contains both the Psalm’s noun phrase (‘fulness of joy’) and a ‘joy… full’ clause close to Acts’ ‘full of joy’ — though that clause is better explained by John 15:11 and 16:24, which the verse also touches.

pericopes.text: and the Holy Ghost beareth record of the Father and me; and the Father giveth the Holy Ghost unto the children of men, because of me.
And it came to pass that when Jesus had spake these words, he touched every one of them with his finger, save it were the three which were to tarry, and then he departed.
And behold, the heavens were opened, and they were caught up into heaven, and saw and heard unspeakable things.

links.text: I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven.

provenance.other: “caught up” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — 2 Corinthians 12:2, 12:4, 1 Thessalonians 4:17 and Revelation 12:5 — and only Paul’s two are ascents of a living man to heaven. “unspeakable words” occurs in exactly one, 2 Corinthians 12:4, and 28:13’s ‘unspeakable things’ is one noun away from it; 28:14’s ‘it was forbidden them that they should utter’ is 12:4’s ‘which it is not lawful for a man to utter’. “the heavens were opened” occurs in exactly two, Ezekiel 1:1 and Matthew 3:16 (Acts 7:56 reads ‘I see the heavens opened’).
provenance.significance: Paul’s rapture is unique in the New Testament and defiantly singular in its telling: one man, fourteen years ago, who cannot be named and cannot say whether he had a body. 3 Nephi 28:13-15 makes it corporate and datable — three men, named as a group, on the day Jesus departed — and keeps every element that made Paul’s account reticent. The prohibition is the tell. At 3 Nephi 19:34 this catalogue records the same verse of 2 Corinthians converted from prohibition to incapacity (the words ‘cannot be uttered by man’); here, fewer than ten chapters later, the prohibition is restored in Paul’s own terms — forbidden, not impossible. The book uses 2 Corinthians 12:4 twice and takes a different half of it each time.

links.note: ‘And behold, the heavens were opened, and they were caught up into heaven, and saw and heard unspeakable things.’ Three of Paul’s four distinctive elements in eighteen words, with the fourth (the uncertainty about the body) following at 28:15 as an eight-word run. Hardy cross-references 2 Corinthians 12:2-4 here. 1830 and 1920 agree.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 3 Ne 28.13 (cross-references 2 Corinthians 12:2-4)

pericopes.text: And it was forbidden them that they should utter; neither was it given unto them power that they could utter the things which they saw and heard;

and whether they were in the body or out of the body, they could not tell: for it did seem unto them like a transfiguration of them, that they were changed from this body of flesh, into an immortal state, that they could behold the things of God.

links.text: And I knew such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;)

provenance.other: Eight consecutive words: ‘whether they were in the body or out of the body’ against ‘whether in the body, or out of the body’. “out of the body” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Job 20:25 (a sword drawn out of a body) and 2 Corinthians 12:2 and 12:3. The KJV’s verb for the other half of this verse is not present: “transfigured” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 17:2 and Mark 9:2, both of Jesus on the mountain, and the noun ‘transfiguration’ does not occur in the King James Bible at all.
provenance.significance: Two changes, and both are arguments. Paul writes ‘I cannot tell: God knoweth’ — a first-person confession of ignorance about his own state, offered as a reason for not boasting. 3 Nephi 28:15 makes it ‘they could not tell’, a narrator’s report about somebody else, and 28:17 then repeats the ignorance in Mormon’s own voice (‘whether they were mortal or immortal… I know not’) before 28:37 removes it by inquiry. Paul’s unresolvable question becomes a question the record answers. The second change is the noun: the chapter calls the event ‘a transfiguration’, a word the KJV never uses, formed from a verb the KJV uses of Christ alone. Paul’s rapture and the Synoptic mountain are fused, and the three disciples undergo in their own persons what in the King James Bible happens only to Jesus.

links.note: ‘And whether they were in the body or out of the body, they could not tell: for it did seem unto them like a transfiguration of them, that they were changed from this body of flesh, into an immortal state.’ An eight-word run from 2 Corinthians 12:3 with the pronoun turned from first person to third, and the strongest single verbal contact in the chapter. The 1830 and 1920 texts agree here.

pericopes.text: But it came to pass that they did again minister upon the face of the earth; nevertheless they did not minister of the things which they had heard and seen, because of the commandment which was given them in heaven.

links.text: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.

provenance.other: “heard and seen” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Luke 2:20, Philippians 4:9 and Revelation 22:8 — and only Luke’s has the full clause ‘the things that they had heard and seen’, against this verse’s ‘the things which they had heard and seen’, a one-word difference over seven. Acts 4:20 reverses the pair (‘the things which we have seen and heard’).
provenance.significance: Luke 2:20 is the KJV’s one sentence about witnesses going home to publish what they heard and saw — the shepherds returning, glorifying and praising God. 3 Nephi 28:16 is that sentence negated: they did again minister, but not of the things which they had heard and seen. The nearer situation is Acts 4:20, where apostles under an official prohibition answer ‘we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard’; the three Nephites are under a prohibition too, and they keep it. So the chapter takes the wording of the Bible’s most exuberant witnesses and the position of its most defiant ones, and produces silence.

links.note: ‘Nevertheless they did not minister of the things which they had heard and seen, because of the commandment which was given them in heaven.’ A seven-word near-run on a pairing the KJV has three times, in the negative.
links.whyNot: ‘Heard and seen’ is ordinary English and the only distinctive thing about the match is the order and the relative clause around it. Luke 2:20 has nothing else in common with this verse, and the situation — witnesses forbidden to speak — belongs to Acts 4, whose word order differs. Neither candidate is decisive on its own.

pericopes.text: And now whether they were mortal or immortal, from the day of their transfiguration, I know not;

but this much I know: According to the record which hath been given, they did go forth upon the face of the land, and did minister unto all the people, uniting as many to the church as would believe in their preaching; baptizing them; and as many as were baptized, did receive the Holy Ghost;
and they were cast into prison by them who did not belong to the church. And the prisons could not hold them, for they were rent in twain,

links.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.

provenance.route: Acts 16:23-26, with Matthew 27:51’s phrase → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “rent in twain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, both of the veil of the temple at the moment of the crucifixion. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase of a building at Alma 14:27, where the prison walls fall on the persecutors, and of the rocks at 3 Nephi 8:18. Acts 16:26 supplies the structure — preachers imprisoned by those outside the church, a violent opening of the prison, and the prisoners unhurt.
provenance.significance: This is the Alma 14 miracle re-run in a new book, and the row is written again for that reason (ADJUDICATING §4: across a book boundary, write the link). What is new here is the local resonance. Within 3 Nephi the phrase ‘rent in twain’ has already been used once, at 8:18, for the rocks that split at Christ’s death — the New World’s version of Matthew 27:51. When 28:19 uses it again for a prison that cannot hold his disciples, the same verb has run from the death of Christ to their deliverance, which is the movement Acts 16 makes in a single night and the Gospels make in three days.

links.note: ‘And they were cast into prison by them who did not belong to the church. And the prisons could not hold them, for they were rent in twain.’ The phrase is Matthew 27:51’s and the episode is Acts 16’s. The full argument for the phrase is made at Alma 14:27, where prison walls are rent in twain over the men who built them; this row records the borrowing re-entering in Mormon’s hand rather than restating it.

pericopes.text: and they were cast down into the earth. But they did smite the earth with the word of God, insomuch that by his power they were delivered out of the depths of the earth; and therefore they could not dig pits sufficiently to hold them.

links.text: Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth.

provenance.other: “depths of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 71:20, whose clause is ‘shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth’ against this verse’s ‘by his power they were delivered out of the depths of the earth’. 1830 reads ‘they could not dig pits sufficiently to hold them’, regularised to ‘sufficient’ in 1920.
provenance.significance: Psalm 71 is the prayer of a servant growing old: ‘Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation’ (71:18), and then the promise of being quickened again and brought up from the depths of the earth. That is precisely the condition the other nine disciples accepted at 28:2-3 — to live unto the age of man and then be taken — and precisely the condition these three declined. So the one KJV verse about being raised out of the earth belongs to a psalm about ageing into a ministry that outlasts a generation, which is the thing this chapter has just made permanent.

links.note: ‘And they were cast down into the earth. But they did smite the earth with the word of God, insomuch that by his power they were delivered out of the depths of the earth.’ A KJV singleton, in the one biblical sentence about being brought up again from where these men are buried.
links.whyNot: Four words, and the deliverance is a different kind: the psalmist is speaking figuratively of revival from trouble and near-death, the Book of Mormon literally of men dug out of pits. Nothing else of Psalm 71 is present.

pericopes.text: And thrice they were cast into a furnace, and received no harm.

links.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

provenance.route: Daniel 3 and Daniel 6 as paired by Hebrews 11:33-34 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Hebrews 11:33-34 sets the two deliverances side by side in adjacent clauses: “stopped the mouths of lions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:33, and “quenched the violence of fire” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 11:34. 3 Nephi 28:21-22 gives the same two in reverse order, furnace then beasts. There is no shared wording with either Daniel or Hebrews: “no harm” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses and none is Daniel’s (Daniel 3:27 has ‘the fire had no power’, Daniel 6:22 ‘they have not hurt me’). tools/mediation-check.py on Daniel 6:22 against Hebrews 11:33 returns no decisive divergence, because the Book of Mormon reproduces neither; the mediation is argued below rather than measured.
provenance.significance: The evidence that this is Hebrews’ catalogue and not Daniel’s stories is inside the Book of Mormon. Ether 12 is the book’s own chapter of faith-exemplars — its Hebrews 11 — and it names these same three men in Hebrews’ vocabulary: ‘it was by faith that the three disciples obtained a promise that they should not taste of death’ (Ether 12:17), where “obtained promises” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:33, the same verse that stops the mouths of lions. So the corpus reads the three Nephites through Hebrews 11 explicitly, and 3 Nephi 28:21-22 is what Hebrews 11:33-34 looks like when its list is turned back into narrative: the two Danielic deliverances, adjacent, unglossed, and multiplied (thrice, twice) because a catalogue of what faith does has no fixed number.

links.note: ‘And thrice they were cast into a furnace, and received no harm.’ With 28:22 this is Daniel 3 and Daniel 6 in two sentences, and the pairing — fire and beasts, in immediate succession, as instances of what happens to men under a promise — exists in the Bible in exactly one place, Hebrews 11:33-34. Catalogued as figural because there is no verbal contact at all; the case is the pairing plus Ether 12:17.
links.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared with Daniel or with Hebrews. Fire and wild beasts are the two standard ancient executions and any writer wanting invulnerable men could reach for both without a source, and the order is reversed from Hebrews’. The link rests entirely on the adjacency of the pair and on the Book of Mormon’s own use of Hebrews 11:33 at Ether 12:17.

pericopes.text: And twice were they cast into a den of wild beasts; and behold they did play with the beasts, as a child with a suckling lamb, and received no harm.

links.text: And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’ den.

provenance.other: “the sucking child shall play” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:8; “sucking child” occurs in exactly four and “shall play” in exactly two, of which Isaiah 11:8 is the only overlap. Isaiah 11:8 supplies the child, the playing and a den (‘the cockatrice’ den’); Isaiah 11:6 supplies the lamb and the little child among wild animals. 3 Nephi 28:22 has all four — a den, beasts, a child and a suckling lamb — in one clause. The Book of Mormon’s ‘suckling’ is not the KJV’s spelling, which is ‘sucking’ throughout, and 1830 and 1920 agree on it.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:6-8 is the peaceable kingdom: the wolf with the lamb, a little child leading them, the sucking child playing at the asp’s hole and the weaned child’s hand on the cockatrice’ den. It is the Book of Mormon’s standing image of the millennial future — the chapter is quoted whole at 2 Nephi 21 and its gathering verse is used as prophecy six chapters earlier at 3 Nephi 21:26. Here it is not prophesied but narrated: three men in a den of wild beasts, playing with them as a child plays with a lamb. The oracle is used as a description of what has already happened to somebody, which is what the chapter does to every eschatological text it touches — 1 Corinthians 15:52 at 28:8, Matthew 16:28 at 28:7.

links.note: ‘And twice were they cast into a den of wild beasts; and behold they did play with the beasts, as a child with a suckling lamb, and received no harm.’ Four of Isaiah 11:6-8’s images compressed into a single simile, including the KJV’s one instance of a child at play among dangerous animals.
links.whyNot: Only ‘play’ and ‘child’ survive in the KJV’s own form; ‘suckling’ is not the King James spelling, the lamb comes from a different verse than the den, and Isaiah’s den belongs to a cockatrice rather than to beasts. A writer describing a man unharmed among animals could reach for a child and a lamb with no Isaiah in view, which is why this is catalogued as an allusion at moderate confidence and marked uncertain for KJV-specificity.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that thus they did go forth among all the people of Nephi, and did preach the gospel of Christ unto all people upon the face of the land: And they were converted unto the Lord, and were united unto the church of Christ: And thus the people of that generation were blessed, according to the word of Jesus.
And now I, Mormon, make an end of speaking concerning these things, for a time.
Behold, I were about to write the names of those who were never to taste of death; but the Lord forbade, therefore I write them not, for they are hid from the world.
But behold I have seen them, and they have ministered unto me;
and behold they will be among the Gentiles, and the Gentiles knoweth them not.
They will also be among the Jews, and the Jews shall know them not.

And it shall come to pass, when the Lord seeth fit in his wisdom, that they shall minister unto all the scattered tribes of Israel, and unto all nations, kindred, tongues and people, and shall bring out of them unto Jesus many souls, that their desire may be fulfilled, and also because of the convincing power of God which is in them;

links.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: “nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:6, and “kindred, and tongue” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 5:9 and 14:6. The KJV’s four nouns at Revelation 14:6 are all singular: ‘to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people’. The 1830 text of 3 Nephi 28:29 reads ‘unto all nations, kindred, tongues and people’ — plural, singular, plural, plural — keeping the KJV’s singular ‘kindred’ stranded between two plurals; the 1920 edition regularised it to ‘kindreds’ and in doing so moved the phrase further from its source. The formula is used across the Book of Mormon and is adjudicated first at 1 Nephi 5:18.
provenance.significance: Worth a row for the orthographic datum rather than for the formula, which by 3 Nephi is the narrator’s own (CONVENTIONS §8). Revelation 14:6’s angel flies with the everlasting gospel to preach to every nation and kindred and tongue and people; 3 Nephi 28:29-30 has three men who ‘are as the angels of God’ doing exactly that among the scattered tribes. The apocalyptic figure and the ministry described are the same figure, and the verse that names it is the verse the Book of Mormon has been quoting for the phrase since 1 Nephi.

links.note: ‘They shall minister unto all the scattered tribes of Israel, and unto all nations, kindred, tongues and people.’ The Revelation 14:6 formula, whose argument is made at 1 Nephi 5:18; recorded here because the 1830 reading preserves the KJV’s singular ‘kindred’ and the modern text does not, and because the angel of Revelation 14:6 is what the next verse calls these men.

pericopes.text: and they are as the angels of God and if they shall pray unto the Father in the name of Jesus they can shew themselves unto whatsoever man it seemeth them good;

links.text: For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.

provenance.route: Matthew 22:30, with Luke 20:36’s argument → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “as the angels of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 22:30, and “in the resurrection they neither marry” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. Mark 12:25 has ‘as the angels which are in heaven’ and Luke 20:36 ‘equal unto the angels’, so Matthew’s is the only form the Book of Mormon could be reproducing. 1830 reads ‘they can shew themselves unto whatsoever man it seemeth them good’, keeping the KJV’s ‘shew’; 1920 modernises it to ‘show’.
provenance.significance: Matthew’s sentence is about the resurrected, and the respect in which they are like angels is that they neither marry nor are given in marriage — which has nothing to do with the three Nephites. Luke’s parallel supplies the respect that does: ‘Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels’ (Luke 20:36). So 28:30 takes Matthew’s words and Luke’s reason. The chapter has done this twice already, at 28:7 (John’s adverb on Matthew’s promise) and 28:34 (Matthew’s verb in Luke’s polarity); it is the composition habit of the whole chapter, and it means the borrowings are being selected clause by clause rather than passage by passage.

links.note: ‘And they are as the angels of God, and if they shall pray unto the Father in the name of Jesus they can shew themselves unto whatsoever man it seemeth them good.’ Five words from the one KJV verse that has them, applied to men who have not died, on the strength of a clause found only in the Lukan parallel.

pericopes.text: therefore great and marvellous works shall be wrought by them, before the great and coming day, when all people must surely stand before the judgement seat of Christ;

links.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, but “stand before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one: Romans 14:10, ‘we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ’. 2 Corinthians 5:10 has ‘appear before’. 3 Nephi 28:31 reads ‘when all people must surely stand before the judgement seat of Christ’ — Romans’ verb and Romans’ universal quantifier. 1830 spells ‘judgement’ and ‘marvellous’, both modernised in 1920.
provenance.significance: Paul’s clause is levelling. Its whole function at Romans 14:10 is to stop Christians from judging one another — why dost thou judge thy brother, seeing we shall all stand there together. Mormon’s use of it is discriminating: all people must surely stand, and the next sentences pronounce woe on those who will not hearken to the words of Jesus and of them whom he hath sent (28:34). The identical clause, with the same universal ‘all’, is turned from a reason not to judge into the warrant of a judgment. The suppressed context is the one that would embarrass the borrowing.

links.note: ‘Therefore great and marvellous works shall be wrought by them, before the great and coming day, when all people must surely stand before the judgement seat of Christ.’ Six words from a KJV singleton. The ‘great and marvellous work’ clause of this verse and the next is Isaiah 29:14’s and is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 21:9; the register cross-references it at 28:32.

pericopes.text: yea, even among the Gentiles shall there be a great and marvellous work wrought by them, before that judgement day.—
And if ye had all the scriptures which gives an account of all the marvellous works of Christ, ye would, according to the words of Christ, know that these things must surely come.—

And wo be unto him that will not hearken unto the words of Jesus, and also to them which he hath chosen and sent among them: for whoso receiveth not the words of Jesus, and the words of them which he hath sent, receiveth not him; and therefore he will not receive them at the last day;

links.text: He that receiveth you receiveth me, and he that receiveth me receiveth him that sent me.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:40 / John 13:20, with the polarity of Luke 10:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “receiveth him that sent me” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 10:40, Luke 9:48 and John 13:20 — and all three run the chain in the same direction and the same positive form: he that receives the messenger receives me, and he that receives me receives him that sent me. Luke 10:16 is the KJV’s only negative version of the chain, and it uses a different verb: ‘he that despiseth you despiseth me; and he that despiseth me despiseth him that sent me’. 3 Nephi 28:34 has ‘whoso receiveth not the words of Jesus, and the words of them which he hath sent, receiveth not him’ — Matthew’s verb in Luke’s polarity. 1830’s relatives ‘them which he hath chosen’ and ‘them which he hath sent’ are modernised to ‘those whom’ in 1920, moving away from the KJV’s ‘which’.
provenance.significance: Two changes and both are pressure on the same point. The KJV’s chain is about receiving persons — ‘he that receiveth you’; 3 Nephi 28:34 makes it about receiving words, twice (‘the words of Jesus, and the words of them which he hath sent’). And it adds a terminus none of the four verses has: ‘and therefore he will not receive them at the last day’, which turns the chain around so that the rejected messenger becomes the one who does the rejecting. It is the same move as 3 Nephi 19:23, where believing on the apostles’ words is made the antecedent of believing in Christ rather than its synonym — a claim about the standing of a text and its witnesses, made by rewriting a saying about persons.

links.note: ‘And wo be unto him that will not hearken unto the words of Jesus, and also to them which he hath chosen and sent among them: for whoso receiveth not the words of Jesus, and the words of them which he hath sent, receiveth not him.’ The Synoptic and Johannine chain of reception, run in the negative and terminated with a clause the KJV does not have.

pericopes.text: and it would be better for them if they had not been born. For do ye suppose that ye can get rid of the justice of an offended God, who hath been trampled under feet of men, that thereby salvation might come?

links.text: The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born.
