provenance.other: “if he had not been born” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:24: ‘it had been good for that man if he had not been born’. The Markan parallel reads ‘good were it for that man if he had never been born’ (Mark 14:21), so the Book of Mormon’s ‘it would be better for them if they had not been born’ is Matthew’s form pluralised, not Mark’s.
provenance.significance: The man of Matthew 26:24 is Judas, and the sentence is passed in the same breath as ‘woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed’. 3 Nephi 28:34 has just pronounced its own woe — on whoever will not hearken to the words of Jesus and of his messengers — and 28:35 completes it with the sentence the KJV reserves for the betrayer. Refusing the record is put on a level with handing Christ over. That reading is strengthened by what the machine turned up two verses into the chapter: the highest-ranked candidate at 28:4 is Matthew 26:15, Judas asking ‘What will ye give me’, which the register declines as coincidence — but it is Matthew 26 that supplies this verse, and the two occurrences frame the chapter.

links.note: ‘And it would be better for them if they had not been born.’ Seven words from a KJV singleton, with the singular made plural, applied to those who reject the words of Jesus and of the disciples he has sent.

links.text: Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?

provenance.route: Hebrews 10:29 for the sense, Matthew 5:13 for the phrase → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sorer punishment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 10:29, which is also the King James Bible’s only sentence about a person trampling Christ: ‘who hath trodden under foot the Son of God’. “under foot of men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:13, of savourless salt. 3 Nephi 28:35 has ‘trampled under feet of men’ — Matthew’s phrase with a plural foot and a different verb; “trample” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Psalm 91:13, Isaiah 63:3, Matthew 7:6) and in none of them is the object a person.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 10:26-29 is the New Testament’s hardest warning about rejecting what one has received — no more sacrifice for sins, a certain looking for of judgment, and a sorer punishment for the man who has trodden under foot the Son of God. That is the argument 3 Nephi 28:34-35 is making: woe to him that will not hearken, and it would be better for him if he had not been born, for the justice of an offended God has been trampled under feet of men. The Book of Mormon says with Matthew’s salt-idiom what Hebrews says of the Son of God, and it substitutes ‘the justice of an offended God’ for Hebrews’ person of the Son.

links.note: ‘For do ye suppose that ye can get rid of the justice of an offended God, who hath been trampled under feet of men, that thereby salvation might come?’ The phrase is Matthew 5:13’s (adjudicated in this book at 3 Nephi 12:13) and the sense is Hebrews 10:29’s; the row records the fusion rather than either half.
links.whyNot: No word of Hebrews 10:29 is reproduced — the Book of Mormon has ‘trampled’ where both candidate verses have ‘trodden’, and ‘feet’ where Matthew has ‘foot’. The trampling idiom is common enough in the Book of Mormon that the writer may simply be reusing his own formula, and the connection to Hebrews rests on the shared argument rather than on shared English. Marked uncertain for KJV-specificity for that reason.

pericopes.text: And now behold, as I spake concerning them whom the Lord had chosen, yea, even three which were caught up into the Heavens, that I knew not whether they were cleansed from mortality to immortality:—

But behold, since I wrote, I have inquired of the Lord, and he hath made it manifest unto me, that there must needs be a change wrought upon their bodies, or else it needs be that they must taste of death;
therefore that they might not taste of death, there was a change wrought upon their bodies, that they might not suffer pain nor sorrow, save it were for the sins of the world.

Now this change was not equal to that which should take place at the last day, but there was a change wrought upon them, insomuch that satan could have no power over them, that he could not tempt them, and they were sanctified in the flesh, that they were holy, and that the powers of the earth could not hold them;

and in this state they were to remain until the judgement day of Christ; and at that day they were to receive a greater change, and to be received into the kingdom of the Father, to go no more out, but to dwell with God eternally in the Heavens.

And now behold, I say unto you, that when the Lord shall see fit, in his wisdom, that these sayings shall come unto the Gentiles, according to his word, then ye may know that the covenant which the Father hath made with the children of Israel, concerning their restoration to the lands of their inheritance, is already beginning to be fulfilled;
and ye may know that the words of the Lord, which have been spoken by the holy prophets, shall all be fulfilled; and ye need not say that the Lord delays his coming unto the children of Israel;

links.text: That ye may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour:

provenance.other: “holy prophets” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Luke 1:70, Acts 3:21, 2 Peter 3:2 and Revelation 22:6 — all of them in the New Testament. “the words which were spoken” occurs in exactly two, 2 Peter 3:2 and Jude 1:17, and only 2 Peter 3:2 attaches it to the prophets. “the promise of his coming” and “not slack concerning his promise” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 3:4 and 3:9.
provenance.alternative: Acts 3:21, which the catalogue took as the source of the same epithet at 3 Nephi 5:1, with 2 Peter 3:2 recorded there as the alternative. Acts 3:21 has ‘by the mouth of all his holy prophets’ and no noun ‘words’; 2 Peter 3:2 has ‘the words’ and no ‘mouth’. The Book of Mormon here has ‘the words of the Lord, which have been spoken by the holy prophets’ — words, no mouth — and tools/mediation-check.py returns 2 Peter 3:2 on both of those points.
provenance.significance: This is where the alternative left open at 3 Nephi 5:1 is decided, and it is decided by what the sentence goes on to say rather than by the epithet itself. 2 Peter 3:2 is not a stray verse: it is the premise of the only scoffing-oracle in the New Testament, and the two verses after it are the scoffers of the last days saying ‘Where is the promise of his coming?’, answered seven verses later by ‘The Lord is not slack concerning his promise’. 3 Nephi 29:2 reproduces that whole movement in one sentence — the words spoken by the holy prophets shall all be fulfilled, and ye need not say that the Lord delays his coming. Mormon has taken 2 Peter 3's premise and 2 Peter 3's objection and 2 Peter 3's answer, and compressed eight verses into a clause and a half. Recovering the source's context tells the reader what Mormon thinks the Gentiles who receive his book will be: not disbelievers but scoffers, and specifically 2 Peter's scoffers, whose complaint is about timing.

links.note: 'The words of the Lord, which have been spoken by the holy prophets, shall all be fulfilled; and ye need not say that the Lord delays his coming.' The epithet on its own is a repeat — the catalogue adjudicated it at 3 Nephi 5:1 and does not restate the argument — but a repeat is not what this verse is. At 5:1 the choice between Acts 3:21 and 2 Peter 3:2 could not be made on the wording alone; here the phrase arrives with 2 Peter 3's own objection attached to it in the same breath, which settles the choice for this verse and is a fresh borrowing in its own right. Held at moderate because the shared string with 3:2 is four words long and the rest of the case is contextual: the argument is the sequence premise-objection-answer, not the clause.

links.text: But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming;

provenance.other: “delayeth his coming” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:48 and Luke 12:45, and they are the same saying in the two synoptics. “say in his heart” occurs in exactly the same two. tools/mediation-check.py returns Matthew 24:48, but only on an absence: the Book of Mormon lacks Luke's long tail about beating the menservants. The two forms differ otherwise by 'evil' and 'shall', and the Book of Mormon has neither, so the assignment to Matthew is the weaker half of this row.
provenance.significance: The evil servant's sentence is not an opinion about eschatology; in Matthew it is the thing a servant says when he has decided the master is not watching, and the parable's point is that the saying is the sin. Mormon has given the Gentiles who scoff at his book the evil servant's line, which means the chapter's charge is not error but presumption — acting as though the delay were licence. Note what the catalogue can see here that a modern reader cannot: the very next verse of 3 Nephi says 'ye need not imagine in your hearts', and the KJV's evil servant says his line 'in his heart'. The saying and its location are both borrowed, split across a verse break.

links.note: 'Ye need not say that the Lord delays his coming.' This is the strongest verbal row in the chapter and the machine stream proposed nothing for the verse at all: the n-gram windows found no run because the Book of Mormon has modernised the verb ('delays' for 'delayeth') and dropped the possessive subject, leaving 'his coming' as the only contiguous survivor. Read as a saying rather than a string it is exact — the KJV has one saying about a lord who delays his coming, it is spoken by a servant in his own heart, and it is quoted only to be condemned. The Book of Mormon quotes it in the same posture, as a thing 'ye need not say'.

pericopes.text: and ye need not imagine in your hearts, that the words which have been spoken are vain, for behold, the Lord will remember his covenant which he hath made unto his people of the house of Israel.

links.text: And let none of you imagine evil in your hearts against his neighbour; and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: “imagine evil in your hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Zechariah 8:17. “in your hearts” occurs in exactly thirteen, and Zechariah 8:17 is the only one of the thirteen whose verb is 'imagine'. The construction ‘imagine … in your hearts’ is therefore a KJV singleton, which is what the Book of Mormon has, with its own object substituted for 'evil'.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 2:1, 'Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?', brings 'imagine' and 'vain' together in one clause and is addressed to exactly 3 Nephi 29's audience, the Gentiles set against the LORD's purpose. It is rejected as the source because its 'vain thing' is the plotting, not the word plotted against, and because it has no 'in your hearts'; but a reader who notices it has noticed something, and the two verses may both be in play.
provenance.significance: Zechariah 8 is the KJV's densest short chapter on precisely 3 Nephi 29's subject: God returning to Zion, the remnant gathered from the east country and the west, 'they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness' (8:8), and the promise that what he has now purposed to do he will not repent of (8:14-15). Its prohibition against imagining evil in the heart sits at the end of that argument as the behaviour the restored covenant forbids. Mormon has taken the prohibition and pointed it at unbelief in the restoration itself — the thing Zechariah 8 forbids you to imagine against your neighbour is what 3 Nephi 29 forbids you to imagine against the promise.

links.note: 'And ye need not imagine in your hearts, that the words which have been spoken are vain.' The verb and its location are the KJV's, from the one verse in which they occur together, and the object has been swapped: Zechariah forbids imagining evil, Mormon forbids imagining vanity. The row is held at moderate because a single verb plus a common prepositional phrase is thin evidence taken alone, and because the immediately preceding verse has already borrowed 'say in his heart' from Matthew 24:48 — the two sources are competing for the same clause, and it is possible that 29:3's 'in your hearts' is simply Matthew's phrase pluralised. What tips it to Zechariah is 'imagine', which Matthew does not have and which the KJV never elsewhere puts in the heart.

pericopes.text: And when ye shall see these sayings coming forth among you, then ye need not any longer spurn at the doings of the Lord, for the sword of his justice is in his right hand, and behold at that day, if ye shall spurn at his doings, he will cause it that it shall soon overtake you.

links.text: But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:

provenance.other: “overtake thee” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and all three are in Deuteronomy 28 — 28:2 of the blessings, 28:15 and 28:45 of the curses. “shall come upon thee, and overtake thee” occurs in exactly one, Deuteronomy 28:15. Outside that chapter the King James Bible does not use the verb of a sanction pursuing a person at all. “take hold on judgment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 32:41, which is the only place in the KJV where God's hand holds judgment as a sword is held.
provenance.alternative: The image of the sword itself is not borrowed. The catalogue's standing entry at Helaman 13:5 records that ‘sword of justice’ occurs in no KJV verse and is a Book of Mormon coinage, and that judgment is not disturbed here; Deuteronomy 32:41 is offered as the nearest KJV picture of the same thing, not as its wording.
provenance.significance: The whole of 3 Nephi 29 is an argument that the covenant is still running, and the verb Mormon picks for its sanction is the one verb the King James Bible reserves for covenant sanctions. Deuteronomy 28 uses it twice in both directions — the blessings 'shall come on thee, and overtake thee' if thou hearken, the curses 'shall come upon thee, and overtake thee' if thou wilt not — and the condition attached to the curse at 28:45 is 'because thou hearkenedst not unto the voice of the LORD thy God', which is what spurning at the doings of the Lord amounts to. Recover the source and the threat in 29:4 stops being a general warning and becomes a clause of the same covenant whose fulfilment 29:1 has just announced. The chapter says the covenant is beginning to be kept; the borrowing says both halves of it are.

links.note: 'If ye shall spurn at his doings, he will cause it that it shall soon overtake you.' A single verb, but a verb that in the KJV belongs to one chapter: every occurrence of 'overtake thee' is in Deuteronomy 28, and the fuller run 'shall come upon thee, and overtake thee' is a KJV singleton there. The rest of the verse is Mormon's own — 'spurn' occurs in no KJV verse, and neither does 'doings of the Lord', which is worth saying because the KJV's fifty uses of 'doings' are almost all human and mostly evil. The 1830 reads 'he will cause it that it shall soon overtake you' where 1920 deletes the first 'it'; the deletion tidies the grammar and does not touch the borrowing.

pericopes.text: Wo unto him that spurneth at the doings of the Lord; yea, wo unto him that shall deny the Christ and his works;

links.text: That say, Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know it!

provenance.other: “Woe unto him that” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Isaiah 45:9 and 45:10, Jeremiah 22:13, Habakkuk 2:15 and 2:19 — and the serial form, one woe after another on a different offence, is Isaiah 5:8-23 and Habakkuk 2:6-19. Note against the KJV that the Book of Mormon spells the interjection 'Wo': “Wo unto” occurs in no KJV verse, which is a fact about orthography rather than about dependence but is worth having on the record. “hasten his work” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 5:19; “regard not the work” in exactly one, Isaiah 5:12.
provenance.alternative: Habakkuk 2:6-19 is the closer formal model for a chain of woes and the closer verbal one for 'Woe to him that', and a reader who prefers it is not wrong about the form. It is not preferred here because Habakkuk's five woes are on greed, violence and idols, and have nothing to do with scoffing at the timing of God's work.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis in the strict sense: the interest is in what Isaiah 5 says that 3 Nephi 29 does not. Isaiah's woe-series contains the KJV's one portrait of men who mock the delay of God's work — 'Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it' — and, seven verses earlier, of men who 'regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands'. Those are the two charges of 3 Nephi 29 exactly, in Isaiah's order: first that the doings of the Lord are not regarded (29:4-5), then that his coming is late (29:2). Isaiah's series ends at 5:25 with 'therefore is the anger of the LORD kindled … and his hand is stretched out still' — a hand held out in judgment, which is what 29:4 has just put a sword into.

links.note: 'Wo unto him that spurneth at the doings of the Lord; yea, wo unto him that shall deny the Christ and his works.' Verses 5, 6 and 7 are a chain of three woes, each on a distinct form of contempt, and that is a form the King James Bible has in exactly two places: Isaiah 5 and Habakkuk 2. Isaiah 5 is preferred because it is the one whose offences are these offences — despising the work of the LORD and jeering at its delay. The link is figural and the wording is not shared: 'spurn' is not a KJV word, 'doings of the Lord' occurs in no KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon's 'Wo' is not the KJV's 'Woe'. It is recorded because a reader hearing a triple woe against scoffers is hearing a scriptural form, and the catalogue should say which one and on what evidence rather than leave the resemblance unclaimed.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact worth the name — not one distinctive shared word between 3 Nephi 29:5-7 and Isaiah 5:11-25. The case rests entirely on the coincidence of a rhetorical form (serial woes) with a subject matter (contempt for God's work, mockery of its delay), and either could have been arrived at independently by a writer who had simply read the prophets. A reader who declines this row and keeps only the verbal links in 29:6-7 has lost nothing the catalogue can prove.

pericopes.text: yea, wo unto him that shall deny the revelations of the Lord, and that shall say, the Lord no longer worketh by revelation, or by prophecy, or by gifts, or by tongues, or by healings, or by the power of the Holy Ghost;

links.text: To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 12:8-30 and 14:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the working of miracles” and “divers kinds of tongues” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:10. “gifts of healing” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 12:9 and 12:30, and nowhere else in the Bible. “by revelation, or by” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 14:6 — 'except I shall speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine' — which is the King James Bible's only serial 'or by' list of ways the Spirit speaks, and it is the syntax 3 Nephi 29:6 is written in. “the power of the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 15:13.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 12:29-30 is where Paul turns his own list into a series of questions expecting the answer no — 'Are all prophets? … Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues?' — which is the one place in the KJV where the catalogue of gifts is put in the negative. 3 Nephi 29:6 is that inversion carried one step further: not 'do all speak with tongues' but 'the Lord no longer worketh by … tongues'. The list Paul assembled to prove that the Spirit is various is quoted by Mormon to name what a later age will deny the Spirit does at all, and the reader who recovers 1 Corinthians 12 finds the same six items being used to make the opposite point. The chapter's charge against the Gentiles is thus put in the Gentiles' own apostle's words.

links.note: 'That shall say, the Lord no longer worketh by revelation, or by prophecy, or by gifts, or by tongues, or by healings, or by the power of the Holy Ghost.' Five of the six items are the vocabulary of one chapter of the New Testament and of no other: healings and gifts and prophecy and tongues are 1 Corinthians 12's inventory, where 'gifts of healing' and 'divers kinds of tongues' are KJV rarities found there and essentially nowhere else. The sixth item, revelation, and the serial 'or by' that strings them all together, come from 1 Corinthians 14:6, whose 'by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine' is a KJV singleton and is the only KJV sentence built the way this one is. Below any quotation threshold — no continuous run exceeds three words — but the composition is unmistakable: it is Paul's list, in Paul's syntax, negated.

pericopes.text: yea, and wo unto him that shall say at that day, that there can be no miracle wrought by Jesus Christ, for to get gain; for he that doeth this, shall become like unto the son of perdition, for whom there was no mercy, according to the word of Christ.

links.text: While I was with them in the world, I kept them in thy name: those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition; that the scripture might be fulfilled.

provenance.other: “son of perdition” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 17:12 and 2 Thessalonians 2:3. “get gain” occurs in exactly one, James 4:13 — adjudicated in this book at 3 Nephi 6:10 and first at 2 Nephi 26:20, and registered here rather than re-argued.
provenance.alternative: 2 Thessalonians 2:3, where the son of perdition is the eschatological man of sin. It is ruled out by the Book of Mormon's own attribution: 29:7 says the doom is 'according to the word of Christ', and of the two KJV verses only John 17:12 is a word of Christ — 2 Thessalonians 2:3 is Paul's. That the phrase 'the word of Christ' is itself Colossians 3:16's does not weaken the point; the clause is a citation formula, and it points where it points.
provenance.significance: Recover John 17:12 and the identity of the son of perdition is Judas, and the sentence Mormon has built becomes exact rather than merely severe. The man 3 Nephi 29:7 condemns is one who denies that Christ works miracles and does it for money; the man John 17:12 calls the son of perdition is one who was with Christ through the miracles and sold him for money. 'For whom there was no mercy' answers John's 'none of them is lost, but the son of perdition' — the single exception to a kept flock. Neither text says the scoffer is Judas. The link says it: to deny Christ's works for gain is to take the one place in the twelve that was not kept.

links.note: 'That there can be no miracle wrought by Jesus Christ, for to get gain; for he that doeth this, shall become like unto the son of perdition, for whom there was no mercy, according to the word of Christ.' The borrowed phrase is short and its rarity does the work: two verses in the King James Bible contain it, and the Book of Mormon tells the reader which of the two it means by attributing the doom to the word of Christ. The 1830 reading matters here and the modern text hides it. In 1830 the sentence runs 'no miracle wrought by Jesus Christ, for to get gain', with the KJV's 'for to' before the infinitive and the gain attached to the denial; 1920 moved the phrase forward to 'shall say at that day, to get gain, that there can be no miracle' and dropped 'for', which both breaks the King James idiom and reassigns the motive from the doctrine to the speaker. The first edition reads as a single accusation of denying Christ's works for money, which is the accusation John 17:12's son of perdition answers to.

pericopes.text: Yea, and ye need not any longer hiss, nor spurn, nor make game of the Jews, nor of any of the remnant of the house of Israel, for behold the Lord remembereth his covenant unto them, and he will do unto them according to that which he hath sworn;

links.text: All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?

provenance.other: “they hiss” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Lamentations 2:15 and 2:16, and they are consecutive. “an hissing” occurs in exactly six, all of them formulae in which a place is made a hissing rather than sentences in which people hiss at somebody. Lamentations 2:15-16 is therefore the King James Bible's only passage where the verb has a human subject deriding a named Jewish object, which is the grammar 3 Nephi 29:8 uses.
provenance.alternative: 1 Kings 9:7-8, whose 'a proverb and a byword' plus 'shall hiss' the catalogue has already adjudicated behind the Book of Mormon's compound 'a hiss and a byword' at 1 Nephi 19:14 and at 3 Nephi 16:9. That compound is not what 29:8 has: here 'hiss' is a finite verb in a list of three things the Gentiles are told to stop doing, with the Jews as its object, and the 1 Kings verses supply a noun, not a verb with a victim.
provenance.significance: In Lamentations the hissers are the enemies who pass by a ruined Jerusalem and say 'we have swallowed her up: certainly this is the day that we looked for'. Their derision is not of the Jews' religion but of their visible ruin, and it is offered in the poem as evidence that God has finished with them. That is precisely the reading 3 Nephi 29:8 forbids: the Gentiles who hiss at the Jews are reading the scattering as an ending, and Mormon's answer is that the covenant is a thing sworn and the ruin is an interval. Recover the source and the prohibition acquires its ground — Lamentations records the hissing at the very moment the covenant looked broken, which is exactly when it was not.

links.note: 'Ye need not any longer hiss, nor spurn, nor make game of the Jews, nor of any of the remnant of the house of Israel.' Two of the three verbs are the Book of Mormon's own — 'spurn' and 'make game' occur in no KJV verse — and the third is the KJV's standing gesture of contempt at a fallen Israel. What identifies Lamentations 2:15-16 rather than the six 'astonishment and an hissing' formulae is the grammar: the Book of Mormon needs people hissing at the Jews, and only Lamentations supplies that, twice in consecutive verses. Held at moderate because one verb is thin, and because the Book of Mormon may simply be using a prophetic commonplace rather than this passage of it.

pericopes.text: therefore ye need not suppose that ye can turn the right hand of the Lord unto the left, that he may not execute judgement unto the fulfilling of the covenant which he hath made unto the house of Israel.

links.text: And the king said, Is not the hand of Joab with thee in all this? And the woman answered and said, As thy soul liveth, my lord the king, none can turn to the right hand or to the left from ought that my lord the king hath spoken: for thy servant Joab, he bade me, and he put all these words in the mouth of thine handmaid:

provenance.other: “to the right hand or to the left” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses. Nine of the ten are the walking idiom — 'thou shalt not turn aside to the right hand, or to the left' — in which the one who might turn is the person addressed and the thing not to be turned from is the law. “none can turn” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 14:19, which is the tenth, and the only one in which the phrase means that a decree already spoken cannot be deflected by anybody.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 5:32, 17:20, 28:14, Joshua 1:7 and 23:6 and the rest of the walking-idiom family. They are the commoner form and any of them could have furnished the words, but none of them furnishes the sense: in all of them the turning is disobedience by the hearer, and in 3 Nephi 29:9 the turning is an attempt to divert the Lord.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has taken a directional idiom and made its 'right hand' a literal hand — 'turn the right hand of the Lord unto the left' — which is why the machine streams could not see the borrowing and why it is worth recording. That literalising is prepared five verses earlier: 29:4 has already put the sword of his justice into the Lord's right hand, so by 29:9 the right hand is an object in the chapter and not a compass point. Recover 2 Samuel 14:19 and the argument sharpens further: the woman of Tekoah is telling David that nothing can deflect what the king has already spoken, and she is saying it at the moment she has been caught staging a parable to change his mind. 3 Nephi 29:9's Gentiles are in her position and are told the same thing, with the added point that the covenant is not a verdict a petitioner might yet talk the king out of.

links.note: 'Ye need not suppose that ye can turn the right hand of the Lord unto the left, that he may not execute judgement unto the fulfilling of the covenant.' The phrase is common and the use is not. In nine of its ten KJV occurrences the right hand and the left are directions a person is told not to stray into; in the tenth, 2 Samuel 14:19, they are the impossibility of deflecting what a king has decreed, which is the sense 3 Nephi 29:9 needs and takes. Held at moderate because the shared string is the commonest form of the idiom and the argument turns on sense rather than rarity. One 1830 detail runs against the usual direction of these findings: the first edition spells 'judgement', which is not the King James spelling, and 1920 changed it to the KJV's 'judgment' — an edition moving the text toward the source rather than away from it, as at 1 Nephi 1:20.

pericopes.text: Hearken, O ye Gentiles, and hear the words of Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, which he hath commanded me that I should speak concerning you: for behold he commandeth me that I should write, saying,

links.text: And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.

provenance.route: Matthew 16:16 (or John 6:69) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the Son of the living God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 16:16 and John 6:69, and both are Peter speaking. The two are not separable on wording here: they differ only at “the Christ” / “that Christ”, and the Book of Mormon has the name “Jesus Christ” in that slot rather than either article, so mediation-check.py returns no decisive point. Matthew 16:16 is named as the source on context alone — Hardy's apparatus cross-references Matthew 16:18 at 3 Nephi 27:8, three chapters earlier in this same book, where Christ names his church; John 6 has no comparable footprint in 3 Nephi. Mark 1:1's “Jesus Christ, the Son of God” is the nearer word order and the wrong title; it is registered as an exclusion.
provenance.alternative: John 6:69, which is the identical six words in a different scene.
provenance.significance: The last chapter of the book opens by naming Jesus with the one title the King James Bible reserves to Peter's confession, and the confession is the one Christ answered by promising to build his church and by handing over the keys. Recover that context and the summons that follows reads differently: a Gentile world that received the church through Peter's confession is addressed under Peter's own words for its founder, and told to turn. The title also closes an arc the corpus opened — Nephi ends his own book with “the example of the Son of the living God” (2 Nephi 31:16), and Mormon opens his last with the same phrase; what was there a pattern for individual endurance is here the authority behind a national demand.

links.note: 'Hearken, O ye Gentiles, and hear the words of Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God.' Six words reproduced exactly, from one of only two KJV verses that contain them, in a sentence that is otherwise Mormon's own. The title is not the ordinary New Testament way of naming Jesus — “Jesus Christ, the Son of God” is Mark 1:1's formula and is what a writer reaching for a generic solemn title would produce — and the extra word 'living' is what makes the phrase countable. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36 quotations; it is catalogued as an allusion, not a quotation, because no clause of Matthew 16:16 comes with it.

pericopes.text: Turn, all ye Gentiles, from your wicked ways, and repent of your evil doings, of your lyings and deceivings, and of your whoredoms, and of your secret abominations, and your idolatries, and of your murders, and your priestcrafts, and your envyings, and your strifes, and from all your wickedness and abominations, and come unto me, and be baptized in my name, that ye may receive a remission of your sins, and be filled with the Holy Ghost, that ye may be numbered with my people, which are of the house of Israel.

links.text: And again, Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles; and laud him, all ye people.

provenance.mt: Psalm 117:1 — 'O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people.' The KJV renders the same word 'nations' in the Psalm and 'Gentiles' in Paul's quotation of it.
provenance.route: Psalm 117:1 → Romans 15:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “all ye Gentiles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 15:11, and “ye Gentiles” as a vocative in exactly two, Romans 15:10 and 15:11 — both inside Paul's four-quotation catena at Romans 15:9-12. mediation-check.py returns one decisive point: where Psalm 117:1 reads 'nations praise' the Book of Mormon has Romans 15:11's 'Gentiles', so the address exists in English only because of the KJV's choice to translate the Psalm's word one way in the Psalter and another way in Romans. The Book of Mormon uses this vocative once in the whole corpus, here.
provenance.significance: The catena Paul builds at Romans 15:9-12 exists to prove one thing: that the Gentiles are brought in to praise God *with* Israel, not instead of it — 'Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people' (15:10, quoting Deuteronomy 32:43), then 'Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles' (15:11), then 'in him shall the Gentiles trust' (15:12). 3 Nephi 30:2 takes its vocative from the second of those verses and its conclusion from the first: 'that ye may be numbered with my people, which are of the house of Israel.' Two contacts with one four-verse passage, split across the whole length of a very long verse, and the argument the passage was written to make is the argument the Book of Mormon's last chapter closes on. This is the chapter, and the n-gram stream cannot see it — the two contacts are ninety words apart (CONVENTIONS §9).

links.note: 'Turn, all ye Gentiles ... that ye may be numbered with my people, which are of the house of Israel.' The opening vocative is a KJV singleton and the closing clause is the point of the passage the singleton comes from. What makes the borrowing visible rather than merely apt is the mediation: the Psalm the KJV translates as 'all ye nations' is the same verse Romans translates as 'all ye Gentiles', and a book whose whole final address is to Gentiles takes the form the KJV only supplies in Paul. Note also that Paul's catena is a promise and 3 Nephi's use is a condition — Romans announces that the Gentiles do rejoice with his people; 3 Nephi says they may be numbered with them if they turn.

links.text: Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings: but they did not hear, nor hearken unto me, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: Two King James singletons meet in one clause. “your evil doings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Zechariah 1:4, and “evil doings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one; “your wicked ways” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 20:44, and “wicked ways” in exactly two, Ezekiel 20:44 and 2 Chronicles 7:14. Zechariah 1:4 supplies the frame — 'Turn ye now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings' — and the Book of Mormon reproduces it with the adjective of the first member swapped for the only other King James adjective that governs 'ways' in this construction. The pronoun decides between the two candidates for that member: the Book of Mormon has 'your wicked ways', which is Ezekiel 20:44's, not 2 Chronicles 7:14's 'their wicked ways'.
provenance.alternative: 2 Chronicles 7:14 ('turn from their wicked ways', and 'my people, which are'), which touches this verse twice and is registered as an exclusion; the pronoun sends the first contact to Ezekiel and Romans 15:10 accounts for the second.
provenance.significance: Zechariah 1:2-6 is the preface to the whole book of Zechariah and it is a summons to a returned people not to repeat their fathers' refusal; 3 Nephi 30 is the closing summons of a book to a people who have the record their fathers refused. Recover the rest of Zechariah 1:4 and the metalepsis is exact: the clause the Book of Mormon borrows ends 'but they did not hear, nor hearken unto me, saith the LORD' — and the two verbs of that failure are the two imperatives with which this chapter opens, 'Hearken, O ye Gentiles, and hear'. The pairing of hearing and hearkening is common prophetic idiom (25 KJV verses hold both words), so this is not itself the evidence; the evidence is the two singletons. But the fit is worth naming, because a chapter that borrows Zechariah's demand opens by asking for precisely what Zechariah says was withheld. Ezekiel 20:44, the source of the swapped adjective, contributes the same shape at its own end: 'not according to your wicked ways, nor according to your corrupt doings, O ye house of Israel' — ways and doings paired, and closing on the house of Israel, which is also where 3 Nephi 30:2 closes.

links.note: 'Turn, all ye Gentiles, from your wicked ways, and repent of your evil doings.' The construction is Zechariah 1:4's entire: an imperative 'turn', 'from your [adjective] ways', 'and ... your evil doings', in that order, and the second member is a King James hapax. The first member is the other King James hapax that fits the slot. Zechariah 1:3's 'Turn ye unto me' also stands behind the verse's later 'come unto me'. Recorded at high because two independent singletons in one construction is about as strong as verbal evidence gets without a reproduced clause, and because neither phrase is Book of Mormon house idiom — 'wicked ways' occurs twice in the whole corpus and 'evil doings' four times.

links.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: No single phrase here is rare: “remission of sins” occurs in exactly 7 KJV verses and “filled with the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly 8 KJV verses, though all eight of the latter are Luke's, five of them in Acts. What is rare is the order. Acts 2:38 puts four members in one sentence — repent, be baptized in the name, remission of sins, receive the Holy Ghost — and 3 Nephi 30:2 has all four in that order and no other Book of Mormon verse does. 3 Nephi 11:23 has the baptismal rubric without the remission or the Spirit; 3 Nephi 12:2 has the Spirit before the remission; 3 Nephi 27:20 has repentance, coming, baptism and sanctification but no remission of sins.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:38 is Peter's answer to the crowd at Pentecost, which is the KJV's one scene of a mass Gentile-facing summons answered by baptism, and it is spoken by the same Peter whose confession supplies the title in 30:1. The book's last words to the Gentiles are the first words the church ever spoke to a crowd.

links.note: Acts 2:38 is adjudicated in this book at 3 Nephi 11:23, where it stands behind the baptismal rubric, and CONVENTIONS' default is that a formula's later occurrences in the same book are the writer using his own formula (ADJUDICATING §4). This row is written anyway, on the ground the Mosiah 29:2 ruling names: the second use is the argument. Every other occurrence in 3 Nephi is partial and in its own order; this one, in the book's closing sentence, restores all four members of Acts 2:38 in Acts' sequence, and does so in an address to Gentiles, which is Acts 2:38's own setting once Acts 10 has extended it. A reader arriving at the last verse of the book should be shown the verse it is built on.
links.whyNot: Nothing here is verbally distinctive on its own; the case rests entirely on the sequence, and the sequence is also standard Christian catechetical order, which a nineteenth-century writer would have had without reaching for a text. The formula is thoroughly naturalised in the corpus (2 Nephi 31:11-17, Mosiah 18:10, 3 Nephi 11:23-27, 12:1-2, 27:20), so this may be the house formula reaching its fullest statement rather than a fresh borrowing. Confidence is held at moderate for that reason.
